case_summary.text: INCOME TAX : Where assessee company, engaged in business of production and telecasting of TV serials, entered into non-compete agreement with two firms belonging to same person for a period of 5 years wherein it acquired copyrights of number of movies owned by two firms and paid certain amount as non-compete fee, since entire business was transferred as a going concern concept, then, nothing was left with transferee firms to carry on business and what was held by them was a copyright

INCOME TAX : Where in view of non-compete agreement entered into by assessee with a company from which it acquired business, non-compete fee paid by assessee would form part of initial outlay on acquisition of business, Assessing Officer was justified in treating said non-compete fee as capital expenditure and disallowing same under section 37(1)
Company which acquired new business couldn't be chosen as comparable: Hyderabad ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee company, engaged in business of production and telecasting of TV serials, entered into non-compete agreement with two firms belonging to same person for a period of 5 years wherein it acquired copyrights of number of movies owned by two firms and paid certain amount as non-compete fee, since entire business was transferred as a going concern concept, then, nothing was left with transferee firms to carry on business and what was held by them was a copyright of a feature film, but, not a product/design or copyright asset, this aspect needed to be examined before allowing depreciation on said non compete fee paid by assessee

INCOME TAX: Where assessee paid a non-compete fee to restrain another party from operating in same business segment, such payment merely protected or enhanced assessee’s business profitability and facilitated more efficient conduct of business, and though it could confer an enduring advantage, same was not in capital field and did not result in creation of any new asset or accretion to profit-earning apparatus; therefore, non-compete fee was allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1)

IT : Where SIFL got amalgamated with assessee-company and Excess of fair value of net assets taken over by assessee-company over paid-up value of allotted equity shares was transferred by assessee to its General Revenue Account, since assessee had acquired business of another company through medium of amalgamation, in view of provisions of section 47(vi), there was no transfer as such of any capital asset and, therefore, question of taxing capital gains did not arise

IT: Where assessee purchased business of one 'T' as a going concern for Rs. 42 crores and it in account books had assigned a sum of Rs. 6 crores as customer relationship rights and further claimed depreciation on said amount stating that it was paid as non compete fees, in absence of any agreement between parties for any consideration on account of non compete fees, payment in question could not be regarded as non compete fees

IT : Where assessee engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure
Sum from transfer of entire undertaking as going concern with non-compete held capital receipt u/s 45 due to loss of business: HC
IT: Transfer of shares with all pervasive control over business being entrusted to purchaser and to complete exclusion of assessee with a non-compete clause fell within realm of section 28(va)

IT : Where assessee claimed to sell its manufacturing unit of edible oil as a going concern on slump sale basis, mere fact that buyer was already in same line of business and thus, was not keen to buy intangible assets such as trade name/logos/trademarks/product name etc. belonging to assessee, it would not take assessee's case out of purview of section 50B

IT/ILT : A company even after being taken over by another company continued providing IT services to a client at predetermined consideration, such transaction could not be considered as an uncontrolled transaction and, therefore, said company could not be regarded as functionally comparable with assessee

IT : Where in pursuance of an agreement entered into between assessee and TATA IBM, a part of business being handled by erstwhile TATA IBM was handed over to assessee company due to bifurcation of software and hardware business, expenditure incurred by assessee on processing domestic customer database and transfer of human skills in terms of said agreement, was to be allowed as business expenditure

IT: Where for assessment year 1996-97 under an agreement, assessee transferred one of its business to other company but continued its business using its own logo, trade name, licenses and permits, no part of non-compete fee received by assessee under aforesaid agreement could be treated as considerations for goodwill and it was not taxable as income

IT: Where High Court upheld Tribunal's order holding that non-compete fee paid by assessee to founder of transferor company constituted business expenditure, SLP filed against said decision of High Court was to be granted
IT/ILT: Where comparable company amalgamated with assessee during relevant year and its provided high level KPO services, same could not be comparable to assessee which was ITES provider

IT/ILT: On sale of shareholding of a company, non-compete fees was to be paid to assessee-company which was controlling business of company over years; same was to be calculated adopting internal CUP method
IT/ILT: A company operating in different business strategy of acquiring companies for inorganic growth was incomparable to assessee rendering ITE services to its AE

IT : Where assessee-company acquired business of another company as a going concern, since valuation of assets was supported by registered valuer's report and, moreover, said amount was higher than book value of assets standing under Companies Act, AO was not justified in making addition in respect of excess claim of depreciation by invoking Explanation 3 to section 43(1)

INCOME TAX : Where consumer mobile business undertaking was acquired by assessee on wholesome basis without valuation of an individual asset and lumpsum consideration through process of demerger was paid, provisions of section 56 would not be applicable

IT : Where assessee sold its manufacturing unit of edible oil as a going concern on slump sale basis, mere fact that buyer was already in same line of business and thus was not keen to buy intangible assets such as trade name/logos/trademarks/product name etc. belonging to assessee, it would not take case out of purview of section 50B
Provisions of sec. 28(va) would not apply if only share transfer was made and no amount was attributed to non-compete clause: ITAT

IT : Where in order to give effect to business transfer agreement, assessee purchased shares of management staff, since impugned amount was non-recoverable and was a loss on account of business transfer, it was required to be deducted from capital gain in respect of slump sale of trading business

IT : Where a company took over the partnership firm along with its assets and liabilities, cost of acquisition of assets in the hands of company would be the cost of acquisition of firm. Any revaluation of assets of the partnership firm shall be ignored to determine cost of acquisition of assets in hands of company

IT : Where assessee entered into an agreement with his employer-company for investment in technical concept developed by assessee for its commercial exploitation and thereafter entire business related to said concept had been sold to a US company, since dominant intention of purchaser for making payment to assessee was to prevent him from engaging in any business which could have competed with business purchased, amount so received was to be taxed as business income under section 28(va)

IT : Where Holding Company and assessee demarcated their areas of business, in view of fact holding company rendered other services also and assessee paid one per cent of turnover, said payment was not just for non competition and, thus, to be allowed as revenue expenditure

IT : Where pussuant to sale of one division of its business by 'C' Ltd. to one 'T', assessee, a director of 'C' Ltd., received certain amount by entering into a non-compete agreement whereby he could not engage in any business activity similar to that of division sold to 'T', amount so received was taxable as business income under section 28(va)

ST : A non-compete clause is normal in a contract for transfer of business; such a clause could not be separated from contract for sale of equity shares of an ongoing concern to deny benefit of Notification No. 25/2012-Service Tax; service tax demand by classification of impugned service as declared service under section 66E(e) of Finance Act, 1994 was to be set aside

TRANSFER PRICING : Companies who were not taken as comparables with company having similar business such as assessee since former one underwent extraordinary merger event whereas latter entity provided high-end KPO services and Departmental fails to rebut same fact in present year then, CIT(A) rightly deleted impugned adjustment after excluding above two comparable entities from array of comparables

IT: Where a company 'S' took over business of assessee-company prior to 1-4-2000 and thereupon assessee received an amount of Rs. 4.50 crores from 'S' and it had bifurcated said amount towards trade mark and technical know-how, copyright and non compete compensation, in given situation it was a case of slump sale and since sale had taken place prior to introduction of section 50B, above amount could not be subjected to tax in hands of assessee under head 'capital gain

IT: Where a company 'S' took over business of assessee-company prior to 1-4-2000 and thereupon assessee received an amount of Rs. 4.50 crores from 'S' and it had bifurcated said amount towards trade mark and technical know-how, copyright and non compete compensation, in given situation it was a case of slump sale and since sale had taken place prior to introduction of section 50B, above amount could not be subjected to tax in hands of assessee under head 'capital gain'

ST : Non compete clause was normal in transfer of business and it could not be separated from contract to deny benefit of Notification No.25/2012-Service Tax; service tax demand by classification of impugned service as Declared Service under Section 66 E(e) of Finance Act, 1994, set aside.

IT : Where assessee, a Chairman cum Managing Director of public company engaged in business of manufacturing IMFL, received huge amount as non-compete jee, in view of fact that real and true nature of transaction was sale of shares and transfer of control and management of company, amount in question was to be taxed as Capital gains in hands of assessee

IT-I : Where assessee engaged in various manufacturing activities, sold only one of its activities to another concern and said activity was not a part of it core activities, non-compete fee received in order to refrain from carrying on said activity for a limited period of five years resulted in revenue receipt liable to tax

IBC : Where applicant - successful bidder had taken over corporate debtor as a going concern and had paid entire sale consideration to liquidator, since as per deed of assignment liquidator was to enable substitute assignee i.e. applicant in place of liquidator in pending cases, applicant was entitled to be substituted in place of liquidator as an applicant in avoidance application and to pursue said application pending before NCLT

IBC : In case of sale of corporate debtor's assets as a going concern, transaction will not be treated as void under section 281 of Income-tax Act, for any claims regarding taxes or other amounts payable by Sellers, thus provisions relating to taking over predecessor’s tax liability under section 170 of Income-tax Act, 1961 would not apply
Sum paid to eliminate competition entailing advantage for specified time was capital in nature, says ITAT

TRANSFER PRICING : A company who was KPO providing structural engineering services wherein during year under consideration, extraordinary events such as amalgamation and demerger have taken place cannot be held comparable to assessee

IT/ILT: Where a company was engaged in KPO segment and further, extraordinary events took place in said concern during year under consideration, it was incomparable with assessee providing software consultancy services

IT : Where assessee-company entered into an agreement to take over business of a proprietory concern, in view of fact that in terms of agreement only a license to use copyright was granted to assessee, however, it had not acquired copyright itself, license fee paid by assessee was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

IT : Where assessee purchased business division of another concern which also included payment to non-compete fee restraining seller from carrying on similar business for three years, said payment was to be regarded as capital expenditure
A Co. is comparable if its financials were prepared without taking effect of extraordinary event of merger: ITAT

IT/ILT : Where a company failed in related party transaction filter and employee cost filter and outsourcing and amalgamation had changed business model of company, same could not be taken as comparable

IT/ILT: Where assessee was providing ITES low end services to its group concerns, companies engaged in providing high end KPO services involving specialized expertise in field coupled with extraordinary event of amalgamation and demerger could not be comparables

IT: Where assessee sold three proprietary concerns in slump sale, section 50B would apply; sale consideration received by assessee in cash being combined net worth of all three concerns and this net worth being also deemed as cost of acquisition and/or improvement under section 50B(2), no capital gain would stand to arise

IT/ILT: Where assessee was engaged in providing analytical solutions to its AEs to lower cost of customer acquisition, a company carrying out diverse range of activities which included financial services and sales and marketing support services, could not be accepted as comparable
HC allows business exp. as assessee was doing new business with retained employees after transfer of old business

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against impugned High Court order that loss on account of permanent diminution in value of investment made in subsidiary company in order to expand business being driven by business expediency, would be allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1)
INCOME TAX : Where business was transferred as a going concern on a slump sale basis and it was not mere transfer of assets, assessee had rightly computed capital gain under section 50B
IT/ILT : Where assessee was rendering ITES services to AE, a company in whose case extraordinary event of amalgamation took place during relevant year, was not acceptable as comparable

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company offering training courses in field of financial services took over business of ‘W’, who was also carrying on similar activities, for a consideration which was claimed by assessee-company as revenue expenditure - Revenue, however, treated it as of capital nature - Whether essence of agreement being taking over of business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, said expenditure fell in category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with the prime purpose of specializing in offering of training courses in the field of financial services and other academic activities relating to financial services, such as offering of distance education courses, organizing conferences in and outside India, developing training facilities and classrooms, etc. ‘W’ was also in the business of carrying on similar activities as that of the assessee- company. The assessee-company took over the business of ‘W’ after payment of consideration amount for such acquisition, and claimed the said payment as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company took over the training courses and educational activities, for a consideration, of a company belonging to the same group and that ‘W’ stopped the activities following the takeover of their business by the assessee-company. It was, thus, held that the consider- ation amount paid by the assessee was for initiation of business to set up profit making apparatus in motion. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member took the view that the said payment was in the nature of revenue expenditure because none of the components of the consideration could be said to be in the nature of creation of any asset, which was of the nature of capital assets. However, the Judicial Member was of the opinion that the amount was paid for taking over the business of imparting and conducting training courses in the field of leasing and hire-purchase of related areas, and that by taking over the business the assessee acquired the right to conduct the commercial activities of another company for an indefinite period and that acquisition of such right was of capital nature. As a result of difference of opinion between the two Members, the matter was referred to the Third Member for his opinion.

HELD (PER THIRD MEMBER)

It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.

HEADNOTE: section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-capital or revenue expenditure-assessee, carrying on business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in licensed public cinema theatres, paid rs. 1,50,000 to a rival to induce the latter not to compete with it for nine years-whether payment was allowable as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1)-held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in the licensed public cinema theatres in the four southern States of Madras, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Mysore. B, another company, was also carrying on the business of exhibition of film shorts on behalf of X & Y in the aforesaid States. The assessee-company felt that it would be commercially profitable to it, if it could eliminate B from the business. The assessee-company, therefore, entered into an agreement with B whereby the latter not only agreed to part with its business of exhibition of film shorts but also agreed not to compete with the assessee-company in the business for a period of nine years for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. The assessee paid the said sum as per the terms of the agreement and claimed the same as a business expenditure. The ITO held that payment was made by the assessee-company for obtaining the right to exhibit advertisement and film shorts and not for the purpose of purchasing any stock-in-trade or raw material and, therefore, the expenditure was of a capital nature. The ITO accordingly disallowed the claim. The AAC upheld the ITO's order. The Tribunal held that the expenditure was not incurred to carry on the business of the exhibiting of film shorts but was incurred to acquire an asset or a right of a permanent character for a period of nine years and, therefore, it could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

On reference, the assessee-company contended that since the expenditure was incurred for acquiring the film shorts, it should be taken to have been expended for acquiring stock-in-trade of the assessee's business :

HELD: The agreement entered into by the assessee-company with B does not indicate that the film shorts as stock-in-trade were the subject-matter of the bargain. In substance and effect, the agreement involved a transfer of the B's business to the assessee-company for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. It cannot be said that the said sum was paid for acquiring the stock-in-trade. The assessee-company has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of nine years in a specified area. By this agreement, the assessee-company has in fact derived an advantage by eliminating the competition and acquired a business which actually generated income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generated income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature.

notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11] Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee-company carried on business in providing education and training for various preparatory examinations - During relevant assessment year, it paid certain amount to its two faculty members as non-compete fees for not entering into a business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005 - Assessee claimed said payment as revenue expenditure but revenue authorities held that elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to assessee and, therefore, payment amounted to capital expenditure - Whether having regard to short period of twelve months during which above two persons were prohibited from competing with assessee, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain amount to its two faculty members, namely, 'V' and 'S' as non-compete fees for not entering into business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005. The assessee claimed that the non-compete fee was paid in respect of a very short period of non-competition and, therefore, payment represented revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to the assessee and, therefore, the payment amounted to capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that those payments were to be made in monthly instalments over a period of time; and that the period involved, during which 'V' and 'S' were not to compete with the assessee in any manner was only a short period of 12 months and, therefore, there could be no enduring benefit enuring to the assessee.

On the revenue's appeal:

HELD: It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA' - Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into Indian compressor market - In said process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh facilities - In accordance with terms of MoU, both parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through assessee-company agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility - Total amount paid by assessee to Whirlpool India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores paid towards non-compete fee - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee being revenue expenditure by separating said amount from main agreement - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether, when an expenditure is made for initial outlay or for expansion of business or for a substantial replacement of equipment, then it would fall under capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since, in instant case, it was apparent from records that non-compete agreement was part and parcel of whole transaction (i.e., main agreement entered into between assessee and Whirlpool), it could be concluded that non-compete fee was paid as a part of initial outlay, and, therefore, it was to be disallowed being in nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether an expenditure incurred on warding off competition in business from a rival dealer will constitute a capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure, it is not necessary that non-compete fee is paid to create monopoly rights - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA'. Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into the Indian compressor market. In the process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell the compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh. In accordance with the terms of the MoU, both the parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through its 'to be an established local Indian entity' agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility including laminations, wire drawings, centralized tool room, overload protectors and relays. The total amount paid by the assessee to Whirlpool-India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which was the total sum agreed to be paid by the assessee for whole of the transaction as per the MoU. The said amount of Rs. 52.50 crores included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores towards non-compete fee. As per terms of non-compete agreement against the receipt of full consideration specified therein, Whirlpool India was to sign and deliver to the assessee an undertaking not to compete with it in the manufacture, sale or repair of compressors in India, except that Whirlpool would be entitled to sell and install compressors purchased from the assessee to the persons under its service arrangements, subject to the provisions of the supply agreements. It was the amount of Rs. 2.65 crores which was claimed by the assessee to be the non-compete fees or revenue expenditure by separating the said amount from the main agreement. The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's claim.

On second appeal :

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1955-56 to 1958-59 - Whether in deciding question whether expenditure was in nature of capital expenditure or business expenditure laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for purpose of assessee’s business, one must not confine one selves only to agreement between parties and said question must be decided in light of facts and circumstances of each case - Held, yes - Whether where assessee-company took over business carried on by a firm and made payment of pension amount to employees of firm in consideration of their past services rendered by them to firm and to abstain them from being engaged or employed in business of kind carried on by assessee-company, it could be said that payment made was for purposes of business and has in nature of business expenditure and would not partake of nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: By an agreement the assessee-company took over the entire business carried on by a firm. There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. He held that by buying off potential competitors the company improved the value of its goodwill and thus brought into existence an advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and, therefore, quite apart from the fact that the payment might have been made out of non-business considerations, the payment was also of the nature of capital expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the view taken by the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: Whether the expenditure was in the nature of a capital expenditure or a business expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee’s business, one must not confine oneselves only to the agreements between the parties. The question must be determined in the light of all the facts and circumstances of each case and there is no rule that if there is a written agreement between the parties the authorities and the High Court must look only to that written agreement and nothing else.

It is now settled law that the question whether the amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each case.

Lifting the Corporate Veil :

Both, the Tribunal and the Assessing Officer, had held that what was done by the assessee-firm was clearly an attempt to evade tax in order to get over the provisions contained under section 55(2). It is a well-settled principle of law that what is permissible is avoidance but not evasion. When an attempt is made by a company to evade tax, it is the bounden duty of the authorities to lift the corporate veil and find out the real intention behind the same. It is the duty of the Court in every case, where ingenuinity is expended to avoid taxing and welfare legislations, to get behind the smoke screen and discover the true state of affairs. The Court is not to be satisfied with form and leave well alone the substance of a transaction. [Para 15.1].

On appeal to the High Court : HELD: Section 55 provides for the sale of goodwill after dissolution. From the definition of goodwill as held by the Apex Court in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India AIR 1970 SC 564 and as seen from the provisions of section 55, it is very clear that after the dissolution of a firm, it shall be included in the assets. Therefore, inasmuch as a goodwill could be quantified by way of a sum, the assessee wanted to avoid the same by terming it as technical know-how and compensation. When a business is destroyed, the goodwill goes with it. A goodwill is determined by the nature of business, character, name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio economy and the absence of competition. A goodwill can be sold along with the business or independently. ‘Goodwill’ was brought into tax with effect from 1-4-1988. Therefore, in a commercial and trading parlance, goodwill plays a pivotal role and that is the reason why it has been brought into the tax net. [Para 12.2]

‘Technical know-how’ is defined as an intangible revenue producing asset which can be put to use so as to produce revenue in two ways. The manufacturer can use it himself to make things for sale and make profit in that way, or he can teach it to others, so that they can make their own things, in which case he gets paid for the knowledge and information which he imparts to them. His fees and rewards are then revenue in his hands. Under the Act, transfer of technical know-how is subject to tax only from the assessment year 1998-99 by the amendment through the Finance Act, 1997. [Para 12.3]

In the instant case, there were only two partners in the assessee-firm which consisted of father and son. The assessee had been making good profit over the years as seen from the assessment made for the assessment year 1993-94 onwards. It was a concern running for the past 25 years profitably. It was taken over as a going concern by the limited company. The partners of the assessee-firm were the directors of the limited company. The limited company continued to function in the very same office in which the assessee-firm was functioning earlier. The entire assets had been taken over by the limited company. The agreement between the assessee and the limited company did not make any mention about the payment received for the goodwill. The assessee was not involved in the sale of technical know-how. [Para 13.1]

Therefore, it was clear that inasmuch as the assessee-firm had been taken over as a going concern, it could not have been taken over without the so-called technical know-how. The assessee could not have sold the other tangible assets keeping with it the so-called technical know-how. Hence, the receipts for technical know-how and the compensation for non-competing fees were nothing but a part of composite receipt to diminish the value of the assets of the assessee-firm. The assessee had termed the said amount as receipts for technical know-how in order to escape from the clutches of the provisions of section 55(2) under which a goodwill amount is taxable. [Para 13.2]

There was no material on record to establish the cost of the technical know-how as observed by the Tribunal. There was also no material to quantify the amount shown as paid to the assessee for the transfer of the alleged technical know-how. There was no explanation as to why no amount had been received towards the goodwill considering the undisputed fact of the good performance of the assessee-firm over the years before the transfer. The assessee had clearly attempted to evade tax by claiming the amount received as goodwill as one of technical know-how in order to evade tax. The assessee had tried to sell the old wine in a new bottle by characterizing the receipt as technical know-how. It was not the case of the assessee that it had been selling the technical know-how to any other third party. The agreement also did not provide a clause to the effect that the assessee would not indulge in the same business. That was for the precise reason that the assessee had merely changed from being a partnership firm into one of a private company due to business and commercial expediency. [Para 13.3]

Elimination of competition from the Trust brought benefit of an enduring nature to the assessee-company, in the field of capital and, therefore, increase in lease rent, to the extent it is attributable to this benefit, would be a capital expenditure. [Para 23] The assessee contended that since elimination of competition from the Trust did not happen simultaneous with acquisition of Katha and Cutch business of the Trust, enhancement of lease rent, even to the extent it is attributable to elimination of competition from the Trust, would not constitute capital expenditure. This is not an absolute proposition of law that in order to constitute capital expenditure, the payment/compensation for elimination of competition should be coupled with acquisition of business of the rival and both the things should happen at the same time. In a given case, either the payment to eliminate competition may be post acquisition of business of the rival or elimination of competition may not be accompanied by acquisition of business of the rival. It is very much possible for a rival to agree not to compete in a given area, while continuing with the same business in other areas. In such a case, there would be no takeover of the business of the rival. In any case, as far as instant case is concerned, as would be seen from the lease deeds executed between the assessee and Trust, that the Trust had leased whole of its production unit which was a profit generating unit to the assessee and not only the building, but the plant and machinery was also leased to the assessee along with all benefits, etc. Even the liability towards gratuity of the employees of the trust was taken over. The Trust had also relinquished its right to purchase Khairwood from the Government in favour of the assessee. This is not the case of the assessee that even after lease deed dated 18-1-1992, the Trust continued with the business of manufacture and trading of Katha and Cutch in areas beyond 1000 kilometres from the leased premises. Therefore, the business being carried by 'Mahesh Udyog' was practically taken over by the assessee-company for an indefinite period. The lease deed also shows that the lessee had approached the Trust that it should stop commercial dealings in Katha and Cutch and in lieu thereof it had agreed to compensate the Trust for the loss that would be caused to it by stopping such commercial dealings. Therefore, this was a case of takeover of the business, coupled with elimination of competition from the rival. It is also evident from a perusal of the lease deed dated 18-1-1992 that the previous lease deed executed between the parties was repealed simultaneous with the execution of the new lease deed on 18-1-1992. Therefore, technically speaking in this case, acquisition of assets of the trust and elimination of competition from the Trust took place simultaneously. In fact, the whole transaction between Trust and assessee was a composite transaction, without apportionment of lease rent into various components of the transaction. Therefore, from whatever point of view, one may examine, there is no escape from the conclusion that increase in lease rent, to the extent it was relatable to elimination of competition from the Trust, constitutes capital expenditure. [Para 27]

Applicability of section 40A(2)

The objective behind section 40A is to address evasion of tax under the cloak or guise of permissible deductions by checking payments made or benefits granted made to closely connected persons and entities ostensibly for the goods sold or services rendered by them. Admittedly, Trust is a charitable trust and by itself the Trust does not hold any share of the assessee-company. The Trust is not entitled to any profit out of the business being run by the assessee-company. Hence, the Trust does not have a substantial interest in the business of the assessee-company. [Para 29]

It is not in dispute that at least some of the trustees are also directors and shareholders of the assessee-company. The maximum shareholding in the assessee-company was owned by the trustees and their relatives as defined in section 2(41). However, clause (v ) of section 40A(2)(b) brings only such companies, firms, HUFs or association of persons within its purview, directors/partners/members of which have a substantial interest in the business or profession of the assessee. The interest of the relatives of a director/partner/member of such company/firm/HUF/association of persons cannot be taken into consideration to ascertain whether the director/partner/member have substantial interest in the business of the assessee or not. The Explanation provides that a person shall be deemed to have a substantial interest in a business if in a case where the business is carried on by a company, he, at any time, during the previous year, was the beneficial owner of shares carrying not less than 20 per cent of the voting power. The Tribunal has not given any finding with respect to exact shareholding of the trustees in the assessee-company during the relevant previous years, and there was no material to indicate the exact shareholding of the trustees in the assessee-company during the years to which these appeals pertain. [Para 30]

In view of this there is no reason to exclude this comparable and, therefore, it is held that the TPO has correctly included this company for comparability analysis.

(x) Asian Business Exhibition Conferences Limited

The functional profile of this company is acceptable to both the parties at the initial stage itself. The assessee did not put any evidence to show that the company is functionally dissimilar. The only grievance of the assessee is that the comparable company has entered into an extraordinary event and therefore it becomes not comparable. It is the contention of the assessee that during the year the company has acquired shares of another company and therefore this is the extraordinary event that makes it not comparable. However, this contention of the assessee is not agreeable for the reason that it is purely an investment decision and it does not have any impact on the function performed by the assessee, assets employed for the revenue earned and risk assumed. The action of putting investment into another company did not have any impact on the profitability of the company, no such impact was shown, and therefore there is no reason to exclude this comparable. Therefore, the contention of the assessee for exclusion of the above comparable is rejected.[Para 22]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

FACT: On incorporation the assessee-company became one of the partners of the firm 'NS', with effect from 1-8-1976. That firm was dissolved on 31-12-1976 and as a consequence the assets and liabilities of the erstwhile firm along with the business vested with the assessee-company. The dissolution deed that was drawn up, specified about the royalty that would be payable to the retiring partners for not doing such business for fifteen years arising out of the business of firm. The assessee by virtue of the dissolution deed, which was agreed to by it, provided royalty in its books by crediting to the two retired partners. The amount of royalty which was so shown as payable to the two retired partners for various assessment years, was claimed as revenue expenditure; but that was not accepted by the ITO. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Note - The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1951 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 to 1999-2000 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns, engaged in similar business as going concern, for certain consideration - In addition, assessee undertook to pay certain amount per month to said concerns for a period of 15 years in consideration of non-compete obligation undertaken by them and claimed said payments as revenue expenditure - Whether said payments, having been made for eliminating competition in same line of business for a sufficiently long period of 15 years, were of capital nature and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired the proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns engaged in same business as going concerns for certain consideration. In addition thereto, the assessee under- took to pay Rs. 3.5 lakh and Rs. 2 lakh per month to the two concerns, respectively, for a period of 15 years in consideration of the non-compete obligation undertaken by the said concerns. In the assessment, the assessee claimed that the said payment made to dissuade the said proprietary concerns from continuing independent business, which would be detrimental to it, was to be allowed as the revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that the expenditure was clearly capital in nature, as the same was incurred by the assessee to ward off competition over a long period of time. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s said claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: From various cases, the legal position which clearly emerges is that any ‘non-compete’ fee, which is paid to ward off competition over a sufficiently long period of time, has to be considered as capital expenditure. Depending upon the facts and circumstances, in some cases, it has been held that even though the period of non-competition may be 2 to 5 years, the non-compete fee would still be in the nature of capital. [Para 13]

On a careful consideration of the legal position, as applied to the facts of the assessee’s case, the payments made by the assessee to the two proprietary concerns for a period of 15 years as per the terms and conditions of the agreement, could not be treated as revenue expenditure. The proprietary concerns had been acquired by the assessee as going concerns. The two proprietors, by virtue of the agreement, had transferred the respective business along with rights, assets and liabilities which included trademarks, etc. In addition to the value of the assets, the assessee had undertaken to pay a sum of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per month to one proprietor and a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs per month to another proprietor, which was clearly for eliminating competition in the same line of business, for a sufficiently long period of 15 years. The use of trademark, if any, by the assessee was only an inseparable part of the entire arrangement. By the ‘non-compete’ clause of the agreement, the erstwhile proprietors were automatically excluded from use of such trademarks and they had bound themselves contractually not to carry on similar business activity, in whatever names, for a period of 15 years. As a consideration, the impugned monthly payments were to be paid by the assessee for a period of 15 years. It means that on the expiry of the non-compete period of 15 years, the payments would also cease to be made. There was not much merit in the arguments of the assessee that the payments were partly attributable to the benefit acquired by the assessee by way of user of the tenanted premises at a nominal rent. There was no reference to that fact in the agreement. Further, the landlord or owner of such premises was not a party to the agreement and even if some benefit had accrued to the assessee, it was entirely on account of the Rent Control Act, which might be applicable. The business premises, either owned or rented, had been taken over by the assessee as part of the overall agreement or arrangement for purchase of proprietary business as going concern along with all assets and liabilities. [Para 16]

The argument submitted by the assessee, that one of the proprietors agreed for inclusion of the amount in its total income for taxation purposes, had only some persuasive value. The treatment given in the hands of the recipient did not determine the nature of the payment in the case of the payee.

Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the issue was to be reversed and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to disallow the relevant expenditure treating it to be capital expenditure. [Para 17]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 2001-02 and 2002-03 - Whether to test whether benefit derived by assessee by making a payment is of enduring nature, only point to be considered is whether threat which is perceived at time of agreement/incurring of expenditure will cease to exist after expiry of period or will re-occur - Held, yes - Whether where threat has potential of re-occurring after expiry of period, then benefit derived cannot be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate - It acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores - Assessee had also entered into another ‘non-compete agreement’ with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them - Under said agreement ‘V’ and ‘M’ were restricted to engage themselves in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with abovesaid chemicals for period of 5 years - In return assessee claimed whole of expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that expenditure was not incurred for improving profitability as there was no existing business and assessee had acquired business of chemicals for first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to company and disallowed claimed expenditure - Whether since ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ both being well in a position financially, as well as otherwise, to compete with assessee even after a period of five years, it could be said that threat which was perceived at time of agreement still subsisted and was liable to re-occur at expiry of period of five years and benefit derived could not be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Whether carrying on of same business prior to entering into non-compete agreement is not necessary to appreciate as to whether non-compete agreement is to enhance assessee’s profitability or not - Held, yes - Whether since benefit to be derived by assessee in consequence upon incurring expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to enhancement of assessee’s profitability in business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals, it could be said that said expenditure was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes

ised for the purpose of suing and of being sued. It is in this light of the legal notion of a partnership firm that the status of an assessee in just a position to the firm has to be adjudged. The constitution of both the firm and the assessee disclosed that there were identical partners in both. The sharing also was reported to be similar. In such circumstances, the law treated them as only one firm, though, for convenience, they transacted business under two different trading styles. When the assessee voluntarily undertook to pay the demand in question as sales tax, it did it because of its conscious identity of the personnel of the firm and that of the assessee. Such unison and identity in purpose and in commerce was the intention behind the undertaking being taken over by the assessee. No doubt, it took over all the liabilities and assets, which included the sales tax reserve. This again was at a time when the statutory liability for sales tax payable for the year was not quantified. Here again the intention was clear that the assessee undertook the liability for sales tax, whatever might be the amount, in order to continue its trade. What may be normally said of an ordinary trade liability cannot be said of a statutory liability or a fiscal liability. Such a liability is assumed not because of the contract of transfer of assets, but because it is a necessary annexure to the incidence of the business having been taken over and continued.

In the instant case, merely because for purposes of taxation laws the assessee and the firm were two different legal entities, it could not be said that in the light of the facts disclosed, the businesses of the firm and the assessee were in any manner different. The nexus interlacing in their business was so conspicuous that their fictional legal individuality in tax laws became submerged in their commercial unison, as understood in the common law of partnership.

It, therefore, follows that, if the business of the firm and the assessee was thus interlocked, then the assessee's claim for deduction of the statutory liability in such a common trading activity between the assessee and the firm had to be upheld under section 37(1).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

running business is taken over or amalgamated, then certainly the assets are valued on the date of amalgamation and in this process sometimes the consideration to be paid is much more than the net assets and such deficit can either be reduced from Capital Reserve of the transferee company as provided under Accounting Standard-14 but if the scheme of amalgamation provides and there being genuine transaction, then Courts have consistently held that such deficit is to be considered as goodwill and eligible for depreciation. [Para 18]

■ However, in the instant case, the facts are different and peculiar. It is not the case of some independent transaction of amalgamation a company 'A' with company 'B' for taking over the business but it is a case where one holding company is having two subsidiaries companies and two subsidiary companies are merged in the process of amalgamation but the owner remains the same. In the process of amalgamation, the 60.72 equity shares have been issued by the Transferee company, i.e. the assessee company -ATPL to transferor company-MLPL and after reducing the face value of equity shares held by shareholder of MLPL, the excess amount of Rs.5.97 crores is treated as goodwill. It is clearly visible from the merger note that only against the creation of goodwill 60.72 equity shares in lieu of 1 equity share of MLPL has been issued. It is a case where the owner himself is claiming that one of its subsidiary company has purchased the business on of its another subsidiary company and such higher amount is basically goodwill and there being no banking transaction except the issue of fresh equity shares in lieu of the goodwill. It apparently seems to be an arrangement made at the instance of the holding company between its two subsidiary companies. Genuineness of the transaction of amalgamation between two independent/unrelated companies is missing in the instant case. [Para 19]

■

It is noted that similar type of transaction came for adjudication before Coordinate Bench, Hyderabad in the case of Invesco (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2025] 176 taxmann.com 784 (Hyderabad - Trib.) wherealso the wholly owned subsidiary of assessee company namely Invesco Hyderabad was amalgamated with the assessee company Invesco (India) under the scheme of amalgamation and against the investment of Rs.244.09 crore in the shares of subsidiary company Invesco Hyderabad the fair market value of intangible net assets of subsidiary company were at Rs.102.86 crore and the excess cost of investment over the value of net tangible asset has been determined as goodwill. [Para 20]

■

It is noted that prior to amalgamation ATPL earned revenue of Rs.2.23 crore whereas the revenue of MLPL was Rs.1.97 crore which shows that turnover of ATPL is higher than MLPL. It is also observed that 100 per cent of the sales of MLPL were effected majorly to the USA holding company where the sales of ATPL are to various customers in India. Interestingly, no sales have been effected to its related parties including the holding company by the assessee company, i.e. ATPL. Also post amalgamation, no sales have been effected to the holding company which indicates that the existing business of the subsidiary company prior to amalgamation has been discontinued post amalgamation and only the facilities or the assets appearing in the balance sheet prior to amalgamation as on 31-3-2014 has been transferred to the transferee company ATPL. These facts again support the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the observation of the Assessing Officer that this is a mere colourable transaction and in the garb of inflating the value of assets and creation of goodwill, assessee has intended to claim depreciation for the year under consideration and to be claimed in the subsequent years also. It is also an admitted fact that if new assets are added to the present set of assets on a running business then certainly some sales ought to increase but due to such amalgamation neither any new business has been added nor the profitability has increased much more than the situation prior to amalgamation as appearing from the records. Therefore, the creation of alleged goodwill is merely a colourable transaction carried out between the holding company and the subsidiary company which is to create an Intangible asset, inflate the value of equity shares of the transferee company and to further evade tax by claiming depreciation on such fictitious asset created through such arrangement of transaction between related parties. Therefore, it is held that claim of creation of goodwill of Rs.5.97 crores is only an artificial creation and is classic case of lifting the corporate wheel as rightly observed by the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, no intangible asset in the form of goodwill is created at Rs.5.97 crores. Further, since no intangible asset has been created in the process of amalgamation, depreciation claimed at Rs.1.49 crores also deserves to be disallowed. [Para 21]

Information given by merchant banker has been looked into

The material made available by the appellants through its merchant banker and the clarifications furnished by them were examined by the Board and the Board came to a definite conclusion that none of the 13 promoter group seller companies carried on the business of paper and pulp which was the product line of the target company. It also came to the conclusion that there is no object clause in the memorandum of association of any of the said 13 promoter group sellers which permits them to carry on the business carried on by the target company. It was further noted that one of these 13 companies is only a charitable and religious trust which had nothing to do with the pulp and paper business carried on by the target company and, therefore, not in a position to offer any competition to the target company. Yet another company is in the business of printing and publishing and yet another company. was carrying on business as composite textile mill which could not have the necessary knowledge or experience relating to paper and pulp business and, therefore, not capable of offering any competition to the target company. The information provided by the merchant banker to the Board has been looked into with regard to the justification sought by the Board for non-compete fee to these thirteen corporate entities. It is found that the merchant banker has stated primary reasons for entering into a non-compete agreement with the promoter group sellers as:

1.

Promoter Group Sellers have substantial experience and understanding of the paper industry in India. As such, their competency and ability to compete with APPM, the Acquirer and the PAC is, not in doubt.

2.

By virtue of their association with APPM and knowledge of its business, understanding of the market, access to market information and industrial connections, the Promoter Group Sellers are capable of offering competition to the Business of APPM, which could cause irreparable harm to APPM.

3.

The Promoter Group Sellers have acknowledged and agreed under the Non Compete Agreement that as controlling shareholders of APPM and by their extensive participation in the management and operations of APPM for a substantial period of time, they have acquired comprehensive expertise of the Business and the crucial trade secrets of the Company, and have been in possession of the confidential information relating to the Company and the Business. The Promoter Group Sellers have further acknowledged that by virtue of their association with the company and by using their expertise and confidential information belonging to the company, they are capable of offering competition to the Business of the company, which could cause irreparable harm to the Company, its continuing shareholders and the Acquirer.

Information made available to the Board with regard to 13 corporate promoter group entities shows that they are directly or indirectly controlled by the same promoter group and held significant equity share capital in each of the said companies but that by itself does not indicate that these promoter group companies which are into separate business are either involved in day-to-day business of the target company or are capable of competing with the business of the target company providing a threat perception to the business of the appellants. It was for the promoter group sellers and its merchant bankers to place material on record about the capacity of these promoter group corporate entities to compete with the business of appellants or their involvement into day-to-day business of the target company. The information made available by the merchant banker, are only bald statements and it does not disclose as to how these entities are privy to the information relating to the target company. Even the information made available with regard to current business of these entities does not make one any wiser as to how they are in a position to offer competition to the business of the target company.

As the promoter group sellers have failed to place sufficient material before the Board in this regard, no fault can be found with the conclusions arrived at by the Board that payment of non-compete fee is a sham depriving other shareholders of their rightful claims to get just price for their shares. [Para 15]

■ Admittedly, the agreement is between the two related parties. In fact, RR is the main person holding substantial interest in all these concerns and companies. The non-compete agreement has been entered into between UEPL represented by RR and UKM and UKE represented by RR HUF as a proprietor. The agreement is for non-compete for the business for a period of 5 years in light of purchase of running business by the appellant company and acquisition of 3700 feature films in different languages what was held by the above two Firms is, satellite rights of feature films and the same has been transferred to the appellant company of erstwhile UEPL as a going concern. Once the entire business is transferred as a going concern concept, then, nothing is left with the transferee firms to carry on the business. Further, what was held by them is a copyright of a feature film, but, not a product/design or copyright asset, patent. In order to restrict any person from doing similar business for a particular period, there should be a business and product. In the present case, going by the nature of business transferred by the above two firms, it is only a sale of copyrights of feature films and once right is sold to a third party, then, nothing is left with the seller or the transferee. Therefore, continuing the business or carrying the business of similar nature under different name does not arise because, what is left with the transferee company is factually nothing by virtue of transferring of all the 3700 feature films owned by them. Further, assuming for a moment by entering into non-compete agreement, the appellant company restricted the erstwhile firms to carry on the business and acquired copy-rights of feature films in future, but, said business can be done by any third party because, the exclusive right of feature film is not with the two firms alone, but, it is with the different people because, the copyrights of feature film is owned by producer of different films, but, not a single party. Therefore, once the business is transferred as a going concern and nothing is left with the transferee firms to carry on business, entering into non-compete agreement with the above two firms for a period of 5 years give rise to various questions including question of tax avoidance plan by the appellant company going by the nature of transactions and financial position of Ramoji Rao HUF. Although, this fact has been brought-out by the Assessing Officer in his order while disallowing depreciation on noncompete fee, but, the Tribunal while setting aside the matter has touched upon the point in light of transfer of 39% equity shares to ETEPL even though the Tribunal admitted in it’s order that, share subscription agreement are not available before the Tribunal to ascertain the correct details as to whether ETEPL a third party or a company belongs to RR group or not. In absence of relevant evidences, the finding of facts given by the Tribunal to hold that, the transaction is not between the related parties, in our considered view, is not based on any evidences, but, purely on the submissions of the appellant company. Therefore, to this extent, we cannot subscribe to the reasons given by the Tribunal to hold that, non-compete agreement between the appellant company and other firms, is not between the related parties and a third party interest is involved and, therefore, it cannot be said that, it is a commercial agreement, cannot be accepted and needs to be further examined by the Assessing Officer. [Para 11]

■

It is further observed that the statute does not prescribe any condition for withdrawal or denial of the exemption granted under section 47(xiv) on account of any alleged discrepancy in the valuation of the assets taken over or the issue price of shares allotted by the successor company. [Para 126]

■ Support is found from the decisions of the Co-ordinate Benches of the Tribunal, wherein it has been consistently held that once the conditions stipulated under section 47(xiv) are duly satisfied, the assessee is entitled to the exemption provided therein, and no addition can be made merely on account of revaluation of assets or valuation of shares. [Para 127]

■

The amount of Rs.93.63 crores does not represent a cash credit as contemplated under section 68, but is merely a book entry arising on account of the succession of the assessee's sole proprietorship business by a company. The impugned entry reflects the accounting treatment of transfer of assets and liabilities pursuant to such succession and does not involve any actual inflow of cash or receipt of money. The scope and applicability of section 68 are confined to cases where any sum is found credited in the books of account of the assessee and such credit represents a real and tangible receipt of money, the nature and source of which remains unexplained. The provisions of section 68 cannot be invoked in respect of notional entries or book adjustments which do not result in the introduction of any fresh funds into the business of the assessee. A mere accounting entry, without any corresponding receipt of cash or equivalent consideration, cannot be brought to tax under section 68. In the present case, it is an undisputed fact that the amount of Rs.93.63 crores has arisen solely on account of the vesting of the proprietorship business in the successor company and represents the difference arising from the revaluation or transfer of assets and liabilities. Such an entry is purely notional in nature and does not partake the character of a cash credit. Therefore, the fundamental pre-condition for invoking the provisions of section 68, namely, the existence of a cash credit, itself remains unfulfilled. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was not justified in invoking the provisions of section 68 to make the addition of Rs.93.63 crores. [Para 130]

■

In view of the foregoing discussion and upon a holistic appreciation of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is opined that the assessee has duly complied with and satisfied all the conditions prescribed under section 47(xiv). Consequently, the transfer of the proprietary concern by the assessee to the company does not constitute a ‘transfer’ within the meaning of section 45 read with section 47(xiv), and therefore, no capital gains tax is chargeable on such transaction. [Para 134]

■

Once the transaction is expressly exempt under the specific provisions governing capital gains, the same falls outside the ambit of taxation under that head. In such circumstances, the provisions of section 68, which operate in a different field, cannot be invoked to tax the very same transaction indirectly. The specific statutory exclusion provided under section 47(xiv) overrides the general provisions, and hence, section 68 has no application in the present facts of the case. [Para 135]

■

In this backdrop, the amount of Rs.93.63 crores credited to the assessee’s capital account, representing the net value of the business transferred, cannot be brought to tax. Accordingly, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and subsequently sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 68 is legally unsustainable, misconceived, and devoid of merit. The impugned addition is therefore liable to be deleted on merits. [Para 136]

■

Accordingly, the Assessing Officer erred in making an addition under section 68 and the same is deleted on merits as well. The ground of appeal raised by the assessee challenging the said addition is, therefore, allowed on merits. [Para 137]
