, as to the applicability of the decision of Karnataka High Court in the case of CIT v. Tata Coffee Ltd. [2010] 326 ITR 214 relied on by the Commissioner (Appeals), the Karnataka High Court has treated the non-compete fees received by the vendor as a revenue receipt for the reason that the discontinuance of the unit has not resulted in the loss of enduring trading asset. Same is the position with the other cases relied by the Commissioner (Appeals). However, in the instant case, the perusal of the material on record clearly reveals that after discontinuing the merchant banking activities, assessee-company did not have any active source of income and its income consisted of income mainly from dividend from shares and mutual funds, profit on sale of shares, interest income and nominal consultancy charges. Hence, there is no substantial fall in profit earning of the assessee after entering into non-compete agreement.

As per the relevant agreement, the assessee had received the impugned receipt for the transfer of its business of merchant banking in the form of employees, contracts in the form of customer and client relationship, a list of ten largest clients and certain know-how related to merchant banking business of the assessee, which necessarily qualify impugned receipt for the transfer of the said intangible assets in the category of 'capital nature' as the subject matter of transfer has resulted in the loss of enduring trading assets.

Regarding the possibility of taxing the said impugned capital receipt under the head of capital gains, since no cost of acquisition is involved by the assessee for these assets, the same cannot be taxed under the head capital gains also.

It is needless to emphasise that the nature of the transfer does not attract the provision of section 50B in relation to slump sale also as there is no transfer of an undertaking by the assessee. Accordingly, this ground is decided in favour of the assessee. [Para 2.4.1]

It was however stated that such assets were appearing in the balance sheet prepared under the Companies Act as on 31-3-2004 at Rs. 4,71,20,059 and if the deduction under section 35(1)(iv)/35(2) is ignored, WDV of such assets as on 31-3-2004 would stand at Rs. 2, 16, 06, 346. [Para 14] From the material on record, i.e., WDV as per the Companies Act as on 31-3-2004 there was force in the contention of the assessee that it is not a case where building as held by the Assessing Officer of Rs. 7,098 were sold at Rs. 66,00,000. On the contrary, it is a case where building having book value of Rs. 74,25,264 was transferred to the assessee company at Rs. 66,00,000 and thus, likewise, it is not a case where plant and machinery of Rs. 59.94 lakhs as noted by the Assessing Officer has been transferred for consideration of Rs. 89.66 lakhs. On the contrary, plant and machinery having book value of Rs. 3,71,66,000 has been transferred for consideration of Rs. 89,66,000. The above value are supported by a registered valuer's report and are not mere arbitrary valuations adopted by the assessee.

The Assessing Officer vis-a-vis registered valuer's report has held that both the companies were engaged in the same kind of electronic business and plant and machinery used by them was unique and they were not ordinarily marketable commodities, so as to have any valuation of their market price. He further observed that both the companies knew that there was no market for the old plant and machinery except for the opinion that the assets of one company doing the same business were used by the other. It will be thus seen that the Assessing Officer has not found any specific defect vis-a-vis valuation adopted by the appellant on the basis of registered valuer's report. It could not be said that an asset though having Nil value under Act would be transferred also Nil value to a third party more particularly when the transfer is not of an asset but of a business on a going concern basis.

The transfer of the business is not in dispute. The genuineness of the transfer of the business was not in dispute. The purpose behind the transfer is also not in dispute. All what has been disputed by the Assessing Officer and upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals) is valuation of the assets adopted for the purpose of transfer. In such circumstances, there was force in the claim that it is not a case of valuation having been adopted by a higher price more particularly when the transaction is between the closely held company and public limited company and price is paid to public limited company by the closely held company.

It is also not a case where price as stated in the agreement has not been paid by the assessee. The valuation is supported by registered valuer's report which valuation had not been shown to be either imaginary or irrational by any cogent evidence. On the contrary, having regard to the book value of the assets standing under the Companies Act, the value as adopted could not otherwise be said to be unreasonable. [Para 15]

Once there is a report by the registered valuer it is encumbent upon the authority to dislodge the same by bringing adequate material on record in the form of a departmental valuation report, because in the absence of the same as technical expert's opinion cannot be dislodged by any authority by merely ignoring the same. In the present case that is what has happened. Neither the Assessing Officer nor the Commissioner (Appeals) has even attempted to state that the valuation report and the values put on the assets are incorrect in any manner whatsoever. [Para 16]

The Assessing Officer has also laid emphasis on the fact that short-term capital gain as declared by the transfer of company namely Deltron has been set off against the losses in the books of the said company. Having regard to the peculiar facts and circumstances in the case of the assessee company as highlighted above, such a factor alone cannot be made a basis to invoke Explanation 3 to section 43(1). Explanation 3 to section 43(1) is not an absolute rule. The Assessing Officer is empowered to substitute the value. However, such a valuation cannot be substituted where there is no intent to reduce the tax liability.

In the instant case, the assets as held by Deltron and transferred to the assessee as part of transfer of electronic business on going concern basis cannot be said to be in any manner with an intent to reduce the tax liability. Certainly, the effect of the transaction was that the gain declared by Deltron Ltd. was set off against the losses in its computation yet that fact cannot undetermine the genuineness of the transaction and in any case empower the Assessing Officer to substitute the valuation as determined in the registered valuer's report which has not been found to be incorrect by any other technical valuation. Hence, the conclusion of the authorities below cannot be accepted. [Para 18]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment years 2004-05 to 2009-10 - Assessee purchased one division of 'N' chemicals by way of slump sale - Assessee paid certain amount as non-compete fee which represented difference in value of tangible and intangible assets and lump sum amount paid for taking over business - It was found that on account of payment of non-compete fee, seller was restrained from carrying on similar type of business for three years - Whether since payment of non-compete fee resulted in enduring benefit to assessee, it could not be allowed as revenue expenditure; it was capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee purchased business division of another concern which also included payment to non-compete fee restraining seller from carrying on similar business for three years, said payment was to be regarded as capital expenditure  IT : Payment made for taking legal and professional advice in connection with purchase of business division, was to be treated as capital expenditure  IT : Where assessee made payment to its holding company for using its trade mark and to obtain expertise in field of commerce, finance, manufacturing etc. for smooth running of business, amount so paid was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where assessee paid commission on export sales at same rate at which it had been paid by seller of business earlier, disallowance made by Assessing Officer taking a view that a part of commission payment was excessive, was to be deleted  IT : Foreign exchange fluctuation loss incurred by assessee in respect of outstanding foreign currency term loan was to be allowed as business loss  IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee in connection to transfer of business such as legal notice charges, performance incentive etc., was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where in order to give effect to business transfer agreement, assessee purchased shares of management staff, since impugned amount was non-recoverable and was a loss on account of business transfer, it was required to be deducted from capital gain in respect of slump sale of trading business  IT : Where Assessing Officer made disallowance in respect of dividend income by relying upon Rule 8D of Income-tax Rules, 1962, since said rule was applicable for assessment year 2008-09 while assessment year under consideration was 2007-08, impugned disallowance was to be deleted

FACT: The assessee purchased one division of 'N' Chemicals which was transferred to the assessee by way of slump sales. The assessee treated the same as capital expenditure in the books of account and claimed depreciation on said amount. For the purpose of computing total income under the Act, the assessee treated Rs. 6.80 crores as non-compete fee on the basis of the value of the intangibles determined by the valuers.

The Assessing Officer treated the said amount as capital expenditure by holding that the amount claimed as fee for non-compete was nothing but goodwill of the business.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, took a view that by entering into a restrictive covenant the assessee had warded off a potential competition from the transferor. He thus held that amount paid as non-compete fee was to be regarded as revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: In the instant case the non-compete fee although identified separately by the valuer but it was inbuilt in the lump sum consideration. The assessee split the lump sum consideration in various tangible and intangible assets on the basis of report of the valuers which was not doubted either by the Assessing Officer or by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In the present case, the only dispute was relating to the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores, the said amount was difference in the value of tangible/intangible assets of the going concern which was purchased by the assessee and the lump sum amount paid for taking over the business, so it was in the nature of the goodwill and since the assessee was having the enduring benefit particularly when there was a covenant on the seller for not to run the similar type of business for three years. Therefore, the said amount cannot be considered as revenue in nature as has been held by the Commissioner (Appeals). Since the amount under consideration was in excess of the value of tangible and intangible asset and was a part of the lump sum consideration for acquiring the business, so it was a goodwill. [Para 30]

Therefore, by considering the totality of the facts, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside on this issue and the view taken by the Assessing Officer that the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores was nothing but goodwill of the business and a capital expenditure is upheld.

The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contentions and set aside the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The facts indicated that the parties were unrelated and the assessee purchased the cement units as a slump scale with effect from 1-11-1999. Under the business transfer agreement the assessee not only acquired the fixed assets of the said unit but also the current assets of the same units including the current liabilities for which the total consideration of Rs. 550 crores was paid. It was also a fact that the said TISCO had arrived at the profit on sale of Rs. 125. 26 crores after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers. This was the basis for Assessing Officer's opinion that the cost of fixed assets acquired by the assessee should be the book value of TISCO. Accordingly, he restricted the cost of the assets to the above amount thereby treating the balance amount as goodwill and denied depreciation. It was also a fact that the agreement did not speak of any goodwill payment and the assessee had adjusted the entire consideration paid between fixed assets and net current assets. It was also a fact that in the next assessment year assessee acquired another unit from 'R' and the assessee treated the difference between the fair market value of the assets and the payment made as goodwill and made entries in the books of account accordingly where as in relevant year the value paid was for fixed assets and net current assets and goodwill was not involved. [Para 6]

Section 43(1) is clear that the actual cost to be considered for the purpose of section 32 should be the actual cost paid by the assessee. Since the cost has not been directly or indirectly met by any other person or authority, the cost paid by the assessee for acquisition of the assets of the units is the cost under section 43(1) . However, Explanation (3) makes it clear that where the assets are used at any time by any other person for the purpose of his business or profession and the Assessing Officer is satisfied that the main purpose of the transfer of such assets directly or indirectly to the assessee was reduction of liability of tax for claiming depreciation with reference to enhanced cost, the actual cost of the assets shall be such an amount as the Assessing Officer may determine having regard to all the circumstances of the case. As rightly considered by the Commissioner (Appeals) the parties were unrelated and the transaction was at arm's length basis. The registered valuer also valued the assets as on 1-11-1999, the price of which was considered to be the cost of fixed asset acquired and the balance to the current assets including the current liabilities. In view of this, there was no reason to invoke Explanation (3) as the Assessing Officer nowhere stated that the main purpose of such a valuation was for reduction of liability to tax. It was a direct acquisition by the assessee company from another public limited company in an open bid, being the highest bidder. As per AS 10 para 35 the assessee was supposed to take the value on the fair basis as determined by competent valuers. [Para 8]

It was with a view to safeguard against that possibility that the appellant as the acquirer entered into the non-compete agreement with the promoters with a view to protect the interest of the target company and its continuing shareholders. Equally, there was nothing that prevented the promoters from divesting their minority stake in the target company if that was to become necessary. The promoters who had been in management of the target company had comprehensive knowledge of how the source of water available to the target company could be exploited. Thus, the argument of the Board that the appellant had acquired a US based flavored water maker 'G' which was a similar line of business as the target company and, therefore, the appellant could not claim that it had no knowledge and expertise in the business of bottled water, had no merits. Thus, the Board had erred in directing the appellant to add to the offer price, the non-compete fee as paid to the promoter sellers. HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1962-63 - During relevant accounting year, assessee company took over business carried on by a firm including its employees - Aforesaid firm had a scheme in force of retiring its employees at age of 57½ years and paying them gratuity at time of retirement - Assessee-company also had a scheme of paying gratuity to its employees on retirement, but there was no fixed age of retirement for employees - As per terms of agreement of taking over business, assessee-company was to retire all its employees who had exceeded age of 57½ years and to pay them gratuity - Assessee-company did so and claimed amount paid as revenue expenditure - ITO taking a view that amount so paid was nothing but part of business consideration held that expenditure in question was capital in nature and not allowable as deduction - AAC as well as Tribunal, however, allowed assessee's claim - On instant reference, it was seen that Tribunal had recorded finding that there was an existing scheme for employees of assessee-company who were paid this amount by way of gratuity - It was also recorded that payment was made under circumstances as would ensure retention of remaining staff and contentment amongst them - Whether in aforesaid findings, order passed by Tribunal allowing assessee's claim was to be upheld - Held, yes

FACT: The business carried on by 'V' firm was taken over by the assessee-company during the relevant assessment year. The assessee took over the plant, machinery and buildings and lands owned by the firm in relation to its cotton and cotton waste business at various places. The staff of 'V' firm also came over to the assessee. The 'V' firm had a scheme in force of retiring its employees at the age of 57½ and paying them gratuity at the time of retirement. The assessee had a scheme of paying gratuity to its employees when their services came to an end, but there was no fixed age of retirement for the employees of the assessee-company. It had thus employees who had exceeded the age of 57½ years. Under the agreement, the assessee was to retire all its employees who had exceeded the age of 57½ years on or before 31-8-1961, and to pay to these employees the gratuity, provident fund, etc. due to them. It was specifically stated that assets and properties of the assessee shall be transferred to IISL. Reading of clause 4 of the MOU made it clear that the business transactions carried out by the assessee that were transferred to IISL would continue with them and IISL shall be entitled to enforce their rights thereunder without any restriction. It meant restriction of time as well. To come to a different conclusion as canvassed by the revenue, was not acceptable. Clauses 7 and 8 of the MOU restricted the promoters of the assessee-company to do similar or identical business carried out earlier by the assessee and now by IISL permanently and even all improvements in technology, etc., would be the property of IISL. [Para 27]

According to the revenue, by virtue of clause 2 of the MOU, the assessee had not transferred the building, motor car and assets and liabilities relating to income-tax matters. This, according to the revenue, fell short of the slump sale for slump consideration. It was not possible to accept the view canvassed by the revenue. The Bombay High Court in CIT v. Narkeshari Prakashan Ltd. [1992] 196 ITR 438 clearly held that the sale of even branches of an undertaking along with its assets and liabilities amounts to sale as a going concern for a slump price. The assessee's business assets were computers, furniture, etc., because the assessee was in the field of software business. It was difficult to hold that the purchaser could not continue with the business in the absence of building and motor car, which had been kept apart. If the purchaser perhaps was prevented from continuing the business, the stand of the revenue that that was not sale of a going concern for a slump price, would have been correct. The question was whether the business would continue in the same line even without the two assets. Reading of the MOU, relevant clauses of which made it clear that the assessee had transferred all the properties relating to its business. Even according to the revenue, the assessee's business assets were in the nature of intellectual properties, codes, formulae, design, etc. These had been transferred for a consideration. [Para 28]

Further, 'slump sale' means transfer of one or more undertakings as a result of sale for a lump sum consideration without values being assigned to the individual assets and liabilities in such sales. In the instant case of the assessee, though in the purchaser's books of account the individual assets had been priced independently, yet the assessee had not assigned separate values and, consequently, sold the items for an independent price. It was not the revenue's case also that individual assets had the price fixed separately and charged. 'Undertaking' is explained in Explanation 1 to section 2(19AA). According to this Explanation, it includes any part of an undertaking or a unit or division of an undertaking or a business activity as a whole. The revenue's case was that some of the items like motor car and building had been retained by the assessee; as such, this could not be treated as a slump sale. But the fact to be considered was that the assessee was in the field of intellectual property rights. Computers, furniture, etc., which were linked with the business of the assessee had been sold. The items that the assessee kept separately had nothing to do with its business which was sold/handed over to the purchaser, i.e., IISL. Thus, only the business had been sold. The purchaser could very well carry on with the business, which was carried by the assessee before the sale, without purchasing any independent items. In view of the above, the plea of the revenue that the assessee had not sold the undertaking as a whole, could not be accepted. [Para 29]

Thus, the claim of the assessee was to be allowed and that of the revenue was to be rejected.

HEADNOTE: Section 43(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Actual cost -  Assessment year 2000-01 - Assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern - TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and assessee was highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores - After acquiring company units as going concern assessee, on basis of valuation report of 'K', determined fair market value of fixed assets as on date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores - Assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores - Assessing Officer obtained information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that said company had shown book value of fixed asset at Rs. 345. 95 crores - Assessing Officer was of view that assessee had paid more amount than book value of difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment - Thereupon, Assessing Officer determined goodwill value at difference between amount adopted by assessee and amount shown in books of TISCO and depreciation on amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order passed by Assessing Officer holding that Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case - On revenue's appeal, it was noted that parties were unrelated and transaction was at arm's length basis - It was also noticed that neither acquisition of their business nor assets comprised therein nor valuation thereof was with purpose of reducing Income-tax liability of assessee by claiming higher depreciation - Further, assessee had arrived at fair market value of assets on basis of valuation report obtained in accordance with accounting standard 10 - Whether, on facts finding of Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer had not made out a case for reducing actual cost was correct and it did not require any interference - Held, yesIncome-tax : In case of acquisition of fixed assets, actual cost of same to be considered for purpose of section 32 should be actual cost paid by assessee.

FACT: The assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern. The TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and the assessee was the highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores. The same was accepted by the TISCO in its Board meeting on 18-12-1998. Thereupon, the cement units were actually taken over and used in its own production activity. After acquiring the company units as going concern as the assessee, on the basis of valuation report of 'K' fixed the fair market value of fixed assets as on the date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores. The balance amount of consideration of Rs. 68. 61 crores was attributed to the net current assets taken over. The assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on the value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores. In the course of assessment the Assessing Officer asked for the WDV of the assets of TISCO. Since the assessee expressed its inability to furnish the details as they purchased the assets on the basis as going concern, the Assessing Officer obtained the information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that the said company had shown the book value of fixed assets at Rs. 345. 95 crores and after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers, offered profits on sale of net assets of cement division at Rs. 125. 25 crores in their books of account. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had paid more amount than the book value and the difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment and accordingly after discussion about the provisions of section 43(1) , report of the registered valuer, determined the goodwill value at the difference between the amount adopted by the assessee and the amount shown in the books of TISCO and depreciation on the amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed thereby making addition of Rs. 16. 39 crores. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) it was contended that the assessee had acquired fixed assets and current assets of the unit in an open bid and on the basis of the report of the registered valuer the value was accordingly capitalized to the extent of Rs. 481. 39 crores and Assessing Officer's action in taking the WDV of TISCO was not correct as Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case as these two companies were independent and not related and further the Assessing Officer had not correctly appreciated the registered valuer's report and the method adopted. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contentions and set aside the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

This will depend on the purpose for which the payment of Rs. 11 crores was made by ICL to assessee and what was the right that was transferred by assessee for which the amount in question was paid and the law as it existed at the relevant point of time viz., 27-10-1999. [Para 17]

The ICL took over RCL as well as SVCL and the takeover was hostile takeover since both RCL and SVCL were public limited companies whose shares were widely spread out in the market and nobody had controlling block of shares. Ultimately the promoters of RCL and SVCL including assessee sold their shares in a negotiated deal to ICL. The three persons were promoters of the two companies. Similar payments were made to other two promoters. The Tribunal had an occasion to consider taxability of such receipts. In the case of other promoters, the Tribunal held that the receipts were not taxable on two counts. (1) The payment in question was a payment as consideration for not indulging in competition (which was chargeable to capital gains tax only with effect from 1-4-2003 by virtue of amendment to section 55(2)(a ) by the Finance Act, 2002] and was not a payment made for a right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing [which was chargeable to capital gains tax with effect from 1-4-1998 by virtue of amendment to section 55(2)(a) of the Act by the Finance Act, 1997]. (2) The Tribunal held that it was only SVCL and RCL that were manufacturing cement and, therefore, when the amount was received by the assessee who were individuals and promoters of those companies not engaged in any manufacturing of cement, it could not be said that the consideration paid for not indulging in competition was a consideration for giving up right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing. [Para 18]

In the instant case, before analyzing the rival contentions and the terms of the agreement dated 27-10-1999, it would be useful to narrate the relevant provisions of the Act as it existed during the relevant assessment year, the law as it existed prior to the insertion of the statutory provisions and the amendments to the relevant provisions of law after the relevant assessment year. It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature.

This amount was not for business expediency but was actually for settlement of the family dispute in between the two groups of ‘S’ brothers and their family members. It had come on record that these four brothers were running the business of assessee-company and three other companies. R was removed from the effective management and control of all the four companies including assessee-company. R filed a suit and got ad interim injunction in his favour and then matter was amicably settled. The fact noted in the compromise application were relevant. No doubt R and his group transferred the shares in favour of G but R group lost more and G group obtained more in the said settlement. A perusal of the assessment order showed that main relief of R was equalisation of shares in the business of family including the four companies referred in the plaint. He claimed 25 per cent of shares but out of compromise he not only lost that claim but he as well as his family members transferred their shareholding to rival group in all other companies. R and his group members discharged their liabilities of sum of Rs. 30 lakhs to the members of G group out of Rs. 1.29 crores and he was discharged of his personal guarantee given to the bank. In the plaint he claimed his reinstatement on the Board of Directors of all the four companies but after compromise he did not remain even an ordinary members of these companies. Another relief sought by R was that he was given all powers to operate bank accounts of all the four companies and to remain in effective control but after compromise he lost all those powers. Contrary to it G group did not make any counter claim in the suit filed by R but they got the shareholdings of R and group members. They got payment of Rs. 30 lakhs from the member of R group and ultimately total and absolute control over the five companies to the total exclusion of R group. About the amount in question, it could be said that the same was not associated with the terms of the compromise but was particularly in respect of terms and conditions given in the compromise application. These facts went to show that this amount was paid in lump sum to R so that G group may get rid off R and his group from effective control of all the five companies including four mentioned in the plaint. Suit filed by R was not in respect of assessee-company alone but three other companies were evolved and compromise had taken into consideration another 5th company of this group. It would not be in the fitness of things to conclude that the amount was relevant to assessee-company alone when compromise application read as a whole went to show the very intention of the parties. Mere mentioning that the amount was being paid to R for his past services and to ward off competition from him for twenty years would alone be not sufficient to conclude the issue but on the facts and circumstances as discussed in the assessment order and sequence of events which had taken place in between the parties, the only irresistible conclusion would be that amount was paid by the assessee to get the family dispute settled and not for special expertise of R as mentioned in the agreement deed.

On the basis of above discussion, it could be concluded that amount in question was not a revenue expenditure but in view of the case law the amount was to be treated as capital expenditure. Apart from it, the amount in question was not given for any business expediency nor wholly and exclusively laid out for business purposes as required under section 37 but was on account of settling the family dispute and, thus, the Assessing Officer was justified in not allowing the claim of the assessee.

The business continued to be the same. Only the ownership was changed. The Apex Court in the case of Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. CIT [1990] 186 ITR 278 has held that in order to attract the provisions of section 41(1), the identity of the assessee in the earlier year in which deduction was granted in relation to a trading liability and in the subsequent year in which benefit is derived, must be the same. If there is change in the identity of the assessee, there would be no tax liability under section 41. If the assessee to whom the trading liability may have been allowed as business expenditure in the earlier year ceases to be in existence or if the assessee has changed on account of the death of the earlier assessee, the benefit received in the subsequent year cannot be treated as income received by the assessee. [Para 10]

The instant case was governed by the old law. Section 41(1) was amended by the Finance Act, 1992, with effect from 1-4-1993. The instant case related to the assessment year 1990-91. Under the provisions of section 41(1), where an assessee who was allowed deduction in respect of any loss, expenditure or trading liability in any year obtained any amount in respect of such loss on expenditure or any benefit in respect of trading liability by way of remission or cessation thereof, the amount obtained by him or the value of benefit accruing to him was deemed to be the profits and gains of business or profession. However, it was held in the case of Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. (supra ), that such an amount or benefit can be charged to tax only if the assessee who receives the amount or benefit is the same person who was allowed the deduction earlier. [Para 11]

With a view to ensure that there is no loss of revenue and undue enrichment, section 41(1) was substituted by the Finance Act, 1922, so as to bring to tax the amount or benefit, as the case may be. [Para 12]

In the instant case, however, there was no undue enrichment to the assessee. The person who sold the business did pay capital gains tax. Besides, the year in question was governed by the law laid down by the Apex Court and the amendment was not applicable to the facts of the instant case.

The assessee categorically objected before the TPO to the effect that this company was mainly into software product business having license of such products. The TPO ignored the assessee's submissions despite the fact that sufficient material taken from the website of this company was placed before him in support of the contention. It can be seen from notes to the balance sheet that this company developed software products in-house. The expenditure so incurred on product development has been duly capitalized. These facts amply bring out that Lucid Software Ltd. cannot be considered as comparable. Therefore, the exclusion of this case is directed from the list of comparables.

Megasoft Ltd. (Consulting/Blue Alley Division)

It is found from the director's report of this company that the financial results for the year include the business performance of Visual Soft Technologies Ltd. with effect from 1-10-2006 consequent to the amalgamation. The Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal in Petro Araldite (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 144 ITD 625/31 taxmann.com 281 (Mum.) has held that a company cannot be considered as comparable because of exceptional financial results due to mergers/demergers etc. since the financial results of Megasoft Ltd. have the impact of the merger of Visual Software Technologies Ltd. with effect from 1-10-2006, obviously, this company cannot be considered as comparable. Accordingly, this company is directed to be excluded. [Para 31.2]

Presistent Systems Ltd.

This company also cannot be considered as comparable because of merger of another company into it. It can be seen that a subsidiary company was merged into this company pursuant to judgment of Bombay High Court. Because of the merger of subsidiary in to this company, the financial position of this company cannot be construed as normal capable of a good comparison. Following the Mumbai Bench decision in Petro Araldite (P.) Ltd. (supra), the exclusion of this company is directed from the list of comparables. [Para 33]

R Systems International Ltd. (Segmental)

The TPO included this company in the list of comparables and determined its OP/OC at 15.07 per cent. The assessee has no objection to the inclusion of this company in the list of comparables. His only objection was confined to the calculation of OP/OC at 15.07 per cent. The assessee contended that the TPO erred in excluding the amount of 'provision for doubtful debts' from operating costs. [Para 36.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 45, read with section 55, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee-firm was manufacturer of transformers - During relevant assessment year, its business was taken over as a going concern by a limited company and its partners became directors of said company - Said company made certain payments to assessee for technical know-how and as compensation by way of non-competing fee - Assessing Officer held that receipt for technical know-how was nothing but a part of composite receipt to cover value of intangible assets and inasmuch as ‘goodwill’ was taxable under section 55(2), an attempt was made to evade payment of tax - He, therefore, treated entire amount as long-term capital gain - On appeal, Tribunal upheld findings of Assessing Officer - Whether inasmuch as assessee-firm had been taken over as a going concern, it could not have been taken over without so-called technical know-how and, hence, receipts for technical know-how were nothing but a part of composite receipt to diminish value of assets of assessee-firm and assessee had termed said amount as receipts for technical know-how in order to escape from clutches of provisions of section 55(2) under which a goodwill amount is taxable - Held, yes - Whether further question of payment of non-competing fee also would not arise, considering fact that assessee-firm had been taken over as a going concern in its entirety by new company and partners of assessee-firm were directors of said company - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in holding that amount representing value of technical know-how
 and amount received as non-competing fee were taxable as long-term capital gains under section 45, read with section 55 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was manufacturer of transformers. During relevant assessment year, its business was taken over as a going concern by a limited company and its partners became directors of the said company. The said company made certain payments to the assessee for technical know-how and as compensation for pending and expected orders, i.e., not to compete and indulge in transformer business. During assessment proceedings, a show-cause notice was issued to the assessee as to why the amounts shown as received for non-competition fee for pending orders, future orders and for the transfer of technical know-how would not be treated as capital gains, inasmuch as no amount had been shown under the head ‘Goodwill’ even though the assessee had been making good profit in the previous years. The assessee contended that it had not received any money towards the goodwill from the company and inasmuch as for the assessment year 1995-96, a transfer of technical know-how was not taxable, it could not be termed as long-term capital gain. The Assessing Officer held that the receipt for technical know-how was nothing but a part of the composite receipt to cover the value of the intangible assets and inasmuch ‘goodwill’ was taxable under section 55(2), an attempt was made to evade the payment of tax. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer treated the entire amount as capital gains. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim in respect of amount received for technical know-how and compensation for pending orders but disallowed the amount of compensation for expected orders. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that there was no indication of the value of the technical know-how in the balance sheet and it had come into existence only at the time of signing the transfer agreement. It held that the agreement was for the transfer of entire business of a going concern and the amount indicated as the payment for technical know-how was nothing but a goodwill amount which was a colourable device to evade tax. The Tribunal further held that in view of the taking over of the going concern, the assessee-firm had come to an end, more so when the partners were also the directors and, therefore, there was no question of paying the non-competing fees, inasmuch as there was no possibility of the assessee-firm doing the very same business again. Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by the revenue and dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1947-48 - Whether where payment was made to a competitor so that assessee may itself secure a contract for making purchases from a certain concern without any competition, payment was an expenditure not in connection with business but was an expenditure in nature of capital expenditure to prepare ground for securing all business - Held, yes

FACT: The family of BP and his two sons CL and MP were carrying on business in the name of a firm referred to as "the family firm". CL started business of his own which would be referred to his ‘Jaipuria firm’. CL, representing "the Jaipuria firm", entered into partnership with BN for purchase and acquisition of armour plates from the Field Liquidation Commission. In the Jaipuria firm the share of CL was eleven annas and of BN five annas in a rupee. BN subscribed Rs. 1,50,000 towards the capital of the partnership but CL did not subscribe any capital himself and the rest of the capital of the partnership was to come from the family firm." The Jaipuria firm made profits on its armour plates business and in that connection, in the assessment year 1947-48, the family firm was assessed to income-tax. The ITO found that the share in the Jaipuria firm was not the personal and individual share of CL but was the share of the family firm. The reasons for coming to this conclusion, inter alia, were (a) that no capital was invested by CL himself in the Jaipuria firm, (b) that on 12-2-1946, the family firm paid Rs. 40,000 to one EV to remove him from competition for the contract for armour plates business, (ii) that on 4-2-1946, Rs. 99,132 were paid as custom duty by the family firm for the Jaipuria firm and (iii) that the total amount of payments made by the family firm to the American Field Commissioner came to about Rs. 3,30,440 as cost of the armour plates purchased in the name of Jaipuria firm, and that all these transactions were entered in full detail in the account books of the family firm, (c) that on dissolution of the Jaipuria firm partnership the five annas share coming to about Rs. 90,000 of BN was paid to the latter by the family firm and not by CL. For these reasons, the ITO came to the conclusion that the eleven annas share in the Jaipuria firm was the share of the family firm and not of CL individually. The profits of the Jaipuria firm of the share of the family firm were taxed in the income of the latter. The family firm did not appeal against that assessment. It was CL alone, in his personal capacity, who filed an appeal to the AAC of Income-tax and in the grounds of appeal his main attack, was that the ITO had erred in his finding that the eleven annas share in the partnership of Jaipuria firm was not his individual share but was that of the family and that the ITO also erred in disallowing a sum of Rs. 40,000 paid to EV as revenue expenditure because he treated it as capital expenditure.

The AAC confirmed the order of ITO on both counts. He found that the payment of Rs. 40,000 to EV was a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure because it was paid to him to oust him as a competitor in obtaining the armour plate business.

On second appeal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the family or the family firm not having appealed against the order of assessment, the AAC was wrong in entertaining appeal by CL, that Rs. 40,000 paid to EV was rightly found to be capital expenditure and not revenue expenditure and that the share in Jaipuria firm was the share of the family firm and not of CL individually. The Tribunal also refused to make a reference to the High Court.

On reference applications under section 66(2) :

the light of the facts of each case. Supposing, the fee is paid to a person who cannot compete, the Board may be entitled to say that it is only a device to reduce the offer price. In such a case, the Board may justifiably direct its addition to the offer price. On the other hand if the payment is made to an outgoing seller who can offer competition to the business of the target company, the Board shall have no occasion to interfere. [Para 5] The recommendations made by the Bhagwati Committee clearly recognize the legitimacy of the non-compete fee payable to the outgoing sellers. Regulation 20(8) based on these recommendations puts a cap on such payments so that an acquirer cannot reduce the cost of acquisition through public offer thereby depriving the public shareholders of their legitimate dues. When examining the validity of the non-compete fee, the question to be addressed is whether the outgoing sellers are capable of providing competition to the business alone or in association with third parties and not whether the business was dependent on the outgoing sellers. When an acquirer takes over a business from the outgoing seller(s), it is obvious that the sellers have specific knowledge of that business and they have access to and are in possession of crucial trade secrets of the target company which if disclosed or misused would be detrimental to and could cause irreparable harm to the target company and its continuing shareholders and by virtue of their association with that business, they (out going sellers) are capable of offering competition to the business being taken over. In such cases, it would be legitimate for the acquirer to enter into a non-compete agreement with the promoter sellers if he feels threatened by a lurking fear of competition from them. It is neither for the Board nor for the Tribunal to analyse the threat perception of the acquirer. A non-compete agreement would then protect not only the target company but also its continuing shareholders. An acquirer has a right to protect his investment/business from competition by a seller of the business and this right is a long standing customary element in business sale transactions and is even recognised by law. Again, the terms of the non-compete agreement have necessarily to be decided between the acquirer and the outgoing promoter sellers and based as they are, on business consideration, the Board and the Tribunal have no role to play. However, if they agree to fix the non-compete fee in excess of 25 per cent of the offer price as determined , under sub-regulation (4) or (5) of regulation 20, the amount in excess of 25 per cent of the offer price shall be added to the offer price which shall be offered to all the public shareholders. It was common ground between the parties that in the instant case, the amount which the appellant as the acquirer had agreed to pay to the promoters as non-compete fee came to Rs. 9.64 per share which was only 6.96 per cent of the offer price as worked out under regulation 20(4). That was far less than the maximum amount prescribed by regulation 20(8) and was in compliance with the provisions. That payment of non-compete fee was not an attempt on the part of the appellant to reduce the cost of acquisition to discriminate against the public shareholders. [Para 6]

The payment and quantum of the non-compete consideration was based on strong business rationale. It was not in dispute that the target company was in possession of a unique source of water and was engaged inter alia in the business of sourcing, manufacture, bottling and distribution of natural mineral water and was owner of the 'Himalayan' brand, a premium luxury brand of natural mineral water. It was rightly argued on behalf of the appellant that the knowledge and expertise of the promoters in managing and exploiting the said source, was critical to the operations and the worth of the target company. The appellant as the acquirer was a new entrant to the business as a strategic player and, hence, it required support and not competition from the promoters to realize its commercial objectives. As on the date of filing of the appeal, the appellant held 34.29 per cent of the equity share capital of the target company and being in control of the target company, it was important for it to ensure that the promoters who continued to hold a much smaller stake in the target company, did not compete with it in any manner. A sum had been paid as non-compete consideration to the seller promoters for not competing for a period of one year from the termination of the shareholders' agreement executed on 6-1-2007 and it could be presumed that during that period, the acquirer would stabilize in the business. [Para 7]

It is true that the directors of a company discharge a fiduciary duty and cannot allow their own interest to conflict with that of the company but such duties cease to exit, the moment they resign from the directorship of the company. In the instant case, there was nothing to prevent the promoters from resigning from the directorship of the target company and setting up a rival business. It was with a view to safeguard against that possibility that the appellant as the acquirer entered into the non-compete agreement with the promoters with a view to protect the interest of the target company and its continuing shareholders. Equally, there was nothing that prevented the promoters from divesting their minority stake in the target company if that was to become necessary. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1975-76 - Assessee, on taking over a going concern, made payments as work incentive to some of its employees - Whether Tribunal having recorded a clear finding after discussing each case that payments were not made out of any business expediency and expenditure incurred was not laid out wholly and exclusively for assessee's business, it was justified in disallowing assessee's claim - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company after taking over the business of a firm as a going concern filed its return and on scrutiny of the accounts the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had made payments of work incentive to some of its employees. The assessee-company explained that the payments were made by it to its employees out of business expediency and wholly and exclusively for business purposes. The Assessing Officer disallowed the expenditure since the payments made were ex gratia and for non-business purposes. On appeal, the AAC deleted the addition. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the payments to the employees were not made for any business consideration and were ex gratia payments and such payments had rightly been disallowed by the Assessing Officer.

On reference:

HELD: The general principle underlying section 37(1) is that an expenditure which is found to have been wholly and exclusively made or laid out by a businessman for purposes of his business, is to be allowed. There can hardly be any dispute on the proposition that the businessman is the best Judge to determine the business expediency and, therefore, when he claims to have incurred a certain expenditure for business expediency, his version should ordinarily be accepted. This principle, however, does not debar the assessing authorities to enquire and investigate as to whether such expenditure was actually incurred by the businessman and if incurred whether the same was incurred wholly and exclusively for business consideration. The doctrine that the businessman is the best Judge of business expenditure does not affect the right, nay, duty of the assessing authorities to know whether it was incurred for business purposes and not for other extraneous considerations.

In the instant case, the Tribunal had recorded a clear finding that the payments on account of work incentive were not made out of any business expediency and the expenditure incurred was not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee. The Tribunal had discussed the cases of each and every concerned employee in sufficient detail and it was after taking into account all the relevant facts that the Tribunal had recorded its finding on the so-called business expediency of the assessee-company.

Since it was the first year of the assessee-company and there was no scheme for making such payments and no such payments had ever been made by the predecessor-firm to any of the employees in the past, the Tribunal could have come to the conclusion which was arrived at by it. The findings recorded by the Tribunal could not be claimed as based on no material. On the facts of the case the Tribunal was justified in holding that the sum paid to the staff was not on account of work incentive and, accordingly, the Tribunal was further justified in disallowing the amount as having not been expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee-company.

Moreover, no evidence was brought on record to show that the increase in sale was entirely due to special efforts by those employees. The work incentive paid to the employees was found disproportionate to the monthly salary and not commensurate with the pay and benefits allowed. The increased incentive had not been paid to other employees. Thus, totality of the circumstances were taken into consideration and it was found that no nexus had been established between the expenditure incurred and the business of the assessee. Simply because certain amount had factually been expended, it could not be allowed as deduction unless it was established that it was wholly and exclusively for business or had intimate connection thereto or was incurred for carrying on such business.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961 - capital or revenue expenditure-assessee-company hpg and two other companies ngp and wg engaged in the same line of business were running in loss as total installed capacity of product manufactured by them was far in excess of demand-under tripartite agreement among them to save their industry from possible annihilation, ngp agreed to withdraw from business for five years in consideration of rs. 25 lakhs to be paid to it by hpg and wg in prescribed instalments-whether rs. 2,50,000 paid by hpg to ngp as first instalment was capital expenditure-held, on facts, yes

FACT: HPG, the assessee-company and two other companies, viz., WG and NGP, were engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling wired and figured glass products. They entered into a tripartite agreement in which it was noticed that the installed capacity in the country for making such products being far in excess of the demand, all these companies were incurring losses and that in order to save this industry from further heavy losses and possible annihilation, it would be in the common interest of these three companies if one of them, viz., NGP, did not make or sell these products for a period of five years. In the interest of commercial expediency, it was agreed that in return, HPG and WG would pay Rs. 12,50,000 each to NGP in instalments as set out in the agreement. The agreement was to remain in force for five years, unless terminated earlier by consent of all the three parties in writing. In pursuance of this agreement, HPG paid a sum of Rs. 2,50,000 to NGP in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1970-71 and claimed it as a revenue deduction. The ITO, however, treated the amount as capital expenditure. On appeal, the Tribunal eventually accepted the assessee's claim.

On reference:

HELD: If a particular outgoing or the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it might be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process and not for acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which was a condition to the carrying on the business, the expenditure might be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

In the instant case, it could be legitimately said that elimination of competition from NGP by preventing it from producing the products manufactured by the assessee for five years at least, under an agreement which was terminable only with the consent of all the parties in writing, would ensure sufficient advantage to the assessee which would enure beyond the period of five years and put the assessee on its feet in the business and prevent "annihilation" as was anticipated by the assessee. It was a crucial period for the industry involved and if NGP, a competitor of the assessee, could be eliminated, the goodwill that would be generated in these five years could, from a practical and business point of view, be considered to be an enduring advantage that would linger beyond the period of five years. The expenditure was, therefore, capital in nature.

I. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment years 2004-05 to 2009-10 - Assessee purchased one division of 'N' chemicals by way of slump sale - Assessee paid certain amount as non-compete fee which represented difference in value of tangible and intangible assets and lump sum amount paid for taking over business - It was found that on account of payment of non-compete fee, seller was restrained from carrying on similar type of business for three years - Whether since payment of non-compete fee resulted in enduring benefit to assessee, it could not be allowed as revenue expenditure; it was capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee purchased business division of another concern which also included payment to non-compete fee restraining seller from carrying on similar business for three years, said payment was to be regarded as capital expenditure  IT : Payment made for taking legal and professional advice in connection with purchase of business division, was to be treated as capital expenditure  IT : Where assessee made payment to its holding company for using its trade mark and to obtain expertise in field of commerce, finance, manufacturing etc. for smooth running of business, amount so paid was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where assessee paid commission on export sales at same rate at which it had been paid by seller of business earlier, disallowance made by Assessing Officer taking a view that a part of commission payment was excessive, was to be deleted  IT : Foreign exchange fluctuation loss incurred by assessee in respect of outstanding foreign currency term loan was to be allowed as business loss  IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee in connection to transfer of business such as legal notice charges, performance incentive etc., was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where in order to give effect to business transfer agreement, assessee purchased shares of management staff, since impugned amount was non-recoverable and was a loss on account of business transfer, it was required to be deducted from capital gain in respect of slump sale of trading business  IT : Where Assessing Officer made disallowance in respect of dividend income by relying upon Rule 8D of Income-tax Rules, 1962, since said rule was applicable for assessment year 2008-09 while assessment year under consideration was 2007-08, impugned disallowance was to be deleted
