As regards management consultancy service (if provided directly by IIM), the service will be taxable w.e.f. May 1, 2006 since this service is taxable if provided by ‘any person’. IIM can certainly fall within the meaning of ‘any person’ (I believe it is registered as Society).

Hence, possible controversy is only in respect of remaining two activities.

Charges for campus interviews 1. IIM arranges campus interviews for students studying for final examination. IIM collects fees from companies which visit IIM for selecting candidates through campus interviews. It seems this activity is said to be falling under ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’s service.

As per section 65(105)( k), any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a manpower recruitment or supply agency in relation to the recruitment or supply of manpower, temporarily or otherwise, in any manner, is a ‘taxable service’.

As per section 65(68) (amended w.e.f. June 16, 2005), ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’ means any person (earlier, the words were ‘commercial concern’ up to May 1, 2006) engaged in providing any service, directly or indirectly, in any manner for recruitment or supply of manpower, temporarily or otherwise, to a client.

Till May 1, 2006, IIM could not fall within the definition since it is not a ‘commercial concern’. However, since May 1, 2006, the words ‘commercial concern’ have been replaced by ‘any person’. Hence, the earlier defence has gone.

The definition of ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’ is very wide. The service can be provided directly or indirectly in any manner for recruitment of manpower. Service is taxable if provided by ‘any person’. In view of this, in my view, the campus interview activity of IIM will be held as taxable w.e.f. May 1, 2006.

Even if it is not covered under this head, it can get covered under ‘Business Support Service’, since as per section 65(104c), ‘Support services of business or commerce’ means services provided in relation to business or commerce. That service is taxable if provided by any person to any person.

Short-term courses to executives and managers

2. IIM arranges short-term residential courses for executives and managers in companies, PSUs and corporations.

As per section 65(105)( zzc), any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a commercial training or coaching centre in relation to commercial training or coaching, is a ‘taxable service’.

‘Commercial training or coaching’ means any training or coaching provided by a commercial training or coaching centre [Section 65(26)].

‘Commercial training or coaching centre’ means any institute or establishment providing commercial training or coaching for imparting skill or knowledge or lessons on any subject or field other than sports, with or without issuance of a certificate and includes coaching or tutorial classes but does not include pre-school coaching and training centre or any institute or establishment which issues any certificate or diploma or degree or any educational qualification recognised by law for the time being in force [Section 65(27 )].

2.1 IIM short-term courses are ‘education’ - not training or coaching - Education is different from training or coaching. The word ‘education’ is much broader than ‘train’ or ‘coach’. ‘Train’ means train in a particular skill like computer repairs, machine operation etc. ‘Coach’ means special or personal tuition. Giving education in a particular subject is not ‘training’ or ‘coaching’.

Train - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘train’ means to teach (a person, animal, oneself etc.) a specified skill especially by practice. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘train’ means cause or grow in particular way; educate, instruct, exercise.

Coach - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘coach’ means an instructor trainer in sport, a private tutor. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘coach’ means tutor, instructor.

Educate - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘educate’ means give an intellectual, moral and social instruction to (a pupil, especially a child) as a formal and prolonged process. If followed by in or to plus infinitive, it means train or instruct for a particular purpose. ‘Education’ means the act or process of educating or being educated, systematic instruction. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘educate’ means bring up, train mentally and morally; provide schooling for.

Education denotes training of mind, in contradistinction to training in manual skills - Barry v. Hughes [1973] 1 All ER 537 (Ch. D).

Education is the systematic instruction, schooling or training given to the young in preparation for the work of life. It also connotes the whole course of scholastic instruction which a person had received. Education is the process of training and developing the knowledge, skill, mind and character of students by formal schooling - Sole Trustee Loka Shikshana Trust v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 10.

Thus, IIM courses cannot be said to be ‘training’ or ‘coaching’. It is education.

The entire Chapter III and all parts thereof were omitted in 1991, with the result that mergers and acquisition of shares became subject only to the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 1956.

It is determined by the geographical area of activity of the undertakings concerned, worldwide and in member States, and by the quantitative thresholds of turnover10, prescribed by articles 1(2) and (3). As part of the share purchase agreement between Hutchison and Vodafone, it was agreed that the call centre being operated by the taxpayer would not be acquired by Vodafone. Accordingly, the taxpayer undertook a slump sale, transferring the business to a newly established Hutchison Group company named HWP (India).

The Revenue took two alternate pleas in contention that the transaction was controlled and hence subject to transfer pricing:

(a) that the call centre business was purchased by the Hutchison Group through a dummy subsidiary incorporated to create the fiction that the taxpayer was transferring the business to an Indian company, and hence the transaction is effectively between Hutchison Whampoa Ltd., Hong Kong, and its Indian associated enterprise, i.e. the taxpayer; and

(b)

that the transaction qualified as a deemed international transaction as it was entered into pursuant to a prior agreement between Vodafone and Hutchison.

The Tribunal held that on account of the share purchase agreement having been entered into in May 2007, the taxpayer became an AE of both the shareholders during the year. That said, despite there being a prior agreement between Hutchison Telecommunications International Limited, Cayman Islands, and Vodafone International Holdings BV, there was no possibility of a deemed international transaction as HWP (India) was not a third party. Surprisingly though, the Tribunal concluded that the transaction qualified as an international transaction between the taxpayer and Hutchison Group overseas, by disregarding HWP (India) on the premise that it was only an arrangement without any substantial business or commercial interest.

It is worthwhile to note that in the context of deemed international transaction under section 92B(2), the amendment made in the Finance Act, 2014 would still not have had any impact, since the provision still requires a prior agreement to be entered into between the overseas AE and a third party, whether resident or non-resident. In this case, the prior agreement was with an AE.

The conclusion of the Tribunal that a sale between two resident entities could be treated as a transaction between the resident entity and its overseas AE can have significant implications. Transactions such as sale between two resident entities pursuant to a global sale agreement between the overseas AEs of the transacting parties are strictly not covered within the deeming provision even under the amended section 92B(2). However, the Tribunal in this case has treated such domestic transactions as international transactions based on the wide meaning of the term 'transaction', which includes an arrangement between the taxpayer and its AE. While the view of the Tribunal appears to be based on the specific facts of the case, it could encourage the Revenue authorities to rely on this view and seek to treat certain domestic transactions as subject to Transfer Pricing even when they do not fall under the meaning of deemed international transaction or specified domestic transaction.

Having determined it to be an international transaction, the Tribunal had occasion to consider the appropriate valuation method. The taxpayer had adopted a combination of Net Asset Value and Profit Earning Capacity Value methods. The TPO was of the view that the capitalization was based on past earning and not on future cash flow and hence rejected these methods. He called for the projected cash flows, but as these were not provided by the taxpayer in the course of the assessment, proceeded to adopt the Comparable Uncontrolled Transaction method by adopting the Price to Earnings ratio and arrived at 3 comparable companies. The DRP ratified the choice of the CUT method, but eliminated two of the companies and also did not take cognizance of the DCF valuation provided by the taxpayer due to time constraints. The Tribunal consequently ruled that Discounted Cash Flow was the most appropriate valuation method and remanded the valuation to the TPO.

Conclusion

6. The new Competition Act has indeed sought to promote a merger-friendly line of thinking. It would be difficult to deny that the Act has made significant advances towards this line of thinking. However, this intention is not clearly conveyed through the Act. A few anomalies and low-points under the Act have been mentioned in the previous section. The points stated therein and the suggestions that follow are not very large in scope, but their significance lies in their power to clarify the intention of the Legislature. The said suggestions are not against the spirit of the Act, but to enhance the same and make the final outcome more meaningful and perhaps more effective.

CASES WHEREIN IT HAS BEEN HELD THAT TRANSACTIONS FELL WITHIN THE AMBIT OF SECTION 50B OF THE ACT

30.9-1 The ITAT Delhi Bench in the case of Asstt CIT v. Smt. Sangeeta Wij [2012] 24 taxmann.com 128/54 SOT 1 (URO) (Delhi-Trib.) held that where under agreement what was transferred was right to carry on business, application of main section 28(va)(a) of the Act was foreclosed and forbidden and the amount was taxable as capital gain under section 50B of the Act.

It is to be stated that the provisions of section 28(va)(a) deal with taxability under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession of "any sum whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, under an agreement for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business or profession."

The assessee was a specialist in designing of structures, public health and fire protection services and her proprietary concern was taken over as going concern by a company and she received lump sum consideration. The Assessing Officer opined that maximum of lump-sum was for Goodwill in view of meagre net worth of proprietary concern at time of take-over and considered lump-sum receipt as business receipt being compensation paid to the assessee for 'not carrying out any activity in relation to business of company' as contemplated under section 28(va)(a) of the Act and not capital receipt as claimed by the assessee. The Tribunal held as under-

(i)

The amount arrived at by the Assessing Officer as representing value of goodwill, in fact, represented long term capital gains within meaning of section 50B of the Act.

(ii)

As per agreement what was transferred was right to carry on business and hence, application of main section 28(va)(a) of the Act was foreclosed and forbidden by proviso (i) thereof.

The proviso(i) referred to above reads as under-

"Provided that sub-clause (a) shall not apply to—(i) any sum, whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, on account of transfer of the right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing or right to carry on or profession, which is chargeable under the head 'Capital gains'"

This order of the Tribunal was affirmed by the Delhi High Court in CIT v. Sangeeta Wig [2014] 42 taxmann.com 146/221 Taxman 159 (Mag.)(Delhi) wherein it was held that "where the assessee parted with controlling interest in business of her proprietary concern and as consideration, along with money, she received shares in new company and assessee had not carried on the said business or received consideration as a non-compete fee, total consideration received was capital gain."

The High Court at para. 3 of its judgment approved the approach of the Tribunal when it (the Tribunal) after a detailed consideration of the law on the subject referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Motors & General Stores (P.) Ltd. [1967] 66 ITR 692 (SC) to the effect that "the real intention of the parties has to be gathered on the appreciation of a background in its entirety instead of focusing either on the nomenclature or concentrating on certain parts of it."

The High Court also approvingly noted that the Tribunal referred to Board Circular 779 dated 14th September, 1999 and after analysing the circular arrived at the right decision after taking into account the contents of this circular.

30.9-2 The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Equinox Solution (P.) Ltd. [2017] 80 taxmann.com 277/247 Taxman 89/393 ITR 566 (SC) held that "whereas the provisions of section 50(2) of the Act apply to a case where any block of assets is transferred by the assessee but where the entire running business with assets and liabilities is sold by the assessee in one go, such sale cannot be considered as sale of 'short term capital assets' as it was a slump sale of a 'long term capital asset' and be taxed accordingly."

30.9-3 The ITAT Cochin Bench in the case of Asstt. CIT v. continuation of the same business in some altered form. This alteration may assume the form of changing the manner or method of carrying on the same business; it may involve change or rationalization of the administrative set-up or business organization. But when its basic nature changes, it cannot be said that the business is 'reconstructed'. It is not every alteration in the mode, method or scope of the activities of a business and it is not every transfer of assets from one unit to another that will involve reconstruction. The expression is no doubt very wide but it does not take in a case of company setting-up or establishing a totally independent and viable industrial unit for carrying on the same or similar business, even though it might be so set-up by way of expanding the already existing business. The expression 'reconstruction', in the context in which it is used, denotes that the original business or an undertaking continues to exist without its identity being lost or abandoned. In the reconstruction of a business, as in the reconstruction of a company, there is an element of transfer of assets and of some change, however partial or restricted it may be, of ownership of the assets. The transfer, however, need not be of all the assets. It is nonetheless imperative that there should be continuity and preservation of the old undertaking, though in an altered form. The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets-up another industrial unit. The new industrial unit would not lose its separate and independent identity, even though it has been set-up by a company which is already running an industrial unit before the setting-up of the new unit.

2.21-3 Whether takeover of a firm by allotting shares to partners is 'reconstruction' ?

In CIT v. Gaekwar Foam Rubber Co. Ltd. [1959] 35 ITR 662 (Bom), under an agreement, assessee-company took over all assets, goodwill and business premises of a partnership for consideration satisfied by allotment of shares to partners of firm and there was no transfer of credits and outstandings nor debts and liabilities of partnership were to be taken over by assessee-company. It was held that the said agree-ment, both in substance and in form, was one of sale and transaction was not of reconstruction of an existing business.

The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be—and this is brought out by the section itself—of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking. The undertaking must continue to carry on the same business though in some altered or varied form. If the alterations and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. Thus for instance if the ownership of a business or an undertaking changes hands not ostensibly but in reality and effectively, that would not be reconstruction or if the very nature of the business is changed, that again would not be reconstruction. On the other hand, reorganization of the business on sounder lines or alterations in the mode or method or scope of the activities of the business or in its personnel or infusion of new blood in the management or control of the business which may even be by some changes in the constitution of persons interested in the undertaking would certainly be no more than reconstruction of the business if it is substantially the same business carried on by substantially the same persons.

In these matters, one has to look at the substance of the transaction and not the form. If looking at the substance of the transaction, it is a sale, then the concept of reconstruction must be ruled out for in such a case there is no scope for speaking about any reconstruction of an existing business. It would be a misnomer to speak of a buyer of an undertaking reconstructing the vendor's business.

Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, which provides that where there are general words following particular and specific words, the meaning of the latter words shall be confined to things of the same kind, as specified for interpreting the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature' specified in section 32(1)(ii), it is seen that such rights need not answer the description of 'know-how, patents, trademarks, licenses or franchises' but must be of similar nature as the specified assets.

CIT v. Ingersoll Rand International Ind. Ltd. [2014] 48 taxmann.com 349/227 Taxman 176 (Mag.)(Kar.)

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

According to the other view, the exemption is available once the conditions are satisfied at the time of succession and subsequent non-fulfilment do not result in withdrawal of the exemption. It may be noted that if the first view is adopted, it would result in double taxation for the same default: the firm is taxable under section 47(xiii) and the company is taxable under section 47A(3) (see para 3.3). Since such double taxation is not permissible unless expressly provided, it appears that the second view is the correct view.

3.1-1u Consideration has to be in the form of allotment of shares - In CIT v. R.R. Ramakrishna Pillai [1967] 66 ITR 725 (SC) it was observed as follows :

“A transaction by which a person carrying on business transfers the assets of that business to another assessable entity may take different forms and may have a different legal effect. The assets of a business may be sold at a fixed price to a company promoted by a person who carried on the business : if the price paid for or attributable to an asset exceeds the written down value of the asset, proviso 2 to section 10(2)(vii) would ex facie be attracted. Where the person carrying on the business transfers the asset to a company in consideration of allotment of shares, it would be a case of exchange and not of sale, and the true nature of the transaction will not be altered, because for the purpose of stamp duty or other reasons the value of assets transferred is shown as equivalent to the face value of the shares allotted. A person carrying on business may agree with a company floated by him that the assets belonging to him shall be transferred to the company for a certain money consideration and that in satisfaction of the liability to pay that money consideration, shares of a certain face value shall be allotted to the transferor. In that case there are in truth two transactions - one a transaction of sale and the other a contract under which shares are accepted in satisfaction of the liability to pay the price”.

Thus, the Supreme Court has clearly distinguished between transfer the consideration of which is money and the transfer where the consideration is allotment of shares. To illustrate, suppose the agreement mentions that the consideration is Rs. 1 crore and it is to be discharged in the form of allotment of shares. In this case, the consideration is in ‘money form’ and is equivalent to Rs. 1 crore. On the other hand, if the agreement mentions that the consideration is allotment of shares of Rs. 1 crore, then the consideration is in the form of allotment of shares. Having regard to the above and in view of the specific condition requiring consideration by way of allotment of shares, it would be prudent to have consideration in the form of allotment of shares rather than consideration in money form to be discharged by allotment of shares.

3.1-1v Intrinsic worth of shares could be considered as consideration - Where the consideration is allotment of shares, the full value of consideration accruing or arising to the transferor would be the intrinsic value of shares and not the book value of net assets. To illustrate,

◆ book value of assets less liability : Rs. 50 lakhs

◆ value of the business after considering market value of assets, profit earning capacity, etc. : Rs. 1 crore

◆ face value of shares allotted : Rs. 50 lakhs

In the aforesaid case, it could be said that Rs. 1 crore is the consideration accruing or arising to the firm. This is relevant for the purposes of computation of capital gains upon withdrawal of exemption in the event of violation of any of the conditions and for computation of benefit availed of by the firm as required for the purpose of taxation of the company under section 47A(3) (see para 4.3).

6.1 Section 47(xi) has been inserted with effect from assessment year 1998-99 to provide that capital gains arising to brokers on transfer of their stock exchange membership shall be exempt if the following conditions are fulfilled :

◆ the transfer is effected on or before 31-12-1997

◆ the membership so transferred is of a stock exchange recognised under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956

4.5-4a Appointed date or effective date - Amalgamation/Demerger - The section applies to any enterprise or undertaking which is transferred in a scheme of amalgamation or demerger on or after 1-4-2007. Suppose the appointed date for a particular amalgamation is before 1-4-2007 but the order of the High Court is received after 1-4-2007. A question that arises is whether the amended provision would apply. According to one view, the transfer takes place pursuant to the High Court order received after 1-4-2007 and hence the undertaking should be considered as transferred on or after 1-4-2007 within the meaning of section 80-IA(12A).

According to other view, the undertaking is legally transferred with retrospective effect and hence it should be regarded as having been transferred on that date. In Marshall Sons & Co. (India) Ltd. v. ITO[1997] 223 ITR 809/[1996] 89 Taxman 619 (SC), the Court observed that “the date of amalgamation/date of transfer is the date specified in the scheme as ‘the transfer date’”. Under the scheme of amalgamation or demerger, the Board of Directors of the transferee-company are considered to be carrying on the business in trust for the transferee-company. If the transferee-company is considered to be the beneficial owner on whose behalf the business is being carried on, the undertaking should be considered as having been transferred on that date for the purpose of section 80-IA(12A).

It is possible that a particular amalgamation or demerger may not have received approval of the High Court before 31st March while another may have received a similar approval before 1st April. In such a situation, the two assessees would face different consequences if the transfer is reckoned with reference to effective date and not appointed date. The date of transfer should be construed in the light of economic risks and rewards and not nominal transfer. If the transfer takes place by virtue of the retrospective nature of the Court order, it is that date which should be reckoned as date of transfer for the purpose of section 80-IA(12A).

4.5-4a Appointed date or effective date - Amalgamation/Demerger - The section applies to any enterprise or undertaking which is transferred in a scheme of amalgamation or demerger on or after 1-4-2007. Suppose the appointed date for a particular amalgamation is before 1-4-2007 but the order of the High Court is received after 1-4-2007. A question that arises is whether the amended provision would apply. According to one view, the transfer takes place pursuant to the High Court order received after 1-4-2007 and hence the undertaking should be considered as transferred on or after 1-4-2007 within the meaning of section 80-IA(12A).

According to other view, the undertaking is legally transferred with retrospective effect and hence it should be regarded as having been transferred on that date. In Marshall Sons & Co. (India) Ltd. v. ITO[1997] 223 ITR 809/[1996] 89 Taxman 619 (SC), the Court observed that “the date of amalgamation/date of transfer is the date specified in the scheme as ‘the transfer date’”. Under the scheme of amalgamation or demerger, the Board of Directors of the transferee-company are considered to be carrying on the business in trust for the transferee-company. If the transferee-company is considered to be the beneficial owner on whose behalf the business is being carried on, the undertaking should be considered as having been transferred on that date for the purpose of section 80-IA(12A).

In such a situation, the two assessees would face different consequences if the transfer is reckoned with reference to effective date and not appointed date. Section is amendatory and not clarificatory - Compensation received under non-competition agreement became taxable as a capital receipt and not as a revenue receipt by specific legislative mandate vide section 28(va) and that too w.e.f. 1-4-2003. Regulation of Combinations [Section 5]

32.6 Section 5 lays down what amounts to a combination, and section 6 sets out the scheme of regulation of such combinations. The acquisition of one or more enterprises by one or more persons or merger or amalgamation of enterprises shall be a combination of such enterprises and persons or enterprises, in terms of control, shares, voting rights or asset values/turnover value acquired or control acquired of an enterprise while controlling another directly or indirectly, in excess of specified monetary limits. So far as registered companies are concerned, a combination includes acquisitions and take-overs under SEBI procedure discussed in Ch. 22, and arrangements and reconstructions or mergers and amalgamations or the reliefs provided in the prevention of oppression and mismanagement under the NCLT procedure discussed in Chs. 25 and 29. As all these changes in ownership and control bring into being new combinations which ought to be subject to the apex Regulation of Combinations provided under the CA, particularly the reference to the CCI by any statutory authority an issue whether suo motu or at the instance of a party to a proceeding before it—on which the CCI should render its opinion in 60 days which shall be considered by the statutory authority making the reference in giving its finding provided for in section 21(1) implying the supremacy of CA over all other laws and procedures.

Here, ‘control’ includes controlling the affairs or management by (i) one or more enterprises, either jointly or singly, over another enterprise or group, (ii) one or more groups, either jointly or singly, over another group or enterprise; and ‘group’ means two or more enterprises which, directly or indirectly, are in a position to (a) exercise twenty-six per cent or more of the voting rights in the other enterprise, or (b ) appoint more than fifty per cent of the members of the Board of directors in the other enterprise, or (c ) control the management or affairs of the other enterprise, or (d) control the management or affairs of the other enterprise. The value of the assets shall be determined by taking the book values of the assets as shown in the audited books of account of the enterprise, in the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the date of proposed merger falls, as reduced by any depreciation, and the value of assets shall include the brand value, value of goodwill, or value of copyright, patent, permitted use, collective mark, registered proprietor, register trade mark, registered user, homonymous geographical indication, geographical indications, design or layout-design or similar other commercial rights, if any.

ACIT [2022]137 taxmann.com 12(Delhi-Trib.), the Tribunal held that 76% Gandhis-held section 25 company Young Indian was an adventure in the nature of trade under a cloak of charity, with real purpose to gain control of properties valued at approx Rs. 357 crores of publication company AJL which had ceased publication by paying a pittance of Rs. 50 lakhs for 99% of shares in AJL in connivance with directors of AJL who were close to Gandhis family and held high positions in AICC also. The acquisition of shares in AJL by YI was merely a step in the entire adventure which was in the nature of trade and commerce. The benefit has arisen to YI the moment the whole transaction had taken place right from purchase of an asset in the form of loan of Rs. 90.21 crores due by AJL to AICC from AICC for a sum of Rs. 50,00,000/- and in lieu of that, almost the entire shares of AJL have been acquired which was nothing but to get entire interest of the immovable assets of AJL. In the circumstances. The Tribunal analysed the entire sequence of events in detail as under:

Here is a company which has been formed and was found to have carried out only one activity, i.e., takeover of a company having huge immovable properties which are otherwise were commercially exploited by the said company for its own business and profession.

A company which is formed in October 2010 and was closely associated with AJL and AICC through their managing personnel and its stake holders and within days of its formation one of the entity, i.e., AICC offered to sell/assign its receivables worth Rs. 90.21 crores from AJL in favour of the appellant who at that point of time did not even not had money to undertake a transaction.

AICC has offered its huge assets (loan of Rs. 90.21 crores) for a mere sum of Rs. 50,00,000/-) and the appellant company did not have any resources to pay the same when the loan was assigned. It was only after assignment of the loan of Rs. 1 crores which was raised from Kolkata based company; out of that, amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- has been paid for acquiring assets worth Rs. 90 crores.

Before that, AJL had already closed its publication business and was having income only from commercial exploitation of property and was not able to pay the loan, which if had taken from any commercial bank or financial institution would have been obliged to liquidate its debt first.

A newly formed Company (YI) buys the loan even before any loan was received.

In fact, appellant had not even opened its bank account when the loan was assigned for Rs.50,00,000/-. Such a transaction, we already observed above, is beyond any prudence in any comparable third-party scenario, where any person would do that.

The AICC immediately extinguished its receivables worth Rs. 90.21 and instead of getting amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- from AJL had assigned the receivables in favour of a new Company and the entire stake in AJL of more than 99% has been taken over by that company in one stroke.

All these transactions have been frowned upon and held to be a colourable device by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court, wherein it has been held that the real intention was to get the possession of the assets of AJL and enjoy these properties which are situated in major cities of the country.

This clearly shows that the intention of the appellant was to enjoy the benefits by commercial exploitation of these properties and to acquire the benefit of these properties which is nothing but adventure in the nature of trade which can be carried out at some future point of time. It is also very clear from the fact that this was the only activity done swiftly within a period of months, which appellant had carried out in all these years starting from 2010 till date.

The word 'benefit' is occurring in section 28(iv) means some kind of adventure or gain or had same value or acquire any interest in any land, chattel, etc. Thus, the benefit is nothing but any form of adventure and here the adventure is clearly getting the underlying huge properties situated all over the country by stroke of one transaction and to enjoy the benefits of all those properties in future.

C. Merger of Foreign Companies with Indian Companies

Now-a-days, a lot of Indian companies are taking over foreign companies having presence in USA, UK and other countries. How is it possible? Is it through a merger process or take over process? The common answer to this question is that both the methods are usually employed by Indian enterprises and we have a whole lot of examples starting from EID Parry in 1976 to Tata’s takeover of Corus in 2007. If the Indian enterprise is willing to go for merger route, then merger of foreign company is possible under the Indian Companies Act, 2013. On the other hand takeover is possible through well laid out procedure available under Foreign Exchange Management Act, (FEMA) inclusive of FIPB route. Although, FIPB has been abolished in February, 2017 to further liberalize the FDI policy.

Under the Indian Companies Act, 2013, there are precedents in the form of judgments of various courts in India sanctioning the merger of companies in UK, USA, Singapore etc. with Indian companies. The only requisite condition for affecting this type of merger is that the transferee company should always be an Indian company.

Takeover Strategies and Practices Meaning and Concept

In the previous Chapter, we have discussed the provisions of law relating to M&As. Although the said legal provisions include corporate takeovers, yet there are several other aspects with respect to takeovers which need to be examined separately. Thus, this chapter aims at exclusively dealing with laws, practices and procedures relating to takeovers and its illustrations through case studies.

Takeover implies acquisition of control of a company. This concept emerged in late nineteenth century in some countries like USA, UK etc, when the M&As started. However, it started in India in the twentieth century. According to M.A. Weinberg(i), “takeover is a transaction or series of transactions whereby a person or individual or group of individuals or company acquirers control over the assets of a company, either directly by becoming the owner of those assets or indirectly by obtaining control of the management of the company. In case of companies whose shares are closely held (by a small number of persons), a takeover will generally be affected by arrangement with the holders of the majority of the shares capital of the company which is being acquired. Where the shares are held by the public, the takeover may be affected (1) by agreement between the acquirer and the controllers of the acquired company; (2) by purchase of shares on the stock exchange; or (3) by means of a take-over bid.

Takeover implies acquisition of control of a company, which is already registered, through the purchase or exchange of shares. Takeover takes place usually by acquisition or purchase from the shareholders of a company, their shares at a specified price to the extent of at least controlling interest in order to gain control of that company. Takeover of management and control of a business enterprise could take place in different modes. The management of a company may be acquired by acquiring the majority stake in the share capital of a company. The acquisition could take place through different methods. A person may acquire the voting shares of a listed company through what is known as the takeover by complying with the regulations meant for such purposes. A company may acquire shares of an unlisted company through what is called the acquisition under sections 235 and 236 of the Companies Act, 2013. Where the shares of the company are closely held by a small number of persons, a takeover may be effected by agreement with the holders of those shares. However, where the shares of a company are widely held by the general public, it involves the process as set out in the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeover) Regulations, 2011.(ii) & (iii)

To 'reorganize' is to organize again and anew.

| This section is not frequently used in practice and hence one often forgets its unique provisions. A recent decision of the Delhi High Court helps one not only understand the rationale of this provision but also is educative on when it can be used and when the court will not permit its use [in the case of AIG (Mauritius) LLC v. Tata Televentures (Holdings) Ltd. (2003) 43 SCL 22 (Del.)]. The facts of the Case: A company C engaged in the cellular telephony business had two groups of shareholders - the T group holding about 92 per cent and the A group holding the rest. The T group formed a new company in which it held 99.99 per cent (company “O”). Thereafter, company O made an offer to buy out the shares of the company C. It relied on the provisions of section 235. Thus, it was stated in the offer that if offers were received for shares constituting 90 per cent or more of the capital of C, then the remaining shares would be acquired at the same price. There was another related issue of giving proper notice as required by section 235 which was also given due importance but there was an important substantive question. Can the provisions of section 235 apply in such a case? Essentially, the scheme can be summarised as follows. There can be an offer to takeover a company which offer would be addressed to its shareholders. It may so happen that 90 per cent or more of the shareholders have agreed to the offer but the rest of the shareholders do not agree to it. In such a case, of course, the offeror can acquire the 90 per cent plus shares offered and live with the remaining shareholders. However, what if he does not wish the remaining shareholders to continue? On the other hand, what if the offeror has offered to acquire only from a group holding 90 per cent or more shares and not offered to the remaining shareholders and in such a situation these 10 per cent or less shareholders want the offer to buy their shares also? It is provided under section 235 that if the offeror wishes, he can compulsorily acquire the shares of the remaining shareholders on the same terms. In the other situation, the remaining shareholders can also require the offeror to acquire their shares. Now, in the first situation, the provision would appear to be drastic and involving expropriation. Also, it may be capable of misuse in the sense that it could be used to eliminate certain minority shareholders by acquiring their shares at a nominal value. Acquisitions under section 235 did sound as acts of expropriation but there was a certain logic to it. If 90 per cent of the shareholders were in favour of a scheme, it would not be fair if the remaining small group held back its approval thus blocking it. The motives may be mala fide. As the Court observed, “In my opinion, it is not legally odious to expect to fall in line with the dictates of the overwhelming majority comprising ninety per cent of the group. Usually, there is wisdom in the strength of numbers. There is every possibility that where nine persons are willing to accept a particular offer, the remaining single person may be standing apart from the others for motives which are not mercantile or commercial”. However, it was very important that for such an act to be allowed, it was a fair and bona fide one. The Court very importantly held that the same group that was in the majority could not use to remove the small majority under this provision. It was very essential that an independent person or group should be the offeror which was not so in the present case. In fact, the court held that “it was this very reason the section is deemed to be constitutional and if this was deviated from, it would amount to violation of fundamental rights and thus be struck down”. The Court rejected the proposal. |

3.1 Section 47(xiii) has been introduced (with effect from 1-4-1999) to provide that transfer of any capital assets/intangible assets to a company where the firm is succeeded by the company in the business carried on by it shall not be regarded as transfer to attract levy of capital gains subject to certain conditions. The conditions are :

◆ all the assets and liabilities of the firm relating to the business immediately before the succession become the assets and liabilities of the company ;

◆ all the partners of the firm immediately before the succession become the shareholders of the company in the same proportion in which their capital accounts stood in the books of the firm on the date of succession ;

◆ the partners of the firm do not receive any consideration or benefit, directly or indirectly, in any form or manner, other than by way of allotment of shares in the company ; and

◆ the aggregate of the shareholding in the company of the partners of the firm is not less than 50% of the total voting power in the company and their shareholding continues to be as such for a period of five years from the date of the succession.

3.1-1 Analysis of new clause - Note the following :

3.1-1a Short-term capital gains are also exempt - The section provides complete exemption from all capital gains, whether long-term or short-term and including those chargeable under section 50.

◆ There should be a change of ownership.

◆ The integrity of the business should remain - the whole business should devolve upon the successor.

◆ The identity and continuity of the business should be substantially preserved - the same business should be carried on by the person succeeding.

The word 'reconstruction' postulates something which is already constructed in a particular manner because where there is no construction, there cannot be any question of 'reconstruction'.

Therefore, while considering the question whether a particular business is or is not 'reconstruction', it is first necessary to enquire what was the nature of the business which was already in existence, the same as the nature of business which acquired a new shape (sic). If the answer is in the negative, there is no scope for holding that there is any 'reconstruction' of the existing business, because 'reconstruction' implies the continuation of the same business in some altered form. This alteration may assume the form of changing the manner or method of carrying on the same business; it may involve change or rationalization of the administrative set-up or business organization. But when its basic nature changes, it cannot be said that the business is 'reconstructed'. It is not every alteration in the mode, method or scope of the activities of a business and it is not every transfer of assets from one unit to another that will involve reconstruction.

The expression is no doubt very wide but it does not take in a case of company setting-up or establishing a totally independent and viable industrial unit for carrying on the same or similar business, even though it might be so set-up by way of expanding the already existing business. The expression 'reconstruction', in the context in which it is used, denotes that the original business or an undertaking continues to exist without its identity being lost or abandoned. In the reconstruction of a business, as in the reconstruction of a company, there is an element of transfer of assets and of some change, however partial or restricted it may be, of ownership of the assets. The transfer, however, need not be of all the assets. It is nonetheless imperative that there should be continuity and preservation of the old undertaking, though in an altered form. The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets-up another industrial unit. The new industrial unit would not lose its separate and independent identity, even though it has been set-up by a company which is already running an industrial unit before the setting-up of the new unit.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company offering training courses in field of financial services took over business of ‘W’, who was also carrying on similar activities, for a consideration which was claimed by assessee-company as revenue expenditure - Revenue, however, treated it as of capital nature - Whether essence of agreement being taking over of business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, said expenditure fell in category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with the prime purpose of specializing in offering of training courses in the field of financial services and other academic activities relating to financial services, such as offering of distance education courses, organizing conferences in and outside India, developing training facilities and classrooms, etc. ‘W’ was also in the business of carrying on similar activities as that of the assessee- company. The assessee-company took over the business of ‘W’ after payment of consideration amount for such acquisition, and claimed the said payment as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company took over the training courses and educational activities, for a consideration, of a company belonging to the same group and that ‘W’ stopped the activities following the takeover of their business by the assessee-company. It was, thus, held that the consider- ation amount paid by the assessee was for initiation of business to set up profit making apparatus in motion. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member took the view that the said payment was in the nature of revenue expenditure because none of the components of the consideration could be said to be in the nature of creation of any asset, which was of the nature of capital assets. However, the Judicial Member was of the opinion that the amount was paid for taking over the business of imparting and conducting training courses in the field of leasing and hire-purchase of related areas, and that by taking over the business the assessee acquired the right to conduct the commercial activities of another company for an indefinite period and that acquisition of such right was of capital nature. As a result of difference of opinion between the two Members, the matter was referred to the Third Member for his opinion.

HELD (PER THIRD MEMBER)

It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.

HEADNOTE: section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-capital or revenue expenditure-assessee, carrying on business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in licensed public cinema theatres, paid rs. 1,50,000 to a rival to induce the latter not to compete with it for nine years-whether payment was allowable as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1)-held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in the licensed public cinema theatres in the four southern States of Madras, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Mysore. B, another company, was also carrying on the business of exhibition of film shorts on behalf of X & Y in the aforesaid States. The assessee-company felt that it would be commercially profitable to it, if it could eliminate B from the business. The assessee-company, therefore, entered into an agreement with B whereby the latter not only agreed to part with its business of exhibition of film shorts but also agreed not to compete with the assessee-company in the business for a period of nine years for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. The assessee paid the said sum as per the terms of the agreement and claimed the same as a business expenditure. The ITO held that payment was made by the assessee-company for obtaining the right to exhibit advertisement and film shorts and not for the purpose of purchasing any stock-in-trade or raw material and, therefore, the expenditure was of a capital nature. The ITO accordingly disallowed the claim. The AAC upheld the ITO's order. The Tribunal held that the expenditure was not incurred to carry on the business of the exhibiting of film shorts but was incurred to acquire an asset or a right of a permanent character for a period of nine years and, therefore, it could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

On reference, the assessee-company contended that since the expenditure was incurred for acquiring the film shorts, it should be taken to have been expended for acquiring stock-in-trade of the assessee's business :

HELD: The agreement entered into by the assessee-company with B does not indicate that the film shorts as stock-in-trade were the subject-matter of the bargain. In substance and effect, the agreement involved a transfer of the B's business to the assessee-company for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. It cannot be said that the said sum was paid for acquiring the stock-in-trade. The assessee-company has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of nine years in a specified area. By this agreement, the assessee-company has in fact derived an advantage by eliminating the competition and acquired a business which actually generated income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generated income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature.

notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11] Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee-company carried on business in providing education and training for various preparatory examinations - During relevant assessment year, it paid certain amount to its two faculty members as non-compete fees for not entering into a business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005 - Assessee claimed said payment as revenue expenditure but revenue authorities held that elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to assessee and, therefore, payment amounted to capital expenditure - Whether having regard to short period of twelve months during which above two persons were prohibited from competing with assessee, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain amount to its two faculty members, namely, 'V' and 'S' as non-compete fees for not entering into business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005. The assessee claimed that the non-compete fee was paid in respect of a very short period of non-competition and, therefore, payment represented revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to the assessee and, therefore, the payment amounted to capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that those payments were to be made in monthly instalments over a period of time; and that the period involved, during which 'V' and 'S' were not to compete with the assessee in any manner was only a short period of 12 months and, therefore, there could be no enduring benefit enuring to the assessee.

On the revenue's appeal:

HELD: It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

results could not be treated as comparables. The co-ordinate bench has also held that such events with have an effect on the profitability of the company in the financial year in which such events take place. As in this case the amalgamation has taken place during the financial year 2006-07 relevant to assessment year 2007-08, therefore following the decision of co-ordinate bench, the TPO is directed to exclude this comparable.

Ashit C. Mehta Financial Services Ltd. The TPO has included this company as it is engaged into ITES and meets all the qualitative filters applied by the TPO. Before DRP assessee raised an objection that it has a high advertisement and marketing expenses and also functionally different. DRP also held that the company performs broadly the same ITES functions. Before Tribunal, assessee submitted that the employee cost to sales ratio of the company is only 22.40 per cent whereas its employee cost is 47.33 per cent.

This is an altogether new argument and same was not at all either before TPO or DRP. Further it is not submitted how the employee cost to sales ratio as impacted the price or the margin of the assessee vis-à-vis comparables. The assessee relied on the decision of C3i Support Services (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt CIT [2014] 151 ITD 348/46 taxmann.com 453 (Hyd.-Trib) and decision of ITAT of Goldman Sech Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 9 (Bang. - Trib.) wherein both the cases it is submitted that the employee cost to sales if less than 25 per cent, the comparable should be rejected.

There cannot be any dispute with respect to the decisions taken by the co-ordinate benches however; such quantitative filter has not been applied by the assessee while preparing its TP Study Report as well as by TPO. Further, while perusing the decision of the co-ordinate bench in C3i Support Services (P.) Ltd., this comparable has been rejected since it belongs to a different vertical. It is not argued that the company is functionally different and belongs to a different vertical. In view of this the argument of the assessee for the exclusion of this comparable is rejected.

Bodhtree Consulting Limited

This comparable is selected by TPO and held that the company belongs to ITES segment. However, assessee objected submitting that the primary business of company is software development services hence, it cannot be compared with the assessee. Against this the TPO has held that it has considered only the data cleansing services and e-paper activities and has only considered the ITES segment.

Before DRP assessee contended that it is earning extraordinary profit, functionally different and has RPT of 38.54 per cent. The DRP rejected the contention of the assessee holding that TPO has taken into consideration only the ITES segment of the comparable. Before Tribunal, it was submitted that the comparable has the unreliable books of account and therefore same should be rejected. It was also submitted that it is functionally different.

It is undisputed that the comparable company is also engaged in software development services. However the TPO has obtained information under section 133(6) and after that he has excluded the segmental information pertaining to software development services and has only considered the information pertaining to segment of data cleansing solution. The argument of assessee that it has unreliable books and has applied the accounting concept of matching wrongly is a new argument which was neither before TPO and nor before the DRP. However, the assessee has relied on the decision of co-ordinate bench of Ciena India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2015] 59 taxmann 92 (Delhi-Trib) for assessment year 2009-10.

On perusal of said order, it is apparent that co-ordinate benche considered the accounting policy of the comparable with respect to software development services for assessment year 2009-10. However in the present case assessment year involved is 2007-08 and furthermore the segment of the comparable of software development is not at all considered by TPO, he has considered ITES segment of the comparable. Therefore, reliance placed upon the above decision of the co-ordinate bench is misplaced. In view of this the argument of assessee for exclusion of the above comparable is rejected.

Eclerx Services Limited

The assessee submitted that the company is operating in data analytics space and provides operations management, audit and reconciliation service. It was submitted that it falls in the domain of KPO segment. It was further submitted that the company is providing high end services and therefore same should be excluded. For this assessee submitted a corporate presentation of the comparable wherein it is apparent that the company became first KPO in 2008 which is listed on BSE and NSE.

From the above it is apparent that the company is engaged in the KPO business and therefore same is not comparable with the appellant which is carrying on admittedly ITES services. The Delhi High Court in case of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 234 Taxman 573/60 taxmann.com 355 has held that KPO segment cannot be compared with ITES segment. Therefore following the decision of the High Court it is directed to exclude this comparable.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA' - Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into Indian compressor market - In said process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh facilities - In accordance with terms of MoU, both parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through assessee-company agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility - Total amount paid by assessee to Whirlpool India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores paid towards non-compete fee - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee being revenue expenditure by separating said amount from main agreement - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether, when an expenditure is made for initial outlay or for expansion of business or for a substantial replacement of equipment, then it would fall under capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since, in instant case, it was apparent from records that non-compete agreement was part and parcel of whole transaction (i.e., main agreement entered into between assessee and Whirlpool), it could be concluded that non-compete fee was paid as a part of initial outlay, and, therefore, it was to be disallowed being in nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether an expenditure incurred on warding off competition in business from a rival dealer will constitute a capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure, it is not necessary that non-compete fee is paid to create monopoly rights - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA'. Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into the Indian compressor market. In the process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell the compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh. In accordance with the terms of the MoU, both the parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through its 'to be an established local Indian entity' agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility including laminations, wire drawings, centralized tool room, overload protectors and relays. The total amount paid by the assessee to Whirlpool-India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which was the total sum agreed to be paid by the assessee for whole of the transaction as per the MoU. The said amount of Rs. 52.50 crores included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores towards non-compete fee. As per terms of non-compete agreement against the receipt of full consideration specified therein, Whirlpool India was to sign and deliver to the assessee an undertaking not to compete with it in the manufacture, sale or repair of compressors in India, except that Whirlpool would be entitled to sell and install compressors purchased from the assessee to the persons under its service arrangements, subject to the provisions of the supply agreements. It was the amount of Rs. 2.65 crores which was claimed by the assessee to be the non-compete fees or revenue expenditure by separating the said amount from the main agreement. The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's claim.

On second appeal :

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1955-56 to 1958-59 - Whether in deciding question whether expenditure was in nature of capital expenditure or business expenditure laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for purpose of assessee’s business, one must not confine one selves only to agreement between parties and said question must be decided in light of facts and circumstances of each case - Held, yes - Whether where assessee-company took over business carried on by a firm and made payment of pension amount to employees of firm in consideration of their past services rendered by them to firm and to abstain them from being engaged or employed in business of kind carried on by assessee-company, it could be said that payment made was for purposes of business and has in nature of business expenditure and would not partake of nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: By an agreement the assessee-company took over the entire business carried on by a firm. There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. He held that by buying off potential competitors the company improved the value of its goodwill and thus brought into existence an advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and, therefore, quite apart from the fact that the payment might have been made out of non-business considerations, the payment was also of the nature of capital expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the view taken by the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: Whether the expenditure was in the nature of a capital expenditure or a business expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee’s business, one must not confine oneselves only to the agreements between the parties. The question must be determined in the light of all the facts and circumstances of each case and there is no rule that if there is a written agreement between the parties the authorities and the High Court must look only to that written agreement and nothing else.

It is now settled law that the question whether the amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each case.

The agreement also did not provide a clause to the effect that the assessee would not indulge in the same business. That was for the precise reason that the assessee had merely changed from being a partnership firm into one of a private company due to business and commercial expediency. Lifting the Corporate Veil :

Both, the Tribunal and the Assessing Officer, had held that what was done by the assessee-firm was clearly an attempt to evade tax in order to get over the provisions contained under section 55(2). It is a well-settled principle of law that what is permissible is avoidance but not evasion. When an attempt is made by a company to evade tax, it is the bounden duty of the authorities to lift the corporate veil and find out the real intention behind the same. It is the duty of the Court in every case, where ingenuinity is expended to avoid taxing and welfare legislations, to get behind the smoke screen and discover the true state of affairs. The Court is not to be satisfied with form and leave well alone the substance of a transaction. [Para 15.1].

[Para 13.1] The Assessing Officer had placed strong reliance on the terms and conditions of the shareholders’ agreement entered into between the parties. Taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of the case in totality, the payment was not made for the transfer of goodwill but was made to restrict the assessee from carrying on its business and, consequently, the same was on account of compensation for not carrying on the business activities and it was, accordingly, on account of non-competing fees.
