Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by the revenue and dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee.

On appeal to the High Court : HELD: Section 55 provides for the sale of goodwill after dissolution. From the definition of goodwill as held by the Apex Court in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India AIR 1970 SC 564 and as seen from the provisions of section 55, it is very clear that after the dissolution of a firm, it shall be included in the assets. Therefore, inasmuch as a goodwill could be quantified by way of a sum, the assessee wanted to avoid the same by terming it as technical know-how and compensation. When a business is destroyed, the goodwill goes with it. A goodwill is determined by the nature of business, character, name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio economy and the absence of competition. A goodwill can be sold along with the business or independently. ‘Goodwill’ was brought into tax with effect from 1-4-1988. Therefore, in a commercial and trading parlance, goodwill plays a pivotal role and that is the reason why it has been brought into the tax net. [Para 12.2]

‘Technical know-how’ is defined as an intangible revenue producing asset which can be put to use so as to produce revenue in two ways. The manufacturer can use it himself to make things for sale and make profit in that way, or he can teach it to others, so that they can make their own things, in which case he gets paid for the knowledge and information which he imparts to them. His fees and rewards are then revenue in his hands. Under the Act, transfer of technical know-how is subject to tax only from the assessment year 1998-99 by the amendment through the Finance Act, 1997. [Para 12.3]

In the instant case, there were only two partners in the assessee-firm which consisted of father and son. The assessee had been making good profit over the years as seen from the assessment made for the assessment year 1993-94 onwards. It was a concern running for the past 25 years profitably. It was taken over as a going concern by the limited company. The partners of the assessee-firm were the directors of the limited company. The limited company continued to function in the very same office in which the assessee-firm was functioning earlier. The entire assets had been taken over by the limited company. The agreement between the assessee and the limited company did not make any mention about the payment received for the goodwill. The assessee was not involved in the sale of technical know-how. [Para 13.1]

Therefore, it was clear that inasmuch as the assessee-firm had been taken over as a going concern, it could not have been taken over without the so-called technical know-how. The assessee could not have sold the other tangible assets keeping with it the so-called technical know-how. Hence, the receipts for technical know-how and the compensation for non-competing fees were nothing but a part of composite receipt to diminish the value of the assets of the assessee-firm. The assessee had termed the said amount as receipts for technical know-how in order to escape from the clutches of the provisions of section 55(2) under which a goodwill amount is taxable. [Para 13.2]

There was no material on record to establish the cost of the technical know-how as observed by the Tribunal. There was also no material to quantify the amount shown as paid to the assessee for the transfer of the alleged technical know-how. There was no explanation as to why no amount had been received towards the goodwill considering the undisputed fact of the good performance of the assessee-firm over the years before the transfer. The assessee had clearly attempted to evade tax by claiming the amount received as goodwill as one of technical know-how in order to evade tax. The assessee had tried to sell the old wine in a new bottle by characterizing the receipt as technical know-how. It was not the case of the assessee that it had been selling the technical know-how to any other third party. The agreement also did not provide a clause to the effect that the assessee would not indulge in the same business. That was for the precise reason that the assessee had merely changed from being a partnership firm into one of a private company due to business and commercial expediency. [Para 13.3]

Elimination of competition from the Trust brought benefit of an enduring nature to the assessee-company, in the field of capital and, therefore, increase in lease rent, to the extent it is attributable to this benefit, would be a capital expenditure. [Para 23] The assessee contended that since elimination of competition from the Trust did not happen simultaneous with acquisition of Katha and Cutch business of the Trust, enhancement of lease rent, even to the extent it is attributable to elimination of competition from the Trust, would not constitute capital expenditure. This is not an absolute proposition of law that in order to constitute capital expenditure, the payment/compensation for elimination of competition should be coupled with acquisition of business of the rival and both the things should happen at the same time. In a given case, either the payment to eliminate competition may be post acquisition of business of the rival or elimination of competition may not be accompanied by acquisition of business of the rival. It is very much possible for a rival to agree not to compete in a given area, while continuing with the same business in other areas. In such a case, there would be no takeover of the business of the rival. In any case, as far as instant case is concerned, as would be seen from the lease deeds executed between the assessee and Trust, that the Trust had leased whole of its production unit which was a profit generating unit to the assessee and not only the building, but the plant and machinery was also leased to the assessee along with all benefits, etc. Even the liability towards gratuity of the employees of the trust was taken over. The Trust had also relinquished its right to purchase Khairwood from the Government in favour of the assessee. This is not the case of the assessee that even after lease deed dated 18-1-1992, the Trust continued with the business of manufacture and trading of Katha and Cutch in areas beyond 1000 kilometres from the leased premises. Therefore, the business being carried by 'Mahesh Udyog' was practically taken over by the assessee-company for an indefinite period. The lease deed also shows that the lessee had approached the Trust that it should stop commercial dealings in Katha and Cutch and in lieu thereof it had agreed to compensate the Trust for the loss that would be caused to it by stopping such commercial dealings. Therefore, this was a case of takeover of the business, coupled with elimination of competition from the rival. It is also evident from a perusal of the lease deed dated 18-1-1992 that the previous lease deed executed between the parties was repealed simultaneous with the execution of the new lease deed on 18-1-1992. Therefore, technically speaking in this case, acquisition of assets of the trust and elimination of competition from the Trust took place simultaneously. In fact, the whole transaction between Trust and assessee was a composite transaction, without apportionment of lease rent into various components of the transaction. Therefore, from whatever point of view, one may examine, there is no escape from the conclusion that increase in lease rent, to the extent it was relatable to elimination of competition from the Trust, constitutes capital expenditure. [Para 27]

Applicability of section 40A(2)

The objective behind section 40A is to address evasion of tax under the cloak or guise of permissible deductions by checking payments made or benefits granted made to closely connected persons and entities ostensibly for the goods sold or services rendered by them. Admittedly, Trust is a charitable trust and by itself the Trust does not hold any share of the assessee-company. The Trust is not entitled to any profit out of the business being run by the assessee-company. Hence, the Trust does not have a substantial interest in the business of the assessee-company. [Para 29]

It is not in dispute that at least some of the trustees are also directors and shareholders of the assessee-company. The maximum shareholding in the assessee-company was owned by the trustees and their relatives as defined in section 2(41). However, clause (v ) of section 40A(2)(b) brings only such companies, firms, HUFs or association of persons within its purview, directors/partners/members of which have a substantial interest in the business or profession of the assessee. The interest of the relatives of a director/partner/member of such company/firm/HUF/association of persons cannot be taken into consideration to ascertain whether the director/partner/member have substantial interest in the business of the assessee or not. The Explanation provides that a person shall be deemed to have a substantial interest in a business if in a case where the business is carried on by a company, he, at any time, during the previous year, was the beneficial owner of shares carrying not less than 20 per cent of the voting power. The Tribunal has not given any finding with respect to exact shareholding of the trustees in the assessee-company during the relevant previous years, and there was no material to indicate the exact shareholding of the trustees in the assessee-company during the years to which these appeals pertain. [Para 30]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

FACT: On incorporation the assessee-company became one of the partners of the firm 'NS', with effect from 1-8-1976. That firm was dissolved on 31-12-1976 and as a consequence the assets and liabilities of the erstwhile firm along with the business vested with the assessee-company. The dissolution deed that was drawn up, specified about the royalty that would be payable to the retiring partners for not doing such business for fifteen years arising out of the business of firm. The assessee by virtue of the dissolution deed, which was agreed to by it, provided royalty in its books by crediting to the two retired partners. The amount of royalty which was so shown as payable to the two retired partners for various assessment years, was claimed as revenue expenditure; but that was not accepted by the ITO. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Note - The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1951 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 to 1999-2000 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns, engaged in similar business as going concern, for certain consideration - In addition, assessee undertook to pay certain amount per month to said concerns for a period of 15 years in consideration of non-compete obligation undertaken by them and claimed said payments as revenue expenditure - Whether said payments, having been made for eliminating competition in same line of business for a sufficiently long period of 15 years, were of capital nature and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired the proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns engaged in same business as going concerns for certain consideration. In addition thereto, the assessee under- took to pay Rs. 3.5 lakh and Rs. 2 lakh per month to the two concerns, respectively, for a period of 15 years in consideration of the non-compete obligation undertaken by the said concerns. In the assessment, the assessee claimed that the said payment made to dissuade the said proprietary concerns from continuing independent business, which would be detrimental to it, was to be allowed as the revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that the expenditure was clearly capital in nature, as the same was incurred by the assessee to ward off competition over a long period of time. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s said claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: From various cases, the legal position which clearly emerges is that any ‘non-compete’ fee, which is paid to ward off competition over a sufficiently long period of time, has to be considered as capital expenditure. Depending upon the facts and circumstances, in some cases, it has been held that even though the period of non-competition may be 2 to 5 years, the non-compete fee would still be in the nature of capital. [Para 13]

On a careful consideration of the legal position, as applied to the facts of the assessee’s case, the payments made by the assessee to the two proprietary concerns for a period of 15 years as per the terms and conditions of the agreement, could not be treated as revenue expenditure. The proprietary concerns had been acquired by the assessee as going concerns. The two proprietors, by virtue of the agreement, had transferred the respective business along with rights, assets and liabilities which included trademarks, etc. In addition to the value of the assets, the assessee had undertaken to pay a sum of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per month to one proprietor and a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs per month to another proprietor, which was clearly for eliminating competition in the same line of business, for a sufficiently long period of 15 years. The use of trademark, if any, by the assessee was only an inseparable part of the entire arrangement. By the ‘non-compete’ clause of the agreement, the erstwhile proprietors were automatically excluded from use of such trademarks and they had bound themselves contractually not to carry on similar business activity, in whatever names, for a period of 15 years. As a consideration, the impugned monthly payments were to be paid by the assessee for a period of 15 years. It means that on the expiry of the non-compete period of 15 years, the payments would also cease to be made. There was not much merit in the arguments of the assessee that the payments were partly attributable to the benefit acquired by the assessee by way of user of the tenanted premises at a nominal rent. There was no reference to that fact in the agreement. Further, the landlord or owner of such premises was not a party to the agreement and even if some benefit had accrued to the assessee, it was entirely on account of the Rent Control Act, which might be applicable. The business premises, either owned or rented, had been taken over by the assessee as part of the overall agreement or arrangement for purchase of proprietary business as going concern along with all assets and liabilities. [Para 16]

The argument submitted by the assessee, that one of the proprietors agreed for inclusion of the amount in its total income for taxation purposes, had only some persuasive value. The treatment given in the hands of the recipient did not determine the nature of the payment in the case of the payee.

Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the issue was to be reversed and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to disallow the relevant expenditure treating it to be capital expenditure. [Para 17]

and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to company and disallowed claimed expenditure - Whether since ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ both being well in a position financially, as well as otherwise, to compete with assessee even after a period of five years, it could be said that threat which was perceived at time of agreement still subsisted and was liable to re-occur at expiry of period of five years and benefit derived could not be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Whether carrying on of same business prior to entering into non-compete agreement is not necessary to appreciate as to whether non-compete agreement is to enhance assessee’s profitability or not - Held, yes - Whether since benefit to be derived by assessee in consequence upon incurring expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to enhancement of assessee’s profitability in business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals, it could be said that said expenditure was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes

ised for the purpose of suing and of being sued. It is in this light of the legal notion of a partnership firm that the status of an assessee in just a position to the firm has to be adjudged. The constitution of both the firm and the assessee disclosed that there were identical partners in both. The sharing also was reported to be similar. In such circumstances, the law treated them as only one firm, though, for convenience, they transacted business under two different trading styles. When the assessee voluntarily undertook to pay the demand in question as sales tax, it did it because of its conscious identity of the personnel of the firm and that of the assessee. Such unison and identity in purpose and in commerce was the intention behind the undertaking being taken over by the assessee. No doubt, it took over all the liabilities and assets, which included the sales tax reserve. This again was at a time when the statutory liability for sales tax payable for the year was not quantified. Here again the intention was clear that the assessee undertook the liability for sales tax, whatever might be the amount, in order to continue its trade. What may be normally said of an ordinary trade liability cannot be said of a statutory liability or a fiscal liability. Such a liability is assumed not because of the contract of transfer of assets, but because it is a necessary annexure to the incidence of the business having been taken over and continued.

In the instant case, merely because for purposes of taxation laws the assessee and the firm were two different legal entities, it could not be said that in the light of the facts disclosed, the businesses of the firm and the assessee were in any manner different. The nexus interlacing in their business was so conspicuous that their fictional legal individuality in tax laws became submerged in their commercial unison, as understood in the common law of partnership.

It, therefore, follows that, if the business of the firm and the assessee was thus interlocked, then the assessee's claim for deduction of the statutory liability in such a common trading activity between the assessee and the firm had to be upheld under section 37(1).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

running business is taken over or amalgamated, then certainly the assets are valued on the date of amalgamation and in this process sometimes the consideration to be paid is much more than the net assets and such deficit can either be reduced from Capital Reserve of the transferee company as provided under Accounting Standard-14 but if the scheme of amalgamation provides and there being genuine transaction, then Courts have consistently held that such deficit is to be considered as goodwill and eligible for depreciation. [Para 18]

■ However, in the instant case, the facts are different and peculiar. It is not the case of some independent transaction of amalgamation a company 'A' with company 'B' for taking over the business but it is a case where one holding company is having two subsidiaries companies and two subsidiary companies are merged in the process of amalgamation but the owner remains the same. In the process of amalgamation, the 60.72 equity shares have been issued by the Transferee company, i.e. the assessee company -ATPL to transferor company-MLPL and after reducing the face value of equity shares held by shareholder of MLPL, the excess amount of Rs.5.97 crores is treated as goodwill. It is clearly visible from the merger note that only against the creation of goodwill 60.72 equity shares in lieu of 1 equity share of MLPL has been issued. It is a case where the owner himself is claiming that one of its subsidiary company has purchased the business on of its another subsidiary company and such higher amount is basically goodwill and there being no banking transaction except the issue of fresh equity shares in lieu of the goodwill. It apparently seems to be an arrangement made at the instance of the holding company between its two subsidiary companies. Genuineness of the transaction of amalgamation between two independent/unrelated companies is missing in the instant case. [Para 19]

■

It is noted that similar type of transaction came for adjudication before Coordinate Bench, Hyderabad in the case of Invesco (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2025] 176 taxmann.com 784 (Hyderabad - Trib.) wherealso the wholly owned subsidiary of assessee company namely Invesco Hyderabad was amalgamated with the assessee company Invesco (India) under the scheme of amalgamation and against the investment of Rs.244.09 crore in the shares of subsidiary company Invesco Hyderabad the fair market value of intangible net assets of subsidiary company were at Rs.102.86 crore and the excess cost of investment over the value of net tangible asset has been determined as goodwill. [Para 20]

■

It is noted that prior to amalgamation ATPL earned revenue of Rs.2.23 crore whereas the revenue of MLPL was Rs.1.97 crore which shows that turnover of ATPL is higher than MLPL. It is also observed that 100 per cent of the sales of MLPL were effected majorly to the USA holding company where the sales of ATPL are to various customers in India. Interestingly, no sales have been effected to its related parties including the holding company by the assessee company, i.e. ATPL. Also post amalgamation, no sales have been effected to the holding company which indicates that the existing business of the subsidiary company prior to amalgamation has been discontinued post amalgamation and only the facilities or the assets appearing in the balance sheet prior to amalgamation as on 31-3-2014 has been transferred to the transferee company ATPL. These facts again support the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the observation of the Assessing Officer that this is a mere colourable transaction and in the garb of inflating the value of assets and creation of goodwill, assessee has intended to claim depreciation for the year under consideration and to be claimed in the subsequent years also. It is also an admitted fact that if new assets are added to the present set of assets on a running business then certainly some sales ought to increase but due to such amalgamation neither any new business has been added nor the profitability has increased much more than the situation prior to amalgamation as appearing from the records. Therefore, the creation of alleged goodwill is merely a colourable transaction carried out between the holding company and the subsidiary company which is to create an Intangible asset, inflate the value of equity shares of the transferee company and to further evade tax by claiming depreciation on such fictitious asset created through such arrangement of transaction between related parties. Therefore, it is held that claim of creation of goodwill of Rs.5.97 crores is only an artificial creation and is classic case of lifting the corporate wheel as rightly observed by the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, no intangible asset in the form of goodwill is created at Rs.5.97 crores. Further, since no intangible asset has been created in the process of amalgamation, depreciation claimed at Rs.1.49 crores also deserves to be disallowed. [Para 21]

It is found that the merchant banker has stated primary reasons for entering into a non-compete agreement with the promoter group sellers as:

1.

Promoter Group Sellers have substantial experience and understanding of the paper industry in India. As such, their competency and ability to compete with APPM, the Acquirer and the PAC is, not in doubt.

2.

Information made available to the Board with regard to 13 corporate promoter group entities shows that they are directly or indirectly controlled by the same promoter group and held significant equity share capital in each of the said companies but that by itself does not indicate that these promoter group companies which are into separate business are either involved in day-to-day business of the target company or are capable of competing with the business of the target company providing a threat perception to the business of the appellants. Further, what was held by them is a copyright of a feature film, but, not a product/design or copyright asset, patent. In order to restrict any person from doing similar business for a particular period, there should be a business and product. In the present case, going by the nature of business transferred by the above two firms, it is only a sale of copyrights of feature films and once right is sold to a third party, then, nothing is left with the seller or the transferee. Therefore, continuing the business or carrying the business of similar nature under different name does not arise because, what is left with the transferee company is factually nothing by virtue of transferring of all the 3700 feature films owned by them. Further, assuming for a moment by entering into non-compete agreement, the appellant company restricted the erstwhile firms to carry on the business and acquired copy-rights of feature films in future, but, said business can be done by any third party because, the exclusive right of feature film is not with the two firms alone, but, it is with the different people because, the copyrights of feature film is owned by producer of different films, but, not a single party. Therefore, once the business is transferred as a going concern and nothing is left with the transferee firms to carry on business, entering into non-compete agreement with the above two firms for a period of 5 years give rise to various questions including question of tax avoidance plan by the appellant company going by the nature of transactions and financial position of Ramoji Rao HUF. Therefore, to this extent, we cannot subscribe to the reasons given by the Tribunal to hold that, non-compete agreement between the appellant company and other firms, is not between the related parties and a third party interest is involved and, therefore, it cannot be said that, it is a commercial agreement, cannot be accepted and needs to be further examined by the Assessing Officer. It is further observed that the statute does not prescribe any condition for withdrawal or denial of the exemption granted under section 47(xiv) on account of any alleged discrepancy in the valuation of the assets taken over or the issue price of shares allotted by the successor company. ■ Support is found from the decisions of the Co-ordinate Benches of the Tribunal, wherein it has been consistently held that once the conditions stipulated under section 47(xiv) are duly satisfied, the assessee is entitled to the exemption provided therein, and no addition can be made merely on account of revaluation of assets or valuation of shares. [Para 127]

■

The amount of Rs.93.63 crores does not represent a cash credit as contemplated under section 68, but is merely a book entry arising on account of the succession of the assessee's sole proprietorship business by a company. The impugned entry reflects the accounting treatment of transfer of assets and liabilities pursuant to such succession and does not involve any actual inflow of cash or receipt of money. The scope and applicability of section 68 are confined to cases where any sum is found credited in the books of account of the assessee and such credit represents a real and tangible receipt of money, the nature and source of which remains unexplained. The provisions of section 68 cannot be invoked in respect of notional entries or book adjustments which do not result in the introduction of any fresh funds into the business of the assessee. A mere accounting entry, without any corresponding receipt of cash or equivalent consideration, cannot be brought to tax under section 68. In the present case, it is an undisputed fact that the amount of Rs.93.63 crores has arisen solely on account of the vesting of the proprietorship business in the successor company and represents the difference arising from the revaluation or transfer of assets and liabilities. Such an entry is purely notional in nature and does not partake the character of a cash credit. Therefore, the fundamental pre-condition for invoking the provisions of section 68, namely, the existence of a cash credit, itself remains unfulfilled. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was not justified in invoking the provisions of section 68 to make the addition of Rs.93.63 crores. [Para 130]

■

In view of the foregoing discussion and upon a holistic appreciation of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is opined that the assessee has duly complied with and satisfied all the conditions prescribed under section 47(xiv). Consequently, the transfer of the proprietary concern by the assessee to the company does not constitute a ‘transfer’ within the meaning of section 45 read with section 47(xiv), and therefore, no capital gains tax is chargeable on such transaction. [Para 134]

■

Once the transaction is expressly exempt under the specific provisions governing capital gains, the same falls outside the ambit of taxation under that head. In such circumstances, the provisions of section 68, which operate in a different field, cannot be invoked to tax the very same transaction indirectly. The specific statutory exclusion provided under section 47(xiv) overrides the general provisions, and hence, section 68 has no application in the present facts of the case. [Para 135]

■

In this backdrop, the amount of Rs.93.63 crores credited to the assessee’s capital account, representing the net value of the business transferred, cannot be brought to tax. Accordingly, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and subsequently sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 68 is legally unsustainable, misconceived, and devoid of merit. The impugned addition is therefore liable to be deleted on merits. [Para 136]

■

Accordingly, the Assessing Officer erred in making an addition under section 68 and the same is deleted on merits as well. The ground of appeal raised by the assessee challenging the said addition is, therefore, allowed on merits. [Para 137]

On the contrary, plant and machinery having book value of Rs. 3,71,66,000 has been transferred for consideration of Rs. 89,66,000. The above value are supported by a registered valuer's report and are not mere arbitrary valuations adopted by the assessee.

The Assessing Officer vis-a-vis registered valuer's report has held that both the companies were engaged in the same kind of electronic business and plant and machinery used by them was unique and they were not ordinarily marketable commodities, so as to have any valuation of their market price. He further observed that both the companies knew that there was no market for the old plant and machinery except for the opinion that the assets of one company doing the same business were used by the other. It will be thus seen that the Assessing Officer has not found any specific defect vis-a-vis valuation adopted by the appellant on the basis of registered valuer's report. It could not be said that an asset though having Nil value under Act would be transferred also Nil value to a third party more particularly when the transfer is not of an asset but of a business on a going concern basis.

The transfer of the business is not in dispute. The genuineness of the transfer of the business was not in dispute. The purpose behind the transfer is also not in dispute. All what has been disputed by the Assessing Officer and upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals) is valuation of the assets adopted for the purpose of transfer. In such circumstances, there was force in the claim that it is not a case of valuation having been adopted by a higher price more particularly when the transaction is between the closely held company and public limited company and price is paid to public limited company by the closely held company.

It is also not a case where price as stated in the agreement has not been paid by the assessee. The valuation is supported by registered valuer's report which valuation had not been shown to be either imaginary or irrational by any cogent evidence. On the contrary, having regard to the book value of the assets standing under the Companies Act, the value as adopted could not otherwise be said to be unreasonable. [Para 15]

Once there is a report by the registered valuer it is encumbent upon the authority to dislodge the same by bringing adequate material on record in the form of a departmental valuation report, because in the absence of the same as technical expert's opinion cannot be dislodged by any authority by merely ignoring the same. In the present case that is what has happened. Neither the Assessing Officer nor the Commissioner (Appeals) has even attempted to state that the valuation report and the values put on the assets are incorrect in any manner whatsoever. [Para 16]

The Assessing Officer has also laid emphasis on the fact that short-term capital gain as declared by the transfer of company namely Deltron has been set off against the losses in the books of the said company. Having regard to the peculiar facts and circumstances in the case of the assessee company as highlighted above, such a factor alone cannot be made a basis to invoke Explanation 3 to section 43(1). Explanation 3 to section 43(1) is not an absolute rule. The Assessing Officer is empowered to substitute the value. However, such a valuation cannot be substituted where there is no intent to reduce the tax liability.

In the instant case, the assets as held by Deltron and transferred to the assessee as part of transfer of electronic business on going concern basis cannot be said to be in any manner with an intent to reduce the tax liability. Certainly, the effect of the transaction was that the gain declared by Deltron Ltd. was set off against the losses in its computation yet that fact cannot undetermine the genuineness of the transaction and in any case empower the Assessing Officer to substitute the valuation as determined in the registered valuer's report which has not been found to be incorrect by any other technical valuation. Hence, the conclusion of the authorities below cannot be accepted. [Para 18]

The assessee treated the same as capital expenditure in the books of account and claimed depreciation on said amount. HELD: In the instant case the non-compete fee although identified separately by the valuer but it was inbuilt in the lump sum consideration. The assessee split the lump sum consideration in various tangible and intangible assets on the basis of report of the valuers which was not doubted either by the Assessing Officer or by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In the present case, the only dispute was relating to the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores, the said amount was difference in the value of tangible/intangible assets of the going concern which was purchased by the assessee and the lump sum amount paid for taking over the business, so it was in the nature of the goodwill and since the assessee was having the enduring benefit particularly when there was a covenant on the seller for not to run the similar type of business for three years. Therefore, the said amount cannot be considered as revenue in nature as has been held by the Commissioner (Appeals). Since the amount under consideration was in excess of the value of tangible and intangible asset and was a part of the lump sum consideration for acquiring the business, so it was a goodwill. [Para 30]

Therefore, by considering the totality of the facts, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside on this issue and the view taken by the Assessing Officer that the non-compete fee of Rs. 6.80 crores was nothing but goodwill of the business and a capital expenditure is upheld.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The facts indicated that the parties were unrelated and the assessee purchased the cement units as a slump scale with effect from 1-11-1999. Under the business transfer agreement the assessee not only acquired the fixed assets of the said unit but also the current assets of the same units including the current liabilities for which the total consideration of Rs. 550 crores was paid. It was also a fact that the said TISCO had arrived at the profit on sale of Rs. 125. 26 crores after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers. This was the basis for Assessing Officer's opinion that the cost of fixed assets acquired by the assessee should be the book value of TISCO. Accordingly, he restricted the cost of the assets to the above amount thereby treating the balance amount as goodwill and denied depreciation. It was also a fact that the agreement did not speak of any goodwill payment and the assessee had adjusted the entire consideration paid between fixed assets and net current assets. It was also a fact that in the next assessment year assessee acquired another unit from 'R' and the assessee treated the difference between the fair market value of the assets and the payment made as goodwill and made entries in the books of account accordingly where as in relevant year the value paid was for fixed assets and net current assets and goodwill was not involved. [Para 6]

Section 43(1) is clear that the actual cost to be considered for the purpose of section 32 should be the actual cost paid by the assessee. Since the cost has not been directly or indirectly met by any other person or authority, the cost paid by the assessee for acquisition of the assets of the units is the cost under section 43(1) . However, Explanation (3) makes it clear that where the assets are used at any time by any other person for the purpose of his business or profession and the Assessing Officer is satisfied that the main purpose of the transfer of such assets directly or indirectly to the assessee was reduction of liability of tax for claiming depreciation with reference to enhanced cost, the actual cost of the assets shall be such an amount as the Assessing Officer may determine having regard to all the circumstances of the case. As rightly considered by the Commissioner (Appeals) the parties were unrelated and the transaction was at arm's length basis. The registered valuer also valued the assets as on 1-11-1999, the price of which was considered to be the cost of fixed asset acquired and the balance to the current assets including the current liabilities. In view of this, there was no reason to invoke Explanation (3) as the Assessing Officer nowhere stated that the main purpose of such a valuation was for reduction of liability to tax. It was a direct acquisition by the assessee company from another public limited company in an open bid, being the highest bidder. As per AS 10 para 35 the assessee was supposed to take the value on the fair basis as determined by competent valuers. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1962-63 - During relevant accounting year, assessee company took over business carried on by a firm including its employees - Aforesaid firm had a scheme in force of retiring its employees at age of 57½ years and paying them gratuity at time of retirement - Assessee-company also had a scheme of paying gratuity to its employees on retirement, but there was no fixed age of retirement for employees - As per terms of agreement of taking over business, assessee-company was to retire all its employees who had exceeded age of 57½ years and to pay them gratuity - Assessee-company did so and claimed amount paid as revenue expenditure - ITO taking a view that amount so paid was nothing but part of business consideration held that expenditure in question was capital in nature and not allowable as deduction - AAC as well as Tribunal, however, allowed assessee's claim - On instant reference, it was seen that Tribunal had recorded finding that there was an existing scheme for employees of assessee-company who were paid this amount by way of gratuity - It was also recorded that payment was made under circumstances as would ensure retention of remaining staff and contentment amongst them - Whether in aforesaid findings, order passed by Tribunal allowing assessee's claim was to be upheld - Held, yes

FACT: The business carried on by 'V' firm was taken over by the assessee-company during the relevant assessment year. The assessee took over the plant, machinery and buildings and lands owned by the firm in relation to its cotton and cotton waste business at various places. The staff of 'V' firm also came over to the assessee. The 'V' firm had a scheme in force of retiring its employees at the age of 57½ and paying them gratuity at the time of retirement. The assessee had a scheme of paying gratuity to its employees when their services came to an end, but there was no fixed age of retirement for the employees of the assessee-company. It had thus employees who had exceeded the age of 57½ years. Under the agreement, the assessee was to retire all its employees who had exceeded the age of 57½ years on or before 31-8-1961, and to pay to these employees the gratuity, provident fund, etc. due to them. Thus, by 31-8-1961, the assessee's employees who had already reached the age of 57½ years were given notices and they were paid gratuity amount in the aggregate. In their assessment for the year 1962-63, the assessee claimed deduction of gratuity paid to its employees, but the claim was rejected by the ITO on the ground that the compulsory retirement or retrenchment of the staff was occasioned by or was directly relatable to the acquisition by the assessee of the new business, that it was done as part of the terms for purchase of the new business, and that it was nothing but a part of the purchase consideration. According to the ITO, the expenditure was capital in nature and not allowable as deduction. However, on appeal the AAC allowed the deduction claimed by the assessee. On appeal, by the revenue, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: In the instant case, it had been found by the Tribunal that there was an existing scheme for the employees of the assessee-company who were paid this amount by way of gratuity. It had been found further that the payment was made under the circumstances as would ensure retention of the remaining staff and contentment amongst them. In view of aforesaid findings, the decision of the Tribunal would be required to be upheld.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

Clause 10 of MOU again put a restriction that in the event of promoters of the assessee ceasing to be in employment of IISL, either by termination or by determination of period of their employment, except on reaching superannuation, they shall not, for a period of one year from the date of ceasing to be in employment of IISL, deal in any manner with any of the clients of IISL. [Para 26] According to the revenue, the transfer of intellectual properties, codes, formulae, designs, etc., to IISL was not permanent. It was difficult to accept the said view. It was specifically stated that assets and properties of the assessee shall be transferred to IISL. Reading of clause 4 of the MOU made it clear that the business transactions carried out by the assessee that were transferred to IISL would continue with them and IISL shall be entitled to enforce their rights thereunder without any restriction. It meant restriction of time as well. To come to a different conclusion as canvassed by the revenue, was not acceptable. Clauses 7 and 8 of the MOU restricted the promoters of the assessee-company to do similar or identical business carried out earlier by the assessee and now by IISL permanently and even all improvements in technology, etc., would be the property of IISL. [Para 27]

According to the revenue, by virtue of clause 2 of the MOU, the assessee had not transferred the building, motor car and assets and liabilities relating to income-tax matters. This, according to the revenue, fell short of the slump sale for slump consideration. It was not possible to accept the view canvassed by the revenue. The Bombay High Court in CIT v. Narkeshari Prakashan Ltd. [1992] 196 ITR 438 clearly held that the sale of even branches of an undertaking along with its assets and liabilities amounts to sale as a going concern for a slump price. The assessee's business assets were computers, furniture, etc., because the assessee was in the field of software business. It was difficult to hold that the purchaser could not continue with the business in the absence of building and motor car, which had been kept apart. If the purchaser perhaps was prevented from continuing the business, the stand of the revenue that that was not sale of a going concern for a slump price, would have been correct. The question was whether the business would continue in the same line even without the two assets. Reading of the MOU, relevant clauses of which made it clear that the assessee had transferred all the properties relating to its business. Even according to the revenue, the assessee's business assets were in the nature of intellectual properties, codes, formulae, design, etc. These had been transferred for a consideration. [Para 28]

Further, 'slump sale' means transfer of one or more undertakings as a result of sale for a lump sum consideration without values being assigned to the individual assets and liabilities in such sales. In the instant case of the assessee, though in the purchaser's books of account the individual assets had been priced independently, yet the assessee had not assigned separate values and, consequently, sold the items for an independent price. It was not the revenue's case also that individual assets had the price fixed separately and charged. 'Undertaking' is explained in Explanation 1 to section 2(19AA). According to this Explanation, it includes any part of an undertaking or a unit or division of an undertaking or a business activity as a whole. The revenue's case was that some of the items like motor car and building had been retained by the assessee; as such, this could not be treated as a slump sale. But the fact to be considered was that the assessee was in the field of intellectual property rights. Computers, furniture, etc., which were linked with the business of the assessee had been sold. The items that the assessee kept separately had nothing to do with its business which was sold/handed over to the purchaser, i.e., IISL. Thus, only the business had been sold. The purchaser could very well carry on with the business, which was carried by the assessee before the sale, without purchasing any independent items. In view of the above, the plea of the revenue that the assessee had not sold the undertaking as a whole, could not be accepted. [Para 29]

Thus, the claim of the assessee was to be allowed and that of the revenue was to be rejected.

Thus, sub-clause (a) of clause (ii) to section 28 would be applicable if one holds that the payment of Rs. 6.60 crores was towards the termination of management or modification of terms and conditions relating thereto. [Para 14] The reasoning given by the Tribunal records that it was an undisputed position that assessee was the Chairman cum Managing Director of CDBL since 1960 and had 35 years of experience. The first MOU states that the assessee and his family members had sold 1,66,102 (sic, 1,86,019) equity shares of Rs. 10 each at the rate of 30 per share and in this manner Rs. 50 lakhs was paid by the SWC group and the remainder Rs. 5,83,270 was paid subsequently, but before execution of the MOU.

In terms of the MOU, the assessee 'handed-over' management and control of the CDBL to the SWC Group. The same MOU records that the respondent assessee and his family members would cooperate with the SWC Group in arranging for effective registration of transfer of shares etc. and the assessee had further agreed to resign as the Chairman cum Managing Director, and his son had agreed to resign as Joint Managing Director. Thus, the assessee forfeited and gave up the control, charge and management to the SWC Group. There was complete change of management. [Para 15]

The thrust and impose of the Tribunal on why Rs. 6.60 crores was payment towards non-compete fee is for the following reasons:—

(1)

The first MOU, relating to transfer of management and shares was a complete document or deed. The second MOU was a separate document with independent and distinct contractual obligation and consideration stipulated;

(2)

Market or quoted price of a share of CDBL, was Rs. 3 whereas the payment received by respondent assessee was Rs. 30 per share;

(3)

The assessee was engaged in business of IMFL and beer for more than 35 years and had necessary proficiency and expertise;

(4)

Inspite of transfer of shares, the assessee was also in control and management of M Ltd., which was engaged in similar business;

(5)

Quantum or reasonableness of non-compete fee should be best left to the perception of the two competing businessman as they were the best judges on the question of business expediency;

(6)

The contention that Rs. 6.60 crores was substantial and huge and could not be correlated to the salary or other remuneration which the assessee was receiving from CDBL should be rejected as the revenue authorities had no business to challenge the perception of the parties, unless it could be shown that the assessee and the SWC group were in collusion and wanted to defraud the revenue, but there was no such finding on record. [Para 18]

The last reason, is inaccurate and fallacious for the reason that the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) had clearly recorded that 'non-compete fee' payment was a sham and a façade to avoid payment of legitimate taxes. Thus, the revenue had questioned and challenged reality of the taxable event as declared. Price per share quoted in the exchanges would not necessarily be the true price of a transaction for purchase of majority shares to acquire controlling interest in a company, which is the competitor. [Para 19]

It is well settled that when the document is plain and clear, and when the legitimacy and genuineness of the document is not in question there is no scope to ignore the legal character of the transaction. The right of the assessee to choose a legitimate taxable event must be respected. However, in the present case, there are two MOUs which were executed on the same day and deception and maladroit trickery is alleged. The facts mandated a more comprehensive and thorough examination. The first MOU was for transfer of 57.29 per cent of paid-up equity share capital in CDBL which was considerably large company having about 350 employees and manufacturing IMFL and beer. No doubt, market price of each share was only Rs. 3 per share and the purchase price under the MOU was Rs. 30, but the total consideration received was merely about Rs. 56 lakhs. What was allegedly paid as non-compete fee was ten times more, i.e. Rs. 6.60 crores. The figure per se does not appear to be a realistic payment made on account of non-compete fee, de hors and without reference to sale of shares, loss of management and control of CDBL.

HEADNOTE: Section 43(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Actual cost -  Assessment year 2000-01 - Assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern - TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and assessee was highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores - After acquiring company units as going concern assessee, on basis of valuation report of 'K', determined fair market value of fixed assets as on date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores - Assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores - Assessing Officer obtained information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that said company had shown book value of fixed asset at Rs. 345. 95 crores - Assessing Officer was of view that assessee had paid more amount than book value of difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment - Thereupon, Assessing Officer determined goodwill value at difference between amount adopted by assessee and amount shown in books of TISCO and depreciation on amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order passed by Assessing Officer holding that Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case - On revenue's appeal, it was noted that parties were unrelated and transaction was at arm's length basis - It was also noticed that neither acquisition of their business nor assets comprised therein nor valuation thereof was with purpose of reducing Income-tax liability of assessee by claiming higher depreciation - Further, assessee had arrived at fair market value of assets on basis of valuation report obtained in accordance with accounting standard 10 - Whether, on facts finding of Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer had not made out a case for reducing actual cost was correct and it did not require any interference - Held, yesIncome-tax : In case of acquisition of fixed assets, actual cost of same to be considered for purpose of section 32 should be actual cost paid by assessee.

FACT: The assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern. The TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and the assessee was the highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores. The same was accepted by the TISCO in its Board meeting on 18-12-1998. Thereupon, the cement units were actually taken over and used in its own production activity. After acquiring the company units as going concern as the assessee, on the basis of valuation report of 'K' fixed the fair market value of fixed assets as on the date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores. The balance amount of consideration of Rs. 68. 61 crores was attributed to the net current assets taken over. The assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on the value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores. In the course of assessment the Assessing Officer asked for the WDV of the assets of TISCO. Since the assessee expressed its inability to furnish the details as they purchased the assets on the basis as going concern, the Assessing Officer obtained the information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that the said company had shown the book value of fixed assets at Rs. 345. 95 crores and after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers, offered profits on sale of net assets of cement division at Rs. 125. 25 crores in their books of account. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had paid more amount than the book value and the difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment and accordingly after discussion about the provisions of section 43(1) , report of the registered valuer, determined the goodwill value at the difference between the amount adopted by the assessee and the amount shown in the books of TISCO and depreciation on the amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed thereby making addition of Rs. 16. 39 crores. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) it was contended that the assessee had acquired fixed assets and current assets of the unit in an open bid and on the basis of the report of the registered valuer the value was accordingly capitalized to the extent of Rs. 481. 39 crores and Assessing Officer's action in taking the WDV of TISCO was not correct as Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case as these two companies were independent and not related and further the Assessing Officer had not correctly appreciated the registered valuer's report and the method adopted. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contentions and set aside the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

There exists an authorization of assessee that the debts were to be adjusted by ICL against the non-compete fee payable to assessee. Therefore, the conclusion of the Assessing Officer that assessee was paid Rs. 11 crores by ICL as non-compete fee, is proper. [Para 15] In the light of the evidence available on record one has to come to the conclusion that amount of Rs. 11 crores accrued to the assessee under the NCA and that was enough to attract the provisions of section 45 to tax capital gain on transfer of a capital asset. Thus, there was an adjustment of the monies payable by ICL to assessee under the NCA by treating the debts payable by debtors of RCL to RCL, as discharged. Therefore, the findings of the Assessing Officer in this regard are restored. Thus, the discrepancies pointed out by the Commissioner (appeals) will not stop accrual of income in the hands of the assessee. [Para 16]

Having held that a sum of Rs. 11 crores accrued in the hands of late assessee during the previous year relevant to assessment year 2000-01, it is necessary to examine the chargeability of the same to tax as income under the head 'Capital Gains'. This will depend on the purpose for which the payment of Rs. 11 crores was made by ICL to assessee and what was the right that was transferred by assessee for which the amount in question was paid and the law as it existed at the relevant point of time viz., 27-10-1999. [Para 17]

The ICL took over RCL as well as SVCL and the takeover was hostile takeover since both RCL and SVCL were public limited companies whose shares were widely spread out in the market and nobody had controlling block of shares. Ultimately the promoters of RCL and SVCL including assessee sold their shares in a negotiated deal to ICL. The three persons were promoters of the two companies. Similar payments were made to other two promoters. The Tribunal had an occasion to consider taxability of such receipts. In the case of other promoters, the Tribunal held that the receipts were not taxable on two counts. (1) The payment in question was a payment as consideration for not indulging in competition (which was chargeable to capital gains tax only with effect from 1-4-2003 by virtue of amendment to section 55(2)(a ) by the Finance Act, 2002] and was not a payment made for a right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing [which was chargeable to capital gains tax with effect from 1-4-1998 by virtue of amendment to section 55(2)(a) of the Act by the Finance Act, 1997]. (2) The Tribunal held that it was only SVCL and RCL that were manufacturing cement and, therefore, when the amount was received by the assessee who were individuals and promoters of those companies not engaged in any manufacturing of cement, it could not be said that the consideration paid for not indulging in competition was a consideration for giving up right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing. [Para 18]

In the instant case, before analyzing the rival contentions and the terms of the agreement dated 27-10-1999, it would be useful to narrate the relevant provisions of the Act as it existed during the relevant assessment year, the law as it existed prior to the insertion of the statutory provisions and the amendments to the relevant provisions of law after the relevant assessment year. [Para 24]

Capital Gain v. Non-Compete Fee:

Further R being MD of the assessee must have been getting salaries for the services rendered by him in the past and question of any amount being assigned for such past services did not arise. There was no scope for recognising the past services of R and to allocate any amount out of the impugned amount given to R. The assessee-company had not brought anything on record to show that R acquired special expertise or experience in the bus-body building activities. It was not the case of the assessee that R had got any special training in India or abroad in the bus-body building operation or he himself had made any research or was personally involved in such activities. If these were the facts, then this was not a ground for giving the amount to R. The assessee was running in losses and even if some salary was being given to R, a sum of Rs. 1.29 crores shall not be in any manner near to the amounts R would have earned as profit from company or would have got emoluments to that extent. What was the criterion of assessee-company to arrive at this figure of Rs. 1.29 crores was not explained.

It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature.

This amount was not for business expediency but was actually for settlement of the family dispute in between the two groups of ‘S’ brothers and their family members. It had come on record that these four brothers were running the business of assessee-company and three other companies. R was removed from the effective management and control of all the four companies including assessee-company. R filed a suit and got ad interim injunction in his favour and then matter was amicably settled. The fact noted in the compromise application were relevant. No doubt R and his group transferred the shares in favour of G but R group lost more and G group obtained more in the said settlement. A perusal of the assessment order showed that main relief of R was equalisation of shares in the business of family including the four companies referred in the plaint. He claimed 25 per cent of shares but out of compromise he not only lost that claim but he as well as his family members transferred their shareholding to rival group in all other companies. R and his group members discharged their liabilities of sum of Rs. 30 lakhs to the members of G group out of Rs. 1.29 crores and he was discharged of his personal guarantee given to the bank. In the plaint he claimed his reinstatement on the Board of Directors of all the four companies but after compromise he did not remain even an ordinary members of these companies. Another relief sought by R was that he was given all powers to operate bank accounts of all the four companies and to remain in effective control but after compromise he lost all those powers. Contrary to it G group did not make any counter claim in the suit filed by R but they got the shareholdings of R and group members. They got payment of Rs. 30 lakhs from the member of R group and ultimately total and absolute control over the five companies to the total exclusion of R group. About the amount in question, it could be said that the same was not associated with the terms of the compromise but was particularly in respect of terms and conditions given in the compromise application. These facts went to show that this amount was paid in lump sum to R so that G group may get rid off R and his group from effective control of all the five companies including four mentioned in the plaint. Suit filed by R was not in respect of assessee-company alone but three other companies were evolved and compromise had taken into consideration another 5th company of this group. It would not be in the fitness of things to conclude that the amount was relevant to assessee-company alone when compromise application read as a whole went to show the very intention of the parties. Mere mentioning that the amount was being paid to R for his past services and to ward off competition from him for twenty years would alone be not sufficient to conclude the issue but on the facts and circumstances as discussed in the assessment order and sequence of events which had taken place in between the parties, the only irresistible conclusion would be that amount was paid by the assessee to get the family dispute settled and not for special expertise of R as mentioned in the agreement deed.

On the basis of above discussion, it could be concluded that amount in question was not a revenue expenditure but in view of the case law the amount was to be treated as capital expenditure. Apart from it, the amount in question was not given for any business expediency nor wholly and exclusively laid out for business purposes as required under section 37 but was on account of settling the family dispute and, thus, the Assessing Officer was justified in not allowing the claim of the assessee.

The business continued to be the same. Only the ownership was changed. The Apex Court in the case of Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. CIT [1990] 186 ITR 278 has held that in order to attract the provisions of section 41(1), the identity of the assessee in the earlier year in which deduction was granted in relation to a trading liability and in the subsequent year in which benefit is derived, must be the same. If there is change in the identity of the assessee, there would be no tax liability under section 41. If the assessee to whom the trading liability may have been allowed as business expenditure in the earlier year ceases to be in existence or if the assessee has changed on account of the death of the earlier assessee, the benefit received in the subsequent year cannot be treated as income received by the assessee. [Para 10]

The instant case was governed by the old law. Section 41(1) was amended by the Finance Act, 1992, with effect from 1-4-1993. The instant case related to the assessment year 1990-91. Under the provisions of section 41(1), where an assessee who was allowed deduction in respect of any loss, expenditure or trading liability in any year obtained any amount in respect of such loss on expenditure or any benefit in respect of trading liability by way of remission or cessation thereof, the amount obtained by him or the value of benefit accruing to him was deemed to be the profits and gains of business or profession. However, it was held in the case of Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. (supra ), that such an amount or benefit can be charged to tax only if the assessee who receives the amount or benefit is the same person who was allowed the deduction earlier. [Para 11]

With a view to ensure that there is no loss of revenue and undue enrichment, section 41(1) was substituted by the Finance Act, 1922, so as to bring to tax the amount or benefit, as the case may be. [Para 12]

In the instant case, however, there was no undue enrichment to the assessee. The person who sold the business did pay capital gains tax. Besides, the year in question was governed by the law laid down by the Apex Court and the amendment was not applicable to the facts of the instant case.

HEADNOTE: Section 45, read with section 55, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee-firm was manufacturer of transformers - During relevant assessment year, its business was taken over as a going concern by a limited company and its partners became directors of said company - Said company made certain payments to assessee for technical know-how and as compensation by way of non-competing fee - Assessing Officer held that receipt for technical know-how was nothing but a part of composite receipt to cover value of intangible assets and inasmuch as ‘goodwill’ was taxable under section 55(2), an attempt was made to evade payment of tax - He, therefore, treated entire amount as long-term capital gain - On appeal, Tribunal upheld findings of Assessing Officer - Whether inasmuch as assessee-firm had been taken over as a going concern, it could not have been taken over without so-called technical know-how and, hence, receipts for technical know-how were nothing but a part of composite receipt to diminish value of assets of assessee-firm and assessee had termed said amount as receipts for technical know-how in order to escape from clutches of provisions of section 55(2) under which a goodwill amount is taxable - Held, yes - Whether further question of payment of non-competing fee also would not arise, considering fact that assessee-firm had been taken over as a going concern in its entirety by new company and partners of assessee-firm were directors of said company - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in holding that amount representing value of technical know-how
 and amount received as non-competing fee were taxable as long-term capital gains under section 45, read with section 55 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was manufacturer of transformers. During relevant assessment year, its business was taken over as a going concern by a limited company and its partners became directors of the said company. The said company made certain payments to the assessee for technical know-how and as compensation for pending and expected orders, i.e., not to compete and indulge in transformer business. During assessment proceedings, a show-cause notice was issued to the assessee as to why the amounts shown as received for non-competition fee for pending orders, future orders and for the transfer of technical know-how would not be treated as capital gains, inasmuch as no amount had been shown under the head ‘Goodwill’ even though the assessee had been making good profit in the previous years. The assessee contended that it had not received any money towards the goodwill from the company and inasmuch as for the assessment year 1995-96, a transfer of technical know-how was not taxable, it could not be termed as long-term capital gain. The Assessing Officer held that the receipt for technical know-how was nothing but a part of the composite receipt to cover the value of the intangible assets and inasmuch ‘goodwill’ was taxable under section 55(2), an attempt was made to evade the payment of tax. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer treated the entire amount as capital gains. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim in respect of amount received for technical know-how and compensation for pending orders but disallowed the amount of compensation for expected orders. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that there was no indication of the value of the technical know-how in the balance sheet and it had come into existence only at the time of signing the transfer agreement. It held that the agreement was for the transfer of entire business of a going concern and the amount indicated as the payment for technical know-how was nothing but a goodwill amount which was a colourable device to evade tax. The Tribunal further held that in view of the taking over of the going concern, the assessee-firm had come to an end, more so when the partners were also the directors and, therefore, there was no question of paying the non-competing fees, inasmuch as there was no possibility of the assessee-firm doing the very same business again. Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by the revenue and dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee.
