HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1947-48 - Whether where payment was made to a competitor so that assessee may itself secure a contract for making purchases from a certain concern without any competition, payment was an expenditure not in connection with business but was an expenditure in nature of capital expenditure to prepare ground for securing all business - Held, yes

FACT: The family of BP and his two sons CL and MP were carrying on business in the name of a firm referred to as "the family firm". CL started business of his own which would be referred to his ‘Jaipuria firm’. CL, representing "the Jaipuria firm", entered into partnership with BN for purchase and acquisition of armour plates from the Field Liquidation Commission. In the Jaipuria firm the share of CL was eleven annas and of BN five annas in a rupee. BN subscribed Rs. 1,50,000 towards the capital of the partnership but CL did not subscribe any capital himself and the rest of the capital of the partnership was to come from the family firm." The Jaipuria firm made profits on its armour plates business and in that connection, in the assessment year 1947-48, the family firm was assessed to income-tax. The ITO found that the share in the Jaipuria firm was not the personal and individual share of CL but was the share of the family firm. The reasons for coming to this conclusion, inter alia, were (a) that no capital was invested by CL himself in the Jaipuria firm, (b) that on 12-2-1946, the family firm paid Rs. 40,000 to one EV to remove him from competition for the contract for armour plates business, (ii) that on 4-2-1946, Rs. 99,132 were paid as custom duty by the family firm for the Jaipuria firm and (iii) that the total amount of payments made by the family firm to the American Field Commissioner came to about Rs. 3,30,440 as cost of the armour plates purchased in the name of Jaipuria firm, and that all these transactions were entered in full detail in the account books of the family firm, (c) that on dissolution of the Jaipuria firm partnership the five annas share coming to about Rs. 90,000 of BN was paid to the latter by the family firm and not by CL. For these reasons, the ITO came to the conclusion that the eleven annas share in the Jaipuria firm was the share of the family firm and not of CL individually. The profits of the Jaipuria firm of the share of the family firm were taxed in the income of the latter. The family firm did not appeal against that assessment. It was CL alone, in his personal capacity, who filed an appeal to the AAC of Income-tax and in the grounds of appeal his main attack, was that the ITO had erred in his finding that the eleven annas share in the partnership of Jaipuria firm was not his individual share but was that of the family and that the ITO also erred in disallowing a sum of Rs. 40,000 paid to EV as revenue expenditure because he treated it as capital expenditure.

The AAC confirmed the order of ITO on both counts. He found that the payment of Rs. 40,000 to EV was a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure because it was paid to him to oust him as a competitor in obtaining the armour plate business.

On second appeal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the family or the family firm not having appealed against the order of assessment, the AAC was wrong in entertaining appeal by CL, that Rs. 40,000 paid to EV was rightly found to be capital expenditure and not revenue expenditure and that the share in Jaipuria firm was the share of the family firm and not of CL individually. The Tribunal also refused to make a reference to the High Court.

On reference applications under section 66(2) :

the light of the facts of each case. Supposing, the fee is paid to a person who cannot compete, the Board may be entitled to say that it is only a device to reduce the offer price. In such a case, the Board may justifiably direct its addition to the offer price. On the other hand if the payment is made to an outgoing seller who can offer competition to the business of the target company, the Board shall have no occasion to interfere. [Para 5] The recommendations made by the Bhagwati Committee clearly recognize the legitimacy of the non-compete fee payable to the outgoing sellers. Regulation 20(8) based on these recommendations puts a cap on such payments so that an acquirer cannot reduce the cost of acquisition through public offer thereby depriving the public shareholders of their legitimate dues. When examining the validity of the non-compete fee, the question to be addressed is whether the outgoing sellers are capable of providing competition to the business alone or in association with third parties and not whether the business was dependent on the outgoing sellers. When an acquirer takes over a business from the outgoing seller(s), it is obvious that the sellers have specific knowledge of that business and they have access to and are in possession of crucial trade secrets of the target company which if disclosed or misused would be detrimental to and could cause irreparable harm to the target company and its continuing shareholders and by virtue of their association with that business, they (out going sellers) are capable of offering competition to the business being taken over. In such cases, it would be legitimate for the acquirer to enter into a non-compete agreement with the promoter sellers if he feels threatened by a lurking fear of competition from them. It is neither for the Board nor for the Tribunal to analyse the threat perception of the acquirer. A non-compete agreement would then protect not only the target company but also its continuing shareholders. An acquirer has a right to protect his investment/business from competition by a seller of the business and this right is a long standing customary element in business sale transactions and is even recognised by law. Again, the terms of the non-compete agreement have necessarily to be decided between the acquirer and the outgoing promoter sellers and based as they are, on business consideration, the Board and the Tribunal have no role to play. However, if they agree to fix the non-compete fee in excess of 25 per cent of the offer price as determined , under sub-regulation (4) or (5) of regulation 20, the amount in excess of 25 per cent of the offer price shall be added to the offer price which shall be offered to all the public shareholders. It was common ground between the parties that in the instant case, the amount which the appellant as the acquirer had agreed to pay to the promoters as non-compete fee came to Rs. 9.64 per share which was only 6.96 per cent of the offer price as worked out under regulation 20(4). That was far less than the maximum amount prescribed by regulation 20(8) and was in compliance with the provisions. That payment of non-compete fee was not an attempt on the part of the appellant to reduce the cost of acquisition to discriminate against the public shareholders. [Para 6]

The payment and quantum of the non-compete consideration was based on strong business rationale. It was not in dispute that the target company was in possession of a unique source of water and was engaged inter alia in the business of sourcing, manufacture, bottling and distribution of natural mineral water and was owner of the 'Himalayan' brand, a premium luxury brand of natural mineral water. It was rightly argued on behalf of the appellant that the knowledge and expertise of the promoters in managing and exploiting the said source, was critical to the operations and the worth of the target company. The appellant as the acquirer was a new entrant to the business as a strategic player and, hence, it required support and not competition from the promoters to realize its commercial objectives. As on the date of filing of the appeal, the appellant held 34.29 per cent of the equity share capital of the target company and being in control of the target company, it was important for it to ensure that the promoters who continued to hold a much smaller stake in the target company, did not compete with it in any manner. A sum had been paid as non-compete consideration to the seller promoters for not competing for a period of one year from the termination of the shareholders' agreement executed on 6-1-2007 and it could be presumed that during that period, the acquirer would stabilize in the business. [Para 7]

It is true that the directors of a company discharge a fiduciary duty and cannot allow their own interest to conflict with that of the company but such duties cease to exit, the moment they resign from the directorship of the company. In the instant case, there was nothing to prevent the promoters from resigning from the directorship of the target company and setting up a rival business. It was with a view to safeguard against that possibility that the appellant as the acquirer entered into the non-compete agreement with the promoters with a view to protect the interest of the target company and its continuing shareholders. Equally, there was nothing that prevented the promoters from divesting their minority stake in the target company if that was to become necessary. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1975-76 - Assessee, on taking over a going concern, made payments as work incentive to some of its employees - Whether Tribunal having recorded a clear finding after discussing each case that payments were not made out of any business expediency and expenditure incurred was not laid out wholly and exclusively for assessee's business, it was justified in disallowing assessee's claim - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company after taking over the business of a firm as a going concern filed its return and on scrutiny of the accounts the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had made payments of work incentive to some of its employees. The assessee-company explained that the payments were made by it to its employees out of business expediency and wholly and exclusively for business purposes. The Assessing Officer disallowed the expenditure since the payments made were ex gratia and for non-business purposes. On appeal, the AAC deleted the addition. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the payments to the employees were not made for any business consideration and were ex gratia payments and such payments had rightly been disallowed by the Assessing Officer.

On reference:

HELD: The general principle underlying section 37(1) is that an expenditure which is found to have been wholly and exclusively made or laid out by a businessman for purposes of his business, is to be allowed. There can hardly be any dispute on the proposition that the businessman is the best Judge to determine the business expediency and, therefore, when he claims to have incurred a certain expenditure for business expediency, his version should ordinarily be accepted. This principle, however, does not debar the assessing authorities to enquire and investigate as to whether such expenditure was actually incurred by the businessman and if incurred whether the same was incurred wholly and exclusively for business consideration. The doctrine that the businessman is the best Judge of business expenditure does not affect the right, nay, duty of the assessing authorities to know whether it was incurred for business purposes and not for other extraneous considerations.

In the instant case, the Tribunal had recorded a clear finding that the payments on account of work incentive were not made out of any business expediency and the expenditure incurred was not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee. The Tribunal had discussed the cases of each and every concerned employee in sufficient detail and it was after taking into account all the relevant facts that the Tribunal had recorded its finding on the so-called business expediency of the assessee-company.

Since it was the first year of the assessee-company and there was no scheme for making such payments and no such payments had ever been made by the predecessor-firm to any of the employees in the past, the Tribunal could have come to the conclusion which was arrived at by it. The findings recorded by the Tribunal could not be claimed as based on no material. On the facts of the case the Tribunal was justified in holding that the sum paid to the staff was not on account of work incentive and, accordingly, the Tribunal was further justified in disallowing the amount as having not been expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee-company.

Moreover, no evidence was brought on record to show that the increase in sale was entirely due to special efforts by those employees. The work incentive paid to the employees was found disproportionate to the monthly salary and not commensurate with the pay and benefits allowed. The increased incentive had not been paid to other employees. Thus, totality of the circumstances were taken into consideration and it was found that no nexus had been established between the expenditure incurred and the business of the assessee. Simply because certain amount had factually been expended, it could not be allowed as deduction unless it was established that it was wholly and exclusively for business or had intimate connection thereto or was incurred for carrying on such business.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961 - capital or revenue expenditure-assessee-company hpg and two other companies ngp and wg engaged in the same line of business were running in loss as total installed capacity of product manufactured by them was far in excess of demand-under tripartite agreement among them to save their industry from possible annihilation, ngp agreed to withdraw from business for five years in consideration of rs. 25 lakhs to be paid to it by hpg and wg in prescribed instalments-whether rs. 2,50,000 paid by hpg to ngp as first instalment was capital expenditure-held, on facts, yes

FACT: HPG, the assessee-company and two other companies, viz., WG and NGP, were engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling wired and figured glass products. They entered into a tripartite agreement in which it was noticed that the installed capacity in the country for making such products being far in excess of the demand, all these companies were incurring losses and that in order to save this industry from further heavy losses and possible annihilation, it would be in the common interest of these three companies if one of them, viz., NGP, did not make or sell these products for a period of five years. In the interest of commercial expediency, it was agreed that in return, HPG and WG would pay Rs. 12,50,000 each to NGP in instalments as set out in the agreement. The agreement was to remain in force for five years, unless terminated earlier by consent of all the three parties in writing. In pursuance of this agreement, HPG paid a sum of Rs. 2,50,000 to NGP in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1970-71 and claimed it as a revenue deduction. The ITO, however, treated the amount as capital expenditure. On appeal, the Tribunal eventually accepted the assessee's claim.

On reference:

HELD: If a particular outgoing or the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it might be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process and not for acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which was a condition to the carrying on the business, the expenditure might be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

In the instant case, it could be legitimately said that elimination of competition from NGP by preventing it from producing the products manufactured by the assessee for five years at least, under an agreement which was terminable only with the consent of all the parties in writing, would ensure sufficient advantage to the assessee which would enure beyond the period of five years and put the assessee on its feet in the business and prevent "annihilation" as was anticipated by the assessee. It was a crucial period for the industry involved and if NGP, a competitor of the assessee, could be eliminated, the goodwill that would be generated in these five years could, from a practical and business point of view, be considered to be an enduring advantage that would linger beyond the period of five years. The expenditure was, therefore, capital in nature.

Section 37(1) of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee entered into an agreement to take over assets and liabilities of a company SVR and assessee claimed deduction of expenses relating to period prior to commencement of manufacturing/trading business of SVR by assessee on ground that the transferee company had undertaken manufacturing on assessee’s behalf and assessee had reimbursed the expenses of the company, assessee’s claim was not allowable
H & R Aromatics (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. Commissioner [1996] 56 TTJ (Ahd.) 636
The assessee-company had purchased assets and liabilities of SVR as per agreement dated 23-5-1987. The Assessing Officer noted that there was no actual purchase. As the very basis of purchase of assets and liabilities of SVR was not proved the Assessing Officer rejected the claim of expenses of Rs. 3,49,017 claimed to have been incurred by SVR on behalf of the assessee. On appeal it was claimed that assets and liabilities of SVR were taken over by the assessee for a consideration of Rs. 8.50 lakhs as per agreement dated 23-5-1987. As the assessee-company was not in a position to depute its staff it was agreed that from 23-5-1987, SVR would continue to manage the affairs of the business taken over. SVR thus incurred expenses of Rs. 4,71,782 during the period from 23-5-1987 to 31-5-1988, on behalf of the assessee-company. It was also claimed that all the assets of company were not taken over. The net worth of the assets taken over was Rs. 14,06,338 excluding the liability of cash credit account with the bank of Rs. 9,75,222 which was settled separately. It was also claimed that since the assessee-company required time to obtain approval for commencement of production in its own name it was agreed that production will be continued by SVR. The unit was kept in working condition and some raw material was converted into finished products. It was, therefore, claimed that total expenses incurred by SVR at Rs. 3,49,017 were wholly and exclusively for keeping the unit in working condition on behalf of the assessee and same being of revenue nature should have been fully allowed.
Held that in the present case though there was an agreement made on 23-5-1987 to take over the assets and liabilities of SVR including the raw material and finished goods but the said goods were in fact purchased by the assessee and possession taken not during the current year but in the succeeding assessment year 1989-90. Thus, the business of manufacturing or trading did not commence during the current year, but the same was commenced only in the following year when the said goods were purchased and manufacturing activity started and in this view of the matter the expenses claimed for the period prior to the commencement of manufacturing/trading business were not admissible. Thus, the claim for the expenses of Rs. 3,49,017 claimed to have been incurred by SVR on behalf of the assessee-company during the year, was rightly disallowed by the ITO.

Section 28(va), read with section 45, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Non-compete fee (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee-employee conceptualized a technical concept namely, ‘Indus Guard’ to safeguard websites from getting infected with virus - It entered into an agreement with his employer, i.e. Indusface (Indusface India), for investment in further development of concept for its commercial exploitation to develop same into a business idea - Thereafter/agreement was entered into between assessee, employer - Indusface India and Trend Micro USA, for sale of entire business related to product Indus Guard against a certain sum - Assessee submitted that sum received on transfer of asset was a capital receipt not chargeable to tax, since asset was a self-generated asset, having no cost of acquisition/improvement and, therefore, any gains arising on its transfer was not chargeable to tax - Whether since Asset Purchase Agreement between assessee and Trend Micro clearly showed that dominant intention of Trend Micro for making payment to assessee was to prevent him from engaging in any business which could have competed with business purchased, consideration received by assessee could at best be treated as business income under section 28(va) - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee entered into an agreement with his employer-company for investment in technical concept developed by assessee for its commercial exploitation and thereafter entire business related to said concept had been sold to a US company, since dominant intention of purchaser for making payment to assessee was to prevent him from engaging in any business which could have competed with business purchased, amount so received was to be taxed as business income under section 28(va)

I. Section 37(1), read with section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Director, payments to) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether where assessee-company entered into an agreement to take over business of a proprietory concern, in view of fact that in terms of agreement, company did not acquire copyright, but only a license to use copyright was granted to assessee, licence fee paid would be a revenue expenditure - Held, yes - [Paras 21 and 22] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 47(xiv), read with section 47A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Transactions not regarded as transfer (Condition precedent) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether section 47A lays down conditions which if violated would result in withdrawal of exemption provided under section 47 and applicability of section 47A would arise only if it is established that section 47 was pressed into service - Held, yes - Whether where there were no findings of fact recorded that provisions of section 47 were invoked for claiming exemption from capital gains while making transfers from sole proprietary concern to assessee company, deeming provision of sub-section (3) of section 47A could not have been invoked - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 2001-02 and 2002-03 - Whether to test whether benefit derived by assessee by making a payment is of enduring nature, only point to be considered is whether threat which is perceived at time of agreement/incurring of expenditure will cease to exist after expiry of period or will re-occur - Held, yes - Whether where threat has potential of re-occurring after expiry of period, then benefit derived cannot be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate - It acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores - Assessee had also entered into another ‘non-compete agreement’ with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them - Under said agreement ‘V’ and ‘M’ were restricted to engage themselves in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with abovesaid chemicals for period of 5 years - In return assessee claimed whole of expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that expenditure was not incurred for improving profitability as there was no existing business and assessee had acquired business of chemicals for first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to company and disallowed claimed expenditure - Whether since ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ both being well in a position financially, as well as otherwise, to compete with assessee even after a period of five years, it could be said that threat which was perceived at time of agreement still subsisted and was liable to re-occur at expiry of period of five years and benefit derived could not be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Whether carrying on of same business prior to entering into non-compete agreement is not necessary to appreciate as to whether non-compete agreement is to enhance assessee’s profitability or not - Held, yes - Whether since benefit to be derived by assessee in consequence upon incurring expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to enhancement of assessee’s profitability in business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals, it could be said that said expenditure was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes

II. Section 28(va) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Non-compete fees - Assessment year 2003-04 - Excess of cost of acquisition over carrying value of net asset on date of merger which had been brought in financial statement of amalgamated company as goodwill could not be treated as income of amalgamated company under section 28(iv) [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of two-wheelers - It entered into a non-compete agreement with 'V', who was an employee of assessee, and 'VCPL', a company promoted by 'V', whereby assessee paid a sum of Rs. 4 crores to 'VCPL' so that 'VCPL' and 'V' would not carry out any business activity with regard to two-wheelers after retirement of 'V' from assessee-company - Assessee claimed said amount as business expenditure - Assessing Officer disallowed claim on ground that expenditure was of capital nature - Whether since assessee did not acquire any capital asset by making payment of non-compete fee and it merely eliminated competition in two-wheeler business, payment of non-compete fee was a business expenditure and not a capital expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1), read with 40(a)(ii), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessee-company took over assets and liabilities of ‘K’ Ltd. and also paid outstanding tax liability of transferor company - Whether payment of tax liability by assessee on behalf of transferor company did not attract provisions of section 40(a)(ii) and therefore, it was allowable as business expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922) - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1953-54 to 1955-56 - Assessee-company took over routes of various private operators and paid compensation to get rid of competition from said operators - Whether compensation so paid was an expenditure of capital nature and, thus, it could not be allowed as deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

I. Section  37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business expenditure  -  Allowability of  (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year  2001-02  - Assessee, a company, was engaged in business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipment in India - It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and L & T - During year, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L &T as consideration for latter not setting up or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years - Said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in return of income filed by assessee as non-compete fee paid to L &T - Assessing Officer held that such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, hence, treated payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure - Whether non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance profitability of business, thereby facilitating carrying on of business more efficiently and profitably and, thus, such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to profit earning apparatus of payer - Held, yes - Whether, further, on facts, assessee had not acquired any new business and there was no addition to profit making apparatus of assessee, assets remained same and expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of same business and, thus, non-compete fee paid by assessee was an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes [Paras 26, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

Section 28(va) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Non-compete fees - Assessment year 2001-02 - Where assessee, an artist and film director, transferred its proprietary business to a company as a going concern and agreed to provide her expertise in film making to said company, non-compete fee received by her would be assessed as revenue receipt in view of fact that (a) assessee was, and continued to be, face of business as proprietrix and (b) thereafter, as a director with substantial shareholding, she retained a firm hold on reins of decision making [In favour of revenue]   The assessee, an artist and film director with a significant presence in the big as well as small screens entered into an agreement with a company RPPL in terms of which she agreed to provide her expertise in film making, tele-serials and discussions to the company, and not to compete with the business of the company in India or elsewhere. The agreement, in force for a period of 5 years, provided for consideration of an amount of Rs. 75 lakhs by way of allotment of 75,000 equity shares of a nominal value of Rs. 100 each. That apart, the parties had entered into a succession agreement that provided for the succession of the company to the business of the assessee as a going concern, taking over all the assets and liabilities in its books for a consideration. In case of the assessee, the Assessing Officer held that the amount of Rs. 75 lakhs was in the nature of a remuneration paid to her for loss of business occasioned to her by virtue of the terms of non-compete. He also noticed that the assessee retained control over the business even after execution of the succession agreement insofar as she continued in the position of a director in the company holding more than 99.99 per cent voting rights. He, therefore, held that the arrangement of payment of non-compete fee was itself a colourable exercise and made addition of said amount in assessee's hands.  Held that the assessee's sole proprietary concern was succeeded to by the company on 31-3-2000. She was duly compensated for the assets transferred. Parallelly, an agreement was entered into between the parties to provide for a more systematic utilization and exploitation of the creative talents and skills of the artist. The artist, who was managing the business as a proprietary concern, continued to be part of the corporate structure, employing the same skill sets as always employed by her. It was only the business setting that was enlarged over the relevant period. The assessee was, and continued to be, the face of the business as proprietrix and thereafter, as a director with substantial shareholding, she retained a firm hold on the reins of decision making. The transaction of non-compete agreement was thus an illusion in the aforesaid facts and circumstances. Therefore, non-compete fee was rightly added to assessee's income.

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1974-75 - Assessee-company took over a firm with its assets and liabilities - It discharged tax liabilities of firm during previous year and claimed expenditure as deduction from its total income - Whether the expenditure representing tax liability of transferor-firm discharged by assessee was in the nature of a revenue expenditure and allowable under section 37(1) - Held, no

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessee-company was manufacturer of front wheel drive axle assembly for vehicles - To expand its business, assessee entered into an agreement with a company, named (SML) to purchase one of its units - Payment was made by assessee to SML towards non-compete fee and for other obligation and recitals imposed upon SML, i.e., obtaining permissions from financial institutions, obtaining approvals from governmental authorities, income tax authorities, indemnity towards other losses, if any, and maintenance of confidentiality about agreement as also all intellectual property and other data and information - Whether payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards non-compete obligation and, thus, capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 15] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee entered into an agreement for purchase of assets and liabilities of a newly set up factory of a company (SML), and paid a certain sum for obtaining requisite permission and approvals in smooth transfer of factory to assessee, said payment was clearly for an enduring benefit and not just towards non-compete obligation

Section 28(va), read with section 2(14), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Non-compete fees [Transfer of business] - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee offered short term as well as long term capital gains on account of sale of shares treating said transfer as transfer of capital asset as per section 2(14) - However, Assessing Officer held that said transfer, was transfer of business from assessee to purchaser with all pervasive control and he treated said income as business income under section 28(va) - A perusal of share purchase agreement revealed that agreement though classified as an agreement for purchase of shares, envisaged purchase of business to complete and absolute exclusion of assessee and it also contained a non-compete clause - Whether agreement was not an innocent transfer of shareholdings that would place it within section 2(14) but a transfer of business with all pervasive control being entrusted to purchaser and fell in realm of section 28(va)- Held, yes [Para 15] [In favour of revenue]IT: Transfer of shares with all pervasive control over business being entrusted to purchaser and to complete exclusion of assessee with a non-compete clause fell within realm of section 28(va)

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - A company 'M' was taken over under an Ordinance - Before final acquisition, assessee was appointed as an administrator of company and was put in charge of establishment - Assessee paid certain amount to 'M' being deprivation charges and claimed said amount as revenue expenditure - Whether since amount had been paid as compensation for deprivation of income which 'M' would have earned, had it not been deprived of possession and no part of said amount was paid towards consideration of transfer of title or property of undertaking of 'M', amount paid by assessee was in nature of revenue expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Non-compete fee - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one on revenue account - Held, yes - Assessee entered into a non-compete agreement with one 'U' for a period of 5 years - It paid a certain sum as non-compete fee to 'U' and claimed same as revenue expenditure - 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to clientele and pricing of products; as a business proposition, assessee entered into non-compete agreement - Whether payment was in respect of performing of business of assessee and, thus, expenditure was on revenue account and not on capital account - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee made payment as non-compete fee for purpose of business of assessee, expenditure was on revenue count

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Assessee-company passed resolution to wind up company and retrench its employees after paying compensation under section 25FFF of the industrial disputes Act, 1947 - After stoppage of work three share holders individually took up company’s business and retrenched employees were taken back by them - Whether assessee was right in contending that retrenchment compensation paid was allowable expenditure since it did not spring from closure of business - Held, no

Section 45, read with section 55, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1995-96 - Under an agreement, assessee-company transferred its business of manufacture of transformers to a company as a going concern - As per agreement, besides value of net assets, assessee received certain amount for transfer of technical know-how and certain amount as non-competing fees in respect of pending orders and future orders - Assessing Officer treated both amounts as goodwill and determining cost of acquisition as nil, brought same to tax as long-term capital gains - Whether since on date of transfer of business of assessee, there was no technical know-how reflected in balance sheet and it came into existence only at time of signing transfer agreement, it could be said that amount termed as consideration for technical know-how was nothing but a colourable device adopted by assessee to evade tax - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Assessing Officer was justified in treating same as goodwill and in making addition in that respect - Held, yes - Whether since on transferring business to new company, existing firm, i.e., assessee, ceased to be in existence, there was no question of competition, and payment to non-existing person for non-competition could not be treated as paid for non-competition - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Assessing Officer was fully justified in treating such transactions as part and parcel of goodwill and making additions accordingly - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business Expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1959-60 - Assessee, a transport company, purchased shares of another transport company with an objective to eliminate competition on route it was plying - Assessee was successful in eliminating competition and thereafter, sold those shares in a loss - Whether loss suffered by assessee was an expenditure of capital in nature - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1946-47 - Assessee-company, dealers in petroleum and mobil oil took over business as agent of kerosene oil in certain area, from a joint family and paid certain sum annually to said joint family to keep it out from undertaking similar business, directly or indirectly, within particular area - Assessee claimed deduction of amount so paid under section 10(2)(xv) - Whether since annual sum paid was not paid for acquiring any assets of business, but was paid with view to keep competitor out of area in which assessee was carrying on its business, it was entitled to deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether once expenditure on account of non-compete fees is incurred restraining recipient for a short or limited period, expenditure incurred can only be called to have been incurred to increase profitability of assessee and is not a capital expenditure - Held, yes - Assessee purchased running business of a firm along with its goodwill and paid certain amount to partners of that firm for not carrying on same line of business for five years - Whether expenditure incurred by assessee was revenue in nature and, hence, allowable - Held, yes - Whether, however, since expenditure was incurred for a period of 5 years, it was to be allowed over a period of 5 years and not in a lumpsum in relevant assessment year as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

Section 28(i) of the income-tax act, 1961-Business loss/allowance-Assessee-company took over under an agreement business of company oc-It paid 5 per cent commission amounting to Rs. 52,966 to oc for being allowed to execute contract worth Rs. 10.59 lakhs pending with oc on date of take over-Whether impugned commission deductible in computing income of assessee-Held, on facts, yes

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Business expenditure-Assessee-firm's running business was taken over by a company with all assets and liabilities and services of assessee's employees were also transferred to said company under agreement-Under conditions stipulated in agreement, assesses was ab initio not liable to pay retrenchment compensation under section 25ff of industrial disputes act-whether provision made by assessee for such payment was allowable as deduction-held, on facts, no

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arms length price - (Comparability factors - Abnormal events) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Whether if company starts its operations ab initio by taking over business of another entity from first day of financial year, without having any pre-existing business, there can be no question of distortion of its financial results because of merger and such a panorama cannot justify exclusion of an otherwise comparable company - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : If company starts its operations ab initio by taking over business of another entity from first day of financial year, without having any pre-existing business, there can be no question of distortion of its financial results because of merger and such a panorama cannot justify exclusion of an otherwise comparable company   TRANSFER PRICING : A company engaged as consultants and advisors of information/internet systems and surveyors of information services and which was also providing technical and software services, cannot be compared with assessee, a software development services provider

I. Section 37(1), read with section 36(1)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Bad debts) - Assessment year 2000-01 - Assessee offered guarantee to 'S' bank on behalf of its subsidiary company - Subsequently, on invocation of guarantee clause, assessee made payment to bank and wrote off said amount in its books of account believing that nothing could be recovered from subsidiary company - Assessee's claim for deduction of said amount as bad debts was rejected by revenue authorities - Tribunal, however, allowed assessee's claim - Whether since amount in question was paid for business expediency of wholly owned subsidiary company, it was to be regarded as directly relatable to business of assessee and, thus, eligible for deduction as business expenditure - Held, yes [Para 9][In favour of assessee]IT: Where subsequent to invocation of guarantee clause, assessee made payment of guarantee on behalf of its subsidiary company, since amount in question was paid for business expediency of wholly owned subsidiary company, it was to be regarded as directly relatable to business of assessee and, thus, eligible for deduction as business expenditure  IT: Where, for assessment year 2000-01, assessee, who was successfully running business of retail supermarket stores, sold their running business to a new company and in terms of restrictive covenant did not carry on competing business in retail, amount received as non-compete fee was to be treated as capital receipt not liable to tax

Section 37(1)  of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where payment of commission was made by assessee to a party for services rendered and not to ward off competition, as alleged by revenue, payment of commission was allowable as deduction
N.K. Rajgarhia v. Dy. Commissioner [1995] 52 TTJ (Delhi) 631
As per memorandum of understanding between the assessee and one GFC the assessee was to pay commission only in respect of supply of quantity of 6,000 MT of detergent powder under contract to USSR and the arrangement did not extend to any similar or repeat contracts for supply of any detergent goods or commodities in future to USSR or any other party and both the parties were free to compete in the manner best suitable to them. It was a matter of record that the assessee received repeat orders for supply of detergent on which he earned commission but no amount was paid to GFC on that account. The amount had been paid by the assessee only in respect of contract for 6,000 MT and was not in respect of any other contract for supply of detergent goods or commodities to USSR or any other party. The commission paid by the assessee to GFC was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that it was paid to ward off competition.
Held that as was manifest, the assessee had not eliminated GFC from carrying on its business activities inasmuch as both were free to compete with each other in the manner best suitable to them but for the contract of 6,000 MT. The assessee admittedly received further commission on supply of detergents subsequent to this contract of 6,000 MT but did not pay any commission to GFC which was not shown to have stopped business activities either as a result of payments made by the assessee. The amount was paid by the assessee to facilitate his business operations to be run more profitably. The payment made by the assessee to GFC was essentially for services rendered. The claim was, thus, clearly revenue in nature and allowable under section 37.

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1979-80 - Assessee-company took over running business of ‘H’ by sale deed - As per sale deed apart from sale consideration assessee had to pay annual overriding charges to wife of transferee on basis of net profits earned by assessee - Overriding charges paid as per sale deed by assessee during relevant assessment year were disallowed by ITO on ground that it was neither allowable as overriding charge nor admissible as revenue expenditure - Whether since payment of amount as overriding charges was an integral part of sale deed by which going concern was transferred to assessee and obligation to pay said amount was attached to very source of income, payment of overriding charges was diversion of income and, hence, deductible from income of assessee - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1962-63 - During relevant accounting year, assessee company took over business carried on by a firm including its employees - Aforesaid firm had a scheme in force of retiring its employees at age of 57½ years and paying them gratuity at time of retirement - Assessee-company also had a scheme of paying gratuity to its employees on retirement, but there was no fixed age of retirement for employees - As per terms of agreement of taking over business, assessee-company was to retire all its employees who had exceeded age of 57½ years and to pay them gratuity - Assessee-company did so and claimed amount paid as revenue expenditure - ITO taking a view that amount so paid was nothing but part of business consideration held that expenditure in question was capital in nature and not allowable as deduction - AAC as well as Tribunal, however, allowed assessee's claim - On instant reference, it was seen that Tribunal had recorded finding that there was an existing scheme for employees of assessee-company who were paid this amount by way of gratuity - It was also recorded that payment was made under circumstances as would ensure retention of remaining staff and contentment amongst them - Whether in aforesaid findings, order passed by Tribunal allowing assessee's claim was to be upheld - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessee bank transferred its banking business to another bank and transferred a sum to transferee bank as gratuity payable to employees who were taken over by said bank - Assessee claimed that amount as deduction - Whether when assessee-bank transferred a part of its business and thereby it compelled employees to retire from its business, gratuity was payable to them, still obligation to pay gratuity arose only by virtue of transfer of business and, as a matter of fact, transfer of business and obligation to pay gratuity were contemporaneous or simultaneous and, therefore, the payment of gratuity could not be said to be an item of expenditure incurred in course of carrying on business or for purpose of carrying on business - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-Compete fee) - Assessee-company, engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors - Assessee's claim for deduction of said expenditure was rejected by Assessing Officer on ground that it was in nature of capital expenditure - Tribunal upheld order passed by Assessing Officer - Whether since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 15] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

Section 37(1), read with  section 36(1)(v), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowable as - Assessment year 1989-90 - Whether legitimate business needs of an assessee must be judged from point of view of business and it is for assessee to consider business expediency and whether a particular expenditure should be incurred for business - Held, yes - Assessee-company took over affairs of an earlier company and services of employees were continued - At time of retirement employees claimed gratuity for earlier period also and initiated legal proceedings - To settle controversy, assessee accepted part of employees' claim and made additional retirement compensation - Whether provision of gratuity to employees for continuous services rendered to company taken over could be said to be either unusual or unnecessary - Held, no - Whether in instant case, excess payment was not made either towards or from gratuity fund, but it was a payment that was required to be made under Payment of Gratuity Act and it was made on basis of legitimate expectations of workmen on one hand and commercial expediency of employer on other - Held, yes - Whether deduction claimed on such a ground would not fall under section 36(1)(v) but would be in nature of revenue expenditure wholly and exclusively for purpose of business - Held, yes

VI. Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Adjustments - Operating profit/cost, computation of) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessee acquired global engineering design services division of M company through business transfer agreement (BTA), which included a pre-existing 3-year consultancy agreement with C - Assessee apportioned consultancy charges into pre and post-BTA periods and treated pre-BTA portion as exceptional item - TPO considered entire consultancy charges as part of operating cost on ground that expenditure was definitely for purpose of business i.e. now in possession of assessee - Whether, since assessee itself had taken over agreement in a slump sale and paid entire amount to C, and services such as drawing, design and recruitment were for furtherance of business in subsequent years, said expenditure was related to business operations and partook of nature of operating cost - Held, yes - Whether TPO/DRP had rightly considered exceptional item, being service charges paid to C as operating in nature - Held, yes [Para 27] [In favour of revenue]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee company was incorporated in pursuance of joint venture agreement by and between LT Ltd. and 'S' Corporation, Japan - Prior to joint venture agreement, LT was engaged in business of developing, manufacturing, marketing, distributing and selling various electric equipments and products in India and it had a well established country-wide sales network in India - LT and 'S' Corporation, Japan established assessee company with limited liability for purpose of importing, marketing and selling in India certain electric and electronic office products - During relevant assessment year assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to LT in lieu of latter, not setting up undertaking/assisting in setting up any undertaking carrying on business of selling, marketing and trading of electronic office product for a period of 7 years in India - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee paid to LT under section 37(1) - Assessing Officer took a view that expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, therefore, amount so paid was to be treated as capital in nature - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer - Whether since payment had been made to ward off competition for a period of 7 years during which assessee company could have set up its products and reputation in market, expenditure in question could not be treated to have been incurred in revenue field - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, authorities below were justified in rejecting assessee's claim - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

facts.text:
The assessee-company was incorporated with the prime purpose of specializing in offering of training courses in the field of financial services and other academic activities relating to financial services, such as offering of distance education courses, organizing conferences in and outside India, developing training facilities and classrooms, etc. ‘W’ was also in the business of carrying on similar activities as that of the assessee- company. The assessee-company took over the business of ‘W’ after payment of consideration amount for such acquisition, and claimed the said payment as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company took over the training courses and educational activities, for a consideration, of a company belonging to the same group and that ‘W’ stopped the activities following the takeover of their business by the assessee-company. It was, thus, held that the consider- ation amount paid by the assessee was for initiation of business to set up profit making apparatus in motion. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member took the view that the said payment was in the nature of revenue expenditure because none of the components of the consideration could be said to be in the nature of creation of any asset, which was of the nature of capital assets. However, the Judicial Member was of the opinion that the amount was paid for taking over the business of imparting and conducting training courses in the field of leasing and hire-purchase of related areas, and that by taking over the business the assessee acquired the right to conduct the commercial activities of another company for an indefinite period and that acquisition of such right was of capital nature. As a result of difference of opinion between the two Members, the matter was referred to the Third Member for his opinion.

HELD (PER THIRD MEMBER)

It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.

(3) If the outgoing is so related to the carrying on or the conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process or operation, and not for the acquisition of an asset of a permanent character, the possession of which is a condition precedent for the running of the business, then it would be expenditure of revenue nature.

(4) Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired by payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trade marks, it would be expenditure of revenue nature.

The electric supply undertaking of the assessee-company was purchased by State Board on the expiry of its licence at midnight of 7/8-6-1963. In view of the impending transfer, the assessee served one month’s notice under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, on its employees on 6-5-1963, and claimed deduction of the amount of retrenchment compensation paid to them, as business expenditure. It further claimed that the said ‘takeover’ did not amount to ‘sale’ within meaning of section 41(2) and that in any event the amount received in excess of the market value of its assets could not be considered for purposes of section 41(2). The Tribunal rejected the assessee’s claims.

TTKB Ltd. which was engaged in manufacturing condoms and gloves had entered into a non-compete agreement with a foreign company for discontinuing its condom business. The foreign company paid Rs. 3.45 crores as a non-compete fee to TTKB. Later on, TTKB merged with the assessee-company and, therefore, the assessee took up the said transaction. The assessee-company in the assessment year 2000-01 claimed that the amount of Rs. 3.45 crores was not taxable in its hands because the whole structure of the profit making apparatus, was given up to foreign company. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim holding, inter alia, that the non-compete fee received by it was a compensation for loss of business profit in the next few years and was taxable in its hands as a receipt under section 10(3) and that the said intention of the Legislature had been incorporated in the Act by introducing section 28(va) with effect from 1-4-2003 whereby the non-compete fee had been made as taxable income. On second appeal :

The assessee-firm was manufacturer of transformers. During relevant assessment year, its business was taken over as a going concern by a limited company and its partners became directors of the said company. The said company made certain payments to the assessee for technical know-how and as compensation for pending and expected orders, i.e., not to compete and indulge in transformer business. During assessment proceedings, a show-cause notice was issued to the assessee as to why the amounts shown as received for non-competition fee for pending orders, future orders and for the transfer of technical know-how would not be treated as capital gains, inasmuch as no amount had been shown under the head ‘Goodwill’ even though the assessee had been making good profit in the previous years. The assessee contended that it had not received any money towards the goodwill from the company and inasmuch as for the assessment year 1995-96, a transfer of technical know-how was not taxable, it could not be termed as long-term capital gain. The Assessing Officer held that the receipt for technical know-how was nothing but a part of the composite receipt to cover the value of the intangible assets and inasmuch ‘goodwill’ was taxable under section 55(2), an attempt was made to evade the payment of tax. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer treated the entire amount as capital gains. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim in respect of amount received for technical know-how and compensation for pending orders but disallowed the amount of compensation for expected orders. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that there was no indication of the value of the technical know-how in the balance sheet and it had come into existence only at the time of signing the transfer agreement. It held that the agreement was for the transfer of entire business of a going concern and the amount indicated as the payment for technical know-how was nothing but a goodwill amount which was a colourable device to evade tax. The Tribunal further held that in view of the taking over of the going concern, the assessee-firm had come to an end, more so when the partners were also the directors and, therefore, there was no question of paying the non-competing fees, inasmuch as there was no possibility of the assessee-firm doing the very same business again. Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by the revenue and dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee.

The assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern. Since the assessee expressed its inability to furnish the details as they purchased the assets on the basis as going concern, the Assessing Officer obtained the information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that the said company had shown the book value of fixed assets at Rs. 345. 95 crores and after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers, offered profits on sale of net assets of cement division at Rs. 125. 25 crores in their books of account. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had paid more amount than the book value and the difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment and accordingly after discussion about the provisions of section 43(1) , report of the registered valuer, determined the goodwill value at the difference between the amount adopted by the assessee and the amount shown in the books of TISCO and depreciation on the amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed thereby making addition of Rs. 16. 39 crores. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) it was contended that the assessee had acquired fixed assets and current assets of the unit in an open bid and on the basis of the report of the registered valuer the value was accordingly capitalized to the extent of Rs. 481. 39 crores and Assessing Officer's action in taking the WDV of TISCO was not correct as Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case as these two companies were independent and not related and further the Assessing Officer had not correctly appreciated the registered valuer's report and the method adopted. The assessee was a firm of exchange brokers. One 'M' was also carrying on business in co-partnership as exchange brokers. ‘J’, a company, had a bottling plant for filling aerated water and it was franchisee of company ‘H’. The assessee was one of the managing directors of company ‘J’. (4) Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired by payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trade marks, it would be expenditure of revenue nature. (5) If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with net sales, the outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of capital expenditure.

(6) If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled and the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the capital nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(7) A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be revenue expenditure or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment.

(8) If the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be revenue expenditure.

(9) An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a capital expenditure.

(10) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as a capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be revenue expenditure. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which facilitates the acquisition of stock, the expenditure is of capital nature.

(11) The expenditure of capital nature is not referable only to tangible assets, but also to intangible assets. The asset acquired may be of impalpable or incalculable nature.

(12) The expenditure to enhance the profit earning capacity or capital base is of capital nature notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11]

Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure.
