The High Court ruled that Tiger Global's transaction was legitimate and not aimed at tax avoidance, allowing it to claim tax benefits under the treaty's 'grandfathering clause' for capital gains on shares acquired before April 1, 2017. The court rejected the AAR's view that Tiger Global was merely a "see-through entity" controlled by a US-based individual. The High Court acknowledged Tiger Global's significant economic activities, compliance with the required thresholds for expenses and liabilities, and the legitimacy of its Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) as proof of its bona fide status in Mauritius. The court further held that treaty shopping is not inherently objectionable unless explicitly shown to be solely for tax evasion.

3. Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1): Supreme Court

Sharp Business System v. Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 181 taxmann.com 657 (SC)

Assessee, a public limited company, was engaged in the business of software development, hardware sales, technical training and engineering services. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year, declaring a net loss. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) computed the assessee's total income and made several disallowances. One of the disallowances concerned the depreciation claim on the non-compete fee.

Aggrieved-assessee preferred an appeal to the CIT(A), where it contended that the non-compete fee was nothing but a license. Assessee could exclusively carry on the business of software development, training and export of technologies by restraining M/s. Pentamedia Graphics Limited is not allowed to carry out the same activities. Thus, the payment of the non-compete fee was held to be an intangible asset entitled to depreciation under Section 32(1)(ii).

The matter, after passing through the ITAT and the High Court, was carried in appeal before the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court ruled that non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. The purpose of a non-compete payment is to give the payer's business a head start. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the payer's business or enhancing its profitability by insulating it from competition.

Thus, the non-compete fee seeks only to protect or enhance the business's profitability, thereby facilitating its carrying on more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in the creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit-earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, of restricting a competitor in business is not in the capital field.

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring such expenditure.

Thus, the Supreme Court held that a payment made by the assessee as a non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Act.

4. Section 44C covers head office expenses, whether common or solely for Indian branches: SC

Director of Income-tax (IT)-I, Mumbai v. American Express Bank Ltd. [2025] 181 taxmann.com 433 (SC)

The assessee, a non-resident banking company, filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year. While computing the income, the assessee claimed a deduction for expenses incurred at the head office directly related to the Indian branches.

The Assessing Officer (AO) contended that the expenses in question should be subject to the ceiling specified in Section 44C. The assessee claimed that the expenses in question could not have been classified as head office expenditure for the reason that Section 44C presupposes that at least a part of the expenditure is attributable to the business outside India. If this presumption does not hold, and the entire expenditure is incurred solely for the business in India, Section 44C would not apply.

The AO passed an assessment order limiting the deduction under Section 44C to 5% of the gross total income. The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that to be brought within the ambit of Section 44C, two broad conditions must be satisfied: (i) The assessee claiming the deduction must be a non-resident; and (ii) The expenditure in question must strictly fall within the definition of 'head office expenditure' as provided in the Explanation to the Section.

However, in the present circumstances, there are two methods as per provisions of the Act, to dissolve the existence of transferor company. Further, the transferor company has to opt which method is to adopted so that compliance can be done accordingly.

As per provisions of section 217 of the Act, till the date of dissolution, the transferee company has to give particulars of subsidiary company in the Director's Report as well as annex the balance sheet of subsidiary company along with the balance sheet of holding company as well as the nature of interest, if any.

6.2 Investment implications under section 372 - As per provisions ofsection 372(14)(d), the provisions of this section are not applicable to investments by a holding company in its subsidiary company.

The transferee company cannot take benefit of this clause since the relationship of holding and subsidiary exists only after transfer is effected, i.e., in the last moments of amalgamation under the provisions of section 395. As such the benefit of exemption is not available to the transferee company and it has to obtain permission of shareholders and also to seek prior approval of the Central Government under section 372. As a matter of management planning, to take benefit of exemption of provisions of section 372(14)(d) is to acquire more than 50 per cent shares in the transferor company even before giving offer to acquire all the shares.

Dissolution of transferor company under sections 394, 497/509

7. In this method, the dissolution is being effected through process of the Court. The transferor company, in this process, has to comply with the requirements of voluntary liquidation/winding up. In the voluntary winding up proceedings, following steps are to be taken :

Amalgamation/Merger Without Approaching Court

ANIL KUMAR POPLI

In the present business scenario, amalgamation/merger is a common phenomenon in the wake of increasing incidences of mergers and acquisitions and takeover attempts by multinationals and existing big groups. However, amalgamation/merger without approaching the Court is not a common phenomenon in the capital market. Today, there are no clear guidelines in respect of amalgamations without Court order nor the provisions of Companies Act, 1956, are very clear. Therefore, in the emerging liberalisation and free enterprise environment, if the circumstances prevail, the corporates can take substantial benefits like saving of time, money and energy by adopting the procedure of amalgamation without approaching the Court. In this article, the author has explained various provisions, legal compliances and procedures for amalgamation without approaching the Court – EDITOR

Amalgamations and present business scenario

1. In the present business scenario, amalgamation/merger is a common phenomenon in the wake of increasing incidences of mergers and acquisitions and takeover attempts by multinationals and existing big groups. However, amalgamations/mergers without approaching the Court is not a common phenomenon in the capital market. Today, there are no clear guidelines in respect of amalgamations without Court order nor the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 are very clear. Therefore, in the emerging liberalisation and free enterprise environment, if the circumstances prevail, the corporates can take substantial benefits like saving of time, money and energy by adopting the procedures of amalgamations without approaching the Court.

Modes of takeover

2. As per provisions of the Companies Act, read with provisions of Listing Agreement, there are three modes for takeover of shares by way of scheme or contract:

(1) Amalgamation or arrangement of takeover through High Court [Sections 391 to 394 of the Act]

(2) Takeover of management

[Acquisition of shares through Stock Exchange - Clauses 40A and 40B of Listing Agreement]

(3) Take over/amalgamation without approaching the Court [Section 395 of the Act]

Amalgamation under clause No. 1 is very common. Under this method, the resolution for approving scheme of amalgamation/arrangement is required to be approved by members/creditors, as the case may be, and then sanction of the concerned High Court is to be obtained. Thereafter on the basis of report of the Registrar of Companies as well as Official Liquidator, the concerned High Court passes the order. This procedure is lengthy as well as time-consuming.

Whereas takeover under clause No. 2 is booming now a days, Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has now made strict with rules and procedures to comply with. It is a matter of great appreciation that recently SEBI has promulgated Takeover Regulations, 1997 whereby there is need for strict compliance of clauses 40A and 40B of Listing Agreement, appointment of Merchant Banker and maintenance of corpus and compliance of specific guidelines so that the minority shareholders should not suffer.

It is submitted that the amalgamation/merger under clause No. 3 is not very common in the capital market. Under the provisions of section 395, takeover of assets and liabilities or amalgamation of two companies can be effected even without adopting lengthy procedures of SEBI as well as the Court. It is also true to say that takeover under this section cannot be adopted by various companies because consent of the shareholders having share value of at least nine-tenth is not practically feasible in each and every company. This is the main reason why companies are notadopting this provision. However, in the view of the author, this provision is not, being common utilized frequently by the companies, though even by the companies which can fulfil the criteria and which can obtain the consent of majority of shareholders because of ignorance or non-popu-larization of this particular provision in the industry. An attempt is made here to clarify various norms and procedures to serve the purpose.

Accounting Standards and amalgamation by merger /purchase

3. As per provisions of clause 3(e) of Accounting Standards (AS-14) Accounting for Amalgamation "Amalgamation in the nature of merger is an amalgamation that satisfies all the following conditions :

(i) All the assets and liabilities of the transferor company become, after amalgamation, the assets and liabilities of the transferee company.

(ii) Shareholders holding not less than 90 per cent of the face value of the equity shares of the transferor company (other than the equity shares already held therein, immediately before the amalgamation, by the transferee company or its subsidiaries or their nominees) become equity shareholders of the transferee company by virtue of the amalgamation.

merger of partnership firm with Indian Company is not recognised as amalgamation under the Income-tax Act.

What is capital gain?

2. Capital gain arises on transfer of capital asset from one person to another. In the amalgamation, assets and liabilities of the transferor company are transferred, by a scheme of arrangement, to the transferee-company. Therefore, when assets of a partnership firm are transferred by scheme of amalgamation to a company, then capital gains may arise to the firm.

Capital gains exempted 3. List of transfers which are not considered as transfer of assets for the purposes of charging capital gain is enlisted in section 47 with conditions for exemption. Amalgamation is exempted under the provisions of section 47(vi) of the IT Act, the provision reads as "Any transfer, in a scheme of amalgamation, of a capital asset by the amalgamating company to the amalgamated company, if the amalgamated company is an Indian company."

Therefore, what is exempted, is capital gain arising on transfer of assets by a scheme of amalgamation to a amalgamating (Transferor) Company. In the present case a partnership firm, which is an unregistered company as per Companies Act, is being merged with the Private/Public Company. Therefore, advantage of section 47(vi) is not available in this case. Rather such merger of firm with the company is not regarded as amalgamation for the purposes of Income-tax Act.

Hence, question remains as when amalgamation of partnership firm with the Company happens, of course through High Court route under sections 391 & 394 of the Companies Act, whether, Capital gains arising from such transfer of capital assets are taxable? Though it is agreed that section 47(vi) of the Income-tax Act is not applicable but certainly the case falls under another listing in the same section 47, i.e., section 47 (xiii). Reasoning for the same is as follows:

Section 47(xiii) reads as follows:

(xiii) any transfer of a capital asset or intangible asset by a firm to a company as a result of succession of the firm by a company in the business carried on by the firm, or any transfer of a capital asset to a company in the course of demutualisation or corporatisation of a recognised stock exchange in India as a result of which an association of persons or body of individuals is succeeded by such company:

Provided that—

(a) all the assets and liabilities of the firm or of the association of persons or body of individuals relating to the business immediately before the succession become the assets and liabilities of the company;

(b) all the partners of the firm immediately before the succession become the shareholders of the company in the same proportion in which their capital accounts stood in the books of the firm on the date of the succession;

(c) the partners of the firm do not receive any consideration or benefit, directly or indirectly, in any form or manner, other than by way of allotment of shares in the company; and

(d) the aggregate of the shareholding in the company of the partners of the firm is not less than fifty per cent of the total voting power in the company and their shareholding continues to be as such for a period of five years from the date of the succession;

(e) the demutualisation or corporatisation of a recognised stock exchange in India is carried out in accordance with a scheme for demutualisation or corporatisation which is approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India established under section 3 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (15 of 1992);

An analysis of section 47(xiii) is as follows:

1. Business is carried on by the firm up to one date

2. Such business in a firm by succession vests in a company and, therefore, all the assets and liabilities of the firm are transferred to a Company

3. Conditions mentioned in proviso from (a) to (e) are followed,

Vesting of assets and liabilities

Consideration

Accounting treatment

Post merger shareholding

Further, the SEBI Circular dated March 10, 2017 (as amended) provides conditions and compliances by listed entities while undertaking Scheme of Arrangement. Further, while considering the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011, Regulation 10(d), exempts listed companies from the obligation to make an open offer where the acquisition is pursuant to a scheme of arrangement.

IAS 22 Business Combinations (1998) provided accounting policy for negative goodwill:

Negative goodwill must always be measured and initially recognized as the full difference between acquirer's interest in fair values of the identifiable assets and liabilities acquired less the cost of acquisition [ IAS 22.59].

To the extent that it relates to expected future losses and expenses that are identified in the acquirer's acquisition plan, the negative goodwill is recognised as income when the future losses and expenses are recognised. [IAS 22.61]

An excess of negative goodwill to the extent of the fair values of acquired identifiable nonmonetary assets is recognised in income over the average live of those nonmonetary assets. [IAS 22.62(a)]

Any remaining excess is recognised as income immediately. [IAS 22.62(b)]

Negative goodwill is presented as a deduction from the assets of the enterprise, in the same balance sheet classification as (positive) goodwill. [IAS 22.64]

IAS 22 was predecessor of IFRS 3 Business Combinations which was then applicable.

IFRS 3 Business Combinations has changed the accounting treatment of bargain purchase gain and require the acquiree to recognise the bargain purchase gain in profit or loss on the acquisition date – the gain shall be attributed to the acquirer [ IFRS3.34]. Thus it prescribes one time credit rather than writing back over the years. Of course, IFRS 3 explains that a bargain purchase might happen, for example, in a business combination that is forced sale in which the seller is acting under compulsion. IFRS 3 offers safeguard of recognizing bargain purchase gain:

-

Before recognising a gain on a bargain purchase, the acquirer shall determine whether there exists clear evidence of the underlying reasons for classifying the business combination as a bargain purchase. If such evidence exists, the acquirer shall reassess whether it has correctly identified all of the assets acquired and all of the liabilities assumed and shall recognise any additional assets or liabilities that are identified in that review. [ IFRS 3.36]

Neither the BHS Group explained the reason for such unusual amount of negative goodwill (bargain purchase gain) booked in the accounts nor did the then independent auditor KPMG offer any reservation. -

AS 14 Accounting for Amalgamation required the negative goodwill to be recognised as capital reserve [ AS14.17]

-

Ind AS 103 Business Combinations made at carve out from IFRS 3 to require bargain purchase gain to be recognised in capital reserve [ Ind AS 103.36A].

Group : The group to which the enterprise whose control, shares, assets or voting rights are being acquired would belong after the acquisition or the group to which the enterprise remaining the merger or amalgamation would belong has either assets of value of more than INR 6000 crores in India or turnover more than INR 18000 crores in India. 8. Therefore, computation of turnover criteria will determine the decision to notify a transaction or not. It is not an easy task to calculate the actual turnover in view of the ambiguous provisions and definitions of turnover and it will be a real challenge to calculate the turnover and to determine whether a transaction requires notifying to the CCI or not.

Further, the thresholds are based on asset/turnover and not on the market share/dominance of the combining parties. This would cover even combinations between two foreign entities in a third country. Such transactions will have to be notified to CCI merely because the combining parties have certain assets/turnover in India, that too not necessarily relatable to the subject matter of the transaction. Thus, it will be necessary to give clarification on this point as well.

Also, only those cross-border combinations in which the combining parties have significant India present in terms of market share in the relevant product /services market should alone be required to file notice with CCI for prior approval. In case an Indian company acquires a foreign entity, the market share in India of such acquired entity i.e. the target entity, may be considered, whereas if a foreign entity is acquiring an Indian entity, the market share of such acquired entity in India i.e. target entity, may be considered as the benchmark for mandatory filing of notice with CCI for prior approval.

Importance of "Turnover"

9. For complying with the provisions of the Act for notifying a transaction, calculation of turnover of the parties is critical from the merger control perspective. The transactions where the parties fail to meet the asset and turnover thresholds under section 5 of the Competition Act need not be notified. Under Ind AS 103 Business Combinations, goodwill is measured as the difference between the consideration transferred in exchange for the net of the acquisition-date amounts of the identifiable assets acquired and the liabilities assumed.

In extremely rare circumstances, an acquirer will make a bargain purchase in a business combination, where the value of acquired identifiable assets and liabilities exceeds the consideration transferred; the acquirer shall recognize a gain (bargain purchase). The gain shall be recognized by the acquirer in Other Comprehensive Income on the acquisition date and accumulate the same in equity as capital reserve, if there exists a clear evidence of the underlying reason for classifying the business combination as a bargain purchase.

If there does not exist clear evidence of the underlying reasons for classifying the business combination as a bargain purchase, then the gain shall be recognised directly in equity as capital reserve.

The question whether such restrictive covenants are allowed or is it violative of provisions of any law or may be prohibited under any Act is to be examined carefully. Further, in terms of the Competition Act, every restraint or every restrictive covenant in an agreement does not restrict competition. The agreements which impose restriction of Trade or the Agreements in Restraint of Trade are covered by section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 states that "Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is to that extent void."

But there are some exceptions to the aforesaid rule. For example, a person who sells the total business may agree with the buyer that he will not carry on a similar business, may be, within a specified local limits till such time the buyer carries on a like business therein, provided such limits appear to the Court reasonable, having regard to the nature and operations of the business. So, in other words, all agreements in restraint of trade will be valid, provided they are reasonable having regard to the nature of business and also reasonable in the interests of the parties and in public interest.

The Supreme Court in the matter of Gujarat Bottling Co. Ltd. v. Coca Cola Co. [1994] 84 Comp. Cas. 618, has in detail analysed the scope of section 27 of the Indian Contract Act and given the judgment reads as under :—

". . . A covenant in restraint of trade must be reasonable with reference to the public policy and it must also be reasonably necessary for the protection of the interest of the covenantee and regard must be had to the interests of the covenantor. Contracts in restraint of trade are prima facie void and the onus of proof is on the party supporting the contract to show that the restraint goes no further than is reasonably necessary to protect the interest of the covenantee and if this onus is discharged the onus of showing that the restraint is nevertheless injurious to the public is on the party attacking the contract. The Court has to decide, as a matter of law, (i) whether a contract is or is not in restraint of trade, and (ii) whether, if in restraint of trade, it is reasonable. . . ." (p. 642)

Thus, in the aforesaid case, the Supreme Court ruled that a negative stipulation contained in a Franchise Agreement restraining the franchisee from dealing with competing goods was to facilitate the distribution of the goods of the franchiser and could not be regarded as a restraint of a right to trade. However, in yet another case, where the defendant and the plaintiff used to carry on the business of ferrying boats and arrived at a business sale settlement, wherein the defendant had to pay a certain amount to the plaintiff in order that the plaintiff should abstain from carrying on his business of boat ferrying for a period of three years, the Court held that the agreement was void as the restraining covenant was a vital part of the agreement itself and did not fall under the ‘goodwill exception’ as mentioned in section 27 of the Indian Contract Act. Thus, while drafting an agreement, care should be taken to see that the restrictive covenants, if at all to be included, should convey correct meaning and fit into the exception module.

Benefits of framing guidelines on Competition Law by Corporates

13. Certain benefits of framing guidelines on Competition Law are :—

(i) Commitment to compliance with Competition Law - Compliance with the law is part of corporate image and an organisation grows only with sound ethical practices combined with adherence to various provisions of laws, which would take it to next league in achieving success. Further, it will earn a better brand image and goodwill in the market. By complying with the requirement of Competition Law, the company can avoid penalties that may be imposed for activities that may curb anti-competitive practices in the Indian market.

(ii) Detection - With the introduction of proper guidelines, education and training, an organisation can carve out appropriate and inappro-priate conduct which will help in early detection of violations. This is because, by this method, the employees are well-informed about the signs of illegal conduct by co-employees and, thus, pave the way for clear and safe ways for reporting suspected violations. Further, the employees would get an indirect message that the company will not tolerate anti-competitive behaviours or conduct.

(iii) Responsibilities - The responsibility for observing the rules and regulations of the Competition Act lies with every employee who encounters issues relating to Competition Law and particularly applies to senior management and managers involved in the department of sales, procurement and merger and acquisition projects. Each and every employee is required to acquire necessary knowledge in order to assess such issues and, in this regard, to consult the legal department/in-house counsel/external law firms, if necessary. The Senior Management Executive must select, instruct and train their employees to ensure that they observe the rules and regulations of the Act.

(iv) Litigation - The adherence to the guidelines of Competition Laws and proper training will alert the unpleasant situation, if any, of being caught for violation of laws of competition. Thus, proper training of the concerned employees and sticking to the guidelines on competition law will help in identifying potential risk in the conduct and would avoid unnecessary litigation costs.

Introduction

1. An accounting standard for financial accounting and reporting of acquisitions of companies is non-existing under the AS (Indian GAAP) framework. Accounting for acquisitions under AS was primarily driven by AS-14, albeit the standard scoped out acquisitions from its purview. Divergent practices arose resulting from issues surrounding recognition and measurement of acquired assets and liabilities as well as the consequential impact on goodwill.

IND-AS, the Indian variant of IFRS has a separate accounting literature that deals with accounting for acquisition that is embedded within IND-AS 103 - Business Combinations. IFRS, on similar lines to USGAAP, requires the acquisition model of accounting to be used in accounting for acquisitions on Day 1.

Background

2. Indian companies are required to compulsorily switch over from AS to IND-AS (Indian Accounting Standards) in two phases commencing April 1, 2016. IND-AS is based on International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).

The second phase of IND-AS convergence that commences on April 1, 2017 encompasses all listed companies that were not part of Phase 1 and all unlisted companies with a net worth in the range of Rs. 250 - 500 crore calculated as of March 31,2014.

The acquisition method of Accounting at a Glance

3. The acquisition method of accounting as per IND-AS 103 is highlighted in the info graphic herein below.

Accounting for business combinations under IND-AS

4. The salient aspects of the acquisition method of accounting are discussed herein below.

Reporting entities need to apply the acquisition method of accounting for each business combination. It may be noted that a business combination is a transaction or other event in which an acquirer obtains "control" of one or more businesses. Transactions sometimes referred to as 'true mergers' or 'mergers of equals' are also business combinations as per IND-AS.

The consideration transferred in a business combination includes the fair value, as on the acquisition date, of the assets and liabilities transferred and of the interests issued by the acquirer, as well as the fair value of any contingent consideration and of the incentives included in share-based payments recognized by the acquiree that have to be replaced in the business combination.

If the business combination settles a pre-existing relationship between the acquirer and the acquiree, the lesser of the settlement provision, as established by contract, and the off-market price of the element is deducted from the consideration transferred and recognized under other costs.

The identifiable assets acquired and the identifiable liabilities assumed are measured at their respective acquisition-date fair values.

A contingent liability of the acquiree is assumed in a business combination only if this liability represents a current obligation deriving from past events and when its fair value can be reliably measured.

For each business combination, any non-controlling interest in the acquiree is measured at fair value or in proportion to its share of the acquiree's net identifiable assets.

Goodwill arising from the acquisition is recognized as an asset and is initially measured as the excess between the consideration transferred and the acquisition-date net amount of the identifiable assets acquired and the identifiable liabilities assumed.

In case of a business combination achieved in stages, the interest previously held in the acquiree is re-measured at its acquisition-date fair value and any resulting gain or loss is recognized in profit or loss.

The costs relating to the acquisition are recognized in profit or loss in the period in which the costs are incurred and the services received, with the exception for the cost of issuing debt securities or equities.

Accounting aspect

4. In case of Amalgamations, Accounting Standard 14 is applicable. AS 14 uses the word 'companies' in its entire text. However, definition of Amalgamation says that Amalgamation means amalgamation pursuant to provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 or any other statute which may be applicable to companies. Therefore, the word 'Companies' for the purposes of AS 14 must be identified as defined in Companies Act, 1956 for the purposes of Amalgamation, i.e., section 390, read with section 582(b), which includes a partnership with 8 or more partners. Therefore, accounting treatment will be same for a merger of a partnership firm with the Company as it is for amalgamation of a Company with another Company.

There is no need to first convert the firm under Chapter IX in a Company, before amalgamation. However, other statutes and standards are also to be studied before effecting such amalgamation. Section 47(xiii) of the Income Tax Act is crucial in all. It requires certain additional compliances to be done for claiming an exemption granted under that section. Therefore, drafting of a scheme for amalgamation, in this case becomes extremely important. Care must be taken while drafting a scheme for amalgamation of a Partnership Firm with a Company. The facts before the EAC involved a case where one closely-held company held 15% of shares in another closely-held company and the former company acquired balance 85% shares in the latter company with the result that the latter company became a 100% subsidiary of the former company. The above principles in EAC's opinion will equally hold good where as a result of acquisition of the shares of closely-held company at a consideration less than fair market value, no holding-subsidiary relationship is established between the investor closely-held company and the investee closely-held company.

When a firm ‘A' ceases to exist and its business is taken over by one of the partners who carries it on as a proprietary concern ‘B’ and then, after a brief interval, the proprietary concern again becomes a partnership firm 'C’ several complex questions arise about the assessments of A, B and C under the Income-tax Act, 1961. In this article, the author discusses some of these questions in the light of the decision of the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. Bison Knitting Co. [1997] 140 CTR (Mad.) 566, in which the facts conformed to the outline given above. The main questions considered by him are:

(i )When firm A is succeeded by proprietary concern B which, after a certain interval is succeeded by another firm C; is it a case of change of constitution of firm A' under section 187(2) ?

(ii )What is the nature of the transaction when the business changes hands from A to B and then from B to C?

(iii )What is the actual cost of depreciable assets of A in the hands of B ? Likewise, what is the actual cost of such assets in the hands of C when these are taken over by it from 'B' ?

(iv )Is there profit under section 41(2) in the hands of 'A' or ‘B' ?

(v)Do chargeable capital gains arise in the hands of A or B ? - EDITOR Madras High Court's decision

1. In CIT v. Bison Knitting Co. [1997] 140 CTR (Mad.) 566, there was a firm A, in which B was the managing partner; it came to an end on March 31, 1975. Thereafter, B took over the business as a proprietary concern from April 1, 1975. On May 1, 1975, the proprietary concern became a partnership C which filed a return for the assessment year 1976-77 disclosing an income of Rs. 88,169. In arriving at this income the firm claimed depreciation of 15 per cent on Rs. 2.71 lakhs which was the cost of the machinery to the firm. The ITO allowed the claim. The Commissioner, acting under section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), took the view that the sum of Rs. 2.71 lakhs represented the book value of the machinery taken over by C from the predecessor-owner B and not their written down value, which alone should have been adopted as cost for purposes of depreciation. The Commissioner directed the ITO to make a fresh assessment keeping in view the change in the constitution of the firm, the additions stated to have been made to the machinery account, the profit under section 41(2) of the Act in the hands of A, etc.

The Tribunal held that when the earlier firm A came to an end and the business was taken over as a proprietary concern by B, it amounted to a sale and so capital gains arising out of the transfer was liable to tax. Likewise, when the proprietary business of B became once again a partnership C, there was also scope for chargeability to tax of capital gains. The tax on capital gains on either or on both of these transactions would be much more than the increase in revenue that might arise by the adoption of the written down value of the assets in the hands of A, even if that be permitted as the basis of the cost in the hands of C.

Holding that there was no prejudice to the revenue, the Tribunal cancelled the Commissioner's order under section 263.

The High Court held that Rs. 2.71 lakhs on which depreciation was claimed by C represented the book value of these assets in the hands of the firm : "If there is a change in the constitution, depreciation can be claimed only on the written down value of the assets of the firm. If there is no change in the firm, depreciation can be claimed either on the book value or on the market value of the machineries of the firm". There is no connection between the assessee C and the erstwhile firm A in which B was the managing partner: "Therefore, there is no change in the constitution of the assessee-firm. In such a case, the assessee is entitled to claim depreciation on the book value. In the present case . . . we consider that the order passed by the Tribunal in setting aside the order passed by the Commissioner under section 263 of the Act is in order".

A case study

2. The facts stated in the judgment have been almost completely reproduced. Certain logical inferences are drawn on the basis of those facts in the discussion which follows. The case raises the following issues, which are dealt with seriatim :

entire business is transferred as a going concern for a lump-sum consideration – cherry picking of assets is not possible.

Transfer of an undertaking or a business unit as a going concern for a lump sum consideration without assigning individual values to each assets and liabilities. Section 2(42C) of the Income-tax Act defines slump sale as a "transfer of one or more undertakings as a result of the sale for a lump sum consideration without values being assigned to the individual assets and liabilities in such sales". 3.2 Rationale: One of the reasons why a slump sale is preferred over an acquisition of shares is that in case of a slump sale the past liabilities of the transferor-company can be left behind and only the assets of the transferor-company can form part of the business transfer.

3.3 Approvals: It would be necessary for more than 50% of the shareholders of the seller- company to pass a resolution approving of such a disposal.

3.4 Transaction Cost: Tax implication under a Slump Sale method is similar to that of Asset Purchase method, except that VAT is not applicable on a Slump-Sale transaction.

3.4.1 Tax chargeable in the hands of Seller

3.4.1.1 CAPITAL GAINS

Here consideration in excess of the net worth of the business is taxed as capital gains. If the undertaking, which is being sold under Slump Sale, was held by the transferor for more than 36 months, the capital gains realized on such sale would be taxed as long-term capital gains at the rate of 20% plus applicable surcharge and education cess at 3 per cent.

No benefit of indexation would be available in case of slump sale while computing long-term capital gain. If, however, the undertaking was to be held for 36 months or less, the capital gains realized would be taxed as short-term capital gains, i.e., at the rate of 30% for a domestic company and at 40 per cent for a foreign company (plus applicable surcharge and education cess at 3 per cent).

For the purpose of computing capital gains, the cost of acquisition would be the 'net worth' of the undertaking on the date of the transfer2.

3.4.2 Tax chargeable in the hands of Acquirer

The implications of transaction cost on the buyer are similar to those borne by the Acquirer in Asset Purchase method as discussed above, except that there is no VAT applicable in a Slump Sale.

4. SHARE PURCHASE METHOD

4.1 Concept: Under this method the acquirer acquires the target company through acquisition of the existing equity shares of the target company from its shareholders or by subscribing to the new equity shares that are issued by the target company.

In ordinary circumstances a Share Purchase Agreement ("SPA") is executed between the two parties. The SHA basically is the definitive agreement that incorporates all terms and conditions related to the purchase and sale of the shares of a company.

An acquisition of shares can be effected by execution and delivery of transfer deeds, which must be duly stamped and registered with the target company. This must happen within the prescribed time set forth in the Companies Act and must be accompanied by share certi?cates. An acquisition of shares is an easier and much quicker transaction. In a transfer of assets, several additional documents may be necessary, depending upon the nature and number of assets involved in the transaction.

Any acquisition of shares, more particularly in an acquisition of majority shares, a comprehensive due diligence on the target company and all its affairs and business operations, including but not limited to pending and threatened litigation against the target company, status of regulatory compliances, direct and indirect tax liabilities and contingent liabilities, if any, are necessary and critical.

4.2 Rationale: If the interest of the acquirer is in the entity as a whole, then the acquisition can be done by acquiring the shares of that entity or merging or amalgamating that entity with the acquirer.

4.3 Approvals

4.3.1 RBI's Approvals :RBI has issued various noti?cations under the Foreign Management Act of 1999, applicable from January 6, 2000, which have liberalized and simpli?ed the provisions regarding acquisition of shares.

Foreign investment in most industries (even up to 100 per cent) is now permitted without any prior approval from the RBI, although there is a sectoral cap, ranging from forty nine per cent to seventy four per cent, for investing in certain industries. Under the Automatic Route Guidelines, RBI needs only be informed about the investment within thirty days of remittance. In the case of purchase of shares from Indian residents, the prior permission of the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) and RBI are required, regardless of the number or value of shares acquired.

4.3.2 SEBI's Approvals

In case of acquisition of shares exceeding a certain percentage in a company listed on the Stock Exchange, the provisions of the Substantial Acquisition of Shares & Takeovers Regulations of 1997 (Takeover Code) must be followed.

4.4 Transaction Cost: The sale of shares is taxed as capital gains in the hands of the seller. No step-up in the cost of the underlying business is possible in a share purchase method because the ownership of the asset is retained by the company itself. No deduction is allowed for a difference between the underlying net asset values and the consideration paid.

The local Nexus 8. The Act provides for a local nexus, i.e., it makes it mandatory for any combination which is having potential to cause any adverse effect on the Indian market irrespective of the fact as to whether the enterprises involved in the combination are non-Indian entities, to be notified to CCI. Therefore, even if the combination is proposed outside India and is completed and approved outside India, it has to be notified to the CCI, provided it should be capable of causing any effect on the relevant Indian market. If the quantitative jurisdiction criterion based on the size of the enterprises is fulfilled, then notwithstanding whether the principal business of the enterprises is carried outside India, it has to be notified and approved by the CCI. The International combinations may have effect in India if the enterprises involved have subsidiaries in India. For example: A Brazilian company acquiring an Argentinean company and if both the companies have their subsidiaries in India having assets above the threshold limit and such an acquisition is expected to have certain adverse effect on the relevant Indian market, then a merger, that is, between two non-Indian companies proposed in a foreign nation and approved by the laws of those nations is mandatorily required to be reported to the CCI.

The market domination, in cases of merger involving a group of companies outside India, is decided on the basis of assets size of two billion or sale of six billion. This as per international standards appears to be very small. The cross-border mergers taking place today involves big giant corporations and the dimensions of the present day mergers is enormous. For example: The combination of Bell Atlantic and GTE is worth $ 71 Billion, the merger between Exon and Mobile was worth $ 86 Billion and Fuji -Daichi-International Bank of Japan - announced their decision to merge with assets of $1,300 Billion34. The rationale behind the introduction of the local nexus system can be inferred from the Commentary of the UN Model Law on Competition :—

Cross frontier acquisitions of control :

"Mergers, takeovers or other acquisitions of control involving transnational corporations should be subject to some kind of scrutiny in all countries where the corporation operates, since such acquisition of control, irrespective of whether they take place solely within the country or abroad, might have direct or indirect effects on the operations of the other unit of economic activities35."

9.1 COMPETITION ACT AND TAKEOVER CODE - The Takeover Code is the principle law governing acquisitions and takeovers in India. The provision of the Competition Act regarding the time-frame of approval will result in extra financial burden on the acquirer. Under the Takeover Code, the acquirer is bound to pay the shareholders their due within 15 days of closure of offer. Regulation 22(12) of the Takeover Code3 6 says that "The Acquirer shall, within a period of fifteen days from the date of the closure of offer, complete all procedures relating to the offer including payment of consideration to the shareholders who have accepted the offer and for the purpose open a special account as provided under regulation 2937 ."

The Takeover Code under the head of general obligations of the acquirer makes it mandatory for the acquirer to fulfil all the formalities including the payment of consideration to the shareholders within 15 days from the closure of offer. The proviso to the abovementioned regulation provides for extension of time to the acquirer under certain conditions.

The proviso to regulation 22(12) says :

"Provided that where the acquirer is unable to make the payment to the shareholders who have accepted the offer before the said period of fifteen days due to non-receipt of requisite statutory approvals, the Board may, if satisfied that non-receipt of requisite statutory approvals was not due to any wilful default or neglect of the acquirer or failure of the acquirer to diligently pursue the applications for such approvals, grant extension of time for the purpose, subject to the acquirer agreeing to pay interest to the shareholders for delay beyond 15 days, as may be specified by the board. . . ."

The proviso clearly lays down the conditions on which an extension could be granted to the acquirer. While applying, the applicant is obliged to disclose all material facts relating to the company. The application can be filed by both the transferor and the transferee company can apply as it was held in the case of Kirloskar Electric Co. Ltd, In re [2003] 43 SCL 186 (Kar.) The tribunal orders for a meeting of the members, after it is satisfied that the scheme is prima facie fair and workable. A report should be received from the registrar of companies stating that the scheme must not be against the interests of the shareholders and the scheme must also be approved by the stakeholders. The tribunal would send the notice of all merger applications which are filed under Section 391 and Section 394 to the Central government, and they have to file its report on the scheme as under Section 394A and the scheme is approved after complying with all the requirements and the certified copy of the order is to file with the concerned authorities.

Perquisite Of Merger And Acquisition To The Corporate World: A Growing Trend

Merger and acquisition purvey dual form of proliferation to the corporate world namely organic growth and inorganic growth. The former occurs due to the internal management and performance of an entity while the latter betides due to the external factors that conceive growth. Merger and acquisition are preferred by copious undertakings as it yields multiple benefits to the entities by enhancing the financial strength, which is also a reason for its growing trend in today's dynamic corporate world. Finalization of mergers provides for several tax deductions to the process of undergoing companies. Merger process also eliminates several entry barriers in a market facilitating new entrants with pristine possibilities and choice. Merger imparts skilled labour potent and promotes integration of employees, diversification is also achieved which ultimately increases market share of the establishment and gains larger access to market.

Impact Of Merger And Acquisition On Competition: A Diluted Perspective

The Competition Act, 2002 intent to promote healthy competition in the market structure and to impede undertakings from having an adverse effect on competition and to obviate abuse of dominant position of an enterprise. The scenario for mergers and acquisitions (regarded as "Combinations" under the act) in prevailing market design may lead to a possible threat to the competition as well as to the provisions enumerated under the act. There endures proximate hazard that a merger would transmute the market to be less competitive in the future whereby limiting consumer choices. Competition prevailing in a relevant market may encounter unilateral effects wherein merged entities attains the potential to increase their prices profitably and unilaterally. This scope to escalate prices is imparted by merger which negates the competitive constraints between the enterprises. Such scaling up of prices is done by entities through merger that produces substitutable products or engages in a similar line of work. Merger and acquisition have the viability to provide a single entity with dominance and ultimate power in the market. Such constraints on the competition may allow an enterprise to abuse its dominance in the relevant market and cause an adverse effect on competition whereby violating sections 3 and 4 of the competition act.

Competition Commission, in the Combination registration dispute of Monsato by Bayer (Combination Registration No. C-2017/08/523), has held that as both entities were active in the vocation of cotton seeds such combination would ensue dilution of competitions and competition.

Merger control regime is nascent in India and is crucial to control combinations to harbour competition in the market. The quiddity of merger control is cardinal due to the impact that merger and acquisition or combination embody on the competition in a market scenario. 3. The CCI is empowered to regulate its own procedure in the light of principles of natural justice and subject to the Rules made by the Central Government2 8. The CCI enacted the Regulations in pursuance of section 64 of the Act to carry out the purposes of the Act. The Regulations allow the combining parties to the combination to file notice under section 6(2) of the Act in Form 1 or Form 2. The Forms differ in terms of the information required to be disclosed by the parties. Form 2 requires the parties to disclose the identity of the parties, nature of products produced by both parties (identical/similar/substitutable), purpose of the combination, do the combining parties have control over another entity engaged in a similar product/service, filing requirements in other jurisdictions, whether the application has been filed in time or not, and why in the opinion of the parties the combination does not have an AAEC amongst others. In addition to the requirements under Form 2, Form 1 requires the combining parties to further furnish details of the main competitors, customers and level of concentration, production capacity of the combining parties in India along with the location of the supply/distribution facilities, price of acquisition, price of main products and competitors’ products, intellectual Property, etc..

The Regulations deem specific transactions not to have an AAEC in India thereby exempting the same from the regulatory framework of the Act2 9. The exempted transactions are :

u Acquisition of shares/voting rights of not more than 15 per cent of the shares/voting rights of the acquired company not leading to the acquirer’s control over the latter, acquisition of assets not related to the business of the acquirer, not leading to the acquirer’s control over the latter except when the acquired assets represent the entire business operations of the acquired entity in a specific area or particular product/service offered by the acquired enterprise, acquisition when the acquirer holds more than 50 per cent of the shares/voting rights of the acquired entity.

u Acquisition in pursuance of a gift, intestate/testamentary succession or transfer by a settler to an irrevocable trust or acquisition of current assets of the acquired company.

u Acquisition of shares/voting rights by a securities underwriter, acquisition of shares/voting rights pursuant to a bonus issue/rights issue/sub-division of shares, acquisition pursuant to an order of the CCI.

u Acquisition of shares/voting rights which would entitle the acquirer to exercise more than 5 per cent of voting rights in any financial year ending March 31, who, with persons acting in concert has acquired 15 per cent or more but less than 55 per cent of the shares/voting rights of additional shares.

Merger control in India : The post-1991 position

6. Part A of Chapter III containing sections 20 to 26 was omitted in 1991. As a result, India, today, has no prior control to bar anti-competitive mergers from taking place. The Statement of Objects and Reasons to the Amendment Act stated thus: "The basic philosophy behind the MRTP Act was never to inhibit industrial growth in any manner but to ensure that such growth is channelised for the public good and is not instrumental in perpetuating concentration of economic power to the common detriment. With the growing complexity of industrial structure and the need for achieving economies of scale for ensuring higher productivity and competitive advantage in the international market, the thrust of the industrial policy has shifted to controlling and regulating the monopolistic, restrictive and unfair trade practices rather than making it necessary for certain undertakings to obtain prior approval of the Central Government for expansion, establishment of new undertakings, merger, amalgamation, takeovers, and appointment of directors. It has been the experience of the Government that pre-entry restriction under the MRTP Act on the investment decision of the corporate sector has outlived its utility and has become a hindrance to the speedy implementation of industrial projects. 'INCOME ARISING FROM AN INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTION' VERSUS 'INCOME CHARGEABLE TO TAX'

It was settled long back that income-tax is only one tax levied on sum total of the income classified and chargeable under various heads. It is not collection of distinct taxes levied separately on each head of income. In Namberumal6 the taxpayer had income from property, other sources and loss from business. Assessing Officer enhanced the property income and in appeal the appellate authority on one hand accepted the plea of taxpayer to restore the amount of property income to the amount returned, however, on the other hand decreased the loss from business, thereby enhancing the business (negative) income. On an overall basis the taxable income of the taxpayer stood reduced after the order of appellate authority. The appeal of the taxpayer against enhancement of business income (reduction of business loss) was rejected as there was no enhancement of the overall total income.

An implication of this principle is that, loss sustained under one head is to be set off against income from another head, as held by Madras High Court7. The principle that income tax is one tax is also upheld by Supreme Court8.

With the help of the above background, when the phrase 'income chargeable to tax' in juxtaposition with word 'loss' is compared to phrase 'income from an international transaction', the Author reaches a conclusion that the former being wider refers to total income which is chargeable to tax while the latter is obviously amount of income from a particular transaction. This is also supported by the fact that the objective of transfer pricing provisions is to counter the ability of multi-national enterprises to allocate profits in different jurisdictions and thereby resulting in erosion of tax revenues9 which would not be the case where net effect of multiple transactions results in reporting a higher than ALP income.

'CASE' VERSUS 'TRANSACTION'

With this background, let's proceed to deal with meaning of phrase "in a case" and conspicuous absence of struck-through words being "to an international transaction".

The word 'transaction' used in sub-section (1) of section 92 is defined to include closely linked transactions while the word 'case' used in sub-section (3) has not been statutorily defined. This is a significant and conscious departure. Thus the presumption is that expression 'case' is not the same is 'closely linked transactions'. Expression 'case' has been used in several legislations in a wider sense, including in Income tax law.

While deciding on the fitness of a case for appeal to Supreme Court the Calcutta High Court10 held that the word 'case' in section 66A(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 is the whole case and not a particular point of law arising in that case. The Supreme Court11 dealing with legality of transfer of case in relation to future proceedings held that the expression 'case' is used in a comprehensive sense of including both pending proceedings as well as proceedings to be instituted in future. In K.L. Jaiswal12 the court interpreted the word 'case' to encompass entire case commencing from filing of the return of wealth-tax till the final adjudication and assessment of the tax liability, penalty proceedings, proceedings for waiver or reduction of the penalty, and not the proceedings which commences from filing of the application under sub-section (4) of section 18B for waiver or reduction of the penalty.

As per section 65(105)( zzc), any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a commercial training or coaching centre in relation to commercial training or coaching, is a ‘taxable service’.

‘Commercial training or coaching’ means any training or coaching provided by a commercial training or coaching centre [Section 65(26)].

‘Commercial training or coaching centre’ means any institute or establishment providing commercial training or coaching for imparting skill or knowledge or lessons on any subject or field other than sports, with or without issuance of a certificate and includes coaching or tutorial classes but does not include pre-school coaching and training centre or any institute or establishment which issues any certificate or diploma or degree or any educational qualification recognised by law for the time being in force [Section 65(27 )].

2.1 IIM short-term courses are ‘education’ - not training or coaching - Education is different from training or coaching. The word ‘education’ is much broader than ‘train’ or ‘coach’. ‘Train’ means train in a particular skill like computer repairs, machine operation etc. ‘Coach’ means special or personal tuition. Giving education in a particular subject is not ‘training’ or ‘coaching’.

Train - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘train’ means to teach (a person, animal, oneself etc.) a specified skill especially by practice. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘train’ means cause or grow in particular way; educate, instruct, exercise.

Coach - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘coach’ means an instructor trainer in sport, a private tutor. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘coach’ means tutor, instructor.

Educate - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘educate’ means give an intellectual, moral and social instruction to (a pupil, especially a child) as a formal and prolonged process. If followed by in or to plus infinitive, it means train or instruct for a particular purpose. ‘Education’ means the act or process of educating or being educated, systematic instruction. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘educate’ means bring up, train mentally and morally; provide schooling for.

Education denotes training of mind, in contradistinction to training in manual skills - Barry v. Hughes [1973] 1 All ER 537 (Ch. D).

Education is the systematic instruction, schooling or training given to the young in preparation for the work of life. It also connotes the whole course of scholastic instruction which a person had received. Education is the process of training and developing the knowledge, skill, mind and character of students by formal schooling - Sole Trustee Loka Shikshana Trust v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 10.

Thus, IIM courses cannot be said to be ‘training’ or ‘coaching’. It is education.

Accordingly, Competition Law seeks to prohibit mergers which are likely to bring about a concentration of market power or an enhanced ability to use market power4.

u MRTP Act, 1969 Section 23 of the MRTP Act, under Chapter III dealing with ‘Concentration for Economic Power’ provided for regulating mergers by undertakings falling under Chapter III of that Act, or mergers that would lead to the creation of Chapter III undertaking. Chapter III also provided for regulating the take over of an undertaking and for acquisition of and transfer of shares above the prescribed threshold levels5.

The entire Chapter III and all parts thereof were omitted in 1991, with the result that mergers and acquisition of shares became subject only to the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 1956.

u Companies Act, 1956

The legislative provisions governing mergers of companies are contained in sections 390 to 396A of the Companies Act.

Under the Companies Act, section 394 read with section 391 provides for approval of the Tribunal (in place of High Court) for any compromise or arrangement proposed between a company and its shareholders and/or its creditors where the compromise or arrangement has been prepared for the purposes of, or in connection with, a scheme for reconstruction of any company or the amalgamation of any two or more companies or where the whole or any part of the undertaking or properties or liabilities of any company concerned in the scheme is to be transferred to another company. The Tribunal may consider the scheme of arrangement or amalgamation after obtaining the consent of shareholders and creditors of the transferor and transferee companies6.

Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)

Under the SEBI, a listed company, that is, a company whose shares are listed for public dealing in any recognised stock exchange is also required to comply with the requirements of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 1997. In terms of these Regulations, if an acquirer acquires 15 per cent or more of the shares or voting rights of any company, the acquirer will make public announcement to acquire shares in accordance with the Regulations. Attention, in particular, is directed to the Takeovers Regulations, Chapter III, regulations 10, 11 and 127.

A comparative study

3. A comparative study of US, EU and UK laws with respect to Merger Regulation is hereinbelow :

u USA - The Clayton Act

Section 7 of the Act is applicable to such transactions which are most instructive8. It lays emphasis on the effect of the acquisition of stock or assets on competition in ‘any line of commerce’. The mere value of the assets or turnover of the enterprises effecting the competition has naturally been ignored as a criterion for determining the effect of the acquisition of stock or assets on competition.

u European Community

Council Regulation (EC) No. 139/2004 of January 20, 2004 discusses the control of concentrations between undertakings (the EC Merger Regulation9). This Regulation will apply to a concentration with a community dimension.

Articles 1(2) and (3) define that when a concentration with a community dimension arises. It is determined by the geographical area of activity of the undertakings concerned, worldwide and in member States, and by the quantitative thresholds of turnover10, prescribed by articles 1(2) and (3). A concentration that would significantly impede effective competition, in the common market or in a substantial part of it, in particular as a result of the creation or strengthening of a dominant position, shall be declared incompatible with common market1 1.

u UK - The Enterprise Act, 2002

It is the duty of the OFT12 to report to the Commission, if it believes that a relevant merger situation is being created which has resulted or may be expected to result, in a substantial lessening of competition within any market or markets in the UK for goods or services13 . Such a reference need not be made on the grounds of de minimis, that is, where adverse effect is negligible, benefit to consumers which is to be determined in accordance with section 30, or when the OFT is considering whether to accept undertakings from the enterprises, and on certain other grounds.

The Tribunal held that on account of the share purchase agreement having been entered into in May 2007, the taxpayer became an AE of both the shareholders during the year. That said, despite there being a prior agreement between Hutchison Telecommunications International Limited, Cayman Islands, and Vodafone International Holdings BV, there was no possibility of a deemed international transaction as HWP (India) was not a third party. Surprisingly though, the Tribunal concluded that the transaction qualified as an international transaction between the taxpayer and Hutchison Group overseas, by disregarding HWP (India) on the premise that it was only an arrangement without any substantial business or commercial interest.

It is worthwhile to note that in the context of deemed international transaction under section 92B(2), the amendment made in the Finance Act, 2014 would still not have had any impact, since the provision still requires a prior agreement to be entered into between the overseas AE and a third party, whether resident or non-resident. In this case, the prior agreement was with an AE.

The conclusion of the Tribunal that a sale between two resident entities could be treated as a transaction between the resident entity and its overseas AE can have significant implications. Transactions such as sale between two resident entities pursuant to a global sale agreement between the overseas AEs of the transacting parties are strictly not covered within the deeming provision even under the amended section 92B(2). However, the Tribunal in this case has treated such domestic transactions as international transactions based on the wide meaning of the term 'transaction', which includes an arrangement between the taxpayer and its AE. While the view of the Tribunal appears to be based on the specific facts of the case, it could encourage the Revenue authorities to rely on this view and seek to treat certain domestic transactions as subject to Transfer Pricing even when they do not fall under the meaning of deemed international transaction or specified domestic transaction.

Conclusion

6. The new Competition Act has indeed sought to promote a merger-friendly line of thinking. It would be difficult to deny that the Act has made significant advances towards this line of thinking. However, this intention is not clearly conveyed through the Act. A few anomalies and low-points under the Act have been mentioned in the previous section. The points stated therein and the suggestions that follow are not very large in scope, but their significance lies in their power to clarify the intention of the Legislature. The said suggestions are not against the spirit of the Act, but to enhance the same and make the final outcome more meaningful and perhaps more effective.

It is to be stated that the provisions of section 28(va)(a) deal with taxability under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession of "any sum whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, under an agreement for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business or profession."

The assessee was a specialist in designing of structures, public health and fire protection services and her proprietary concern was taken over as going concern by a company and she received lump sum consideration. The Assessing Officer opined that maximum of lump-sum was for Goodwill in view of meagre net worth of proprietary concern at time of take-over and considered lump-sum receipt as business receipt being compensation paid to the assessee for 'not carrying out any activity in relation to business of company' as contemplated under section 28(va)(a) of the Act and not capital receipt as claimed by the assessee. The Tribunal held as under-

(i)

The amount arrived at by the Assessing Officer as representing value of goodwill, in fact, represented long term capital gains within meaning of section 50B of the Act.

The procedure of three variants of takeover by a single transferee-company provided in section 395 of the Companies Act holds good as a transparent method for private companies also. In any such case the larger the number of members in the target company proposed to be taken over, the more difficult it will be to achieve unanimity. continuation of the same business in some altered form. This alteration may assume the form of changing the manner or method of carrying on the same business; it may involve change or rationalization of the administrative set-up or business organization. But when its basic nature changes, it cannot be said that the business is 'reconstructed'. It is not every alteration in the mode, method or scope of the activities of a business and it is not every transfer of assets from one unit to another that will involve reconstruction. The expression is no doubt very wide but it does not take in a case of company setting-up or establishing a totally independent and viable industrial unit for carrying on the same or similar business, even though it might be so set-up by way of expanding the already existing business. The expression 'reconstruction', in the context in which it is used, denotes that the original business or an undertaking continues to exist without its identity being lost or abandoned. In the reconstruction of a business, as in the reconstruction of a company, there is an element of transfer of assets and of some change, however partial or restricted it may be, of ownership of the assets. The transfer, however, need not be of all the assets. It is nonetheless imperative that there should be continuity and preservation of the old undertaking, though in an altered form. The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets-up another industrial unit. The new industrial unit would not lose its separate and independent identity, even though it has been set-up by a company which is already running an industrial unit before the setting-up of the new unit.

2.21-3 Whether takeover of a firm by allotting shares to partners is 'reconstruction' ?

In CIT v. Gaekwar Foam Rubber Co. Ltd. [1959] 35 ITR 662 (Bom), under an agreement, assessee-company took over all assets, goodwill and business premises of a partnership for consideration satisfied by allotment of shares to partners of firm and there was no transfer of credits and outstandings nor debts and liabilities of partnership were to be taken over by assessee-company. It was held that the said agree-ment, both in substance and in form, was one of sale and transaction was not of reconstruction of an existing business.

The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be—and this is brought out by the section itself—of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking. The undertaking must continue to carry on the same business though in some altered or varied form. If the alterations and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. Thus for instance if the ownership of a business or an undertaking changes hands not ostensibly but in reality and effectively, that would not be reconstruction or if the very nature of the business is changed, that again would not be reconstruction. On the other hand, reorganization of the business on sounder lines or alterations in the mode or method or scope of the activities of the business or in its personnel or infusion of new blood in the management or control of the business which may even be by some changes in the constitution of persons interested in the undertaking would certainly be no more than reconstruction of the business if it is substantially the same business carried on by substantially the same persons.

In these matters, one has to look at the substance of the transaction and not the form. If looking at the substance of the transaction, it is a sale, then the concept of reconstruction must be ruled out for in such a case there is no scope for speaking about any reconstruction of an existing business. It would be a misnomer to speak of a buyer of an undertaking reconstructing the vendor's business.

The instant case was of transfer of building, machinery, plant and other implements of a shoe factory. The agreement was both in substance and in form one of out and out sale. It was the case of a business of a firm ceasing after the sale of its machinery, etc. when it could not possibly carry on business. The goodwill of the firm was also sold to the assessee-company. The only relation that remained between the vendors and the assessee-company was that the vendors became some of the shareholders in the assessee-company they having been allotted 1,500 ordinary shares of the face value of Rs. 100 each.

The object was to benefit newly established industrial undertakings.

Therefore, this was not reconstruction of an existing business

Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, which provides that where there are general words following particular and specific words, the meaning of the latter words shall be confined to things of the same kind, as specified for interpreting the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature' specified in section 32(1)(ii), it is seen that such rights need not answer the description of 'know-how, patents, trademarks, licenses or franchises' but must be of similar nature as the specified assets.

CIT v. Ingersoll Rand International Ind. Ltd. [2014] 48 taxmann.com 349/227 Taxman 176 (Mag.)(Kar.)

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.
