FACT: By an agreement the assessee-company took over the entire business carried on by a firm. There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. "37 (1) Any expenditure (not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee), laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession shall be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession".

case, the assessee has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of 9 years in a specified area. By this arrangement the assessee has not only derived an advantage by eliminating the competition but also acquired a business which actually generates income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generates income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature. This follows from the decision of the Supreme Court referred to above. The learned counsel for the assessee refers to the decision of the Kerala High Court in V. Damodaran v. CIT [1967] 64 ITR 26 as supporting his stand that if an expenditure is incurred for avoiding rivalry it will be a revenue expenditure. In that case, an assessee, a forest contractor, carrying on business in timber paid a sum of Rs. 2,577 to each of two rival forest contractors in order to persuade them not to compete in an auction of a coupe held by the forest department. The question arose as to the character of the said expenditure. The court held that the expenditure had been incurred to secure a portion of the stock-in-trade of the assessee's timber business at an advantageous price and, therefore, the expenditure was in the nature of business expenditure and allowable as such. We do not see how that decision will help the assessee in this case. There the amount has been spent for acquiring stock-in-trade at an advantageous price by avoiding a competition in an auction to be held by the forest department. In this case, we have already seen that there is no question of any stock-in-trade. The acquisition was of the right to carry on the business owned by a rival on condition that the rival should not carry on the same business for a period of 9 years. These facts clearly attract the decision of the Full Bench of this court in Alagapan Chetty v. CIT [1928] 3 ITC 44 ; AIR 1928 Mad. 902. In that case, the assessee, a carrying contractor, paid a sum of Rs. 12,000 to a rival contractor to induce the latter not to compete with him. As a result of the non-competition of this rival, the assessee obtained the carrying contract at a rate higher than the previous year's rate and this enabled him to make larger profits. The said sum of Rs. 12,000 was claimed as deduction in the computation of the taxable profits under section 10(2)(ix) of the 1922 Act. The Full Bench took the view that the payment of Rs. 12,000 not being for the purpose of working the contract but for obtaining the same, the expenditure was capital in nature and, therefore, not a permissible allowance under section 10(2)(ix). In support of its view the Full Bench had relied on the decision in City of London Contract Corporation Ltd. v. Styles [1887] 2 TC 239 (CA), wherein a payment made by a company for taking over a business of another rival company on payment of certain sum was held to be a capital expenditure. In our view, therefore, the Tribunal is right in holding that the sum of Rs. 1,50,000 was not deductible as an allowable expenditure.

The question is, therefore, answered in the affirmative and against the assessee. The assessee will pay the costs of the revenue which we fix at Rs. 250.

From the above, it may be seen that all fixed assets as per annexure A have to be valued by a valuer. It is true that the assessee-company would also get the benefit of the exclusive use of trademarks as also the tenanted premises, which are inseparable part of the proprietary business as a going concern. The consideration for this obligation has to be calculated as per clauses 6 and 7 reproduced above. On appeal to the High Court : HELD: Section 55 provides for the sale of goodwill after dissolution. From the definition of goodwill as held by the Apex Court in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India AIR 1970 SC 564 and as seen from the provisions of section 55, it is very clear that after the dissolution of a firm, it shall be included in the assets. Therefore, inasmuch as a goodwill could be quantified by way of a sum, the assessee wanted to avoid the same by terming it as technical know-how and compensation. When a business is destroyed, the goodwill goes with it. A goodwill is determined by the nature of business, character, name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio economy and the absence of competition. A goodwill can be sold along with the business or independently. ‘Goodwill’ was brought into tax with effect from 1-4-1988. Therefore, in a commercial and trading parlance, goodwill plays a pivotal role and that is the reason why it has been brought into the tax net. [Para 12.2]

‘Technical know-how’ is defined as an intangible revenue producing asset which can be put to use so as to produce revenue in two ways. The manufacturer can use it himself to make things for sale and make profit in that way, or he can teach it to others, so that they can make their own things, in which case he gets paid for the knowledge and information which he imparts to them. His fees and rewards are then revenue in his hands. Under the Act, transfer of technical know-how is subject to tax only from the assessment year 1998-99 by the amendment through the Finance Act, 1997. [Para 12.3]

In the instant case, there were only two partners in the assessee-firm which consisted of father and son. The assessee had been making good profit over the years as seen from the assessment made for the assessment year 1993-94 onwards. It was a concern running for the past 25 years profitably. It was taken over as a going concern by the limited company. The partners of the assessee-firm were the directors of the limited company. The limited company continued to function in the very same office in which the assessee-firm was functioning earlier. The entire assets had been taken over by the limited company. The agreement between the assessee and the limited company did not make any mention about the payment received for the goodwill. The assessee was not involved in the sale of technical know-how. [Para 13.1]

Therefore, it was clear that inasmuch as the assessee-firm had been taken over as a going concern, it could not have been taken over without the so-called technical know-how. The assessee could not have sold the other tangible assets keeping with it the so-called technical know-how. Hence, the receipts for technical know-how and the compensation for non-competing fees were nothing but a part of composite receipt to diminish the value of the assets of the assessee-firm. The assessee had termed the said amount as receipts for technical know-how in order to escape from the clutches of the provisions of section 55(2) under which a goodwill amount is taxable. [Para 13.2]

There was no material on record to establish the cost of the technical know-how as observed by the Tribunal. There was also no material to quantify the amount shown as paid to the assessee for the transfer of the alleged technical know-how. There was no explanation as to why no amount had been received towards the goodwill considering the undisputed fact of the good performance of the assessee-firm over the years before the transfer. The assessee had clearly attempted to evade tax by claiming the amount received as goodwill as one of technical know-how in order to evade tax. The assessee had tried to sell the old wine in a new bottle by characterizing the receipt as technical know-how. It was not the case of the assessee that it had been selling the technical know-how to any other third party. The agreement also did not provide a clause to the effect that the assessee would not indulge in the same business. That was for the precise reason that the assessee had merely changed from being a partnership firm into one of a private company due to business and commercial expediency. [Para 13.3]

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) further noted that the assessee-company had not completely given up the whole structure of its profit making apparatus as per some of the clauses of the non-compete agreement. Accordingly, he upheld the Assessing Officer’s action.

The agreement entered into by the assessee-company with B does not indicate that the film shorts as stock-in-trade were the subject-matter of the bargain. In substance and effect, the agreement involved a transfer of the B's business to the assessee-company for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. It cannot be said that the said sum was paid for acquiring the stock-in-trade. The assessee-company has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of nine years in a specified area. By this agreement, the assessee-company has in fact derived an advantage by eliminating the competition and acquired a business which actually generated income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generated income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature.

The assessee-firm was manufacturer of transformers. During relevant assessment year, its business was taken over as a going concern by a limited company and its partners became directors of the said company. The said company made certain payments to the assessee for technical know-how and as compensation for pending and expected orders, i.e., not to compete and indulge in transformer business. During assessment proceedings, a show-cause notice was issued to the assessee as to why the amounts shown as received for non-competition fee for pending orders, future orders and for the transfer of technical know-how would not be treated as capital gains, inasmuch as no amount had been shown under the head ‘Goodwill’ even though the assessee had been making good profit in the previous years. The assessee contended that it had not received any money towards the goodwill from the company and inasmuch as for the assessment year 1995-96, a transfer of technical know-how was not taxable, it could not be termed as long-term capital gain. The Assessing Officer held that the receipt for technical know-how was nothing but a part of the composite receipt to cover the value of the intangible assets and inasmuch ‘goodwill’ was taxable under section 55(2), an attempt was made to evade the payment of tax. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer treated the entire amount as capital gains. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim in respect of amount received for technical know-how and compensation for pending orders but disallowed the amount of compensation for expected orders. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that there was no indication of the value of the technical know-how in the balance sheet and it had come into existence only at the time of signing the transfer agreement. It held that the agreement was for the transfer of entire business of a going concern and the amount indicated as the payment for technical know-how was nothing but a goodwill amount which was a colourable device to evade tax. The Tribunal further held that in view of the taking over of the going concern, the assessee-firm had come to an end, more so when the partners were also the directors and, therefore, there was no question of paying the non-competing fees, inasmuch as there was no possibility of the assessee-firm doing the very same business again. Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by the revenue and dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee.

On appeal to the High Court :

In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Note - The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

Section 43(1)  of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee-company took over assets of dissolved firm of which it was partner at book value and it was not found that the whole thing was colourable device, assessee was entitled to depreciation on assets at book value at which they were taken over and Explanation 3 to section 43(1) was not applicable
Dy. Commissioner v. Metalizing Equipment Co. (P.) Ltd. [1996] 54 TTJ (Jp.) 620
Any device which has the effect of reducing the incidence of tax, is not necessarily a colourful device liable to be demolished by the ratio of the Supreme Court’s decision in McDowell & Co. Ltd. v. CTO [1985] 154 ITR 148/22 Taxman 11.
In order to invoke the provisions of Explanation 3 to section 43(1), it is incumbent upon the Assessing Officer first to establish that the device adopted by the assessee was either contrary to any law, or against accounting principles or against accepted practices and by using such device, singly or in combination with others, one had deprived the exchequer of its legitimate revenue. Unless these two conditions are fulfilled, the Assessing Officer is not empowered to charge the assessee with the allegation of dodging the revenue.
Where the assessee took over assets and liabilities of dissolved firm of which he was partner at book value and there was no finding by the Assessing Officer that entering in the firm as a partner, dissolution of the firm, taking over of the business of the firm by the assessee-company and its assets and liabilities and so on, were a set of transactions, though lawful, yet aimed at deceiving the Department, the assessee was entitled to claim depreciation on book value at which they were taken and Explanation 3 to section 43(1) was not applicable to the case.

A bare perusal of the agreement entered into between the parties would show that the sole aim of floating the JVC was to carry on the business of manufacture and sale of refrigeration equipment. It was stipulated in the agreement that ‘A’ would pay a sum of Rs. ninty lakhs to the assessee for agreeing not to undertake the competing business of refrigeration equipment and refrigeration systems.

The essence of the agreement between the parties was to stop the assessee from competing in the business in the field of JVC. ‘A’ had a world presence and had better reputation in the market and, consequently, better goodwill than the assessee. The said company incorporated in Switzerland, having wider operations and business in refrigeration systems, had agreed to the inclusion of its part name in the name of the JVC in order to promote the business of JVC. From the conduct of the parties, it was clear that the assessee and ‘A’ had jointly set up the JVC in India using their respective technical expertise and as the assessee was already carrying on the business of refrigeration in India, in order to stop its operation in India, it was necessary to compensate the assessee for foregoing its right to continue its business activity and, consequently, a sum of Rs. ninty lakhs was paid as consideration to it. [Para 13.1]

The terms and conditions in shareholders’ agreement were in furtherance to the agreement entered into between the parties which stipulated the rights and duties of the assessee and ‘A’ for smooth carrying on the business in the JVC. The agreement was the basic document determining the terms and conditions agreed upon between the assessee and ‘A’ and it clearly stipulated that the payment was being made to the assessee for agreeing not to carry on the competing business of refrigeration equipment and refrigeration systems. That, by no stretch of imagination, could be treated as payment for ‘goodwill’, although, the term ‘goodwill ’ had been used both in the agreement and the books of account. Taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of the case in totality, the payment was not made for the transfer of goodwill but was made to restrict the assessee from carrying on its business and, consequently, the same was on account of compensation for not carrying on the business activities and it was, accordingly, on account of non-competing fees. [Para 14]

The assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern. The TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and the assessee was the highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores. The same was accepted by the TISCO in its Board meeting on 18-12-1998. Thereupon, the cement units were actually taken over and used in its own production activity. After acquiring the company units as going concern as the assessee, on the basis of valuation report of 'K' fixed the fair market value of fixed assets as on the date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores. The balance amount of consideration of Rs. 68. 61 crores was attributed to the net current assets taken over. The assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on the value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores. In the course of assessment the Assessing Officer asked for the WDV of the assets of TISCO. Since the assessee expressed its inability to furnish the details as they purchased the assets on the basis as going concern, the Assessing Officer obtained the information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that the said company had shown the book value of fixed assets at Rs. 345. 95 crores and after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers, offered profits on sale of net assets of cement division at Rs. 125. 25 crores in their books of account. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had paid more amount than the book value and the difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment and accordingly after discussion about the provisions of section 43(1) , report of the registered valuer, determined the goodwill value at the difference between the amount adopted by the assessee and the amount shown in the books of TISCO and depreciation on the amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed thereby making addition of Rs. 16. 39 crores. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) it was contended that the assessee had acquired fixed assets and current assets of the unit in an open bid and on the basis of the report of the registered valuer the value was accordingly capitalized to the extent of Rs. 481. 39 crores and Assessing Officer's action in taking the WDV of TISCO was not correct as Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case as these two companies were independent and not related and further the Assessing Officer had not correctly appreciated the registered valuer's report and the method adopted. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contentions and set aside the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

On appeal it was claimed that assets and liabilities of SVR were taken over by the assessee for a consideration of Rs. 8.50 lakhs as per agreement dated 23-5-1987. As the assessee-company was not in a position to depute its staff it was agreed that from 23-5-1987, SVR would continue to manage the affairs of the business taken over. SVR thus incurred expenses of Rs. 4,71,782 during the period from 23-5-1987 to 31-5-1988, on behalf of the assessee-company. It was also claimed that all the assets of company were not taken over. The net worth of the assets taken over was Rs. 14,06,338 excluding the liability of cash credit account with the bank of Rs. 9,75,222 which was settled separately. It was also claimed that since the assessee-company required time to obtain approval for commencement of production in its own name it was agreed that production will be continued by SVR. The unit was kept in working condition and some raw material was converted into finished products. It was, therefore, claimed that total expenses incurred by SVR at Rs. 3,49,017 were wholly and exclusively for keeping the unit in working condition on behalf of the assessee and same being of revenue nature should have been fully allowed.
Held that in the present case though there was an agreement made on 23-5-1987 to take over the assets and liabilities of SVR including the raw material and finished goods but the said goods were in fact purchased by the assessee and possession taken not during the current year but in the succeeding assessment year 1989-90. Thus, the business of manufacturing or trading did not commence during the current year, but the same was commenced only in the following year when the said goods were purchased and manufacturing activity started and in this view of the matter the expenses claimed for the period prior to the commencement of manufacturing/trading business were not admissible. Thus, the claim for the expenses of Rs. 3,49,017 claimed to have been incurred by SVR on behalf of the assessee-company during the year, was rightly disallowed by the ITO.

3. Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1): Supreme Court

Sharp Business System v. Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 181 taxmann.com 657 (SC)

Assessee, a public limited company, was engaged in the business of software development, hardware sales, technical training and engineering services. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year, declaring a net loss. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) computed the assessee's total income and made several disallowances. One of the disallowances concerned the depreciation claim on the non-compete fee.

Aggrieved-assessee preferred an appeal to the CIT(A), where it contended that the non-compete fee was nothing but a license. Assessee could exclusively carry on the business of software development, training and export of technologies by restraining M/s. Pentamedia Graphics Limited is not allowed to carry out the same activities. Thus, the payment of the non-compete fee was held to be an intangible asset entitled to depreciation under Section 32(1)(ii).

The matter, after passing through the ITAT and the High Court, was carried in appeal before the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court ruled that non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. The purpose of a non-compete payment is to give the payer's business a head start. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the payer's business or enhancing its profitability by insulating it from competition.

Thus, the non-compete fee seeks only to protect or enhance the business's profitability, thereby facilitating its carrying on more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in the creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit-earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, of restricting a competitor in business is not in the capital field.

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring such expenditure.

Thus, the Supreme Court held that a payment made by the assessee as a non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Act.

4. Section 44C covers head office expenses, whether common or solely for Indian branches: SC

Director of Income-tax (IT)-I, Mumbai v. American Express Bank Ltd. [2025] 181 taxmann.com 433 (SC)

The assessee, a non-resident banking company, filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year. While computing the income, the assessee claimed a deduction for expenses incurred at the head office directly related to the Indian branches.

The Assessing Officer (AO) contended that the expenses in question should be subject to the ceiling specified in Section 44C. The assessee claimed that the expenses in question could not have been classified as head office expenditure for the reason that Section 44C presupposes that at least a part of the expenditure is attributable to the business outside India. If this presumption does not hold, and the entire expenditure is incurred solely for the business in India, Section 44C would not apply.

The AO passed an assessment order limiting the deduction under Section 44C to 5% of the gross total income. The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that to be brought within the ambit of Section 44C, two broad conditions must be satisfied: (i) The assessee claiming the deduction must be a non-resident; and (ii) The expenditure in question must strictly fall within the definition of 'head office expenditure' as provided in the Explanation to the Section.

CASES WHEREIN IT HAS BEEN HELD THAT TRANSACTIONS FELL WITHIN THE AMBIT OF SECTION 50B OF THE ACT

30.9-1 The ITAT Delhi Bench in the case of Asstt CIT v. Smt. Sangeeta Wij [2012] 24 taxmann.com 128/54 SOT 1 (URO) (Delhi-Trib.) held that where under agreement what was transferred was right to carry on business, application of main section 28(va)(a) of the Act was foreclosed and forbidden and the amount was taxable as capital gain under section 50B of the Act.

It is to be stated that the provisions of section 28(va)(a) deal with taxability under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession of "any sum whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, under an agreement for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business or profession."

The assessee was a specialist in designing of structures, public health and fire protection services and her proprietary concern was taken over as going concern by a company and she received lump sum consideration. The Assessing Officer opined that maximum of lump-sum was for Goodwill in view of meagre net worth of proprietary concern at time of take-over and considered lump-sum receipt as business receipt being compensation paid to the assessee for 'not carrying out any activity in relation to business of company' as contemplated under section 28(va)(a) of the Act and not capital receipt as claimed by the assessee. The Tribunal held as under-

(i)

The amount arrived at by the Assessing Officer as representing value of goodwill, in fact, represented long term capital gains within meaning of section 50B of the Act.

(ii)

As per agreement what was transferred was right to carry on business and hence, application of main section 28(va)(a) of the Act was foreclosed and forbidden by proviso (i) thereof.

The proviso(i) referred to above reads as under-

"Provided that sub-clause (a) shall not apply to—(i) any sum, whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, on account of transfer of the right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing or right to carry on or profession, which is chargeable under the head 'Capital gains'"

This order of the Tribunal was affirmed by the Delhi High Court in CIT v. Sangeeta Wig [2014] 42 taxmann.com 146/221 Taxman 159 (Mag.)(Delhi) wherein it was held that "where the assessee parted with controlling interest in business of her proprietary concern and as consideration, along with money, she received shares in new company and assessee had not carried on the said business or received consideration as a non-compete fee, total consideration received was capital gain."

The High Court at para. 3 of its judgment approved the approach of the Tribunal when it (the Tribunal) after a detailed consideration of the law on the subject referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Motors & General Stores (P.) Ltd. [1967] 66 ITR 692 (SC) to the effect that "the real intention of the parties has to be gathered on the appreciation of a background in its entirety instead of focusing either on the nomenclature or concentrating on certain parts of it."

The High Court also approvingly noted that the Tribunal referred to Board Circular 779 dated 14th September, 1999 and after analysing the circular arrived at the right decision after taking into account the contents of this circular.

30.9-2 The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Equinox Solution (P.) Ltd. [2017] 80 taxmann.com 277/247 Taxman 89/393 ITR 566 (SC) held that "whereas the provisions of section 50(2) of the Act apply to a case where any block of assets is transferred by the assessee but where the entire running business with assets and liabilities is sold by the assessee in one go, such sale cannot be considered as sale of 'short term capital assets' as it was a slump sale of a 'long term capital asset' and be taxed accordingly."

30.9-3 The ITAT Cochin Bench in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Ooty Gate Hotel [2019] 101 taxmann.com 163/174 ITD 513 (Cochin-Trib.) held that "where assessee sold its hotel premises along with licences for boarding, lodging, bar etc. as a going concern to a buyer who was also engaged in hotel business, it could be regarded as a case of slump sale and, thus, Assessing Officer was justified in applying provisions of section 50B of the Act to the assessee's case."

It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

were also the trustees of the trust, could have continued for an indefinite period. Therefore, it is difficult to dispute that elimination of competition from Trust brought benefits of an enduring nature to the assessee company. [Para 22]

Elimination of competition from the Trust brought benefit of an enduring nature to the assessee-company, in the field of capital and, therefore, increase in lease rent, to the extent it is attributable to this benefit, would be a capital expenditure. [Para 23] The assessee contended that since elimination of competition from the Trust did not happen simultaneous with acquisition of Katha and Cutch business of the Trust, enhancement of lease rent, even to the extent it is attributable to elimination of competition from the Trust, would not constitute capital expenditure. This is not an absolute proposition of law that in order to constitute capital expenditure, the payment/compensation for elimination of competition should be coupled with acquisition of business of the rival and both the things should happen at the same time. In a given case, either the payment to eliminate competition may be post acquisition of business of the rival or elimination of competition may not be accompanied by acquisition of business of the rival. It is very much possible for a rival to agree not to compete in a given area, while continuing with the same business in other areas. In such a case, there would be no takeover of the business of the rival. In any case, as far as instant case is concerned, as would be seen from the lease deeds executed between the assessee and Trust, that the Trust had leased whole of its production unit which was a profit generating unit to the assessee and not only the building, but the plant and machinery was also leased to the assessee along with all benefits, etc. Even the liability towards gratuity of the employees of the trust was taken over. The Trust had also relinquished its right to purchase Khairwood from the Government in favour of the assessee. This is not the case of the assessee that even after lease deed dated 18-1-1992, the Trust continued with the business of manufacture and trading of Katha and Cutch in areas beyond 1000 kilometres from the leased premises. Therefore, the business being carried by 'Mahesh Udyog' was practically taken over by the assessee-company for an indefinite period. The lease deed also shows that the lessee had approached the Trust that it should stop commercial dealings in Katha and Cutch and in lieu thereof it had agreed to compensate the Trust for the loss that would be caused to it by stopping such commercial dealings. Therefore, this was a case of takeover of the business, coupled with elimination of competition from the rival. It is also evident from a perusal of the lease deed dated 18-1-1992 that the previous lease deed executed between the parties was repealed simultaneous with the execution of the new lease deed on 18-1-1992. Therefore, technically speaking in this case, acquisition of assets of the trust and elimination of competition from the Trust took place simultaneously. In fact, the whole transaction between Trust and assessee was a composite transaction, without apportionment of lease rent into various components of the transaction. Therefore, from whatever point of view, one may examine, there is no escape from the conclusion that increase in lease rent, to the extent it was relatable to elimination of competition from the Trust, constitutes capital expenditure. [Para 27]

Applicability of section 40A(2)

The objective behind section 40A is to address evasion of tax under the cloak or guise of permissible deductions by checking payments made or benefits granted made to closely connected persons and entities ostensibly for the goods sold or services rendered by them. Admittedly, Trust is a charitable trust and by itself the Trust does not hold any share of the assessee-company. The Trust is not entitled to any profit out of the business being run by the assessee-company. Hence, the Trust does not have a substantial interest in the business of the assessee-company. [Para 29]

It is not in dispute that at least some of the trustees are also directors and shareholders of the assessee-company. The maximum shareholding in the assessee-company was owned by the trustees and their relatives as defined in section 2(41). However, clause (v ) of section 40A(2)(b) brings only such companies, firms, HUFs or association of persons within its purview, directors/partners/members of which have a substantial interest in the business or profession of the assessee. The interest of the relatives of a director/partner/member of such company/firm/HUF/association of persons cannot be taken into consideration to ascertain whether the director/partner/member have substantial interest in the business of the assessee or not. The Explanation provides that a person shall be deemed to have a substantial interest in a business if in a case where the business is carried on by a company, he, at any time, during the previous year, was the beneficial owner of shares carrying not less than 20 per cent of the voting power. The Tribunal has not given any finding with respect to exact shareholding of the trustees in the assessee-company during the relevant previous years, and there was no material to indicate the exact shareholding of the trustees in the assessee-company during the years to which these appeals pertain. [Para 30]

The functional profile of this company is acceptable to both the parties at the initial stage itself. The assessee did not put any evidence to show that the company is functionally dissimilar. The only grievance of the assessee is that the comparable company has entered into an extraordinary event and therefore it becomes not comparable. It is the contention of the assessee that during the year the company has acquired shares of another company and therefore this is the extraordinary event that makes it not comparable. However, this contention of the assessee is not agreeable for the reason that it is purely an investment decision and it does not have any impact on the function performed by the assessee, assets employed for the revenue earned and risk assumed. The action of putting investment into another company did not have any impact on the profitability of the company, no such impact was shown, and therefore there is no reason to exclude this comparable. Therefore, the contention of the assessee for exclusion of the above comparable is rejected.[Para 22]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922) - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1953-54 to 1955-56 - Assessee-company took over routes of various private operators and paid compensation to get rid of competition from said operators - Whether compensation so paid was an expenditure of capital nature and, thus, it could not be allowed as deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

FACT: On incorporation the assessee-company became one of the partners of the firm 'NS', with effect from 1-8-1976. That firm was dissolved on 31-12-1976 and as a consequence the assets and liabilities of the erstwhile firm along with the business vested with the assessee-company. The dissolution deed that was drawn up, specified about the royalty that would be payable to the retiring partners for not doing such business for fifteen years arising out of the business of firm. The assessee by virtue of the dissolution deed, which was agreed to by it, provided royalty in its books by crediting to the two retired partners. The amount of royalty which was so shown as payable to the two retired partners for various assessment years, was claimed as revenue expenditure; but that was not accepted by the ITO. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Note - The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1951 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 to 1999-2000 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns, engaged in similar business as going concern, for certain consideration - In addition, assessee undertook to pay certain amount per month to said concerns for a period of 15 years in consideration of non-compete obligation undertaken by them and claimed said payments as revenue expenditure - Whether said payments, having been made for eliminating competition in same line of business for a sufficiently long period of 15 years, were of capital nature and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired the proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns engaged in same business as going concerns for certain consideration. In addition thereto, the assessee under- took to pay Rs. 3.5 lakh and Rs. 2 lakh per month to the two concerns, respectively, for a period of 15 years in consideration of the non-compete obligation undertaken by the said concerns. In the assessment, the assessee claimed that the said payment made to dissuade the said proprietary concerns from continuing independent business, which would be detrimental to it, was to be allowed as the revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that the expenditure was clearly capital in nature, as the same was incurred by the assessee to ward off competition over a long period of time. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s said claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: From various cases, the legal position which clearly emerges is that any ‘non-compete’ fee, which is paid to ward off competition over a sufficiently long period of time, has to be considered as capital expenditure. Depending upon the facts and circumstances, in some cases, it has been held that even though the period of non-competition may be 2 to 5 years, the non-compete fee would still be in the nature of capital. [Para 13]

On a careful consideration of the legal position, as applied to the facts of the assessee’s case, the payments made by the assessee to the two proprietary concerns for a period of 15 years as per the terms and conditions of the agreement, could not be treated as revenue expenditure. The proprietary concerns had been acquired by the assessee as going concerns. The two proprietors, by virtue of the agreement, had transferred the respective business along with rights, assets and liabilities which included trademarks, etc. In addition to the value of the assets, the assessee had undertaken to pay a sum of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per month to one proprietor and a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs per month to another proprietor, which was clearly for eliminating competition in the same line of business, for a sufficiently long period of 15 years. The use of trademark, if any, by the assessee was only an inseparable part of the entire arrangement. By the ‘non-compete’ clause of the agreement, the erstwhile proprietors were automatically excluded from use of such trademarks and they had bound themselves contractually not to carry on similar business activity, in whatever names, for a period of 15 years. As a consideration, the impugned monthly payments were to be paid by the assessee for a period of 15 years. It means that on the expiry of the non-compete period of 15 years, the payments would also cease to be made. There was not much merit in the arguments of the assessee that the payments were partly attributable to the benefit acquired by the assessee by way of user of the tenanted premises at a nominal rent. There was no reference to that fact in the agreement. Further, the landlord or owner of such premises was not a party to the agreement and even if some benefit had accrued to the assessee, it was entirely on account of the Rent Control Act, which might be applicable. The business premises, either owned or rented, had been taken over by the assessee as part of the overall agreement or arrangement for purchase of proprietary business as going concern along with all assets and liabilities. [Para 16]

The argument submitted by the assessee, that one of the proprietors agreed for inclusion of the amount in its total income for taxation purposes, had only some persuasive value. The treatment given in the hands of the recipient did not determine the nature of the payment in the case of the payee.

Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the issue was to be reversed and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to disallow the relevant expenditure treating it to be capital expenditure. [Para 17]

From the finding of the Assessing Officer, it is clear that the assessee's commodity trading was transferred entirely along with its clientele to the new floated company GCL. The new company, though not a subsidiary of the assessee or its parent company, was promoted by the promoters of the holding company of the assessee. In the new company, 53.13 per cent of the share belongs to the wife of one C.J.George, who is the promoter of the holding company of the assessee. Though the assessee-company had surrendered its license with various commodity exchanges in the month of December, 2008, at the very same time, the new company GCL had obtained license, as a member of commodity exchanges where the assessee had surrendered its license. The entire clientele consisting of 6000 clients were transferred in toto to the new company GCL. The credit balance in respect of the clients of the assessee-company were transferred to the books of account of the GCL. The new company, GCL had entered into an agreement with the assessee's parent company for the use of trademark 'Geojit' and therefore, as rightly pointed out by the Assessing Officer, in the eyes of the clients, the business is carried on in the same name. Moreover, the business of the new company was carried out in the same premises of the parent company, making uses of the administrative set up, the equipments and the manpower etc. of the parent company of the assessee. This categorical finding of the Assessing Officer has not been dispelled by the assessee by placing any contra evidence. In this context, the Assessing Officer had come to a conclusion that there is no impairment in the loss of commodity trade to the group concern namely 'Geojit'. Therefore, it was held that the profit making apparatus of the assessee-company/the group company was not impaired by the discontinuance of commodity trade business of the assessee per se. Since there is no sterilization of income/profit earning apparatus from the consolidate perspective of the group concerns, viz., `Geojit', the amount so received by the assessee as compensation cannot be termed as a capital receipt not liable to be taxed under the provisions of the I.T.Act. Therefore, the finding of the Assessing Officer in this context is upheld.[Para 6.3]

As regards the issue whether the amount was taxable under section 28(va), the assessee referring to CBDT Circular No. 8 of 2002, submitted that the said provision is only applicable to a situation wherein the assessee receives payment from a competitor in the same business in lieu of accepting restrictive/negative covenant not to carry any particular activity in relation to the business, without there being any transfer of right to carry on the business. It was submitted that such payment restrains the recipient payee from carrying on competitive business for the period for which non-compete agreement was to last, in order to protect the profitability of the payer who is a competitor/rival in the same business. In other words, it was submitted that the amount of compensation would be taxable under the provisions of section 28(va) only if it is found that the compensation is paid as a non-compete fee.[Para 6.4]

The assessee-company in the instant case, had received the compensation for not carrying on any activities in relation to its commodity trading business. The compensation so paid for not carrying any activity in relation to any business (commodity trading business) would be taxable going by the plain meaning of section 28(va)(a). Section 28(va) was introduced with effect from 1-4-2003. Though there was no written agreement for payment of compensation, the letters of BNP Paribas dated 23-5-2008 and 27-5-2008 and the Board Resolution of the assessee-company stating that it would discontinue the commodity trading business of the assessee on receipt of compensation of Rs. 40 crores, would come within the ambit of an arrangement/undertaking/action in concert, whether or not, the same was formal or in writing or it was intended to be enforceable by legal proceedings and that would tantamount to an agreement for the purpose of section 28(va). The wordings of section 28(va) is unambiguous and clear. The said section does not restrict, the bringing to tax only the non-compete fee but any sum that was received or receivable in cash or kind for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business. The exception for such taxation is only the cash received on account of transfer of right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing or right to carry on any business, which is chargeable under the head 'Capital gains'.[Para 6.5]

The assessee's proprietary concern SD through which she provided consultancy in Civil Engineering was taken over as going concern by ICT-SD w.e.f. 31-10-2007. In this respect, assessee received a compensation of Rs. 1,20,00,000 being the total enterprise value of SD including goodwill vide Agreement dated 4-12-2007. The Assessing Officer observed that against the net worth of SD being Rs. 4,73,725 as on 31-10-2007 the value of goodwill was calculated at Rs. 1,15,26,275 which was grossly over-valued.

The Assessing Officer further observed that as per the Agreement, the assessee was required to work exclusively as a whole-time Director of the ICT-SD at least for five years on salary plus perks, and that in case she was relieved earlier, she would be adequately compensated; that she shall not carry out any activity or engage, directly or indirectly in any other business directly or indirectly related to the business of ICT-SD, and that however, she would be at liberty to do any business whatsoever after quitting. From these contents, the Assessing Officer opined that the compensation of Rs. 1,20,00,000 was not a capital receipt liable for capital gains as claimed by the assessee, but a business receipt and that rather, the compensation was for 'not carrying out any activity in relation to the business of the Company' as contemplated under section 28(va)(a). Accordingly, the compensation amount was added to the total income of the assessee under the head 'business income'. Commissioner (Appeals), however, deleted the addition.

On appeal by the revenue:

The assessee-company, whose main business was as contractors, became a partner in a firm on 1-4-1980, with the sole intention of taking over the firm’s business, which comprised, inter alia, business in cotton and kapas. On the dissolution of the firm on 11-11-1980, the assessee took over the firm’s business, and its share in the firm’s business amounted to a loss of Rs. 16,005. The assessee claimed set off of this loss against its business income, but the ITO disallowed the claim on the ground that, since it related to the acquisition of a business, it was a capital expenditure. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the assessee’s claim.

On the revenue’s appeal:
[2004] 91 ITD 153 (Kolkata) (TM)[04-08-2003] Vinod Kothari Consultants Ltd. vs. Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax

INCOME TAX : Where in view of non-compete agreement entered into by assessee with a company from which it acquired business, non-compete fee paid by assessee would form part of initial outlay on acquisition of business, Assessing Officer was justified in treating said non-compete fee as capital expenditure and disallowing same under section 37(1)

An overall analysis of the agreements did not anywhere manifest the intention of the parties that the assessee wants to continue to carry on the same business or that the assessee received the consideration Rs. 1.20 crores as a non-compete fee as is being contended by the Revenue. The transaction was, to put it plainly, one whereby she parted with her controlling interest in the concerned business which was taken over by ICT-SD. As part of the consideration payable, she had received shares to the tune of 45% of the said company. There is no infirmity in the appellate order of the Tribunal. [Para5]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Whether where business carried on by a firm on its dissolution was transferred to assessee partner company, amount of royalty payable to out going partners for restraining them from carrying on similar business for 15 years was not allowable as business expenditure, but was to be treated as capital expenditure it being paid for purpose of out bidding competitors - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 2001-02 and 2002-03 - Whether to test whether benefit derived by assessee by making a payment is of enduring nature, only point to be considered is whether threat which is perceived at time of agreement/incurring of expenditure will cease to exist after expiry of period or will re-occur - Held, yes - Whether where threat has potential of re-occurring after expiry of period, then benefit derived cannot be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate - It acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores - Assessee had also entered into another ‘non-compete agreement’ with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them - Under said agreement ‘V’ and ‘M’ were restricted to engage themselves in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with abovesaid chemicals for period of 5 years - In return assessee claimed whole of expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that expenditure was not incurred for improving profitability as there was no existing business and assessee had acquired business of chemicals for first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to company and disallowed claimed expenditure - Whether since ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ both being well in a position financially, as well as otherwise, to compete with assessee even after a period of five years, it could be said that threat which was perceived at time of agreement still subsisted and was liable to re-occur at expiry of period of five years and benefit derived could not be said to be of enduring nature - Held, yes - Whether carrying on of same business prior to entering into non-compete agreement is not necessary to appreciate as to whether non-compete agreement is to enhance assessee’s profitability or not - Held, yes - Whether since benefit to be derived by assessee in consequence upon incurring expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to enhancement of assessee’s profitability in business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals, it could be said that said expenditure was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes

ised for the purpose of suing and of being sued. It is in this light of the legal notion of a partnership firm that the status of an assessee in just a position to the firm has to be adjudged. The constitution of both the firm and the assessee disclosed that there were identical partners in both. The sharing also was reported to be similar. In such circumstances, the law treated them as only one firm, though, for convenience, they transacted business under two different trading styles. When the assessee voluntarily undertook to pay the demand in question as sales tax, it did it because of its conscious identity of the personnel of the firm and that of the assessee. Such unison and identity in purpose and in commerce was the intention behind the undertaking being taken over by the assessee. No doubt, it took over all the liabilities and assets, which included the sales tax reserve. This again was at a time when the statutory liability for sales tax payable for the year was not quantified. Here again the intention was clear that the assessee undertook the liability for sales tax, whatever might be the amount, in order to continue its trade. What may be normally said of an ordinary trade liability cannot be said of a statutory liability or a fiscal liability. Such a liability is assumed not because of the contract of transfer of assets, but because it is a necessary annexure to the incidence of the business having been taken over and continued.

In the instant case, merely because for purposes of taxation laws the assessee and the firm were two different legal entities, it could not be said that in the light of the facts disclosed, the businesses of the firm and the assessee were in any manner different. The nexus interlacing in their business was so conspicuous that their fictional legal individuality in tax laws became submerged in their commercial unison, as understood in the common law of partnership.

It, therefore, follows that, if the business of the firm and the assessee was thus interlocked, then the assessee's claim for deduction of the statutory liability in such a common trading activity between the assessee and the firm had to be upheld under section 37(1).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

I. Section  37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business expenditure  -  Allowability of  (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year  2001-02  - Assessee, a company, was engaged in business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipment in India - It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and L & T - During year, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L &T as consideration for latter not setting up or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years - Said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in return of income filed by assessee as non-compete fee paid to L &T - Assessing Officer held that such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, hence, treated payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure - Whether non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance profitability of business, thereby facilitating carrying on of business more efficiently and profitably and, thus, such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to profit earning apparatus of payer - Held, yes - Whether, further, on facts, assessee had not acquired any new business and there was no addition to profit making apparatus of assessee, assets remained same and expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of same business and, thus, non-compete fee paid by assessee was an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes [Paras 26, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

Section 28(va) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Non-compete fees - Assessment year 2001-02 - Where assessee, an artist and film director, transferred its proprietary business to a company as a going concern and agreed to provide her expertise in film making to said company, non-compete fee received by her would be assessed as revenue receipt in view of fact that (a) assessee was, and continued to be, face of business as proprietrix and (b) thereafter, as a director with substantial shareholding, she retained a firm hold on reins of decision making [In favour of revenue]   The assessee, an artist and film director with a significant presence in the big as well as small screens entered into an agreement with a company RPPL in terms of which she agreed to provide her expertise in film making, tele-serials and discussions to the company, and not to compete with the business of the company in India or elsewhere. The agreement, in force for a period of 5 years, provided for consideration of an amount of Rs. 75 lakhs by way of allotment of 75,000 equity shares of a nominal value of Rs. 100 each. That apart, the parties had entered into a succession agreement that provided for the succession of the company to the business of the assessee as a going concern, taking over all the assets and liabilities in its books for a consideration. In case of the assessee, the Assessing Officer held that the amount of Rs. 75 lakhs was in the nature of a remuneration paid to her for loss of business occasioned to her by virtue of the terms of non-compete. He also noticed that the assessee retained control over the business even after execution of the succession agreement insofar as she continued in the position of a director in the company holding more than 99.99 per cent voting rights. He, therefore, held that the arrangement of payment of non-compete fee was itself a colourable exercise and made addition of said amount in assessee's hands.  Held that the assessee's sole proprietary concern was succeeded to by the company on 31-3-2000. She was duly compensated for the assets transferred. Parallelly, an agreement was entered into between the parties to provide for a more systematic utilization and exploitation of the creative talents and skills of the artist. The artist, who was managing the business as a proprietary concern, continued to be part of the corporate structure, employing the same skill sets as always employed by her. It was only the business setting that was enlarged over the relevant period. The assessee was, and continued to be, the face of the business as proprietrix and thereafter, as a director with substantial shareholding, she retained a firm hold on the reins of decision making. The transaction of non-compete agreement was thus an illusion in the aforesaid facts and circumstances. Therefore, non-compete fee was rightly added to assessee's income.

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1974-75 - Assessee-company took over a firm with its assets and liabilities - It discharged tax liabilities of firm during previous year and claimed expenditure as deduction from its total income - Whether the expenditure representing tax liability of transferor-firm discharged by assessee was in the nature of a revenue expenditure and allowable under section 37(1) - Held, no

running business is taken over or amalgamated, then certainly the assets are valued on the date of amalgamation and in this process sometimes the consideration to be paid is much more than the net assets and such deficit can either be reduced from Capital Reserve of the transferee company as provided under Accounting Standard-14 but if the scheme of amalgamation provides and there being genuine transaction, then Courts have consistently held that such deficit is to be considered as goodwill and eligible for depreciation. [Para 18]

■ However, in the instant case, the facts are different and peculiar. It is not the case of some independent transaction of amalgamation a company 'A' with company 'B' for taking over the business but it is a case where one holding company is having two subsidiaries companies and two subsidiary companies are merged in the process of amalgamation but the owner remains the same. In the process of amalgamation, the 60.72 equity shares have been issued by the Transferee company, i.e. the assessee company -ATPL to transferor company-MLPL and after reducing the face value of equity shares held by shareholder of MLPL, the excess amount of Rs.5.97 crores is treated as goodwill. It is clearly visible from the merger note that only against the creation of goodwill 60.72 equity shares in lieu of 1 equity share of MLPL has been issued. It is a case where the owner himself is claiming that one of its subsidiary company has purchased the business on of its another subsidiary company and such higher amount is basically goodwill and there being no banking transaction except the issue of fresh equity shares in lieu of the goodwill. It apparently seems to be an arrangement made at the instance of the holding company between its two subsidiary companies. Genuineness of the transaction of amalgamation between two independent/unrelated companies is missing in the instant case. [Para 19]

■

It is noted that similar type of transaction came for adjudication before Coordinate Bench, Hyderabad in the case of Invesco (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2025] 176 taxmann.com 784 (Hyderabad - Trib.) wherealso the wholly owned subsidiary of assessee company namely Invesco Hyderabad was amalgamated with the assessee company Invesco (India) under the scheme of amalgamation and against the investment of Rs.244.09 crore in the shares of subsidiary company Invesco Hyderabad the fair market value of intangible net assets of subsidiary company were at Rs.102.86 crore and the excess cost of investment over the value of net tangible asset has been determined as goodwill. [Para 20]

■

It is noted that prior to amalgamation ATPL earned revenue of Rs.2.23 crore whereas the revenue of MLPL was Rs.1.97 crore which shows that turnover of ATPL is higher than MLPL. It is also observed that 100 per cent of the sales of MLPL were effected majorly to the USA holding company where the sales of ATPL are to various customers in India. Interestingly, no sales have been effected to its related parties including the holding company by the assessee company, i.e. ATPL. Also post amalgamation, no sales have been effected to the holding company which indicates that the existing business of the subsidiary company prior to amalgamation has been discontinued post amalgamation and only the facilities or the assets appearing in the balance sheet prior to amalgamation as on 31-3-2014 has been transferred to the transferee company ATPL. These facts again support the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the observation of the Assessing Officer that this is a mere colourable transaction and in the garb of inflating the value of assets and creation of goodwill, assessee has intended to claim depreciation for the year under consideration and to be claimed in the subsequent years also. It is also an admitted fact that if new assets are added to the present set of assets on a running business then certainly some sales ought to increase but due to such amalgamation neither any new business has been added nor the profitability has increased much more than the situation prior to amalgamation as appearing from the records. Therefore, the creation of alleged goodwill is merely a colourable transaction carried out between the holding company and the subsidiary company which is to create an Intangible asset, inflate the value of equity shares of the transferee company and to further evade tax by claiming depreciation on such fictitious asset created through such arrangement of transaction between related parties. Therefore, it is held that claim of creation of goodwill of Rs.5.97 crores is only an artificial creation and is classic case of lifting the corporate wheel as rightly observed by the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, no intangible asset in the form of goodwill is created at Rs.5.97 crores. Further, since no intangible asset has been created in the process of amalgamation, depreciation claimed at Rs.1.49 crores also deserves to be disallowed. [Para 21]

provided, the Board is entitled to determine whether a person is capable of competing or not and whether payment of non-compete fee, payable to the promoter group sellers, was only a device to reduce the price payable to the other shareholders.

Issue Involved

Whether the appellants were liable to pay to the public shareholders the non-compete fee that had been agreed to be paid to the outgoing promoters of the company being takenover?

HELD: Offer Price in conformity with regulation 20(1) It is not in dispute that the price of Rs. 544.20 arrived at by the appellant is in conformity with the regulation 20(1). However, sub-regulation (8) thereof further provides that any payment made to a person other than the target company in respect of non-compete agreement in excess of 25 percent of the offer price arrived at under sub-regulation (4), (5) or (6) shall also be added to the offer price. [Para 13]

Information given by merchant banker has been looked into

The material made available by the appellants through its merchant banker and the clarifications furnished by them were examined by the Board and the Board came to a definite conclusion that none of the 13 promoter group seller companies carried on the business of paper and pulp which was the product line of the target company. It also came to the conclusion that there is no object clause in the memorandum of association of any of the said 13 promoter group sellers which permits them to carry on the business carried on by the target company. It was further noted that one of these 13 companies is only a charitable and religious trust which had nothing to do with the pulp and paper business carried on by the target company and, therefore, not in a position to offer any competition to the target company. Yet another company is in the business of printing and publishing and yet another company. was carrying on business as composite textile mill which could not have the necessary knowledge or experience relating to paper and pulp business and, therefore, not capable of offering any competition to the target company. The information provided by the merchant banker to the Board has been looked into with regard to the justification sought by the Board for non-compete fee to these thirteen corporate entities. It is found that the merchant banker has stated primary reasons for entering into a non-compete agreement with the promoter group sellers as:

1.

Promoter Group Sellers have substantial experience and understanding of the paper industry in India. As such, their competency and ability to compete with APPM, the Acquirer and the PAC is, not in doubt.

2.

By virtue of their association with APPM and knowledge of its business, understanding of the market, access to market information and industrial connections, the Promoter Group Sellers are capable of offering competition to the Business of APPM, which could cause irreparable harm to APPM.

3.

The Promoter Group Sellers have acknowledged and agreed under the Non Compete Agreement that as controlling shareholders of APPM and by their extensive participation in the management and operations of APPM for a substantial period of time, they have acquired comprehensive expertise of the Business and the crucial trade secrets of the Company, and have been in possession of the confidential information relating to the Company and the Business. The Promoter Group Sellers have further acknowledged that by virtue of their association with the company and by using their expertise and confidential information belonging to the company, they are capable of offering competition to the Business of the company, which could cause irreparable harm to the Company, its continuing shareholders and the Acquirer.

Information made available to the Board with regard to 13 corporate promoter group entities shows that they are directly or indirectly controlled by the same promoter group and held significant equity share capital in each of the said companies but that by itself does not indicate that these promoter group companies which are into separate business are either involved in day-to-day business of the target company or are capable of competing with the business of the target company providing a threat perception to the business of the appellants. It was for the promoter group sellers and its merchant bankers to place material on record about the capacity of these promoter group corporate entities to compete with the business of appellants or their involvement into day-to-day business of the target company. The information made available by the merchant banker, are only bald statements and it does not disclose as to how these entities are privy to the information relating to the target company. Even the information made available with regard to current business of these entities does not make one any wiser as to how they are in a position to offer competition to the business of the target company.

As the promoter group sellers have failed to place sufficient material before the Board in this regard, no fault can be found with the conclusions arrived at by the Board that payment of non-compete fee is a sham depriving other shareholders of their rightful claims to get just price for their shares. [Para 15]

No entitlement for non-compete merely because persons belonged to promoter group

All the four assessees were directors and principal promoter-shareholders of the company ‘MPIL’, which was earlier engaged in the business of doing bottling work for ‘HCC’ in its unit. Since ‘MPIL’ suffered heavy losses, as per the BIFR order, business and assets of the company relating to the bottling unit were vested in HCC.
