10.4-3 Some points to be noted in connection with the deductions:

10.4-3a Section 35DD - Section 44DB refers to deduction under section 35DD which refers to expenses of amalgamation/demerger. However, it applies only to Indian Companies. It is not clear how this section would apply to co-operative banks.

10.4-3b Actual cost of assets in the hands of successor - Explanations 7 and 7A to section 43(1) provide for actual cost to the successor in case of amalgamation/demerger of companies. No such provision is made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3c WDV of the amalgamating/resulting co-operative bank - Explanations 2 and 2B in section 43(6) provides for computation of written down value in the hands of the amalgamated company or resulting company. No such provision has been made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3d Tax liability under section 41(1) - If an amalgamating company/demerged company has been granted an allowance or deduction and subsequently the amalgamated company/resulting company obtains any amount in respect of such loss or expenditure by way of remission or cessation of such trading liability, the amalgamated company/resulting company is liable to tax under section 41(1) in respect of the said sum. This is because section 41(1) provides inter alia, that, in case of a succession in business (which has been defined to include amalgamation/demerger) the successor is chargeable under section 41(1) even if the deduction was allowed to the person succeeded to. However, no express amendment has been made to cover reorganisation of co-operative banks. It may be noted that Explanation 2(ii) to section 41(1) does provide that where a person is succeeded by any other person, such other person is a successor in business for the purposes of section 41(1). Since amalgamation/demerger result in succession, it may be possible for the revenue to argue that the case of reorganisation of co-operative banks is covered under this general Explanation.

10.4-4 Capital gains to predecessor - Section 47(vica) provides that section 45 is not applicable to transfer of a capital asset in a business reorganization by the predecessor to the successor. Hence, there is no capital gains to the predecessor on transfer of its capital assets to the successor.

The appellant was a global paper and package company and its business includes manufacturing of uncoated papers, industrial and consumer packaging.

The appellants entered into a share purchase agreement (SPA) with the promoters of the target company to acquire equity shares forming 53.46 per cent share capital of the target company at a price of Rs. 523 per share. An exclusivity fee of Rs. 21.20 per share was also to be paid to the promoter group sellers and, therefore, it was decided by the appellants to add the same to the offer price.

The equity shares proposed to be acquired under the share purchase agreement represented the equity shareholding of the promoter group sellers in the target company.

In terms of regulation 10 and 12, a public announcement was published with regard to the proposed open offer for acquisition of shares of the target company from the existing shareholders representing 21.54 per cent of the voting capital at a price of Rs. 544.20 per fully paid-up equity share.

The said offer price was arrived at in accordance with the provisions of sub-regulation(4) of regulation 20.

It was the case of the appellants that the promoter group sellers of the target company had been the controlling shareholders and had extensive participation in the management and operation of the target company for a substantial period of time and had gained deep knowledge of the paper and pulp industry in India and experience in the business and affairs of the target company and were capable of offering competition. In consideration for the non-compete undertakings of the sellers as set out in the SPA as well as in the Non-Compete Agreement, the appellants agreed to pay an amount to the promoter group sellers as non-compete fee.

The said non-compete fee, to be paid to the promoter group sellers, came to Rs. 130.74 per share and same was within the limits of 25 per cent of the offer price arrived at in accordance with the provisions of the Takeover Code.

The SEBI asked the appellants to revise the offer price from Rs. 544.20 to Rs. 674.93, i.e., by adding the amount of Rs. 130.73 in the offer price, being paid to the promoter group sellers as non-compete fee as out of twenty promoter entities only 5 entities were eligible to get the non-complete fees.

Arguments of the appellants

The SEBI had incorrectly observed that out of 20 promoter group sellers, only 5 individuals were eligible for payment of non-compete fee and that the remaining 15 promoters, 13 of which were corporate entities and two individuals were not capable of offering any competition.

The Board would have no occasion to interfere if payment was made to the outgoing seller within the limits prescribed under the regulation and was made to a seller who would offer competition to the business of the target company.

Arguments of SEBI

On the basis of information provided, the Board is entitled to determine whether a person is capable of competing or not and whether payment of non-compete fee, payable to the promoter group sellers, was only a device to reduce the price payable to the other shareholders.

Issue Involved

Whether the appellants were liable to pay to the public shareholders the non-compete fee that had been agreed to be paid to the outgoing promoters of the company being takenover?

The non-competition receipt of Rs. 30 crores was received by the assessee in cash and section 28(iv) does not apply to benefits in cash or money. [Para 18]

The non-competition fee was in fact a payment for sharing customer database and sharing of trained employees. The receipt towards the said transfer is not attributable to transfer of any assets or right and the mere fact that the receipt is not attributable to non-compete covenant, it cannot be automatically concluded that the receipt was either from business or income of an activity recurring in nature. [Para 19]

For the aforesaid reasons, no exception could be found with actions of the Tribunal in setting aside the addition made by the Assessing Officer with regard to non-competition fee of Rs. 30 crores as revenue receipt. Thus, the substantial question of law No. 2 is answered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue. [Para 20]

31.1 Background Note31.1 Background Note

The procedure of three variants of takeover by a single transferee-company provided in section 395 of the Companies Act holds good as a transparent method for private companies also. In any such case the larger the number of members in the target company proposed to be taken over, the more difficult it will be to achieve unanimity. Therefore, this statutory cut off point set down is the consent of three-fourths in number comprised of nine-tenths in value of members for the take-over in a straight and open deal under a Scheme, isolating the dissentients to fall in line with or without a bicker on the price of their shares with none of a veto power left to nullify the majority decision in favour of the takeover even when they move the Court or the Tribunal with any cause for complaint made out under section 395 or other sections of the Act.

31.2 Procedure31.2 Procedure

The offer procedure is common to all the three variants of takeover provided under section 395, that is, where the acquirer’s holding of the same class of shares as are targeted for acquisition being less than 10 % or more or are to the extent of 90% of the total of the class of shares by value comprising 75% in number of the holders. Of course, valuation of the shares to be acquired forms the crux in the takeover in this procedure, and the principles of valuation extensively laid out in CWT v. Mahadeo Jalan [1972] 86 ITR 621 (SC) as well as those given in the SEBI Takeover Regulations would be of valuable guidance in that behalf.

If the business of the vendor is sold as such as a going concern, it will tantamount to a slump sale. If the sale is a slump sale, then provisions of section 50B of the I.T. Act will have application. The impugned sale deed executed on 18.01.2013, mentions only the sale of land and building for a total consideration of Rs. 20 crores. On sale of the property, the business of the assessee was closed down and the assets of the assessee as whole was transferred to the purchaser, viz., M/s. BKR Hotels and Resorts Private Limited. It is an admitted fact that the purchaser is in hotel business. It is also admitted fact that purchaser, after substantial investment on the property carried on the hotel business in the said premises. It is clear from reading of the entire clause of the sale deed that the assets of the assessee, including the license for boarding, lodging, bar etc. were also transferred to the purchaser along with land and building as a going concern. The entire business was sold for a total consideration of Rs. 20 crores consisting of land and building which includes furniture, equipments, kitchen equipments, telephone instruments, television, computer, etc. The building and other amenities are valued as a whole, without assigning value to any item of the assets. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 40 (Delhi) held that "In a case of slump sale if certain defunct assets or properties are left out because they would cause inconvenience or lead to some kind of trouble for buyer, it is well within right of seller to exclude such asset from list and such sale would qualify for treatment under section 50B of the Act."

The following pertinent observations made at paras 10 and 11 from this judgment are worth noticing-

"10........... To expect a purchaser to buy and pay value for defunct or superfluous assets flies in the face of commercial sense. Unfortunately, the Revenue's understanding is that in a going concern the buyer is bound to pay good money, transact and purchase bad and irrecoverable debts. Not only does it fly in the face of common and commercial understanding, but it is not even a pre-condition, as is evident from the definition of "undertaking", cited in Explanation (1) to Section 2(19) (A) of the Act.

11. This definition of "undertaking" is what has been engrafted into by reference, under section 2(42C) of the Act. Therefore, if certain assets or properties are left out because they would cause inconvenience or lead to some kind of a trouble for the purchasing party, it is well within its right to exclude it from the list of assets."

It is clear from various cases that payment made to ward off competition in business to a rival dealer would constitute capital expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee itself contended that amount was paid to R so that he might not come in competition for twenty years and if the amount was to ward off the competition, then as laid down in various cases, the amount was to be treated as capital in nature.

This amount was not for business expediency but was actually for settlement of the family dispute in between the two groups of ‘S’ brothers and their family members. It had come on record that these four brothers were running the business of assessee-company and three other companies. R was removed from the effective management and control of all the four companies including assessee-company. R filed a suit and got ad interim injunction in his favour and then matter was amicably settled. The fact noted in the compromise application were relevant. No doubt R and his group transferred the shares in favour of G but R group lost more and G group obtained more in the said settlement. A perusal of the assessment order showed that main relief of R was equalisation of shares in the business of family including the four companies referred in the plaint. He claimed 25 per cent of shares but out of compromise he not only lost that claim but he as well as his family members transferred their shareholding to rival group in all other companies. R and his group members discharged their liabilities of sum of Rs. 30 lakhs to the members of G group out of Rs. 1.29 crores and he was discharged of his personal guarantee given to the bank. In the plaint he claimed his reinstatement on the Board of Directors of all the four companies but after compromise he did not remain even an ordinary members of these companies. Another relief sought by R was that he was given all powers to operate bank accounts of all the four companies and to remain in effective control but after compromise he lost all those powers. Contrary to it G group did not make any counter claim in the suit filed by R but they got the shareholdings of R and group members. They got payment of Rs. 30 lakhs from the member of R group and ultimately total and absolute control over the five companies to the total exclusion of R group. About the amount in question, it could be said that the same was not associated with the terms of the compromise but was particularly in respect of terms and conditions given in the compromise application. These facts went to show that this amount was paid in lump sum to R so that G group may get rid off R and his group from effective control of all the five companies including four mentioned in the plaint. Suit filed by R was not in respect of assessee-company alone but three other companies were evolved and compromise had taken into consideration another 5th company of this group. It would not be in the fitness of things to conclude that the amount was relevant to assessee-company alone when compromise application read as a whole went to show the very intention of the parties. Mere mentioning that the amount was being paid to R for his past services and to ward off competition from him for twenty years would alone be not sufficient to conclude the issue but on the facts and circumstances as discussed in the assessment order and sequence of events which had taken place in between the parties, the only irresistible conclusion would be that amount was paid by the assessee to get the family dispute settled and not for special expertise of R as mentioned in the agreement deed.

On the basis of above discussion, it could be concluded that amount in question was not a revenue expenditure but in view of the case law the amount was to be treated as capital expenditure. Apart from it, the amount in question was not given for any business expediency nor wholly and exclusively laid out for business purposes as required under section 37 but was on account of settling the family dispute and, thus, the Assessing Officer was justified in not allowing the claim of the assessee.

(4) Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired by payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trade marks, it would be expenditure of revenue nature. (5) If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with net sales, the outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of capital expenditure.

(6) If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled and the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the capital nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(7) A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be revenue expenditure or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment.

(8) If the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be revenue expenditure.

(9) An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a capital expenditure.

(10) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as a capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be revenue expenditure. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which facilitates the acquisition of stock, the expenditure is of capital nature.

(11) The expenditure of capital nature is not referable only to tangible assets, but also to intangible assets. The asset acquired may be of impalpable or incalculable nature.

(12) The expenditure to enhance the profit earning capacity or capital base is of capital nature notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11]

Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. [Para 12]

The business continued to be the same. Only the ownership was changed. The Apex Court in the case of Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. CIT [1990] 186 ITR 278 has held that in order to attract the provisions of section 41(1), the identity of the assessee in the earlier year in which deduction was granted in relation to a trading liability and in the subsequent year in which benefit is derived, must be the same. If there is change in the identity of the assessee, there would be no tax liability under section 41. If the assessee to whom the trading liability may have been allowed as business expenditure in the earlier year ceases to be in existence or if the assessee has changed on account of the death of the earlier assessee, the benefit received in the subsequent year cannot be treated as income received by the assessee. [Para 10]

The instant case was governed by the old law. Section 41(1) was amended by the Finance Act, 1992, with effect from 1-4-1993. The instant case related to the assessment year 1990-91. Under the provisions of section 41(1), where an assessee who was allowed deduction in respect of any loss, expenditure or trading liability in any year obtained any amount in respect of such loss on expenditure or any benefit in respect of trading liability by way of remission or cessation thereof, the amount obtained by him or the value of benefit accruing to him was deemed to be the profits and gains of business or profession. However, it was held in the case of Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. (supra ), that such an amount or benefit can be charged to tax only if the assessee who receives the amount or benefit is the same person who was allowed the deduction earlier. [Para 11]

With a view to ensure that there is no loss of revenue and undue enrichment, section 41(1) was substituted by the Finance Act, 1922, so as to bring to tax the amount or benefit, as the case may be. [Para 12]

In the instant case, however, there was no undue enrichment to the assessee. The person who sold the business did pay capital gains tax. Besides, the year in question was governed by the law laid down by the Apex Court and the amendment was not applicable to the facts of the instant case.

The assessee was the owner of the proprietary concern which used to provide civil engineering consultancy. The concern was taken over by ICT-SD. The assessee received Rs. 1,20,00,000 in terms of the memorandum of understanding as consideration. Out of the said consideration of Rs. 1,20,00,000, a sum of Rs. 54,00,000 was to be paid by 54,000 fully paid up equity shares of ICT-SD. While two other individuals were entitled to shareholding aggregating to 55% shares in the said company, 45% was held by the assessee. In the return filed the assessee claimed that the amount received by her was on capital account which gave rise to capital gains. She computed long term capital gains qua the slump sale under section 50B.

The Assessing Officer rejected the claim holding that it was not a capital receipt but business receipt and represented compensation for not carrying out any activity in relation to the business or profession, assessable under section 28(va).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reversed the findings of the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal found that the newly formed company had taken over the assets and liabilities of the business of the asseessee's concern as a going concern on the close of business for a total consideration of Rs. 1,20,00,000, inclusive of good-will, empanelments, receivables, work in progress and all other rights and entitlements. It was further found that the sum received was not for carrying out any activity in relation to any business. Rather, the business itself was transferred by the assessee, for a lump-sum consideration, from the date when the firm of the assessee ceased to operate consequent upon the slump sale of the business as a going concern. The intention of the assessee was eloquently clear from the Disclosure of the Accounting Policies (APB 27) filed before the AO. As per clause 1B thereof the firm ceased its operations consequent to the slump sale of the business. The Tribunal held that the assessee's business was itself transferred as a going concern to ICT-SD and that the right to carry on any business has been recognized by the Legislature as a capital asset, taxable under section 55 (2)(a) and not taxable under section 28(va).

 and amount received as non-competing fee were taxable as long-term capital gains under section 45, read with section 55 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was manufacturer of transformers. During relevant assessment year, its business was taken over as a going concern by a limited company and its partners became directors of the said company. The said company made certain payments to the assessee for technical know-how and as compensation for pending and expected orders, i.e., not to compete and indulge in transformer business. During assessment proceedings, a show-cause notice was issued to the assessee as to why the amounts shown as received for non-competition fee for pending orders, future orders and for the transfer of technical know-how would not be treated as capital gains, inasmuch as no amount had been shown under the head ‘Goodwill’ even though the assessee had been making good profit in the previous years. The assessee contended that it had not received any money towards the goodwill from the company and inasmuch as for the assessment year 1995-96, a transfer of technical know-how was not taxable, it could not be termed as long-term capital gain. The Assessing Officer held that the receipt for technical know-how was nothing but a part of the composite receipt to cover the value of the intangible assets and inasmuch ‘goodwill’ was taxable under section 55(2), an attempt was made to evade the payment of tax. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer treated the entire amount as capital gains. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim in respect of amount received for technical know-how and compensation for pending orders but disallowed the amount of compensation for expected orders. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that there was no indication of the value of the technical know-how in the balance sheet and it had come into existence only at the time of signing the transfer agreement. It held that the agreement was for the transfer of entire business of a going concern and the amount indicated as the payment for technical know-how was nothing but a goodwill amount which was a colourable device to evade tax. The Tribunal further held that in view of the taking over of the going concern, the assessee-firm had come to an end, more so when the partners were also the directors and, therefore, there was no question of paying the non-competing fees, inasmuch as there was no possibility of the assessee-firm doing the very same business again. Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by the revenue and dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee.

continuation of the same business in some altered form. This alteration may assume the form of changing the manner or method of carrying on the same business; it may involve change or rationalization of the administrative set-up or business organization. But when its basic nature changes, it cannot be said that the business is 'reconstructed'. It is not every alteration in the mode, method or scope of the activities of a business and it is not every transfer of assets from one unit to another that will involve reconstruction. The expression is no doubt very wide but it does not take in a case of company setting-up or establishing a totally independent and viable industrial unit for carrying on the same or similar business, even though it might be so set-up by way of expanding the already existing business. The expression 'reconstruction', in the context in which it is used, denotes that the original business or an undertaking continues to exist without its identity being lost or abandoned. In the reconstruction of a business, as in the reconstruction of a company, there is an element of transfer of assets and of some change, however partial or restricted it may be, of ownership of the assets. The transfer, however, need not be of all the assets. It is nonetheless imperative that there should be continuity and preservation of the old undertaking, though in an altered form. The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets-up another industrial unit. The new industrial unit would not lose its separate and independent identity, even though it has been set-up by a company which is already running an industrial unit before the setting-up of the new unit.

2.21-3 Whether takeover of a firm by allotting shares to partners is 'reconstruction' ?

In CIT v. Gaekwar Foam Rubber Co. Ltd. [1959] 35 ITR 662 (Bom), under an agreement, assessee-company took over all assets, goodwill and business premises of a partnership for consideration satisfied by allotment of shares to partners of firm and there was no transfer of credits and outstandings nor debts and liabilities of partnership were to be taken over by assessee-company. It was held that the said agree-ment, both in substance and in form, was one of sale and transaction was not of reconstruction of an existing business.

The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be—and this is brought out by the section itself—of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking. The undertaking must continue to carry on the same business though in some altered or varied form. If the alterations and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. Thus for instance if the ownership of a business or an undertaking changes hands not ostensibly but in reality and effectively, that would not be reconstruction or if the very nature of the business is changed, that again would not be reconstruction. On the other hand, reorganization of the business on sounder lines or alterations in the mode or method or scope of the activities of the business or in its personnel or infusion of new blood in the management or control of the business which may even be by some changes in the constitution of persons interested in the undertaking would certainly be no more than reconstruction of the business if it is substantially the same business carried on by substantially the same persons.

In these matters, one has to look at the substance of the transaction and not the form. If looking at the substance of the transaction, it is a sale, then the concept of reconstruction must be ruled out for in such a case there is no scope for speaking about any reconstruction of an existing business. It would be a misnomer to speak of a buyer of an undertaking reconstructing the vendor's business.

The instant case was of transfer of building, machinery, plant and other implements of a shoe factory. The agreement was both in substance and in form one of out and out sale. It was the case of a business of a firm ceasing after the sale of its machinery, etc. when it could not possibly carry on business. The goodwill of the firm was also sold to the assessee-company. The only relation that remained between the vendors and the assessee-company was that the vendors became some of the shareholders in the assessee-company they having been allotted 1,500 ordinary shares of the face value of Rs. 100 each.

The object was to benefit newly established industrial undertakings.

Therefore, this was not reconstruction of an existing business

Section 395 is invoked in a scheme of merger or reorganisation of a company between several transferor-companies with the transferee company. This scheme may envisage the purchase of the entire shareholding of one or more of the transferor-companies. In an altogether different scenario section 395 may also be invoked in a ‘takeover situation’ where company A offers to buy out all the shares of all the shareholders of company B. In this event company A would make an offer for the purchase of the shares at a certain price and if 90 per cent of the shareholders of company B agree to sell their shares at the said price, a contract would come into existence which neither party could resile from. By the operation of section 395, takeover contract would be enforceable not only for the 90 per cent shareholders but also for the dissentient shareholders if the transferee-company voices and expresses its intent to do so by giving a notice to the dissenting 10 per cent within two months of the expiry of the four months period. Once the notice is issued, the transferee- company would not be empowered to withdraw the offer. The transferee-company may not issue the notice with the result that the dissentients would retain their shares. In the instant case, it was the second stage that had transpired, since respondent No. 1 had exercised the option to buy out the dissentient petitioner, by the issuance of the notice dated 24-7-2001. [Para 14]

Section 395 has already withstood a constitutional assault and has been held not to impinge upon the rights recognised in article 19 of the Constitution. It is extremely important that the 90 per cent majority should comprise of different and distinct persons since this would then fall in line with the rationale of the section and justify overriding the rights and interests of the dissentients. It is also imperative that this majority should not be the same as the party seeking to acquire the shares. The offerer must be substantially different to the majority. It is for this very reason that section 395 itself stipulates that those who approved the scheme or contract besides holding not less than 9/10th of the value of the shares whose transfer is involved, are not less than 3/4th in number of the holders of those shares. So far as respondent No. 2 was concerned, TIL held over 81.23 per cent together with other concerns of same group who held 11.5 per cent of the equity, the remaining 7.27 per cent being held by the petitioner 99.993 per cent of respondent No. 1 was held by TIL which, independently held 81.23 per cent of respondent No. 2. Quite appropriately, the phrase ‘TI Group’ had been ubiquitously used by the respondents themselves. In the entire transaction only two faces could be seen, one of the dissentient petitioner and the other of the TI Group. It was one ‘T’ company which was buying up the shares of another ‘T’ company. The consequence was that not only was there no independent determination of the value of the shares, but more importantly the wisdom behind stipulating and prescribing the majority to be not less than 90 per cent was rendered wholly illusory.

By way of illustration, let one substitute respondent No. 1 with the BCAL. In such an event, if 90 per cent of shareholders of respondent No. 2, namely, the ‘TI’ Group, had agreed to sell their shareholding to BCAL, the purpose and intendment behind section 395 would have been fulfilled. It would be inconceivable that ‘T’ would agree to sell their 90 per cent holding at an unrealistic price. It was this dialectic that had primarily persuaded one to conclude that section 395 could not have been legitimately invoked in the circumstances of the instant case. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1947-48 - Whether where payment was made to a competitor so that assessee may itself secure a contract for making purchases from a certain concern without any competition, payment was an expenditure not in connection with business but was an expenditure in nature of capital expenditure to prepare ground for securing all business - Held, yes

FACT: The family of BP and his two sons CL and MP were carrying on business in the name of a firm referred to as "the family firm". CL started business of his own which would be referred to his ‘Jaipuria firm’. CL, representing "the Jaipuria firm", entered into partnership with BN for purchase and acquisition of armour plates from the Field Liquidation Commission. In the Jaipuria firm the share of CL was eleven annas and of BN five annas in a rupee. BN subscribed Rs. 1,50,000 towards the capital of the partnership but CL did not subscribe any capital himself and the rest of the capital of the partnership was to come from the family firm." The Jaipuria firm made profits on its armour plates business and in that connection, in the assessment year 1947-48, the family firm was assessed to income-tax. The ITO found that the share in the Jaipuria firm was not the personal and individual share of CL but was the share of the family firm. The reasons for coming to this conclusion, inter alia, were (a) that no capital was invested by CL himself in the Jaipuria firm, (b) that on 12-2-1946, the family firm paid Rs. 40,000 to one EV to remove him from competition for the contract for armour plates business, (ii) that on 4-2-1946, Rs. 99,132 were paid as custom duty by the family firm for the Jaipuria firm and (iii) that the total amount of payments made by the family firm to the American Field Commissioner came to about Rs. 3,30,440 as cost of the armour plates purchased in the name of Jaipuria firm, and that all these transactions were entered in full detail in the account books of the family firm, (c) that on dissolution of the Jaipuria firm partnership the five annas share coming to about Rs. 90,000 of BN was paid to the latter by the family firm and not by CL. For these reasons, the ITO came to the conclusion that the eleven annas share in the Jaipuria firm was the share of the family firm and not of CL individually. The profits of the Jaipuria firm of the share of the family firm were taxed in the income of the latter. The family firm did not appeal against that assessment. It was CL alone, in his personal capacity, who filed an appeal to the AAC of Income-tax and in the grounds of appeal his main attack, was that the ITO had erred in his finding that the eleven annas share in the partnership of Jaipuria firm was not his individual share but was that of the family and that the ITO also erred in disallowing a sum of Rs. 40,000 paid to EV as revenue expenditure because he treated it as capital expenditure.

The AAC confirmed the order of ITO on both counts. He found that the payment of Rs. 40,000 to EV was a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure because it was paid to him to oust him as a competitor in obtaining the armour plate business.

On second appeal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the family or the family firm not having appealed against the order of assessment, the AAC was wrong in entertaining appeal by CL, that Rs. 40,000 paid to EV was rightly found to be capital expenditure and not revenue expenditure and that the share in Jaipuria firm was the share of the family firm and not of CL individually. The Tribunal also refused to make a reference to the High Court.

In such a case, the Board may justifiably direct its addition to the offer price. On the other hand if the payment is made to an outgoing seller who can offer competition to the business of the target company, the Board shall have no occasion to interfere. [Para 5] The recommendations made by the Bhagwati Committee clearly recognize the legitimacy of the non-compete fee payable to the outgoing sellers. Regulation 20(8) based on these recommendations puts a cap on such payments so that an acquirer cannot reduce the cost of acquisition through public offer thereby depriving the public shareholders of their legitimate dues. When examining the validity of the non-compete fee, the question to be addressed is whether the outgoing sellers are capable of providing competition to the business alone or in association with third parties and not whether the business was dependent on the outgoing sellers. When an acquirer takes over a business from the outgoing seller(s), it is obvious that the sellers have specific knowledge of that business and they have access to and are in possession of crucial trade secrets of the target company which if disclosed or misused would be detrimental to and could cause irreparable harm to the target company and its continuing shareholders and by virtue of their association with that business, they (out going sellers) are capable of offering competition to the business being taken over. In such cases, it would be legitimate for the acquirer to enter into a non-compete agreement with the promoter sellers if he feels threatened by a lurking fear of competition from them. It is neither for the Board nor for the Tribunal to analyse the threat perception of the acquirer. A non-compete agreement would then protect not only the target company but also its continuing shareholders. An acquirer has a right to protect his investment/business from competition by a seller of the business and this right is a long standing customary element in business sale transactions and is even recognised by law. Again, the terms of the non-compete agreement have necessarily to be decided between the acquirer and the outgoing promoter sellers and based as they are, on business consideration, the Board and the Tribunal have no role to play. However, if they agree to fix the non-compete fee in excess of 25 per cent of the offer price as determined , under sub-regulation (4) or (5) of regulation 20, the amount in excess of 25 per cent of the offer price shall be added to the offer price which shall be offered to all the public shareholders. It was common ground between the parties that in the instant case, the amount which the appellant as the acquirer had agreed to pay to the promoters as non-compete fee came to Rs. 9.64 per share which was only 6.96 per cent of the offer price as worked out under regulation 20(4). That was far less than the maximum amount prescribed by regulation 20(8) and was in compliance with the provisions. That payment of non-compete fee was not an attempt on the part of the appellant to reduce the cost of acquisition to discriminate against the public shareholders. [Para 6]

The payment and quantum of the non-compete consideration was based on strong business rationale. It was not in dispute that the target company was in possession of a unique source of water and was engaged inter alia in the business of sourcing, manufacture, bottling and distribution of natural mineral water and was owner of the 'Himalayan' brand, a premium luxury brand of natural mineral water. It was rightly argued on behalf of the appellant that the knowledge and expertise of the promoters in managing and exploiting the said source, was critical to the operations and the worth of the target company. The appellant as the acquirer was a new entrant to the business as a strategic player and, hence, it required support and not competition from the promoters to realize its commercial objectives. As on the date of filing of the appeal, the appellant held 34.29 per cent of the equity share capital of the target company and being in control of the target company, it was important for it to ensure that the promoters who continued to hold a much smaller stake in the target company, did not compete with it in any manner. A sum had been paid as non-compete consideration to the seller promoters for not competing for a period of one year from the termination of the shareholders' agreement executed on 6-1-2007 and it could be presumed that during that period, the acquirer would stabilize in the business. [Para 7]

It is true that the directors of a company discharge a fiduciary duty and cannot allow their own interest to conflict with that of the company but such duties cease to exit, the moment they resign from the directorship of the company. In the instant case, there was nothing to prevent the promoters from resigning from the directorship of the target company and setting up a rival business. It was with a view to safeguard against that possibility that the appellant as the acquirer entered into the non-compete agreement with the promoters with a view to protect the interest of the target company and its continuing shareholders. Equally, there was nothing that prevented the promoters from divesting their minority stake in the target company if that was to become necessary. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1975-76 - Assessee, on taking over a going concern, made payments as work incentive to some of its employees - Whether Tribunal having recorded a clear finding after discussing each case that payments were not made out of any business expediency and expenditure incurred was not laid out wholly and exclusively for assessee's business, it was justified in disallowing assessee's claim - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company after taking over the business of a firm as a going concern filed its return and on scrutiny of the accounts the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had made payments of work incentive to some of its employees. The assessee-company explained that the payments were made by it to its employees out of business expediency and wholly and exclusively for business purposes. The Assessing Officer disallowed the expenditure since the payments made were ex gratia and for non-business purposes. On appeal, the AAC deleted the addition. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the payments to the employees were not made for any business consideration and were ex gratia payments and such payments had rightly been disallowed by the Assessing Officer.

On reference:

HELD: The general principle underlying section 37(1) is that an expenditure which is found to have been wholly and exclusively made or laid out by a businessman for purposes of his business, is to be allowed. There can hardly be any dispute on the proposition that the businessman is the best Judge to determine the business expediency and, therefore, when he claims to have incurred a certain expenditure for business expediency, his version should ordinarily be accepted. This principle, however, does not debar the assessing authorities to enquire and investigate as to whether such expenditure was actually incurred by the businessman and if incurred whether the same was incurred wholly and exclusively for business consideration. The doctrine that the businessman is the best Judge of business expenditure does not affect the right, nay, duty of the assessing authorities to know whether it was incurred for business purposes and not for other extraneous considerations.

In the instant case, the Tribunal had recorded a clear finding that the payments on account of work incentive were not made out of any business expediency and the expenditure incurred was not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee. The Tribunal had discussed the cases of each and every concerned employee in sufficient detail and it was after taking into account all the relevant facts that the Tribunal had recorded its finding on the so-called business expediency of the assessee-company.

Since it was the first year of the assessee-company and there was no scheme for making such payments and no such payments had ever been made by the predecessor-firm to any of the employees in the past, the Tribunal could have come to the conclusion which was arrived at by it. The findings recorded by the Tribunal could not be claimed as based on no material. On the facts of the case the Tribunal was justified in holding that the sum paid to the staff was not on account of work incentive and, accordingly, the Tribunal was further justified in disallowing the amount as having not been expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee-company.

Moreover, no evidence was brought on record to show that the increase in sale was entirely due to special efforts by those employees. The work incentive paid to the employees was found disproportionate to the monthly salary and not commensurate with the pay and benefits allowed. The increased incentive had not been paid to other employees. Thus, totality of the circumstances were taken into consideration and it was found that no nexus had been established between the expenditure incurred and the business of the assessee. Simply because certain amount had factually been expended, it could not be allowed as deduction unless it was established that it was wholly and exclusively for business or had intimate connection thereto or was incurred for carrying on such business.

Sub-section (1) of section 43 lays down that actual cost in the hands of an assessee means the actual cost of the assets as reduced by that portion of the cost which may have been met directly or indirectly by any other person. Explanation 3 to the said sub-section stipulates that:-

(i)

The assets which are acquired by the assessee were used by any other person before the date of acquisition;

(ii)

The income-tax officer arrives at objective satisfaction that such assets were transferred with the main purpose of reducing tax liability by claiming depreciation with reference to enhanced cost;

(iii)

Then the Income-tax Officer is empowered to determine the actual cost having regard to all the circumstances of the case. [Para 10]

So from a perusal of the aforesaid provision, it is found that the Assessing Officer needs to satisfy that the main purpose of the transfer of such assets directly or indirectly to the assessee was for the reduction of a liability of tax by claiming depreciation with reference to an enhanced cost. Then only, the Assessing Officer can invoke Explanation 3 to fix the actual cost. So, the requirement of law is that the main purpose of the transfer of assets was for the reduction of a liability to tax without satisfying the same, the Assessing Officer cannot invoke Explanation 3 to section 43(1). [Para 11]

Here, in this case, the Assessing Officer's observation that neither in the audit report nor in the papers filed along with the return the acquisition was not mentioned, is not correct. In the Director's report, it has been reported that the assessee had acquired business of Deltron Ltd. as a going concern. Similarly, in Schedule 'T' of balance sheet being notes on accounts as Note 10, assessee-company has disclosed that it has purchased electronic business of Deltron at a net consideration of Rs. 7.54 cores. Thus, the observation of the Assessing Officer that the assessee did not disclose the transaction is factually incorrect. [Para 12]

A perusal of the agreement entered into between assessee and Deltron makes it abundantly clear that the purport of the transfer of electronic business from the public limited company namely Deltron to the assessee was on account of lack of sufficient financial source to run the said business as a profitable unit by the public limited company. This purpose as stated in the agreement has not been found to be rejected, commented or disputed by any of the authorities below. There is no material to dispute the assertion that Deltron, a public limited company had no resources to invest heavily in R&D or develop process capability to keep pace with the advancing technology.

No doubt, the ground of common management and common office is a relevant consideration but the same is not of conclusive nature. The prime requirement under Explanation to section 43(1) is that the transfer of a going concern has been effected to defraud the revenue and such defraud had been attempted by claiming depreciation at an enhanced cost. As stated above, it was a case of transfer by a public limited company and the purpose stated in the agreement is not a matter of dispute. The Assessing Officer in the order has opined that the assets as reflected in the books of Deltron as on 1-4-2004 at Rs. 66, 95, 884 were transferred for a consideration of Rs. 1,76,84,338 though the assessee claims that such a finding is incorrect.

It has been pointed out that Deltron is a public limited company and had been allowed 100 per cent deduction under section 35(1)(iv)/35(2) as expenditure and as such, there was certain assets which appeared at Nil cost in the books of Deltron Ltd. It was however stated that such assets were appearing in the balance sheet prepared under the Companies Act as on 31-3-2004 at Rs. 4,71,20,059 and if the deduction under section 35(1)(iv)/35(2) is ignored, WDV of such assets as on 31-3-2004 would stand at Rs. 2, 16, 06, 346. [Para 14]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961 - capital or revenue expenditure-assessee-company hpg and two other companies ngp and wg engaged in the same line of business were running in loss as total installed capacity of product manufactured by them was far in excess of demand-under tripartite agreement among them to save their industry from possible annihilation, ngp agreed to withdraw from business for five years in consideration of rs. 25 lakhs to be paid to it by hpg and wg in prescribed instalments-whether rs. 2,50,000 paid by hpg to ngp as first instalment was capital expenditure-held, on facts, yes

FACT: HPG, the assessee-company and two other companies, viz., WG and NGP, were engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling wired and figured glass products. They entered into a tripartite agreement in which it was noticed that the installed capacity in the country for making such products being far in excess of the demand, all these companies were incurring losses and that in order to save this industry from further heavy losses and possible annihilation, it would be in the common interest of these three companies if one of them, viz., NGP, did not make or sell these products for a period of five years. In the interest of commercial expediency, it was agreed that in return, HPG and WG would pay Rs. 12,50,000 each to NGP in instalments as set out in the agreement. The agreement was to remain in force for five years, unless terminated earlier by consent of all the three parties in writing. In pursuance of this agreement, HPG paid a sum of Rs. 2,50,000 to NGP in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1970-71 and claimed it as a revenue deduction. The ITO, however, treated the amount as capital expenditure. On appeal, the Tribunal eventually accepted the assessee's claim.

On reference:

HELD: If a particular outgoing or the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it might be regarded as an integral part of the profit earning process and not for acquisition of an asset or a right of a permanent character, the possession of which was a condition to the carrying on the business, the expenditure might be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

In the instant case, it could be legitimately said that elimination of competition from NGP by preventing it from producing the products manufactured by the assessee for five years at least, under an agreement which was terminable only with the consent of all the parties in writing, would ensure sufficient advantage to the assessee which would enure beyond the period of five years and put the assessee on its feet in the business and prevent "annihilation" as was anticipated by the assessee. It was a crucial period for the industry involved and if NGP, a competitor of the assessee, could be eliminated, the goodwill that would be generated in these five years could, from a practical and business point of view, be considered to be an enduring advantage that would linger beyond the period of five years. The expenditure was, therefore, capital in nature.

Therefore, there was no evidence to suggest that internal audit practice carried out by the buyer was enjoying the goodwill acquired over the year by the assessee firm. Further it could not be said that PCPL bought the practice of the assessee as it did not get all the clients of the assessee firm nor the assessee requested its clients to move over to that particular entity. The buyer also did not use any of the brand name or trade name of the assessee, if any. Therefore, whether client relationship was actually transferred was not clear. The Assessing Officer was further of the view that as the entire internal audit team of the assessee did not shift to the new buyer but only a partner, therefore, it could not be said that a vertical was actually transferred by the assessee firm. He therefore was of the view that a sum received by the assessee was paid to the assessee to make itself absent from the field of internal audit practice. Therefore, he held that the claim of the assessee of the sale of the client relationship and goodwill of the internal audit practice was a non-compete fee received for not to carry out a specific business activity and was chargeable to tax under section 28(va). Information made available to the Board with regard to 13 corporate promoter group entities shows that they are directly or indirectly controlled by the same promoter group and held significant equity share capital in each of the said companies but that by itself does not indicate that these promoter group companies which are into separate business are either involved in day-to-day business of the target company or are capable of competing with the business of the target company providing a threat perception to the business of the appellants. It was for the promoter group sellers and its merchant bankers to place material on record about the capacity of these promoter group corporate entities to compete with the business of appellants or their involvement into day-to-day business of the target company. The information made available by the merchant banker, are only bald statements and it does not disclose as to how these entities are privy to the information relating to the target company. Even the information made available with regard to current business of these entities does not make one any wiser as to how they are in a position to offer competition to the business of the target company.

As the promoter group sellers have failed to place sufficient material before the Board in this regard, no fault can be found with the conclusions arrived at by the Board that payment of non-compete fee is a sham depriving other shareholders of their rightful claims to get just price for their shares. The Assessing Officer had determined the book value of shares and had treated the difference between the sale price of shares and their book value as consideration towards non-compete fees. Admittedly, in the share purchase agreement no consideration was assigned towards non-compete fees and the parties had entered into the share purchase agreement after mutually settling the price of shares. The Assessing Officer had primarily relied on article 11.1 of the share purchase agreement to infer that the assessee had been paid certain amount towards non-compete fees. The said clause clearly showed that in the purchase price of shares, consideration towards restraint clause was embedded, but the same was not specifically mentioned in the share purchase agreement. As rightly pointed by the assessee, non-compete fees was payable primarily with respect to manufacturing company. As regards other two IPR companies, since value of IPR was not reflected in the balance sheet, which constituted major part of the share price, the same had to be determined before arriving at the true book value of shares of these two companies. The Assessing Officer had computed approximately 80 per cent of the consideration towards non-compete fees which, in any case, was not in conformity with the settled principles of valuation of shares. Therefore, it was to be held that the basis adopted for assigning consideration towards non-compete fees was not correct. Now the question would be how to assign the consideration towards non-compete fees. There was no need to enter this area particularly because the difference between the sale price of share and the true book value of the share, if allocated towards non-compete fees, was to be computed under section 55(2)(a). Admittedly, the assessee on her own was not carrying on business and it was the company in which she was shareholder which was carrying on the business. Thus, it was evident that where capital asset was in the nature of right to carry on business, then the same would come within the ambit of capital gain tax. Section 28(va) would be attracted where the assessee was carrying on business and not where the assessee only had right to carry on business in the form of capital asset. Further, as per Circular No. 763, dated 18-2-1998 by the Finance Act, 1997 the amendments were made to section 55(2)(a) to bring extinguishment of right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing or right to carry on any business within the ambit of capital gains tax. Similarly, Circular No. 8 of 2002, dated 27-8-2002 explaining the provisions of the Finance Act, 2002 by which clause (va ) was inserted in section 28 of the Act, clarifies that receipts for transfer of rights to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing or right to carry on any business, which are chargeable to tax under the head ‘Capital gain’ would not be taxable as profits and gains of business. Thus, the difference between the sale consideration and true value of shares was chargeable as capital gains. Since, in the instant case, the date of transfer of shares was 1/15-4-2005 and the investment in the specified securities had, accordingly, been made within the specified period in any view of the matter, no tax was payable. [Para 17]

The assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate. The assessee had acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores. The assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them. The said agreement provided forrestriction on ‘V’ and ‘M’ to engage in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate directly or indirectly for a period of 5 years for a cash consideration of Rs. 6 crores to be paid upfront. In the books of account, the assessee wrote off one-fifth of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores because the period during which agreement was to remain in force was 5 years but in the computation of income furnished along with return, the assessee claimed whole of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that the expenditure was not incurred for improving the profitability, as there was no existing business and the assessee had acquired the business of chemicals for the first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to the company and disallowed the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores claimed as revenue expenditure and treated it as capital expenditure. The Assessing Officer also disallowed the alternative claim made by the assessee that if the expenditure in question was not considered as revenue expenditure, then the assessee by having entered into non-compete agreement as per which ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ were not to carry on either manufacturing or trading business in the two chemicals for a period of five years, the assessee had acquired commercial/business rights for a period of 5 years to carry on manufacturing and trading activities in both the chemicals undisturbed and freely for a period of five years, which were of intangible nature entitled to depreciation under section 32 and, therefore, the assessee might be allowed depreciation. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not acquired any specific intellectual right by making payment of Rs. 6 crores, which was eligible for depreciation under section 32.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. He held that no doubt the assessee earlier was doing only some trading business in the chemicals but it was not much; another group concern ‘D’ was manufacturing and selling the two chemicals in western India; by making a payment of Rs. 6 crores to ‘V’ the advantage had accrued to the assessee and that too of enduring nature and, accordingly, the expenditure was capital in nature and; the impugned expenditure could not be considered as deferred revenue expenditure and, accordingly, could not be allowed proportionately in five years as contended by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) further held that the non-compete fees of Rs. 6 crores paid by the assessee to ‘V’ did not bring in any asset as mentioned in section 32(1)(ii) so as to qualify for depreciation.

Therefore, the provisions of section 50B(2) and (3) are machinery provisions and, hence, would have retroactive operation and apply to all pending matters.

Sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 50B require the computation of cost of acquisition and improvement to be done in the manner prescribed therein which, inter alia, requires the assessee to furnish in the prescribed form a report of a chartered accountant indicating the computation of net worth of the undertaking or division, as the case may be. In the present case, there was no loss, expenditure or trading liability incurred by the assessee in respect of which allowance or deduction has been made in the assessment for any year and thereafter assessee received some benefit qua this loss or expenditure. These creditors were taken over by the assessee from vendor companies and subsequently written off in the books of account. Nevertheless, undisputedly, the assessee never claimed any loss or expenditure qua those sundry creditors.

Hence, the same is clearly not covered by clause (a) of section 41(1). Clause (b) covers a situation where the assessee has been allowed allowance or deduction of certain expenditure and subsequently his 'successor in business' receives certain benefits out of the same. The expression 'Successor in business', as per Explanation-2, covers four types of situation. Clause (iii) is related with firms which is not the case here and hence, not applicable. Clauses (i) & (iv) applies in case of amalgamation/demerger of company, but here the Tribunal is dealing with a case of 'outright purchase' as event from 'business transfer agreement' and financial statements and therefore, the same is also not applicable. Clause (ii) covers case of 'succession' by other person in that business' which is also not the case here.

The issue can be looked from another angle. Hypothetically assuming that the assessee took over certain fictitious liabilities meaning thereby that actual liabilities stood at lower value. In that case, the value of 'net asset' i.e. 'Value of Assets taken over less value of liabilities taken over' would have been at higher value and consequently, the value of goodwill, which was nothing but 'total consideration less net assets' would have been at lesser value thereby resulting into less depreciation claim for the assessee.

Even in that situation, depreciation is neither a loss, nor an expenditure, nor a trading liability, referred to in section 41(1). Hence, the same further supports the stand of the assessee. Even otherwise, neither clause (a) nor clause (b) of section 41(1) applies to the assessee on the facts and circumstances of the case. Hence, from any angle, the impugned addition is not sustainable. Amalgamation/Merger Without Approaching Court

ANIL KUMAR POPLI

In the present business scenario, amalgamation/merger is a common phenomenon in the wake of increasing incidences of mergers and acquisitions and takeover attempts by multinationals and existing big groups. However, amalgamation/merger without approaching the Court is not a common phenomenon in the capital market. Today, there are no clear guidelines in respect of amalgamations without Court order nor the provisions of Companies Act, 1956, are very clear. Therefore, in the emerging liberalisation and free enterprise environment, if the circumstances prevail, the corporates can take substantial benefits like saving of time, money and energy by adopting the procedure of amalgamation without approaching the Court. In this article, the author has explained various provisions, legal compliances and procedures for amalgamation without approaching the Court – EDITOR

Amalgamations and present business scenario

1. In the present business scenario, amalgamation/merger is a common phenomenon in the wake of increasing incidences of mergers and acquisitions and takeover attempts by multinationals and existing big groups. However, amalgamations/mergers without approaching the Court is not a common phenomenon in the capital market. Today, there are no clear guidelines in respect of amalgamations without Court order nor the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 are very clear. Therefore, in the emerging liberalisation and free enterprise environment, if the circumstances prevail, the corporates can take substantial benefits like saving of time, money and energy by adopting the procedures of amalgamations without approaching the Court.

Modes of takeover

2. As per provisions of the Companies Act, read with provisions of Listing Agreement, there are three modes for takeover of shares by way of scheme or contract:

(1) Amalgamation or arrangement of takeover through High Court [Sections 391 to 394 of the Act]

(2) Takeover of management

[Acquisition of shares through Stock Exchange - Clauses 40A and 40B of Listing Agreement]

(3) Take over/amalgamation without approaching the Court [Section 395 of the Act]

Amalgamation under clause No. 1 is very common. Under this method, the resolution for approving scheme of amalgamation/arrangement is required to be approved by members/creditors, as the case may be, and then sanction of the concerned High Court is to be obtained. Thereafter on the basis of report of the Registrar of Companies as well as Official Liquidator, the concerned High Court passes the order. This procedure is lengthy as well as time-consuming.

Whereas takeover under clause No. 2 is booming now a days, Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has now made strict with rules and procedures to comply with. It is a matter of great appreciation that recently SEBI has promulgated Takeover Regulations, 1997 whereby there is need for strict compliance of clauses 40A and 40B of Listing Agreement, appointment of Merchant Banker and maintenance of corpus and compliance of specific guidelines so that the minority shareholders should not suffer.

It is submitted that the amalgamation/merger under clause No. 3 is not very common in the capital market. Under the provisions of section 395, takeover of assets and liabilities or amalgamation of two companies can be effected even without adopting lengthy procedures of SEBI as well as the Court. It is also true to say that takeover under this section cannot be adopted by various companies because consent of the shareholders having share value of at least nine-tenth is not practically feasible in each and every company. This is the main reason why companies are notadopting this provision. However, in the view of the author, this provision is not, being common utilized frequently by the companies, though even by the companies which can fulfil the criteria and which can obtain the consent of majority of shareholders because of ignorance or non-popu-larization of this particular provision in the industry. An attempt is made here to clarify various norms and procedures to serve the purpose.

Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, which provides that where there are general words following particular and specific words, the meaning of the latter words shall be confined to things of the same kind, as specified for interpreting the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature' specified in section 32(1)(ii), it is seen that such rights need not answer the description of 'know-how, patents, trademarks, licenses or franchises' but must be of similar nature as the specified assets.

CIT v. Ingersoll Rand International Ind. Ltd. [2014] 48 taxmann.com 349/227 Taxman 176 (Mag.)(Kar.)

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, which provides that where there are general words following particular and specific words, the meaning of the latter words shall be confined to things of the same kind, as specified for interpreting the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature' specified in section 32(1)(ii), it is seen that such rights need not answer the description of 'know-how, patents, trademarks, licenses or franchises' but must be of similar nature as the specified assets.

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.
