Hence, if a firm having a company as a partner is dissolved pursuant to which the business is taken over by the company, since the condition of allotment to all the partners would not be satisfied, in such a case, the firm will continue to be liable under section 45(4) of the Act and it will not get benefit of exemption under section 47(xiii). 3.1-1s Business profits are not exempt - An amendment corresponding to this amendment is not made in the provisions relating to computation of business income. Hence, if a transfer of a business results in business income (say, transfer of inventory at a price higher than its carrying cost), such income would be liable to tax.

3.1-1t Consequences of non-fulfilment of conditions - According to one view if any of the conditions is violated in the period of 5 years, the exemption is lost and the Assessing Officer would be entitled to reopen the assessment of the year of transfer and tax the capital gains considered as exempt. According to the other view, the exemption is available once the conditions are satisfied at the time of succession and subsequent non-fulfilment do not result in withdrawal of the exemption. It may be noted that if the first view is adopted, it would result in double taxation for the same default: the firm is taxable under section 47(xiii) and the company is taxable under section 47A(3) (see para 3.3). Since such double taxation is not permissible unless expressly provided, it appears that the second view is the correct view.

3.1-1u Consideration has to be in the form of allotment of shares - In CIT v. R.R. Ramakrishna Pillai [1967] 66 ITR 725 (SC) it was observed as follows :

“A transaction by which a person carrying on business transfers the assets of that business to another assessable entity may take different forms and may have a different legal effect. The assets of a business may be sold at a fixed price to a company promoted by a person who carried on the business : if the price paid for or attributable to an asset exceeds the written down value of the asset, proviso 2 to section 10(2)(vii) would ex facie be attracted. Where the person carrying on the business transfers the asset to a company in consideration of allotment of shares, it would be a case of exchange and not of sale, and the true nature of the transaction will not be altered, because for the purpose of stamp duty or other reasons the value of assets transferred is shown as equivalent to the face value of the shares allotted. A person carrying on business may agree with a company floated by him that the assets belonging to him shall be transferred to the company for a certain money consideration and that in satisfaction of the liability to pay that money consideration, shares of a certain face value shall be allotted to the transferor. In that case there are in truth two transactions - one a transaction of sale and the other a contract under which shares are accepted in satisfaction of the liability to pay the price”.

Thus, the Supreme Court has clearly distinguished between transfer the consideration of which is money and the transfer where the consideration is allotment of shares. To illustrate, suppose the agreement mentions that the consideration is Rs. 1 crore and it is to be discharged in the form of allotment of shares. In this case, the consideration is in ‘money form’ and is equivalent to Rs. 1 crore. On the other hand, if the agreement mentions that the consideration is allotment of shares of Rs. 1 crore, then the consideration is in the form of allotment of shares. Having regard to the above and in view of the specific condition requiring consideration by way of allotment of shares, it would be prudent to have consideration in the form of allotment of shares rather than consideration in money form to be discharged by allotment of shares.

3.1-1v Intrinsic worth of shares could be considered as consideration - Where the consideration is allotment of shares, the full value of consideration accruing or arising to the transferor would be the intrinsic value of shares and not the book value of net assets. To illustrate,

◆ book value of assets less liability : Rs. 50 lakhs

◆ value of the business after considering market value of assets, profit earning capacity, etc. : Rs. 1 crore

◆ face value of shares allotted : Rs. 50 lakhs

In the aforesaid case, it could be said that Rs. 1 crore is the consideration accruing or arising to the firm. This is relevant for the purposes of computation of capital gains upon withdrawal of exemption in the event of violation of any of the conditions and for computation of benefit availed of by the firm as required for the purpose of taxation of the company under section 47A(3) (see para 4.3).

Section 80-IA(12A) has been inserted with effect from assessment year 2008-09 to provide that the provisions of section 80-IA(12) shall not apply to any undertaking or enterprise which is transferred in a scheme of amalgamation or demerger after 31-3-2007. The heading in the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill states that ‘Tax benefit under section 80-IA not available to undertakings/enterprises of Indian Companies undergoing amalgamation or demerger after 31-3-2007’. However, this is not borne out by the plain reading of section 80-IA(12A) which states that section 80-IA(12) shall not apply in respect of amalgamation or demerger after 31-3-2007. It means that no cognizance should be taken of section 80-IA(12A) and the general provisions in relation to availability of deduction in a post-amalgamation and post-demerger situation should be considered. Now, Courts have held that takeover of a business by an assessee does not amount to reconstruction of a business already in existence:

(a) CIT v. Gaekwar Foam & Rubber Co. Ltd.[1959] 35 ITR 662 (Bom.)

(b) CIT v. Devson Ltd.[1975] 98 ITR 311 (J&K)

(c) CIT v. N. Guru Investment (P.) Ltd.[1979] 117 ITR 522 (Cal.).

Again, the CBDT has also clarified that ‘The Board agrees that the benefit of section 84 (now section 80J) attaches to the undertaking and not to the owner thereof. The successor will be entitled to the benefit for the unexpired period of five years provided the undertaking is taken over as a ‘running concern’ [F. No. 15/563-IT(AT), dated 13-12-1963 issued by CBR]

Applying the ratio of the Circular and the judgments, and on a plain reading of the amendment it could be argued that the transferee-company would be entitled to deduction in respect of profits and gains of newly established industrial undertaking of the amalgamated company and demerged company even after the amendment. However, as mentioned above, this is unintended.

4.5-4a Appointed date or effective date - Amalgamation/Demerger - The section applies to any enterprise or undertaking which is transferred in a scheme of amalgamation or demerger on or after 1-4-2007. Suppose the appointed date for a particular amalgamation is before 1-4-2007 but the order of the High Court is received after 1-4-2007. A question that arises is whether the amended provision would apply. According to one view, the transfer takes place pursuant to the High Court order received after 1-4-2007 and hence the undertaking should be considered as transferred on or after 1-4-2007 within the meaning of section 80-IA(12A).

According to other view, the undertaking is legally transferred with retrospective effect and hence it should be regarded as having been transferred on that date. In Marshall Sons & Co. (India) Ltd. v. ITO[1997] 223 ITR 809/[1996] 89 Taxman 619 (SC), the Court observed that “the date of amalgamation/date of transfer is the date specified in the scheme as ‘the transfer date’”. Under the scheme of amalgamation or demerger, the Board of Directors of the transferee-company are considered to be carrying on the business in trust for the transferee-company. If the transferee-company is considered to be the beneficial owner on whose behalf the business is being carried on, the undertaking should be considered as having been transferred on that date for the purpose of section 80-IA(12A).

It is possible that a particular amalgamation or demerger may not have received approval of the High Court before 31st March while another may have received a similar approval before 1st April. In such a situation, the two assessees would face different consequences if the transfer is reckoned with reference to effective date and not appointed date. The date of transfer should be construed in the light of economic risks and rewards and not nominal transfer. If the transfer takes place by virtue of the retrospective nature of the Court order, it is that date which should be reckoned as date of transfer for the purpose of section 80-IA(12A).

It may be noted that the High Court has the power to reject an amalgamation or demerger if it finds that it is proposed for tax avoidance [see Wood Polymer Ltd., In re [1977] 109 ITR 177 (Guj.)]. Hence, in a particular situation where the scheme of amalgamation is filed after 31-3-2007 but proposing an amalgamation or demerger with retrospective effect before 31-3-2007, a Court may seek to satisfy that the amalgamation or demerger is not for tax avoidance.

Amalgamation reserve - Amalgamation reserve, being the difference in value of share capital of amalgamated companies prior and post amalgamation, coming into existence consequent to the merger could not be regarded as profit and gains from business profession u/s 28(iv) [CIT v. STADS Ltd. [2015] 61 taxmann.com 33 (Mad.)].

EMOLUMENTS TO PARTNER OF A FIRM FROM SUCH FIRM [SECTION 28(v)]

Retirement benefits - Payment made to partner in realization of his share in net value of assets upon his retirement from a firm do not fall u/s 28(v) [Prashant S. Joshi v. ITO [2010] 189 Taxman 1 (Bom.)].

NON-COMPETE FEES [SECTION 28(va)]

Section is amendatory and not clarificatory - Compensation received under non-competition agreement became taxable as a capital receipt and not as a revenue receipt by specific legislative mandate vide section 28(va) and that too w.e.f. 1-4-2003. Hence, the section is amendatory and not clarificatory [CIT v. Bisleri Sales Ltd. [2016] 66 taxmann.com 364 (Bom.)].

Illustrations - (1) Transfer of shares with all pervasive control over business being entrusted to purchaser and to complete exclusion of assessee with a non-compete clause fell within the realm of section 28(va) [Sumeet Taneja v. CIT [2013] 38 taxmann.com 149 (P&H)].

(2) Where C Ltd., pursuant to sale of one division to its director, received certain amount by entering into a non-compete agreement whereby it could not engage in any business activity similar to that of division sold to such director, amount so received was taxable as business income u/s 28(va) [Arun Toshniwal v. DCIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 274 (Bom.)].

32.6 Section 5 lays down what amounts to a combination, and section 6 sets out the scheme of regulation of such combinations. The acquisition of one or more enterprises by one or more persons or merger or amalgamation of enterprises shall be a combination of such enterprises and persons or enterprises, in terms of control, shares, voting rights or asset values/turnover value acquired or control acquired of an enterprise while controlling another directly or indirectly, in excess of specified monetary limits. So far as registered companies are concerned, a combination includes acquisitions and take-overs under SEBI procedure discussed in Ch. 22, and arrangements and reconstructions or mergers and amalgamations or the reliefs provided in the prevention of oppression and mismanagement under the NCLT procedure discussed in Chs. 25 and 29. As all these changes in ownership and control bring into being new combinations which ought to be subject to the apex Regulation of Combinations provided under the CA, particularly the reference to the CCI by any statutory authority an issue whether suo motu or at the instance of a party to a proceeding before it—on which the CCI should render its opinion in 60 days which shall be considered by the statutory authority making the reference in giving its finding provided for in section 21(1) implying the supremacy of CA over all other laws and procedures.

Here, ‘control’ includes controlling the affairs or management by (i) one or more enterprises, either jointly or singly, over another enterprise or group, (ii) one or more groups, either jointly or singly, over another group or enterprise; and ‘group’ means two or more enterprises which, directly or indirectly, are in a position to (a) exercise twenty-six per cent or more of the voting rights in the other enterprise, or (b ) appoint more than fifty per cent of the members of the Board of directors in the other enterprise, or (c ) control the management or affairs of the other enterprise, or (d) control the management or affairs of the other enterprise. The value of the assets shall be determined by taking the book values of the assets as shown in the audited books of account of the enterprise, in the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the date of proposed merger falls, as reduced by any depreciation, and the value of assets shall include the brand value, value of goodwill, or value of copyright, patent, permitted use, collective mark, registered proprietor, register trade mark, registered user, homonymous geographical indication, geographical indications, design or layout-design or similar other commercial rights, if any.

ana Rao v. Sri Ramanuja Ginning (1986) 60 Comp Cas 568 (AP HC) = AIR 1984 AP 176, it was held that the word 'company' used in section 565 includes partnership firm. And hence can be registered under the Companies Act - quoted with approval in Salim Akbarali Nanji v. UOI (2003) 48 SCL 1 = 2003 CLC 395 (Bom HC DB). Section 368 of Companies Act, 2013 [similar section 575 of the 1956 Act] provides that all property (movable and immovable) including actionable claims, belonging or vested in the firm shall, on registration, pass and vest in the company incorporated under the Act.

Since there is statutory vesting of property (movable and immovable) of the firm into the limited company, no conveyance is necessary. The conversion of partnership firm into a limited company is not a 'transfer' within the meaning of Transfer of Property Act, 1882 since 'transfer' requires presence of two persons. - Valli Pattabhirama Rao v. Sri Ramanuja Ginning & Rice Factory (1986) 60 Comp Cas 568 (AP HC) = AIR 1984 AP 176 - quoted with approval in Prem Lata Bhatia v. UOI (2006) 71 SCL 142 (Del HC DB). - also quoted and followed in LKS Gold House P Ltd. v. LKS Gold Palace (2005) 57 SCL 362 (Mad HC), where it was held that when firm is converted into company, there is no transfer of copyright which was originally with firm. Any written assignment under section 19 of Copyright Act is not required.

It has been clarified that Registrar of Companies will continue to register partnership firms under Part IX of the Companies Act, if they fulfil conditions prescribed under Companies Act. Such registration cannot be refused, if it fulfils all other requirements of company law - PIB press release dated 5-8-1999.

No Capital Gains - Since vesting of property in new company is automatic, deed of conveyance for transfer of immovable property is not required, since the partnership itself is registered as a company. There is no sale or purchase and hence no capital gain arises. - - As per section 47(xiii) of Income Tax Act, conversion of a partnership firm into a limited company is exempt from capital gains tax, if prescribed conditions are fulfilled.

In CIT v. Texspin Engg (2003) 129 Taxman 1 = 44 SCL 239 = 180 CTR 497 = 263 ITR 345 (Bom HC DB), it was held that when a firm is converted into a limited company, it is not transfer by way of distribution under section 45(4) of Income Tax Act. There is no transfer of asset as contemplated under section 45(1) of Income Tax Act. Hence, question of capital gains tax does not arise. It was also held that depreciation for the year is allowable to the firm for the year. Section 34 of Income Tax Act does not apply as the assets are not 'sold, discarded, demolished or destroyed'.

Same view has been taken in CIT v. S Koder (1998) 233 ITR 620 (Ker HC) and CIT v. Hansa Footwear (2012) 344 ITR 30 (AP HC).

If there is no change in partners, there is no transfer of assets. Hence, tax on capital gains is not payable - CADD Centre v. ACIT (2016) 237 Taxman 401 = 65 taxmann.com 291 (Mad HC DB).

Sale of assessee firm as a going concern to company for consideration of paid up capital does not amount to transfer liable as capital gains - DCIT v. R L Kalathia and Co (2016) 237 Taxman 621 = 66 taxmann.com 249 (Guj HC DB).

Memorandum must contain the object of takeover - Often, a partnership firm or an association is converted into a limited company. In such cases, the fact that the company is being specifically formed to takeover business, property or affairs of the firm or body must be specified in memorandum. In absence of such mention, the company cannot be deemed to be continuation of earlier body or firm.

In Electrical Cable Dev. Corpn. v. Arun Commercial Premises Coop Soc. AIR 1998 SC 1998 = 94 Comp Cas 53 = (1968) 5 SCC 396, an unregistered body (an association) had leased premises in a cooperative society. Later, a section 25 company was formed to take over business of the association. However, the Cooperative Society declined to accept the new company as the same earlier body. It was held by Supreme Court that in absence of any mention of such intention in articles of the company (like providing that all members of unregistered body will become members of new company), the limited company cannot be taken to be same as the earlier unregistered body. It was held that the unregistered body and company are different legal entities. (And hence, it has no right of lease which was in favour of earlier unregistered body).

10.4-3 Some points to be noted in connection with the deductions:

10.4-3a Section 35DD - Section 44DB refers to deduction under section 35DD which refers to expenses of amalgamation/demerger. However, it applies only to Indian Companies. It is not clear how this section would apply to co-operative banks.

10.4-3b Actual cost of assets in the hands of successor - Explanations 7 and 7A to section 43(1) provide for actual cost to the successor in case of amalgamation/demerger of companies. No such provision is made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3c WDV of the amalgamating/resulting co-operative bank - Explanations 2 and 2B in section 43(6) provides for computation of written down value in the hands of the amalgamated company or resulting company. No such provision has been made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3d Tax liability under section 41(1) - If an amalgamating company/demerged company has been granted an allowance or deduction and subsequently the amalgamated company/resulting company obtains any amount in respect of such loss or expenditure by way of remission or cessation of such trading liability, the amalgamated company/resulting company is liable to tax under section 41(1) in respect of the said sum. This is because section 41(1) provides inter alia, that, in case of a succession in business (which has been defined to include amalgamation/demerger) the successor is chargeable under section 41(1) even if the deduction was allowed to the person succeeded to. However, no express amendment has been made to cover reorganisation of co-operative banks. It may be noted that Explanation 2(ii) to section 41(1) does provide that where a person is succeeded by any other person, such other person is a successor in business for the purposes of section 41(1). Since amalgamation/demerger result in succession, it may be possible for the revenue to argue that the case of reorganisation of co-operative banks is covered under this general Explanation.

10.4-4 Capital gains to predecessor - Section 47(vica) provides that section 45 is not applicable to transfer of a capital asset in a business reorganization by the predecessor to the successor. Hence, there is no capital gains to the predecessor on transfer of its capital assets to the successor.

If the accumulated loss or unabsorbed depreciation is not directly relatable to the undertaking, the same will be apportioned between the demerged co-operative bank and the resulting co-operative bank in the same proportion in which the value of the assets have been transferred.

ACIT [2022]137 taxmann.com 12(Delhi-Trib.), the Tribunal held that 76% Gandhis-held section 25 company Young Indian was an adventure in the nature of trade under a cloak of charity, with real purpose to gain control of properties valued at approx Rs. 357 crores of publication company AJL which had ceased publication by paying a pittance of Rs. 50 lakhs for 99% of shares in AJL in connivance with directors of AJL who were close to Gandhis family and held high positions in AICC also. The acquisition of shares in AJL by YI was merely a step in the entire adventure which was in the nature of trade and commerce. The benefit has arisen to YI the moment the whole transaction had taken place right from purchase of an asset in the form of loan of Rs. 90.21 crores due by AJL to AICC from AICC for a sum of Rs. 50,00,000/- and in lieu of that, almost the entire shares of AJL have been acquired which was nothing but to get entire interest of the immovable assets of AJL. In the circumstances. The Tribunal analysed the entire sequence of events in detail as under:

Here is a company which has been formed and was found to have carried out only one activity, i.e., takeover of a company having huge immovable properties which are otherwise were commercially exploited by the said company for its own business and profession.

A company which is formed in October 2010 and was closely associated with AJL and AICC through their managing personnel and its stake holders and within days of its formation one of the entity, i.e., AICC offered to sell/assign its receivables worth Rs. 90.21 crores from AJL in favour of the appellant who at that point of time did not even not had money to undertake a transaction.

AICC has offered its huge assets (loan of Rs. 90.21 crores) for a mere sum of Rs. 50,00,000/-) and the appellant company did not have any resources to pay the same when the loan was assigned. It was only after assignment of the loan of Rs. 1 crores which was raised from Kolkata based company; out of that, amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- has been paid for acquiring assets worth Rs. 90 crores.

Before that, AJL had already closed its publication business and was having income only from commercial exploitation of property and was not able to pay the loan, which if had taken from any commercial bank or financial institution would have been obliged to liquidate its debt first.

A newly formed Company (YI) buys the loan even before any loan was received.

In fact, appellant had not even opened its bank account when the loan was assigned for Rs.50,00,000/-. Such a transaction, we already observed above, is beyond any prudence in any comparable third-party scenario, where any person would do that.

The AICC immediately extinguished its receivables worth Rs. 90.21 and instead of getting amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- from AJL had assigned the receivables in favour of a new Company and the entire stake in AJL of more than 99% has been taken over by that company in one stroke.

All these transactions have been frowned upon and held to be a colourable device by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court, wherein it has been held that the real intention was to get the possession of the assets of AJL and enjoy these properties which are situated in major cities of the country.

This clearly shows that the intention of the appellant was to enjoy the benefits by commercial exploitation of these properties and to acquire the benefit of these properties which is nothing but adventure in the nature of trade which can be carried out at some future point of time. It is also very clear from the fact that this was the only activity done swiftly within a period of months, which appellant had carried out in all these years starting from 2010 till date.

The word 'benefit' is occurring in section 28(iv) means some kind of adventure or gain or had same value or acquire any interest in any land, chattel, etc. Thus, the benefit is nothing but any form of adventure and here the adventure is clearly getting the underlying huge properties situated all over the country by stroke of one transaction and to enjoy the benefits of all those properties in future.

What is capital gain?

2. Capital gain arises on transfer of capital asset from one person to another. In the amalgamation, assets and liabilities of the transferor company are transferred, by a scheme of arrangement, to the transferee-company. Therefore, when assets of a partnership firm are transferred by scheme of amalgamation to a company, then capital gains may arise to the firm.

Capital gains exempted 3. List of transfers which are not considered as transfer of assets for the purposes of charging capital gain is enlisted in section 47 with conditions for exemption. Amalgamation is exempted under the provisions of section 47(vi) of the IT Act, the provision reads as "Any transfer, in a scheme of amalgamation, of a capital asset by the amalgamating company to the amalgamated company, if the amalgamated company is an Indian company."

Therefore, what is exempted, is capital gain arising on transfer of assets by a scheme of amalgamation to a amalgamating (Transferor) Company. In the present case a partnership firm, which is an unregistered company as per Companies Act, is being merged with the Private/Public Company. Therefore, advantage of section 47(vi) is not available in this case. Rather such merger of firm with the company is not regarded as amalgamation for the purposes of Income-tax Act.

Hence, question remains as when amalgamation of partnership firm with the Company happens, of course through High Court route under sections 391 & 394 of the Companies Act, whether, Capital gains arising from such transfer of capital assets are taxable? Though it is agreed that section 47(vi) of the Income-tax Act is not applicable but certainly the case falls under another listing in the same section 47, i.e., section 47 (xiii). Reasoning for the same is as follows:

Section 47(xiii) reads as follows:

(xiii) any transfer of a capital asset or intangible asset by a firm to a company as a result of succession of the firm by a company in the business carried on by the firm, or any transfer of a capital asset to a company in the course of demutualisation or corporatisation of a recognised stock exchange in India as a result of which an association of persons or body of individuals is succeeded by such company:

Provided that—

(a) all the assets and liabilities of the firm or of the association of persons or body of individuals relating to the business immediately before the succession become the assets and liabilities of the company;

(b) all the partners of the firm immediately before the succession become the shareholders of the company in the same proportion in which their capital accounts stood in the books of the firm on the date of the succession;

(c) the partners of the firm do not receive any consideration or benefit, directly or indirectly, in any form or manner, other than by way of allotment of shares in the company; and

(d) the aggregate of the shareholding in the company of the partners of the firm is not less than fifty per cent of the total voting power in the company and their shareholding continues to be as such for a period of five years from the date of the succession;

(e) the demutualisation or corporatisation of a recognised stock exchange in India is carried out in accordance with a scheme for demutualisation or corporatisation which is approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India established under section 3 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (15 of 1992);

An analysis of section 47(xiii) is as follows:

1. Business is carried on by the firm up to one date

2. Such business in a firm by succession vests in a company and, therefore, all the assets and liabilities of the firm are transferred to a Company

3. Conditions mentioned in proviso from (a) to (e) are followed,

Then such transfer of assets is not considered as transfer for charging the capital gains tax.

What section 47(xiii) contemplates is succession of business and not transfer or take over of business only. Word 'succession' has wider meaning and in its ambit, it includes transfer as well as take over. Word 'succession' is not defined in Income-tax Act. Therefore, applying rules of interpretation of statutes, general meaning of a word "succession" must be applied in this case.

As per Black's law dictionary, word 'successor' means a corporation that, through amalgamation, consolidation, or other assumptions on interests, is vested with the rights and duties (obviously properties) of the earlier corporation.

C. Merger of Foreign Companies with Indian Companies

Now-a-days, a lot of Indian companies are taking over foreign companies having presence in USA, UK and other countries. How is it possible? Is it through a merger process or take over process? The common answer to this question is that both the methods are usually employed by Indian enterprises and we have a whole lot of examples starting from EID Parry in 1976 to Tata’s takeover of Corus in 2007. If the Indian enterprise is willing to go for merger route, then merger of foreign company is possible under the Indian Companies Act, 2013. On the other hand takeover is possible through well laid out procedure available under Foreign Exchange Management Act, (FEMA) inclusive of FIPB route. Although, FIPB has been abolished in February, 2017 to further liberalize the FDI policy.

Under the Indian Companies Act, 2013, there are precedents in the form of judgments of various courts in India sanctioning the merger of companies in UK, USA, Singapore etc. with Indian companies. The only requisite condition for affecting this type of merger is that the transferee company should always be an Indian company.

Regulatory Framework

5. Several provisions of various Acts deal with M&A. The regulatory landscape is represented below:-

5.1 A brief understanding of the various applicable regulatory regimes 5.1-1 Companies Act - Sections 391-394 of the CA, 1956 dealt with the provisions of mergers and amalgamations and were considered as "A complete code" or "Single Window Clearance System". Whereas, Sections 230 - 232 of CA, 2013, read with the Companies (Compromise, Arrangements and Amalgamations) Rules, 2016 deal with the power to make compromise and arrangement of companies along with the procedure of merger and amalgamation. Under CA, 1956, the scheme of arrangement was to be approved by respective High Court which had jurisdiction over Acquirer and Target companies. Under CA, 2013 the National Company Law Tribunal deals with the matters related to M & A. It is pertinent to note that the scheme of arrangement is the most important document in the process of merger. The scheme shall, inter alia, contain specific clauses w.r.t. the following:-

Vesting of assets and liabilities

Consideration

Appointed date and effective date

Accounting treatment

Post merger shareholding

The step-wise procedure under the CA, 2013 shall include the following:

5.1-2 Securities laws - The provisions of the SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (LODR, 2015) shall only be applicable in case of listed entities, which provide the requirement to comply with Regulations 11, 37 and 94 of LODR for every Scheme of Arrangement. Further, the SEBI Circular dated March 10, 2017 (as amended) provides conditions and compliances by listed entities while undertaking Scheme of Arrangement. The listed entity shall not file any scheme of arrangement, with any Court or Tribunal unless it has obtained observation letter or No-objection letter from the stock exchange(s). The validity of the same shall be 6 months.

Further, while considering the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011, Regulation 10(d), exempts listed companies from the obligation to make an open offer where the acquisition is pursuant to a scheme of arrangement.

5.1-3 Accounting and Income Tax implications - Accounting standard ('AS')-14 issued by the ICAI deals with two types of amalgamations-

amalgamation in the nature of merger, and

amalgamation in the name of purchase

Also, IND- AS 103 deals with the aspects of accounting in case of business combinations. Further, Considering the perspective of the Income-tax Act, 1961, section 2(1B), section 47, section 35DD and Section 72A deal with the taxation aspects in case of amalgamation. The accounting treatments and tax implications are an essential part of the valuation report. The Act, 2013 makes it mandatory that notice of meeting to discuss the scheme must be accompanied by valuation report. Also, as per section 232 of the Act, 2013 no compromise or arrangement shall be sanctioned by the Tribunal unless a certificate by the company's auditor has been filed with the Tribunal to the effect that the accounting treatment, if any, proposed in the scheme is in conformity with the accounting standards prescribed under section 133.

5.1-4 Competition Act, 2002 - Section 5 of the Act deals with "combinations" which means acquisition of control, shares, voting rights or assets, acquisition of control by a person over an enterprise where such person has direct or indirect control over another enterprise engaged in competing businesses and mergers and amalgamation between or among the enterprises when combining parties exceed the threshold set in the Act. Also, pursuant to section 6 of the said Act, any enterprise(s) which proposes to enter into a combination, shall give notice to the Commission, disclosing the details of the proposed combination, within 30 days approval of the proposal relating to merger or amalgamation, as per section 5, by the board of the enterprise(s).

5.1-5 Stamp duty implications - Stamp duty is another considerable aspect in the regulatory regime of M & A. The duty shall be payable in the States where the order approving the scheme is passed and where the properties of transferor-company are located. At present there are two schools of thought prevailing for the implication of the same, the Indian Stamp Act does not mention 'amalgamation as a stampable article, however, the term 'conveyance' covers any instrument which purports to transfer inter vivos. Due to lack of clarity on the subject, the rulings of the High Courts are generally resorted to. Some of the well known rulings on the subject are-

CHAPTER 6

Takeover Strategies and Practices Meaning and Concept

In the previous Chapter, we have discussed the provisions of law relating to M&As. Although the said legal provisions include corporate takeovers, yet there are several other aspects with respect to takeovers which need to be examined separately. Thus, this chapter aims at exclusively dealing with laws, practices and procedures relating to takeovers and its illustrations through case studies.

Takeover implies acquisition of control of a company. This concept emerged in late nineteenth century in some countries like USA, UK etc, when the M&As started. However, it started in India in the twentieth century. According to M.A. Weinberg(i), “takeover is a transaction or series of transactions whereby a person or individual or group of individuals or company acquirers control over the assets of a company, either directly by becoming the owner of those assets or indirectly by obtaining control of the management of the company. In case of companies whose shares are closely held (by a small number of persons), a takeover will generally be affected by arrangement with the holders of the majority of the shares capital of the company which is being acquired. Where the shares are held by the public, the takeover may be affected (1) by agreement between the acquirer and the controllers of the acquired company; (2) by purchase of shares on the stock exchange; or (3) by means of a take-over bid.

Takeover implies acquisition of control of a company, which is already registered, through the purchase or exchange of shares. Takeover takes place usually by acquisition or purchase from the shareholders of a company, their shares at a specified price to the extent of at least controlling interest in order to gain control of that company. Takeover of management and control of a business enterprise could take place in different modes. The management of a company may be acquired by acquiring the majority stake in the share capital of a company. The acquisition could take place through different methods. A person may acquire the voting shares of a listed company through what is known as the takeover by complying with the regulations meant for such purposes. A company may acquire shares of an unlisted company through what is called the acquisition under sections 235 and 236 of the Companies Act, 2013. Where the shares of the company are closely held by a small number of persons, a takeover may be effected by agreement with the holders of those shares. However, where the shares of a company are widely held by the general public, it involves the process as set out in the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeover) Regulations, 2011.(ii) & (iii)

6.10-9 No acquisition of business from other person

6.10-9a ACQUISITION OF BUSINESS BY WAY OF TRANSFER - In terms of the provision, the deduction will not be available in respect of business is acquired by way of transfer from any other person. The word 'transfer' is defined under the Act [section 2(47)]. The said definition is in relation to the transfer of capital asset. The business/undertaking is also held as capital asset [CIT v. F.X. Periera & Sons (Travancore) (P.) Ltd. [1990] 184 ITR 461/[1991] 55 Taxman 242 (Ker.)/West Coast Electric Supply Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 107 ITR 483 (Mad.)/Karvalves Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 197 ITR 95/60 Taxman 483 (Ker.)/Syndicate Bank Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [1985] 155 ITR 681/[1986] 29 Taxman 32 (Kar.)].

Prima facie, the section intends to deny deduction in case where business is acquired from any other person. For the purpose, it states that the provision of section will not apply if such business is acquired by way of transfer.

To illustrate, if an assessee, engaged in business 'A'; also acquired business 'B' from another person during the year. In such circumstances, he can claim deduction only in case of additional employee cost incurred in business 'A'; However, in subsequent years, both business will qualify for deduction, if the conditions are fulfilled.

6.10-9b BUSINESS REORGANISATION - 'Reorganisation' has been defined in McMillan's Online Dictionary as 'the process of organizing something again in a different way'.

It has been explained in Permanent Edition of Words & Phrases as follows:

To 'reorganize' is to organize again and anew.

'Reorganization', indicates corporate readjustment of existing interests.

In Dictionary for Accountants by Eric L Kohler, the term "reorganization" is defined as follows:

"reorganization 1. A major change in the financial structure of a corporation or a group of associated corporations resulting in alterations in the rights and interests of security holders; a recapitalization, merger or consolidation."

Generally, the business re-organization means re-structuring of the business, partly or fully, internally or externally. In the following circumstances, it can be said that there is business reorganization:

Conversion

Amalgamation

Merger/Demerger

It should be noted that mere change of ownership is not relevant for the purpose of business re-organisation.

In view of the above, it appears that if the business is acquired pursuant to the business reorganisation, the deduction will not be allowed in respect of such business in year of business reorganization. However, as said above, in subsequent year, the deduction can be claimed, if other conditions are fulfilled.

6.10-10 Report from an Accountant

The deduction under section 80JJAA is admissible only if the assessee obtains a report from an accountant as defined in the Explanation below section 288(2), giving the prescribed particulars and such report is furnished along with the return of income.

Hitherto, Rule 19AB prescribed Form 10DA which was required to be furnished by the assessee along with the return of income. The Form was required to be furnished online.

Whether filing of the report along with return of income is mandatory?

Prima facie, filing of Audit Report is procedural and directive in nature, as held by various judicial authorities in context of different provisions under the Act. It was further held that audit report can be filed before the assessment is completed or even at appellate stage also [see CIT v. Medicaps Ltd. [2010] 323 ITR 554 (MP), CIT v. Deduction to the LLP in respect of expenditure relating to company

2.11-5 In Amin Machinery (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2008] 114 ITD 413 (Ahd. - Trib.), the assessee company was incorporated through conversion of a partnership firm. On the other hand, if the scheme was sanctioned, the accounts of the transferee-company would reflect an exorbitant and inflated income, but as the transferee-company is an infrastructure company, it could claim deductions under the various provisions of Chapter VI-A of the Income-tax Act, 1961. It was also alleged that once the assets are transferred from the transferor-companies, they would stand removed from their record. The net worth of some companies might be rendered negative, thereby defeating the purpose of law and also evading income-tax. The objection was overruled. It was held that since the scheme was just, fair and reasonable and conformed to public interest and was approved by the equity shareholders, secured and unsecured creditors of the petitioner-companies, it could not challenged on the alleged grounds. Moreover, the Government policy was in favour of the scheme, as its object was to promote exchange of infrastructure and not to avoid taxes. The high earnings of the transferee-company’s assets would naturally be subjected to tax in the hands of the transferee-company, and the liabilities that remain behind with the transferor-companies would not be available to the transferee-company for adjustment against profit before tax. However, if the transferee-company is further entitled to any other benefits or deductions notified by the Government in its wisdom, the Income-tax authorities cannot complain. As regards the accounting principles used and the validity of their adoption by the petitioners the question is left open to the Income-tax authorities to enquire into the correctness or otherwise of the same, independent of the sanction of the scheme. The approval of the scheme would not legitimize any statutory violation committed by the petitioners. The scheme was sanctioned with the condition that Income-tax authorities would be at liberty to exercise their power of investigation under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

2.1-6 A dispute between ex-employee and the transferor-company not a bar to the sanction of the scheme of amalgamation - In Webneuron Services Ltd. v. Monster.com (India) (P.) Ltd. [2008] 85 SCL 35 (Delhi), an ex-employee of the transferred company claimed that the company owed Rs. 4,48,040 to him. The Court directed the company to deposit Rs. 4,48,040 with the Court so that the same may be adjusted against the claim of the ex-employee, if he succeeded. The company deposited the amount as directed by the Court. Even then the ex-employee raised an objection that the scheme of amalgamation could not be sanctioned as the terms and conditions of service of employees would be affected by such sanction. Objection was overruled. It was held that the terms and conditions of service of the employees of the transferor-company were not affected and there was no legal impediment to sanctioning the scheme of amalgamation.

2.1-7 A partnership firm can be merged with a company - In Kirtilal Kalidas Diamonds Exports (P) Ltd., In re. [2009] 148 Comp. Cas. 607 (Bom.), the Bombay High Court held that the amalgamation scheme proposed between four transferor-companies and a partnership firm and transferee-company and their respective shareholders and partners could not be refused because it was a fair and reasonable scheme, not violative of any statutory provisions or contrary to public policy. The partnership firm was to be dissolved and succeeded by the transferee-company. While according sanction to the scheme the Court directed the Registrar of Firms to transfer all documents of the firm to the Registrar of Companies.

1.1-4 Non-compete for profession - The amendment provides for taxing any sum received for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business. Does it cover any sum received for not carrying out any activity in relation to any profession? The matter is not free from doubt. The Supreme Court has held in Barendra Prasad Ray v. ITO [1981] 129 ITR 295 that the expression 'business' is one of wide import and it means an activity carried on continuously and systematically by a person by the application of his labour and skill with a view to earning an income. In that case the Supreme Court held that the expression 'business connection' used in section 9(1) of the Act includes professional connection. On the other hand, the CBDT has clarified that section 55 (which provides that the cost of acquisition of goodwill of a business shall be nil) shall not apply to professional firms (para 28.3 of Circular No. 495, dated 22-9-1987). This indicates that the Board has interpreted the term business to exclude profession.

1.1-5 Tax implication in the hands of the payer - The new provision has been introduced to override the Court judgments, which held that sum received for restrictive covenant is a capital receipt. However, there is no corresponding amendment to provide that the payee would get deduction as revenue expenditure. In many cases, Courts have held that amount paid by assessee as non-compete charges is capital expenditure and hence not allowable as deduction [Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT 27 ITR 34 (SC), CIT v. Hindustan Pilkington Glass Works 139 ITR 601 (Cal.), Chelpark Co. Ltd. v. CIT 191 ITR 249 (Mad.)]. Hence, while the recipient will get taxed under the new provisions, the payer may not get a deduction on the basis of the aforesaid judgments.

| --- |
| This section is not frequently used in practice and hence one often forgets its unique provisions. A recent decision of the Delhi High Court helps one not only understand the rationale of this provision but also is educative on when it can be used and when the court will not permit its use [in the case of AIG (Mauritius) LLC v. Tata Televentures (Holdings) Ltd. (2003) 43 SCL 22 (Del.)]. The facts of the Case: A company C engaged in the cellular telephony business had two groups of shareholders - the T group holding about 92 per cent and the A group holding the rest. The T group formed a new company in which it held 99.99 per cent (company “O”). Thereafter, company O made an offer to buy out the shares of the company C. It relied on the provisions of section 235. Thus, it was stated in the offer that if offers were received for shares constituting 90 per cent or more of the capital of C, then the remaining shares would be acquired at the same price. There was another related issue of giving proper notice as required by section 235 which was also given due importance but there was an important substantive question. Can the provisions of section 235 apply in such a case? Essentially, the scheme can be summarised as follows. There can be an offer to takeover a company which offer would be addressed to its shareholders. It may so happen that 90 per cent or more of the shareholders have agreed to the offer but the rest of the shareholders do not agree to it. In such a case, of course, the offeror can acquire the 90 per cent plus shares offered and live with the remaining shareholders. However, what if he does not wish the remaining shareholders to continue? On the other hand, what if the offeror has offered to acquire only from a group holding 90 per cent or more shares and not offered to the remaining shareholders and in such a situation these 10 per cent or less shareholders want the offer to buy their shares also? It is provided under section 235 that if the offeror wishes, he can compulsorily acquire the shares of the remaining shareholders on the same terms. In the other situation, the remaining shareholders can also require the offeror to acquire their shares. Now, in the first situation, the provision would appear to be drastic and involving expropriation. Also, it may be capable of misuse in the sense that it could be used to eliminate certain minority shareholders by acquiring their shares at a nominal value. Acquisitions under section 235 did sound as acts of expropriation but there was a certain logic to it. If 90 per cent of the shareholders were in favour of a scheme, it would not be fair if the remaining small group held back its approval thus blocking it. The motives may be mala fide. As the Court observed, “In my opinion, it is not legally odious to expect to fall in line with the dictates of the overwhelming majority comprising ninety per cent of the group. Usually, there is wisdom in the strength of numbers. There is every possibility that where nine persons are willing to accept a particular offer, the remaining single person may be standing apart from the others for motives which are not mercantile or commercial”. However, it was very important that for such an act to be allowed, it was a fair and bona fide one. The Court very importantly held that the same group that was in the majority could not use to remove the small majority under this provision. It was very essential that an independent person or group should be the offeror which was not so in the present case. In fact, the court held that “it was this very reason the section is deemed to be constitutional and if this was deviated from, it would amount to violation of fundamental rights and thus be struck down”. The Court rejected the proposal. |

Negative goodwill must always be measured and initially recognized as the full difference between acquirer's interest in fair values of the identifiable assets and liabilities acquired less the cost of acquisition [ IAS 22.59].

To the extent that it relates to expected future losses and expenses that are identified in the acquirer's acquisition plan, the negative goodwill is recognised as income when the future losses and expenses are recognised. [IAS 22.61]

An excess of negative goodwill to the extent of the fair values of acquired identifiable nonmonetary assets is recognised in income over the average live of those nonmonetary assets. [IAS 22.62(a)]

Any remaining excess is recognised as income immediately. [IAS 22.62(b)]

Negative goodwill is presented as a deduction from the assets of the enterprise, in the same balance sheet classification as (positive) goodwill. [IAS 22.64]

IAS 22 was predecessor of IFRS 3 Business Combinations which was then applicable.

IFRS 3 Business Combinations has changed the accounting treatment of bargain purchase gain and require the acquiree to recognise the bargain purchase gain in profit or loss on the acquisition date – the gain shall be attributed to the acquirer [ IFRS3.34]. Thus it prescribes one time credit rather than writing back over the years. Of course, IFRS 3 explains that a bargain purchase might happen, for example, in a business combination that is forced sale in which the seller is acting under compulsion. IFRS 3 offers safeguard of recognizing bargain purchase gain:

-

Before recognising a gain on a bargain purchase, the acquirer shall determine whether there exists clear evidence of the underlying reasons for classifying the business combination as a bargain purchase. If such evidence exists, the acquirer shall reassess whether it has correctly identified all of the assets acquired and all of the liabilities assumed and shall recognise any additional assets or liabilities that are identified in that review. [ IFRS 3.36]

Neither the BHS Group explained the reason for such unusual amount of negative goodwill (bargain purchase gain) booked in the accounts nor did the then independent auditor KPMG offer any reservation. Of course, prudential accounting policies were lacking in both FRS 6 and IAS 22 (1998). Here an important point to be noted is the accounting conservatism followed in India:

-

AS 14 Accounting for Amalgamation required the negative goodwill to be recognised as capital reserve [ AS14.17]

-

Ind AS 103 Business Combinations made at carve out from IFRS 3 to require bargain purchase gain to be recognised in capital reserve [ Ind AS 103.36A].

Amendment in special provision relating to business of prospecting, etc.

5.8 Section 42 dealing with special provisions for deduction in the case of business for prospecting, etc., for mineral oil has been amended with effect from assessment year 1999-2000.

Hitherto, where the Central Government has entered into an agreement with any person for the association or participation of the Central Government or any person authorised by it in the business of prospecting for or extraction or production of mineral oils, the expenses and allowances in relation to such business as are specified in the agreement were allowed in lieu of or in addition to those admissible under the Act. Further, any agreement entered into after 31st March 1981, could provide also for allowance in lieu of or in addition to depreciation allowance admissible under section 32 of the Act.

Section 42 has been amended to provide that, subject to the provisions of the agreement entered into by the Central Government, where the business of assessee consisting of the prospecting for or extraction or production of petroleum and natural gas is transferred or any interest therein is transferred, wholly or partly, or any interest in such business is transferred in accordance with the aforesaid agreement entered into by the Central Government and the proceeds of the transfer are less than the expenditure incurred remaining unallowed, a deduction equal to the expenditure remaining unallowed as reduced by the proceeds of transfer, shall be allowed in respect of the previous year, in which the business or an interest therein has been transferred. Further, where such business or any interest therein is transferred and proceeds of the transfer exceed the amount of expenditure incurred remaining unallowed, the excess amount shall be chargeable to tax as profits and gains of business in the previous year in which such business or interest therein has been transferred. The amendment also provides that no deduction shall be allowed in the previous year in which the business or any interest therein is transferred in case the proceeds of transfer are not less than the expenditure remaining unallowed.

The provisions in relation to transfer of aforesaid business or any interest therein shall not apply in a scheme of amalgamation whereby the business or interest therein is transferred by the amalgamating company to the amalgamated company, the latter being an Indian company.

Exemption to capital gains upon conversion of a firm into a company

3.1 Section 47(xiii) has been introduced (with effect from 1-4-1999) to provide that transfer of any capital assets/intangible assets to a company where the firm is succeeded by the company in the business carried on by it shall not be regarded as transfer to attract levy of capital gains subject to certain conditions. The conditions are :

◆ all the assets and liabilities of the firm relating to the business immediately before the succession become the assets and liabilities of the company ;

◆ all the partners of the firm immediately before the succession become the shareholders of the company in the same proportion in which their capital accounts stood in the books of the firm on the date of succession ;

◆ the partners of the firm do not receive any consideration or benefit, directly or indirectly, in any form or manner, other than by way of allotment of shares in the company ; and

◆ the aggregate of the shareholding in the company of the partners of the firm is not less than 50% of the total voting power in the company and their shareholding continues to be as such for a period of five years from the date of the succession.

3.1-1 Analysis of new clause - Note the following :

3.1-1a Short-term capital gains are also exempt - The section provides complete exemption from all capital gains, whether long-term or short-term and including those chargeable under section 50.

3.1-1b The firm should be ‘succeeded’ by the company in the business carried on by it - The requisites of succession, as laid down in CIT v. K.H. Chambers [1965] 55 ITR 674 (SC), are as follows :

◆ There should be a change of ownership.

◆ The integrity of the business should remain - the whole business should devolve upon the successor.

◆ The identity and continuity of the business should be substantially preserved - the same business should be carried on by the person succeeding.

3.1-1c Existing Company - The transferee company can be any company, including an existing company; what is required is that the partners hold not less than 50% of the total equity capital upon allotment to the partners.

3.1-1d Are all the businesses to be transferred or will the provision apply even if only some of the businesses are transferred ? - The section requires the firm to be succeeded by a company in the business carried on by it. According to one view, if the firm carries on two activities which can be termed as two separate businesses, it could be argued that the benefit of the exemption will be available even if one of the two businesses is transferred.

According to the other view, having regard to the other provisions, especially, section 72A(3), it appears that the exemption will be available only if all the businesses are transferred. Even if only one of the businesses is transferred by the firm, under section 72A(3), the entire loss/depreciation of the firm including the loss of the business not transferred is also allowed to be carry forward in the hands of the company. The Legislative intention could not have been to allow carry forward of losses to the company of a business not transferred to it. Hence, the exemption under section 47 will be available only if all the businesses are transferred.

3.1-1e Non-business assets need not be transferred - The section requires that all the assets of the firm ‘relating to the business’ become the assets of the company. It does not state that all the assets of the firm should be transferred to the company. Hence, it is not necessary that non-business assets (e.g. investments out of surplus funds) should also be transferred to the company.

3.1-1f Novation of liabilities may not be necessary - Under section 62 of the Indian Contract Act,1872, a debtor is not released from his liability to the creditor until there is novation, that is, release of the debtor by the creditor by an express agreement. Hence, the firm is not released from its liabilities until the creditor consents to the transfer of the business to the company. In such a case, where there is no novation, can it be said that the liabilities of the firm have become liabilities of the company as required by the section ? It appears that while the creditor may have recourse against the firm, it cannot be denied that the company has certainly become liable to pay liability of the firm. Hence, the condition should be considered to be satisfied even if there is no express novation.

Shamrock [2009] 32 SOT 1 (Mum.-Trib.), it was held that the reconstruction of a business must necessarily involve the concept that the original business is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be - and this is brought out by the section itself of a 'business already in existence'. There must be continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking. The undertaking must continue to carry on the same business, though in some altered or varied form. If the alterations and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. The word 'reconstruction' postulates something which is already constructed in a particular manner because where there is no construction, there cannot be any question of 'reconstruction'.

Therefore, while considering the question whether a particular business is or is not 'reconstruction', it is first necessary to enquire what was the nature of the business which was already in existence, the same as the nature of business which acquired a new shape (sic). If the answer is in the negative, there is no scope for holding that there is any 'reconstruction' of the existing business, because 'reconstruction' implies the continuation of the same business in some altered form. This alteration may assume the form of changing the manner or method of carrying on the same business; it may involve change or rationalization of the administrative set-up or business organization. But when its basic nature changes, it cannot be said that the business is 'reconstructed'. It is not every alteration in the mode, method or scope of the activities of a business and it is not every transfer of assets from one unit to another that will involve reconstruction.

The expression is no doubt very wide but it does not take in a case of company setting-up or establishing a totally independent and viable industrial unit for carrying on the same or similar business, even though it might be so set-up by way of expanding the already existing business. The expression 'reconstruction', in the context in which it is used, denotes that the original business or an undertaking continues to exist without its identity being lost or abandoned. In the reconstruction of a business, as in the reconstruction of a company, there is an element of transfer of assets and of some change, however partial or restricted it may be, of ownership of the assets. The transfer, however, need not be of all the assets. It is nonetheless imperative that there should be continuity and preservation of the old undertaking, though in an altered form. The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets-up another industrial unit. The new industrial unit would not lose its separate and independent identity, even though it has been set-up by a company which is already running an industrial unit before the setting-up of the new unit.

2.7-5 Whether takeover of a firm by allotting shares to partners is 'reconstruction' ?

In CIT v. Gaekwar Foam Rubber Co. Ltd. [1959] 35 ITR 662 (Bom.), under an agreement, assessee-company took over all assets, goodwill and business premises of a partnership for consideration satisfied by allotment of shares to partners of firm and there was no transfer of credits and outstandings nor debts and liabilities of partnership were to be taken over by assessee-company. It was held that the said agree-ment, both in substance and in form, was one of sale and transaction was not of reconstruction of an existing business.

The reconstruction of a business or an industrial undertaking must necessarily involve the concept that the original business or undertaking is not to cease functioning, and its identity is not to be lost or abandoned. The concept essentially rests on changes but the changes must be constructive and not destructive. There must be something positive about the whole matter as opposed to negative. The underlying idea of a reconstruction evidently must be—and this is brought out by the section itself—of a 'business already in existence'. There must be a continuation of the activities and business of the same industrial undertaking. The undertaking must continue to carry on the same business though in some altered or varied form. If the alterations and changes are substantial, there would be little scope for describing what emerges as a reconstruction of the business. Thus for instance if the ownership of a business or an undertaking changes hands not ostensibly but in reality and effectively, that would not be reconstruction or if the very nature of the business is changed, that again would not be reconstruction.

Support for this view can be had from the judgments in the case of Mir Gulam Ali Khan v. CIT [1987] 165 ITR 228 (AP) and C.V.Ramanathan v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 191 (Mad.). In these judgments the Courts gave a liberal interpretation to the word ‘assessee’ for the purposes of section 54 and held that the term ‘assessee’ would include his legal representative after his death. 3.1-1p Increase in equity capital of the company is not prohibited - The section requires that the shareholding of the partners should not be less than 50% of the total voting power. It does not impose a further condition that such voting power cannot be increased and hence, subsequent increase in capital will not per se result in violation of the condition, as long as the partners continue to hold atleast 50% of such increased capital.

3.1-1q Transfer of shares by partners may not affect the exemption if aggregate shareholding is maintained - The section requires that the aggregate of shareholding of the partners is not less than 50% of the total voting power in the company and ‘their shareholding continues to be as such for a period of 5 years from the date of the succession’. A question that arises is whether each partner has to maintain his shareholding as it is or should the aggregate of shareholding be not less than 50%. In other words, if a particular partner transfers the shares to non-partners, can it be said that the condition is fulfilled as long as the other partners continue to hold not less than 50% of the voting power ?

The expression ‘as such’ has been defined in Webster’s Encyclopedic Unabridged Dictionary as ‘as being what is indicated’. Thus, what is required is that the partner’s shareholding should continue to be as being what is indicated in the preceding part of the sentence. What is indicated there is that the aggregate of shareholding should not be less than 50% of the total voting power and hence, on a combined reading, as long as the aggregate of shareholding is not less than 50% of the total voting power, the condition should be deemed to be have been fulfilled. This interpretation is also supported by the Memorandum explaining the provision in Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1998 which states that ‘the aggregate shareholding of the partners is at least 50% for a period of 5 years from the date of succession’.

3.1-1r Takeover by a corporate partner upon dissolution is not covered - The section requires all partners to become shareholders in the firm. A company cannot become a shareholder in the company itself. Hence, if a firm having a company as a partner is dissolved pursuant to which the business is taken over by the company, since the condition of allotment to all the partners would not be satisfied, in such a case, the firm will continue to be liable under section 45(4) of the Act and it will not get benefit of exemption under section 47(xiii).

3.1-1s Business profits are not exempt - An amendment corresponding to this amendment is not made in the provisions relating to computation of business income. Hence, if a transfer of a business results in business income (say, transfer of inventory at a price higher than its carrying cost), such income would be liable to tax.

3.1-1t Consequences of non-fulfilment of conditions - According to one view if any of the conditions is violated in the period of 5 years, the exemption is lost and the Assessing Officer would be entitled to reopen the assessment of the year of transfer and tax the capital gains considered as exempt. According to the other view, the exemption is available once the conditions are satisfied at the time of succession and subsequent non-fulfilment do not result in withdrawal of the exemption. It may be noted that if the first view is adopted, it would result in double taxation for the same default: the firm is taxable under section 47(xiii) and the company is taxable under section 47A(3) (see para 3.3). Since such double taxation is not permissible unless expressly provided, it appears that the second view is the correct view.

The Act does not define anti-competitive combination with reference to market share. Section 5 of the Act defines it as : "Acquisitions of one or more enterprises by one or more persons or merger or amalgamation of enterprises, with reference to threshold criteria of the value of assets and turnover of the enterprise involved1 4."

EMPLOYEES COST 11. In Electronics Data Processing (I) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [IT Appeal No. 420/Hyd/07] the Tribunal held that there was no dispute to the fact that the employees cost to the total turnover of the selected company worked out to be 1.42% as against the industry's average of 30-40% and the assessee's employees cost to turnover percentage was 43%. This fact implied that the selected company had outsourced major portion of its work to third party vendors. Therefore, the company could not be treated as a comparable.

In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that any company with employee cost less than 25% could not be compared with an ITES company – in this case Vishal IT Limited had been adopted by the TPO. This company outsourced its call centre work and, therefore, the employees cost was less than 25% as was the common practice among other ITES. When company had outsourced its ITES, it could not be said that its business results would be comparable to any other ITES provider rendering the services entirely on its own. In such circumstances the net margins of the two comparables could not be on the same basis.

BUSINESS MODEL

12. In Capital IQ Infrastructure Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2013] 57 SOT 14/ 32 taxmann.com 21 (Hyd. – Trib.) the Tribunal found that Dispute Resolution Panel, in the proceedings for the assessment year 2008-09 in the assessee's own case, after taking note of the composition of the vendor payments of Coral Hub for the last three years and the fact that it also commenced a new line of business of printing on demand, wherein it printed upon clients request, in view of the major difference in functionality and the business model the Panel was of the view that 'Coral Hub' was not a suitable comparable to the taxpayer and, hence, it needed to be dropped from the final list of comparables.

SUPER PROFIT COMPANIES

13. In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that the super profit margin companies were to be excluded from the list of comparables for the purposes of transfer pricing study – in this case two companies showed profit of more than 100% as compared to other companies taken by the TPO.

EXTRAORDINARY EVENTS

14. In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that in respect of two companies Datamatics Financial Services and Allsec Technologies Limited, the Tribunal found that merely because there were extraordinary events during the financial year without demonstrating as to how these extraordinary events had influenced the profit margin of the companies they could not be excluded from the list of comparables, but the adjustments for such extraordinary events had to be made to the profits of the companies to bring them on par with the assessee before comparing them with the assessee.

ARITHMETIC MEAN

15. First proviso to section 92C(2) provides that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price shall be taken to be the arithmetical mean of such prices.

In Simphony Marketing Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 38 taxmann.com 55 (Bang. – Trib.)the assessee had selected nine comparables identified by it at arithmetical mean of 14.84% in relation to the disclosed margins of 14.91%, the difference being within the tolerance limit of 5%. The TPO added 18 more comparables to the two accepted by him. The TPO worked out the arithmetical mean at 22.28% after making an adjustment to the benchmark for working capital. If nine comparables which according to the assessee were wrongly included were excluded, it would work out to be an arithmetical mean of 7.97% only as against 14.91% disclosed by the assessee, so that there could have been no addition. The DRP affirmed the addition of TPO. The Tribunal found that out of 20 companies chosen by the TPO as comparables only 11 companies were found to be comparables and their arithmetic mean was only 7.97%. The profit margin cost of the assessee was 14.91% which was made higher than the arithmetic mean of comparable companies chosen by the TPO after the exclusion of some of the comparable companies. The reasons for exclusions of 9 companies were on the following grounds:

During the previous year, there were extraordinary events that took place which warranted exclusion as a comparable;

The comparable company performed knowledge process outsourcing and the assessee was doing business process outsourcing;

The comparable company outsourced most of the work and the assessee was carrying out work by itself;

Videnotification S.O. 482(E), dated 4th March, 2011, the government has enhanced the value of assets and turnover mentioned in section 5 by fifty percent.

The current thresholds for the combined assets/turnover of the combining parties are as follows:– Individual : Either the combined assets of the enterprises would value more than (INR) 1500 crores in India or the combined turnover of the enterprise is more than (INR) 4500 crores in India. In case either or both of the enterprises have assets/turnover outside India also, then the combined assets of the enterprises value more than US$ 750 million, including at least (INR) 750 crores in India or turnover is more than US$ 2250 million, including at least (INR) 2250 crores in India.

Group : The group to which the enterprise whose control, shares, assets or voting rights are being acquired would belong after the acquisition or the group to which the enterprise remaining the merger or amalgamation would belong has either assets of value of more than INR 6000 crores in India or turnover more than INR 18000 crores in India. Where the group has presence in India as well as outside India then the group has assets more than US$ 3 billion including at least INR 750 crores in India or turnover more than US$ 9 billion including at least INR 2250 crores in India.

The term Group has been explained in the Competition Act. Two enterprises belong to a 'Group' if one is in position to exercise at least 26 per cent voting rights or appoint at least 50 per cent of the directors or controls the management or affairs in the other.[Explanation (b) to section 5 of the Competition Act]. Vide notification S.O. 481(E), dated 4th March, 2011, the Government has exempted "Group" exercising less than fifty percent of voting rights in other enterprise from the provisions of section 5 of the Competition Act for a period of five years.

The turnover shall be determined by taking into account the values of sales of goods or services. The value of assets shall be determined by taking the book value of the assets as shown in the audited books of account of the enterprise, in the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the date of proposed merger falls, as reduced by any depreciation. The value of assets shall include the brand value, value of goodwill or Intellectual Property Rights etc. referred to in Explanation (C) to section 5 of the Competition Act.

Comments

8. Therefore, computation of turnover criteria will determine the decision to notify a transaction or not. It is not an easy task to calculate the actual turnover in view of the ambiguous provisions and definitions of turnover and it will be a real challenge to calculate the turnover and to determine whether a transaction requires notifying to the CCI or not.

Further, the thresholds are based on asset/turnover and not on the market share/dominance of the combining parties. This would cover even combinations between two foreign entities in a third country. Such transactions will have to be notified to CCI merely because the combining parties have certain assets/turnover in India, that too not necessarily relatable to the subject matter of the transaction. Thus, it will be necessary to give clarification on this point as well.

Also, only those cross-border combinations in which the combining parties have significant India present in terms of market share in the relevant product /services market should alone be required to file notice with CCI for prior approval. In case an Indian company acquires a foreign entity, the market share in India of such acquired entity i.e. the target entity, may be considered, whereas if a foreign entity is acquiring an Indian entity, the market share of such acquired entity in India i.e. target entity, may be considered as the benchmark for mandatory filing of notice with CCI for prior approval.

Importance of "Turnover"

9. For complying with the provisions of the Act for notifying a transaction, calculation of turnover of the parties is critical from the merger control perspective. The transactions where the parties fail to meet the asset and turnover thresholds under section 5 of the Competition Act need not be notified. It is to be noted that the given the potentially substantial penalties i.e. up to 1% of the turnover of the combination that may be attracted for not notifying a transaction to the CCI, it is all the more necessary that the business house should know how to calculate the turnover so as to comply with the provisions. Further, entering into a combination which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within the relevant market in India is prohibited and such combination shall be void.
