running business is taken over or amalgamated, then certainly the assets are valued on the date of amalgamation and in this process sometimes the consideration to be paid is much more than the net assets and such deficit can either be reduced from Capital Reserve of the transferee company as provided under Accounting Standard-14 but if the scheme of amalgamation provides and there being genuine transaction, then Courts have consistently held that such deficit is to be considered as goodwill and eligible for depreciation. [Para 18]

■ However, in the instant case, the facts are different and peculiar. It is not the case of some independent transaction of amalgamation a company 'A' with company 'B' for taking over the business but it is a case where one holding company is having two subsidiaries companies and two subsidiary companies are merged in the process of amalgamation but the owner remains the same. In the process of amalgamation, the 60.72 equity shares have been issued by the Transferee company, i.e. the assessee company -ATPL to transferor company-MLPL and after reducing the face value of equity shares held by shareholder of MLPL, the excess amount of Rs.5.97 crores is treated as goodwill. It is clearly visible from the merger note that only against the creation of goodwill 60.72 equity shares in lieu of 1 equity share of MLPL has been issued. It is a case where the owner himself is claiming that one of its subsidiary company has purchased the business on of its another subsidiary company and such higher amount is basically goodwill and there being no banking transaction except the issue of fresh equity shares in lieu of the goodwill. It apparently seems to be an arrangement made at the instance of the holding company between its two subsidiary companies. Genuineness of the transaction of amalgamation between two independent/unrelated companies is missing in the instant case. [Para 19]

■

It is noted that similar type of transaction came for adjudication before Coordinate Bench, Hyderabad in the case of Invesco (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2025] 176 taxmann.com 784 (Hyderabad - Trib.) wherealso the wholly owned subsidiary of assessee company namely Invesco Hyderabad was amalgamated with the assessee company Invesco (India) under the scheme of amalgamation and against the investment of Rs.244.09 crore in the shares of subsidiary company Invesco Hyderabad the fair market value of intangible net assets of subsidiary company were at Rs.102.86 crore and the excess cost of investment over the value of net tangible asset has been determined as goodwill. [Para 20]

■

It is noted that prior to amalgamation ATPL earned revenue of Rs.2.23 crore whereas the revenue of MLPL was Rs.1.97 crore which shows that turnover of ATPL is higher than MLPL. It is also observed that 100 per cent of the sales of MLPL were effected majorly to the USA holding company where the sales of ATPL are to various customers in India. Interestingly, no sales have been effected to its related parties including the holding company by the assessee company, i.e. ATPL. Also post amalgamation, no sales have been effected to the holding company which indicates that the existing business of the subsidiary company prior to amalgamation has been discontinued post amalgamation and only the facilities or the assets appearing in the balance sheet prior to amalgamation as on 31-3-2014 has been transferred to the transferee company ATPL. These facts again support the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the observation of the Assessing Officer that this is a mere colourable transaction and in the garb of inflating the value of assets and creation of goodwill, assessee has intended to claim depreciation for the year under consideration and to be claimed in the subsequent years also. It is also an admitted fact that if new assets are added to the present set of assets on a running business then certainly some sales ought to increase but due to such amalgamation neither any new business has been added nor the profitability has increased much more than the situation prior to amalgamation as appearing from the records. Therefore, the creation of alleged goodwill is merely a colourable transaction carried out between the holding company and the subsidiary company which is to create an Intangible asset, inflate the value of equity shares of the transferee company and to further evade tax by claiming depreciation on such fictitious asset created through such arrangement of transaction between related parties. Therefore, it is held that claim of creation of goodwill of Rs.5.97 crores is only an artificial creation and is classic case of lifting the corporate wheel as rightly observed by the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, no intangible asset in the form of goodwill is created at Rs.5.97 crores. Further, since no intangible asset has been created in the process of amalgamation, depreciation claimed at Rs.1.49 crores also deserves to be disallowed. [Para 21]

for consideration of the Tribunal was in relation to the transfer of the Call Centre business. As part of the share purchase agreement between Hutchison and Vodafone, it was agreed that the call centre being operated by the taxpayer would not be acquired by Vodafone. Accordingly, the taxpayer undertook a slump sale, transferring the business to a newly established Hutchison Group company named HWP (India).

The Revenue took two alternate pleas in contention that the transaction was controlled and hence subject to transfer pricing:

(a) that the call centre business was purchased by the Hutchison Group through a dummy subsidiary incorporated to create the fiction that the taxpayer was transferring the business to an Indian company, and hence the transaction is effectively between Hutchison Whampoa Ltd., Hong Kong, and its Indian associated enterprise, i.e. the taxpayer; and

(b)

that the transaction qualified as a deemed international transaction as it was entered into pursuant to a prior agreement between Vodafone and Hutchison.

The Tribunal held that on account of the share purchase agreement having been entered into in May 2007, the taxpayer became an AE of both the shareholders during the year. That said, despite there being a prior agreement between Hutchison Telecommunications International Limited, Cayman Islands, and Vodafone International Holdings BV, there was no possibility of a deemed international transaction as HWP (India) was not a third party. Surprisingly though, the Tribunal concluded that the transaction qualified as an international transaction between the taxpayer and Hutchison Group overseas, by disregarding HWP (India) on the premise that it was only an arrangement without any substantial business or commercial interest.

It is worthwhile to note that in the context of deemed international transaction under section 92B(2), the amendment made in the Finance Act, 2014 would still not have had any impact, since the provision still requires a prior agreement to be entered into between the overseas AE and a third party, whether resident or non-resident. In this case, the prior agreement was with an AE.

The conclusion of the Tribunal that a sale between two resident entities could be treated as a transaction between the resident entity and its overseas AE can have significant implications. Transactions such as sale between two resident entities pursuant to a global sale agreement between the overseas AEs of the transacting parties are strictly not covered within the deeming provision even under the amended section 92B(2). However, the Tribunal in this case has treated such domestic transactions as international transactions based on the wide meaning of the term 'transaction', which includes an arrangement between the taxpayer and its AE. While the view of the Tribunal appears to be based on the specific facts of the case, it could encourage the Revenue authorities to rely on this view and seek to treat certain domestic transactions as subject to Transfer Pricing even when they do not fall under the meaning of deemed international transaction or specified domestic transaction.

Having determined it to be an international transaction, the Tribunal had occasion to consider the appropriate valuation method. The taxpayer had adopted a combination of Net Asset Value and Profit Earning Capacity Value methods. The TPO was of the view that the capitalization was based on past earning and not on future cash flow and hence rejected these methods. He called for the projected cash flows, but as these were not provided by the taxpayer in the course of the assessment, proceeded to adopt the Comparable Uncontrolled Transaction method by adopting the Price to Earnings ratio and arrived at 3 comparable companies. The DRP ratified the choice of the CUT method, but eliminated two of the companies and also did not take cognizance of the DCF valuation provided by the taxpayer due to time constraints. The taxpayer protested the choice of the third comparable, First Source Solutions Ltd. on grounds of functional differences. The Tribunal consequently ruled that Discounted Cash Flow was the most appropriate valuation method and remanded the valuation to the TPO.

Continuing from the esoteric to the mundane, the other material ground of appeal before Tribunal was in respect of an adjustment made to the ITES services rendered by the taxpayer to its associated enterprises. The Tribunal has made some pertinent observations on filters, in addition to adjudicating on comparables:

(a)

the Tribunal has accepted the adoption of a 75 per cent export filter, on the premise that the taxpayer was wholly engaged in export of its ITES services and hence for comparability reasons, comparables should also be predominantly exporters of services. The Tribunal also observed that the adoption of such filter was neither prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue or the taxpayer as it would apply uniformly to all comparables;

(b)

the Tribunal has accepted a related party transaction filter of 25 per cent, holding that anywhere between 10 per cent and 25 per cent of RPT were in order so as to obtain a reasonable set of comparable companies, and that the adoption of a 25 per cent filter by the TPO amounted to taking the most liberal approach.

[Para 26] According to the revenue, the transfer of intellectual properties, codes, formulae, designs, etc., to IISL was not permanent. It was difficult to accept the said view. It was specifically stated that assets and properties of the assessee shall be transferred to IISL. Reading of clause 4 of the MOU made it clear that the business transactions carried out by the assessee that were transferred to IISL would continue with them and IISL shall be entitled to enforce their rights thereunder without any restriction. It meant restriction of time as well. To come to a different conclusion as canvassed by the revenue, was not acceptable. Clauses 7 and 8 of the MOU restricted the promoters of the assessee-company to do similar or identical business carried out earlier by the assessee and now by IISL permanently and even all improvements in technology, etc., would be the property of IISL. [Para 27]

According to the revenue, by virtue of clause 2 of the MOU, the assessee had not transferred the building, motor car and assets and liabilities relating to income-tax matters. This, according to the revenue, fell short of the slump sale for slump consideration. It was not possible to accept the view canvassed by the revenue. The Bombay High Court in CIT v. Narkeshari Prakashan Ltd. [1992] 196 ITR 438 clearly held that the sale of even branches of an undertaking along with its assets and liabilities amounts to sale as a going concern for a slump price. The assessee's business assets were computers, furniture, etc., because the assessee was in the field of software business. It was difficult to hold that the purchaser could not continue with the business in the absence of building and motor car, which had been kept apart. If the purchaser perhaps was prevented from continuing the business, the stand of the revenue that that was not sale of a going concern for a slump price, would have been correct. The question was whether the business would continue in the same line even without the two assets. Reading of the MOU, relevant clauses of which made it clear that the assessee had transferred all the properties relating to its business. Even according to the revenue, the assessee's business assets were in the nature of intellectual properties, codes, formulae, design, etc. These had been transferred for a consideration. [Para 28]

Further, 'slump sale' means transfer of one or more undertakings as a result of sale for a lump sum consideration without values being assigned to the individual assets and liabilities in such sales. In the instant case of the assessee, though in the purchaser's books of account the individual assets had been priced independently, yet the assessee had not assigned separate values and, consequently, sold the items for an independent price. It was not the revenue's case also that individual assets had the price fixed separately and charged. 'Undertaking' is explained in Explanation 1 to section 2(19AA). According to this Explanation, it includes any part of an undertaking or a unit or division of an undertaking or a business activity as a whole. The revenue's case was that some of the items like motor car and building had been retained by the assessee; as such, this could not be treated as a slump sale. But the fact to be considered was that the assessee was in the field of intellectual property rights. Computers, furniture, etc., which were linked with the business of the assessee had been sold. The items that the assessee kept separately had nothing to do with its business which was sold/handed over to the purchaser, i.e., IISL. Thus, only the business had been sold. The purchaser could very well carry on with the business, which was carried by the assessee before the sale, without purchasing any independent items. In view of the above, the plea of the revenue that the assessee had not sold the undertaking as a whole, could not be accepted. [Para 29]

Thus, the claim of the assessee was to be allowed and that of the revenue was to be rejected.

The potential benefit of the acquiree's income tax loss carry forwards or other deferred tax assets might not satisfy the criteria for separate recognition when a business combination is initially accounted for but might be realised subsequently. An entity shall recognise acquired deferred tax benefits that it realises after the business combination as follows: (a)

Acquired deferred tax benefits recognised within the measurement period that result from new information about facts and circumstances that existed at the acquisition date shall be applied to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill related to that acquisition. If the carrying amount of that goodwill is zero, any remaining deferred tax benefits shall be recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity as capital reserve or recognised directly in capital reserve, depending on whether paragraph 34 or paragraph 36A of Ind AS 103, would have applied had the measurement period adjustments been known on the date of acquisition itself.

(b)

All other acquired deferred tax benefits realised shall be recognised in profit or loss (or, if this Standard so requires, outside profit or loss).

Current and deferred tax arising from share-based payment transactions

68A. In some tax jurisdictions, an entity receives a tax deduction (i.e. an amount that is deductible in determining taxable profit) that relates to remuneration paid in shares, share options or other equity instruments of the entity. The amount of that tax deduction may differ from the related cumulative remuneration expense, and may arise in a later accounting period. For example, in some jurisdictions, an entity may recognise an expense for the consumption of employee services received as consideration for share options granted, in accordance with Ind AS 102, Share-based Payment, and not receive a tax deduction until the share options are exercised, with the measurement of the tax deduction based on the entity's share price at the date of exercise.

68B. As with the preliminary expenses discussed in paragraphs 9 and 26(b) of this Standard, the difference between the tax base of the employee services received to date (being the amount permitted as a deduction in future periods under taxation laws), and the carrying amount of nil, is a deductible temporary difference that results in a deferred tax asset. If the amount permitted as a deduction in future periods under taxation laws is not known at the end of the period, it shall be estimated, based on information available at the end of the period. For example, if the amount permitted as a deduction in future periods under taxation laws is dependent upon the entity's share price at a future date, the measurement of the deductible temporary difference should be based on the entity's share price at the end of the period.

68C. As noted in paragraph 68A, the amount of the tax deduction (or estimated future tax deduction, measured in accordance with paragraph 68B) may differ from the related cumulative remuneration expense. Paragraph 58 of the Standard requires that current and deferred tax should be recognised as income or an expense and included in profit or loss for the period, except to the extent that the tax arises from (a) a transaction or event that is recognised, in the same or a different period, outside profit or loss, or (b) a business combination (other than the acquisition by an investment entity of a subsidiary that is required to be measured at fair value through profit or loss). If the amount of the tax deduction (or estimated future tax deduction) exceeds the amount of the related cumulative remuneration expense, this indicates that the tax deduction relates not only to remuneration expense but also to an equity item. In this situation, the excess of the associated current or deferred tax should be recognised directly in equity.

y Gate Hotel [2019] 101 taxmann.com 163/174 ITD 513 (Cochin-Trib.) held that "where assessee sold its hotel premises along with licences for boarding, lodging, bar etc. as a going concern to a buyer who was also engaged in hotel business, it could be regarded as a case of slump sale and, thus, Assessing Officer was justified in applying provisions of section 50B of the Act to the assessee's case." The following observations made by the Hon'ble Members at para 4.3 are worth noticing (and) which enabled the Tribunal to decide in favour of the Revenue-

"4.3 In order to understand whether the sale was a slump sale or sale of independent items of assets, necessarily we have to examine the intention of the parties to the sale agreement. If the business of the vendor is sold as such as a going concern, it will tantamount to a slump sale. If the sale is a slump sale, then provisions of section 50B of the I.T. Act will have application. The impugned sale deed executed on 18.01.2013, mentions only the sale of land and building for a total consideration of Rs. 20 crores. However, we notice from page 9 of the sale deed, what was sold by vendor includes also license for boarding, lodging, bar etc. The assessee was running a hotel business in Ooty. On sale of the property, the business of the assessee was closed down and the assets of the assessee as whole was transferred to the purchaser, viz., M/s. BKR Hotels and Resorts Private Limited. It is an admitted fact that the purchaser is in hotel business. It is also admitted fact that purchaser, after substantial investment on the property carried on the hotel business in the said premises. It is clear from reading of the entire clause of the sale deed that the assets of the assessee, including the license for boarding, lodging, bar etc. were also transferred to the purchaser along with land and building as a going concern. The entire business was sold for a total consideration of Rs. 20 crores consisting of land and building which includes furniture, equipments, kitchen equipments, telephone instruments, television, computer, etc. The building and other amenities are valued as a whole, without assigning value to any item of the assets. As mentioned earlier, consequent to the sale of the hotel premises, the business of assessee was closed down. Therefore, it is clear from the sale deed executed, the intention of the parties was to sell the hotel business as a going concern and the same is nothing but a slump sale."

30.9-4 The ITAT Kolkata Bench in the case of Ambo Agro Products Ltd. v. Principal CIT [2017] 81 taxmann.com 305/165 ITD 20 (Kol.-Trib.) held that where the assessee claimed to sell its manufacturing unit of edible oil as a going concern on slump sale basis, the mere fact that buyer was already in the same line of business and thus, was not keen to buy intangible assets such as trade name/logos/trademarks/product name etc. belonging to assessee, it would not take assessee's case out of purview of section 50B of the Act.

30.9-5 The Delhi High Court in the case of Triune Projects (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 40 (Delhi) held that "In a case of slump sale if certain defunct assets or properties are left out because they would cause inconvenience or lead to some kind of trouble for buyer, it is well within right of seller to exclude such asset from list and such sale would qualify for treatment under section 50B of the Act."

The following pertinent observations made at paras 10 and 11 from this judgment are worth noticing-

"10........... To expect a purchaser to buy and pay value for defunct or superfluous assets flies in the face of commercial sense. Unfortunately, the Revenue's understanding is that in a going concern the buyer is bound to pay good money, transact and purchase bad and irrecoverable debts. Not only does it fly in the face of common and commercial understanding, but it is not even a pre-condition, as is evident from the definition of "undertaking", cited in Explanation (1) to Section 2(19) (A) of the Act.

11. This definition of "undertaking" is what has been engrafted into by reference, under section 2(42C) of the Act. Therefore, if certain assets or properties are left out because they would cause inconvenience or lead to some kind of a trouble for the purchasing party, it is well within its right to exclude it from the list of assets."

■ However, the stated business transfer agreement in its Non Compete and Non solicit states that the purchaser (RIO) shall be exclusive vehicle engaged in the transferred business. Each of the promoters and the seller shall not and shall procure that their affiliates do not, directly, indirectly or beneficially by themselves or in association with or through any person; (a) commence, establish engage in, invest in, carry on, won, manage, operate, join, assist and/or. This leads to an interpretation as to whether this business agreement is only restricted to the business transferred or its proceeds also as there is no provision as to how the effect of gain made if any is to be shared between the parties. It is also mentioned that the R 9 is the group company and a related entity. RIO might have in all prudence obtained consent of the shareholders before offering its shares to the other entities, it is alleged that it has been sold at a huge value, which raises doubt as within 2 months of the business transfer the alleged allotment has taken place. Similarly, there is no valuation report produced either on the transfer of Rs.35 lakh of the business nor the sale after the transfer of funds at a huge premium. The question is whether the act of R 10 violates the clause 9.1 of the agreement. Since the business agreement is silent, there cannot be abuse of circumstances to bring in fresh entities by evicting the petitioner/s rights if any which is confined to R 9. However, there could be a violation of Section 188 (related party transactions) as the new entity brought in as shareholder by sale at a high premium by R 10 of its shares/issue of shares within 2 months and it would have been in order if the shareholders of R 9 would have accordingly consented for such sale as the creation of SPV by a slump sale could have been utilised to bring in other related party shareholders at the cost of the Petitioner/s who are stated to be promoters of R 9 which is a group company.

■

Prima facie it appears that R 1 and R 4 have acted independently as Directors of R 10 in increasing the shares and issuing at a premium. There are two possibilities of nullifying the act by either : the transfer of the proceeds back to R 9 which is sought in prayer of the applicant to enable the shareholders of R 9 hold the shares which will eliminate LLP A which are stated to be holding 90% of the shares and related to RI.

■

The Court also observes that R 4 has filed another application IA wherein he has made allegations against these transactions even though he has been party to the same and was respondent a matter which is yet to be taken up whether to be allowed as the same is now filed under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, which turns the respondent 4 as agreeing with the pleadings of the petitioner and his prayers. All the three groups which appeared created ample commotions during the arguments on the status of R 9 and R 10 and this application has been prolonged for long time and one of the contentions is that this application is filed to prevent IPO issue.

■

The Court concludes that the process by which the R 1 and R 4 had implemented the business agreement, isolating the interests of the R 9 being a group company which permitted the sale of its business or brand value through slump sale is not in accordance with the provisions of the Group/Subsidiary Companies as defined in Sec 2(87) and other provisions.

■

By way of nullifying the profits that could have come to R 9 by transferring the business on slump basis and immediately issuing shares to certain other LLPs which are related party, there seems to be injustice cause to the applicant, and to R 9 as an entity. This act is not backed by any proper board resolution of R 9 and a new entity created as SPV cannot sell its shares at high premium. Hence the amount of such realisation ought to be reverted back to the R 9 as they are not profits out of business but on account of inter change of brand value and franchise at a cost of Rs 35 lakhs but not properly explained through appropriate valuation. Hence the rights of the applicant needs to be protected along with other shareholders, as the Court observes that there was no unanimous resolution to this arrangement to transfer the assets/liabilities of tea business to R 10. On revenue's appeal : HELD: The facts indicated that the parties were unrelated and the assessee purchased the cement units as a slump scale with effect from 1-11-1999. Under the business transfer agreement the assessee not only acquired the fixed assets of the said unit but also the current assets of the same units including the current liabilities for which the total consideration of Rs. 550 crores was paid. It was also a fact that the said TISCO had arrived at the profit on sale of Rs. 125. 26 crores after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers. This was the basis for Assessing Officer's opinion that the cost of fixed assets acquired by the assessee should be the book value of TISCO. Accordingly, he restricted the cost of the assets to the above amount thereby treating the balance amount as goodwill and denied depreciation. It was also a fact that the agreement did not speak of any goodwill payment and the assessee had adjusted the entire consideration paid between fixed assets and net current assets. It was also a fact that in the next assessment year assessee acquired another unit from 'R' and the assessee treated the difference between the fair market value of the assets and the payment made as goodwill and made entries in the books of account accordingly where as in relevant year the value paid was for fixed assets and net current assets and goodwill was not involved. [Para 6]

Section 43(1) is clear that the actual cost to be considered for the purpose of section 32 should be the actual cost paid by the assessee. Since the cost has not been directly or indirectly met by any other person or authority, the cost paid by the assessee for acquisition of the assets of the units is the cost under section 43(1) . However, Explanation (3) makes it clear that where the assets are used at any time by any other person for the purpose of his business or profession and the Assessing Officer is satisfied that the main purpose of the transfer of such assets directly or indirectly to the assessee was reduction of liability of tax for claiming depreciation with reference to enhanced cost, the actual cost of the assets shall be such an amount as the Assessing Officer may determine having regard to all the circumstances of the case. As rightly considered by the Commissioner (Appeals) the parties were unrelated and the transaction was at arm's length basis. The registered valuer also valued the assets as on 1-11-1999, the price of which was considered to be the cost of fixed asset acquired and the balance to the current assets including the current liabilities. In view of this, there was no reason to invoke Explanation (3) as the Assessing Officer nowhere stated that the main purpose of such a valuation was for reduction of liability to tax. It was a direct acquisition by the assessee company from another public limited company in an open bid, being the highest bidder. As per AS 10 para 35 the assessee was supposed to take the value on the fair basis as determined by competent valuers. [Para 8]

Sub-section (1) of section 43 lays down that actual cost in the hands of an assessee means the actual cost of the assets as reduced by that portion of the cost which may have been met directly or indirectly by any other person. Explanation 3 to the said sub-section stipulates that:-

(i)

The assets which are acquired by the assessee were used by any other person before the date of acquisition;

(ii)

The income-tax officer arrives at objective satisfaction that such assets were transferred with the main purpose of reducing tax liability by claiming depreciation with reference to enhanced cost;

(iii)

Then the Income-tax Officer is empowered to determine the actual cost having regard to all the circumstances of the case. [Para 10]

So from a perusal of the aforesaid provision, it is found that the Assessing Officer needs to satisfy that the main purpose of the transfer of such assets directly or indirectly to the assessee was for the reduction of a liability of tax by claiming depreciation with reference to an enhanced cost. Then only, the Assessing Officer can invoke Explanation 3 to fix the actual cost. So, the requirement of law is that the main purpose of the transfer of assets was for the reduction of a liability to tax without satisfying the same, the Assessing Officer cannot invoke Explanation 3 to section 43(1). [Para 11]

Here, in this case, the Assessing Officer's observation that neither in the audit report nor in the papers filed along with the return the acquisition was not mentioned, is not correct. In the Director's report, it has been reported that the assessee had acquired business of Deltron Ltd. as a going concern. Similarly, in Schedule 'T' of balance sheet being notes on accounts as Note 10, assessee-company has disclosed that it has purchased electronic business of Deltron at a net consideration of Rs. 7.54 cores. Thus, the observation of the Assessing Officer that the assessee did not disclose the transaction is factually incorrect. [Para 12]

A perusal of the agreement entered into between assessee and Deltron makes it abundantly clear that the purport of the transfer of electronic business from the public limited company namely Deltron to the assessee was on account of lack of sufficient financial source to run the said business as a profitable unit by the public limited company. This purpose as stated in the agreement has not been found to be rejected, commented or disputed by any of the authorities below. There is no material to dispute the assertion that Deltron, a public limited company had no resources to invest heavily in R&D or develop process capability to keep pace with the advancing technology.

No doubt, the ground of common management and common office is a relevant consideration but the same is not of conclusive nature. The prime requirement under Explanation to section 43(1) is that the transfer of a going concern has been effected to defraud the revenue and such defraud had been attempted by claiming depreciation at an enhanced cost. As stated above, it was a case of transfer by a public limited company and the purpose stated in the agreement is not a matter of dispute. The Assessing Officer in the order has opined that the assets as reflected in the books of Deltron as on 1-4-2004 at Rs. 66, 95, 884 were transferred for a consideration of Rs. 1,76,84,338 though the assessee claims that such a finding is incorrect.

It has been pointed out that Deltron is a public limited company and had been allowed 100 per cent deduction under section 35(1)(iv)/35(2) as expenditure and as such, there was certain assets which appeared at Nil cost in the books of Deltron Ltd. It was however stated that such assets were appearing in the balance sheet prepared under the Companies Act as on 31-3-2004 at Rs. 4,71,20,059 and if the deduction under section 35(1)(iv)/35(2) is ignored, WDV of such assets as on 31-3-2004 would stand at Rs. 2, 16, 06, 346. [Para 14]

Appendix A

Defined terms

This Appendix is an integral part of the Ind AS.

Acquiree

The business or businesses that the acquirer obtains control of in a business combination.

Acquirer

The entity that obtains control of the acquiree.

Acquisition date

The date on which the acquirer obtains control of the acquiree.

19[Business

An integrated set of activities and assets that is capable of being conducted and managed for the purpose of providing goods or services to customers, generating investment income (such as dividends or interest) or generating other income from ordinary activities.]

Business combination

A transaction or other event in which an acquirer obtains control of one or more businesses. Transactions sometimes referred to as 'true mergers' or 'mergers of equals' are also business combinations as that term is used in this Ind AS.

Contingent consideration

Usually, an obligation of the acquirer to transfer additional assets or equity interests to the former owners of an acquiree as part of the exchange for control of the acquiree if specified future events occur or conditions are met. However, contingent consideration also may give the acquirer the right to the return of previously transferred consideration if specified conditions are met.

Equity interests

For the purposes of this Ind AS, equity interests is used broadly to mean ownership interests of investor-owned entities and owner, member or participant interests of mutual entities.

Fair value

Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. (See Ind AS 113.)

The assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern. The TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and the assessee was the highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores. The same was accepted by the TISCO in its Board meeting on 18-12-1998. Thereupon, the cement units were actually taken over and used in its own production activity. After acquiring the company units as going concern as the assessee, on the basis of valuation report of 'K' fixed the fair market value of fixed assets as on the date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores. The balance amount of consideration of Rs. 68. 61 crores was attributed to the net current assets taken over. The assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on the value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores. In the course of assessment the Assessing Officer asked for the WDV of the assets of TISCO. Since the assessee expressed its inability to furnish the details as they purchased the assets on the basis as going concern, the Assessing Officer obtained the information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that the said company had shown the book value of fixed assets at Rs. 345. 95 crores and after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers, offered profits on sale of net assets of cement division at Rs. 125. 25 crores in their books of account. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had paid more amount than the book value and the difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment and accordingly after discussion about the provisions of section 43(1) , report of the registered valuer, determined the goodwill value at the difference between the amount adopted by the assessee and the amount shown in the books of TISCO and depreciation on the amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed thereby making addition of Rs. 16. 39 crores. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) it was contended that the assessee had acquired fixed assets and current assets of the unit in an open bid and on the basis of the report of the registered valuer the value was accordingly capitalized to the extent of Rs. 481. 39 crores and Assessing Officer's action in taking the WDV of TISCO was not correct as Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case as these two companies were independent and not related and further the Assessing Officer had not correctly appreciated the registered valuer's report and the method adopted. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contentions and set aside the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

6.1-5 ICDS

Income Computation Disclosure Standards (ICDS) IV issued under section 145(2) is silent regarding taxability of the compensation covered by section 28(ii)(e).

Section 28(ii) provides for taxation of any compensation or other payment "due" to or received by an assessee. Hence, the compensation, etc., covered by section 28(ii)(e) would be taxable in the year in which it becomes "due" or in the year of receipt under section 145(1), if the assessee has adopted cash basis of accounting.

6.1-6 Termination of contracts of 'professionals'

Section 28(ii)(e) provides for taxation in respect of any contract relating to "business".

Now,

section 28 provides that profits and gains of business or "profession" shall be chargeable to tax.

section 28(i) provides for taxation of profits and gains of any business or profession.

section 28(iv) refers to taxation of benefit or perquisite arising from the exercise of a profession.

section 28(va)(a) refers to any activity in relation to business or profession.

However, the new section 28(ii)(e) is consciously restricted to business.

There is a controversy as to whether the term 'business' includes 'profession'. It has been held that :

(a)

business does not include profession for the purposes of section 28(va) [Satya Sheel Khosla v. ITO [2015] 63 taxmann.com 293 (Delhi - Trib.); Dr. K. Premraj v. Dy. CIT [2014] 41 taxmann.com 81/149 ITD 339 (Chennai - Trib.)];

(b)

business includes profession for the purposes of section 9(1)(i) [Barendra Prosad Ray v. ITO [1981] 6 Taxman 19 (SC)];

(c)

business does not include profession for the purposes of section 32(1)(iv) [G.K. Choksi Co. v. CIT [2007] 165 Taxman 299 (SC)].

Hence it is a moot point as to whether the amendment covers compensation upon termination or modification of any term relating to a profession.

All the four assessees were directors and principal promoter-shareholders of the company ‘MPIL’, which was earlier engaged in the business of doing bottling work for ‘HCC’ in its unit. Since ‘MPIL’ suffered heavy losses, as per the BIFR order, business and assets of the company relating to the bottling unit were vested in HCC. All the assessees agreed to desist from using the confidential information regarding the bottling and distribution of Coca Cola trade mark beverages provided to them by Coca Cola company for a consideration of Rs. 1.5 crores each and an agreement to that effect was entered into between the HCC and the assessees. For the relevant assessment year, the Assessing Officer accepted the assessees’ claim that the consideration amount received from the HCC was capital receipt not liable to tax. However, the Commissioner, exercising powers under section 263, set aside those orders of the Assessing Officer on the ground that the agreement entered into between the assessees and HCC constituted extinguishment of assessees’ right to manufacture, produce or process and, therefore, the consideration amount received by them as non-compete fee was liable to capital gain tax. Amalgamation after the Balance Sheet Date

27. When an amalgamation is effected after the balance sheet date but before the issuance of the financial statements of either party to the amalgamation, disclosure is made in accordance with AS 4, 'Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date', but the amalgamation is not incorporated in the financial statements. In certain circumstances, the amalgamation may also provide additional information affecting the financial statements themselves, for instance, by allowing the going concern assumption to be maintained.

Main Principles

28. An amalgamation may be either -

(a)

an amalgamation in the nature of merger, or

(b)

an amalgamation in the nature of purchase.

29. An amalgamation should be considered to be an amalgamation in the nature of merger when all the following conditions are satisfied:

(i)

All the assets and liabilities of the transferor company become, after amalgamation, the assets and liabilities of the transferee company.

(ii)

Shareholders holding not less than 90% of the face value of the equity shares of the transferor company (other than the equity shares already held therein, immediately before the amalgamation, by the transferee company or its subsidiaries or their nominees) become equity shareholders of the transferee company by virtue of the amalgamation.

(iii)

The consideration for the amalgamation receivable by those equity shareholders of the transferor company who agree to become equity shareholders of the transferee company is discharged by the transferee company wholly by the issue of equity shares in the transferee company, except that cash may be paid in respect of any fractional shares.

(iv)

The business of the transferor company is intended to be carried on, after the amalgamation, by the transferee company.

(v)

No adjustment is intended to be made to the book values of the assets and liabilities of the transferor company when they are incorporated in the financial statements of the transferee company except to ensure uniformity of accounting policies.

30. An amalgamation should be considered to be an amalgamation in the nature of purchase, when any one or more of the conditions specified in paragraph 29 is not satisfied.

9. In Brigade Global Services (P.) Ltd. (supra)the assessee introduced the company F.I. Sofex but it was rejected by the Assessing Officer on the ground that no segmental details were available. The fact remained that the assessee had furnished the segmental data. The Revenue contended that segmental total cost was not available and that the subsidiary in India incurred a loss due to which the entire investment as well as recoverable advance had been fully provided for in the books of account. Being so it was not comparable with the assessee-company. The Tribunal held that for computing the net margin of the assessee for the purpose of transfer pricing only the cost related to the transaction with the associated enterprises had to be considered and, accordingly, the Tribunal agreed with the argument that segmental financial data was to be considered for the purpose of arriving at net margin on an international transaction with the assessee's enterprises in respect of transactions carried out by the assessee. The Tribunal held that the segmental data of the company F.I. Sofex Limited ought to be considered as comparable if there was normal loss. In this case, there was abnormal loss on account of extraordinary reasons and it was not comparable and was to be excluded from comparables. As such, F.I. Sofex Limited had to be excluded by the Assessing Officer.

In Onward Technologies Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 35 taxmann.com 584 (Mum.–Trib.)the assessee was engaged in engineering design services and information technology consultancy services. It is the fundamental rule that the comparable cases can be those which are engaged in similar or as close as possible to the nature of the business of the assessee. The Tribunal took two companies as samples from the companies selected by the TPO for comparison. The first company was engaged in educational software focused on adult best skill remediation and employability skills. Another company was consultancy and information technology service provider in life and general insurance sector. The Tribunal held that the two companies were ex facie, functionally different from the assessee. Without going into the factual position qua each of these 20 companies, as to whether they were comparable or not, the justice would be done adequately if the impugned order was set aside and the matter was restored to the file of the Assessing Officer/TPO so that the comparability or otherwise of such cases might be discussed and decided in the light of the objectives of the assessee on these issues. The AO/TPO would determine the arm's length price of ITES segment afresh by primarily considering the correct figures of operating profit to total cost in respect of ITES segment alone and thereafter, consider the mean of the operating profit/total cost of such cases out of 20 cases noted by TPO which were really comparables.

Section 43(1) is clear that the actual cost to be considered for the purpose of section 32 should be the actual cost paid by the assessee. Since the cost has not been directly or indirectly met by any other person or authority, the cost paid by the assessee for acquisition of the assets of the units is the cost under section 43(1) . However, Explanation (3) makes it clear that where the assets are used at any time by any other person for the purpose of his business or profession and the Assessing Officer is satisfied that the main purpose of the transfer of such assets directly or indirectly to the assessee was reduction of liability of tax for claiming depreciation with reference to enhanced cost, the actual cost of the assets shall be such an amount as the Assessing Officer may determine having regard to all the circumstances of the case. As rightly considered by the Commissioner (Appeals) the parties were unrelated and the transaction was at arm's length basis. The registered valuer also valued the assets as on 1-11-1999, the price of which was considered to be the cost of fixed asset acquired and the balance to the current assets including the current liabilities. In view of this, there was no reason to invoke Explanation (3) as the Assessing Officer nowhere stated that the main purpose of such a valuation was for reduction of liability to tax. It was a direct acquisition by the assessee company from another public limited company in an open bid, being the highest bidder. As per AS 10 para 35 the assessee was supposed to take the value on the fair basis as determined by competent valuers. [Para 8]

Introduction

Recently, the Delhi bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (the Tribunal) in the case of Cash Edge India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO1, held that the Assessing Officer (AO) had erred in adding back the Transfer Pricing (TP) adjustment to book profits under section 115JB` of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) [Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT)] and directed the AO to exclude the TP adjustment from the book profits computed under section 115JB of the Act.

Further, the Mumbai Tribunal, in the case of Koch Chemical Technology Group (India) Ltd. v. ACIT2 held that when the taxpayer has submitted a report from the approved valuer indicating the fair market value of machineries purchased, then before rejecting such a valuation report, the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) was duty bound to refer the valuation of the machineries to the Departmental Valuation Officer (DVO) as per the procedure laid down under the statutory provisions of the Act.

After lot of deliberations and representations, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has issued the rules3, for computation of arm's length price of international transactions or specified domestic transactions, undertaken on or after 1 April 2014, based on range of comparable data, median and multiple year data. These rules have provided clarifications on various areas as well as bring into play areas that may result into disputes.

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on 5 October 2015 issued a final package of reports in connection with its action plan to address Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS), together with a plan for follow-up work by 2020 and a timetable for implementation from 2016.

(1) Assessing Officer erred in adding back TP adjustment to book profits under section 115JB of the Act

The taxpayer rendered software development and business support services to its associated enterprise (AE) on a cost plus basis. The arm's length price (ALP) of the said transaction was determined by considering transactional net margin method (TNMM). The TPO, rejecting the TP study, carried out a fresh benchmarking analysis and made an adjustment. The Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP) upheld the adjustment made by the TPO, subject to: (a) exclusion of the two comparables, (b) granting working capital adjustment as per the OECD Methodology (c) furnishing the annual report of Wipro Technology Services Ltd. to the taxpayer and (d) re-computing the operating margin of the taxpayer as well as comparable companies as per the guidelines provided by Safe Harbor Notification dated 18 September 2013. The AO determined the total income under MAT provisions after including the TP addition.

Tribunal ruling

Dispute on comparables - The Tribunal directed to exclude Persistent Systems Limited and Wipro Technology Services from the comparables set. For Zylog Systems Limited (Zylog), Tribunal set-aside the issue back to the file of the TPO for reconsideration, subject to the availability of the audited segment data of Zylog's software development services segment and it qualifying all the filters applied by the TPO.

Nature of foreign exchange gain/loss (operating or not) - Relying on the decisions in the case of Westfalia Separator India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT4 and Fiserv India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT5, the Tribunal directed the AO/TPO to treat foreign exchange gain/loss as an operating item.

Addition of TP adjustment by the AO, to the income assessed under section 115JB (MAT) - The Tribunal, stated that except for adjustments provided in Explanation1 to section 115JB(2) of the Act, no other adjustment can be made to book profits under section 115JB and held that the TP adjustment could not have been added back to the book profits under section 115JB of the Act. The case law relied upon by Revenue of Rain Commodities v. Dy. CIT6 is not applicable in the present case as the Special Bench, following the decision of the Apex Court in Apollo Tyres v. CIT7 and CIT v. HCL Comnet System & Services Ltd. 8, held that the AO cannot travel beyond the net profits declared by the taxpayer unless (a) it is discovered that profit and loss (P&L) account is not drawn up in accordance with Part II and Part III of Schedule VI of the Companies Act or (b) incorrect accounting policies, accounting standards have been adopted for preparing such accounts and the method/rate of depreciation has been adopted incorrectly. In the present case, there is no such allegation or any such finding by the AO in the assessment order. Tribunal directed AO to exclude the TP adjustment from the book profits computed under section 115JB of the Act.

10.4-3 Some points to be noted in connection with the deductions:

10.4-3a Section 35DD - Section 44DB refers to deduction under section 35DD which refers to expenses of amalgamation/demerger. However, it applies only to Indian Companies. It is not clear how this section would apply to co-operative banks.

10.4-3b Actual cost of assets in the hands of successor - Explanations 7 and 7A to section 43(1) provide for actual cost to the successor in case of amalgamation/demerger of companies. No such provision is made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3c WDV of the amalgamating/resulting co-operative bank - Explanations 2 and 2B in section 43(6) provides for computation of written down value in the hands of the amalgamated company or resulting company. No such provision has been made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3d Tax liability under section 41(1) - If an amalgamating company/demerged company has been granted an allowance or deduction and subsequently the amalgamated company/resulting company obtains any amount in respect of such loss or expenditure by way of remission or cessation of such trading liability, the amalgamated company/resulting company is liable to tax under section 41(1) in respect of the said sum. This is because section 41(1) provides inter alia, that, in case of a succession in business (which has been defined to include amalgamation/demerger) the successor is chargeable under section 41(1) even if the deduction was allowed to the person succeeded to. However, no express amendment has been made to cover reorganisation of co-operative banks. It may be noted that Explanation 2(ii) to section 41(1) does provide that where a person is succeeded by any other person, such other person is a successor in business for the purposes of section 41(1). Since amalgamation/demerger result in succession, it may be possible for the revenue to argue that the case of reorganisation of co-operative banks is covered under this general Explanation.

10.4-4 Capital gains to predecessor - Section 47(vica) provides that section 45 is not applicable to transfer of a capital asset in a business reorganization by the predecessor to the successor. Hence, there is no capital gains to the predecessor on transfer of its capital assets to the successor.

(3) The provisions of this section shall not apply in relation an international transaction in a case1 where the computation of income under sub-section (1)....., has the effect of reducing the income arising from that international transaction income chargeable to tax or increasing the loss2, as the case may be, computed on the basis of entries made in the books of account in respect of the previous year in which the international transaction or specified domestic transaction was entered into. [Emphasis supplied - The struck-through words are meaningful variations.]

A comparison of sub-sections (1) and (3) reveals significant variations in the phrases used. In Indian jurisprudence, there is a presumption that when in relation to the same subject matter, different words are used in the same statute they are not used in the same sense5. We now proceed to analyse the significance of varied phrases.

'INCOME ARISING FROM AN INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTION' VERSUS 'INCOME CHARGEABLE TO TAX'

It was settled long back that income-tax is only one tax levied on sum total of the income classified and chargeable under various heads. It is not collection of distinct taxes levied separately on each head of income. In Namberumal6 the taxpayer had income from property, other sources and loss from business. Assessing Officer enhanced the property income and in appeal the appellate authority on one hand accepted the plea of taxpayer to restore the amount of property income to the amount returned, however, on the other hand decreased the loss from business, thereby enhancing the business (negative) income. On an overall basis the taxable income of the taxpayer stood reduced after the order of appellate authority. The appeal of the taxpayer against enhancement of business income (reduction of business loss) was rejected as there was no enhancement of the overall total income.

An implication of this principle is that, loss sustained under one head is to be set off against income from another head, as held by Madras High Court7. The principle that income tax is one tax is also upheld by Supreme Court8.

With the help of the above background, when the phrase 'income chargeable to tax' in juxtaposition with word 'loss' is compared to phrase 'income from an international transaction', the Author reaches a conclusion that the former being wider refers to total income which is chargeable to tax while the latter is obviously amount of income from a particular transaction. This is also supported by the fact that the objective of transfer pricing provisions is to counter the ability of multi-national enterprises to allocate profits in different jurisdictions and thereby resulting in erosion of tax revenues9 which would not be the case where net effect of multiple transactions results in reporting a higher than ALP income.

'CASE' VERSUS 'TRANSACTION'

With this background, let's proceed to deal with meaning of phrase "in a case" and conspicuous absence of struck-through words being "to an international transaction".

The word 'transaction' used in sub-section (1) of section 92 is defined to include closely linked transactions while the word 'case' used in sub-section (3) has not been statutorily defined. This is a significant and conscious departure. Thus the presumption is that expression 'case' is not the same is 'closely linked transactions'. Expression 'case' has been used in several legislations in a wider sense, including in Income tax law.

While deciding on the fitness of a case for appeal to Supreme Court the Calcutta High Court10 held that the word 'case' in section 66A(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 is the whole case and not a particular point of law arising in that case. The Supreme Court11 dealing with legality of transfer of case in relation to future proceedings held that the expression 'case' is used in a comprehensive sense of including both pending proceedings as well as proceedings to be instituted in future. In K.L. Jaiswal12 the court interpreted the word 'case' to encompass entire case commencing from filing of the return of wealth-tax till the final adjudication and assessment of the tax liability, penalty proceedings, proceedings for waiver or reduction of the penalty, and not the proceedings which commences from filing of the application under sub-section (4) of section 18B for waiver or reduction of the penalty.

HEADNOTE: Section 43(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Actual cost -  Assessment year 2000-01 - Assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern - TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and assessee was highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores - After acquiring company units as going concern assessee, on basis of valuation report of 'K', determined fair market value of fixed assets as on date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores - Assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores - Assessing Officer obtained information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that said company had shown book value of fixed asset at Rs. 345. 95 crores - Assessing Officer was of view that assessee had paid more amount than book value of difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment - Thereupon, Assessing Officer determined goodwill value at difference between amount adopted by assessee and amount shown in books of TISCO and depreciation on amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order passed by Assessing Officer holding that Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case - On revenue's appeal, it was noted that parties were unrelated and transaction was at arm's length basis - It was also noticed that neither acquisition of their business nor assets comprised therein nor valuation thereof was with purpose of reducing Income-tax liability of assessee by claiming higher depreciation - Further, assessee had arrived at fair market value of assets on basis of valuation report obtained in accordance with accounting standard 10 - Whether, on facts finding of Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer had not made out a case for reducing actual cost was correct and it did not require any interference - Held, yesIncome-tax : In case of acquisition of fixed assets, actual cost of same to be considered for purpose of section 32 should be actual cost paid by assessee.

FACT: The assessee had entered into a business transfer agreement with TISCO for acquisition of their cement units as going concern. The TISCO had invited bids through its merchant bankers and the assessee was the highest bidder at Rs. 550 crores. The same was accepted by the TISCO in its Board meeting on 18-12-1998. Thereupon, the cement units were actually taken over and used in its own production activity. After acquiring the company units as going concern as the assessee, on the basis of valuation report of 'K' fixed the fair market value of fixed assets as on the date of acquisition at Rs. 481. 39 crores. The balance amount of consideration of Rs. 68. 61 crores was attributed to the net current assets taken over. The assessee accordingly claimed depreciation on the value of assets at Rs. 481. 39 crores. In the course of assessment the Assessing Officer asked for the WDV of the assets of TISCO. Since the assessee expressed its inability to furnish the details as they purchased the assets on the basis as going concern, the Assessing Officer obtained the information regarding WDV from TISCO and noticed that the said company had shown the book value of fixed assets at Rs. 345. 95 crores and after claiming transfer expenses and fees to merchant bankers, offered profits on sale of net assets of cement division at Rs. 125. 25 crores in their books of account. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the assessee had paid more amount than the book value and the difference amount was to be considered as goodwill payment and accordingly after discussion about the provisions of section 43(1) , report of the registered valuer, determined the goodwill value at the difference between the amount adopted by the assessee and the amount shown in the books of TISCO and depreciation on the amount of goodwill determined at Rs. 135. 44 crores was disallowed thereby making addition of Rs. 16. 39 crores. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) it was contended that the assessee had acquired fixed assets and current assets of the unit in an open bid and on the basis of the report of the registered valuer the value was accordingly capitalized to the extent of Rs. 481. 39 crores and Assessing Officer's action in taking the WDV of TISCO was not correct as Explanation 3 to section 43(1) did not apply in assessee's case as these two companies were independent and not related and further the Assessing Officer had not correctly appreciated the registered valuer's report and the method adopted. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contentions and set aside the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

The Pooling of Interests Method

33. In preparing the transferee company's financial statements, the assets, liabilities and reserves (whether capital or revenue or arising on revaluation) of the transferor company should be recorded at their existing carrying amounts and in the same form as at the date of the amalgamation. 36. In preparing the transferee company's financial statements, the assets and liabilities of the transferor company should be incorporated at their existing carrying amounts or, alternatively, the consideration should be allocated to individual identifiable assets and liabilities on the basis of their fair values at the date of amalgamation. The reserves (whether capital or revenue or arising on revaluation) of the transferor company, other than the statutory reserves, should not be included in the financial statements of the transferee company except as stated in paragraph 39.

37. Any excess of the amount of the consideration over the value of the net assets of the transferor company acquired by the transferee company should be recognised in the transferee company's financial statements as goodwill arising on amalgamation. If the amount of the consideration is lower than the value of the net assets acquired, the difference should be treated as Capital Reserve.

38. The goodwill arising on amalgamation should be amortised to income on a systematic basis over its useful life. The amortisation period should not exceed five years unless a somewhat longer period can be justified.

39. Where the requirements of the relevant statute for recording the statutory reserves in the books of the transferee company are complied with, statutory reserves of the transferor company should be recorded in the financial statements of the transferee company. The corresponding debit should be given to a suitable account head (e.g., 'Amalgamation Adjustment Account') which should be disclosed as a part of 'miscellaneous expenditure' or other similar category in the balance sheet. When the identity of the statutory reserves is no longer required to be maintained, both the reserves and the aforesaid account should be reversed.

Common Procedures

40. The consideration for the amalgamation should include any non-cash element at fair value. In case of issue of securities, the value fixed by the statutory authorities may be taken to be the fair value. In case of other assets, the fair value may be determined by reference to the market value of the assets given up. Where the market value of the assets given up cannot be reliably assessed, such assets may be valued at their respective net book values.

41. Where the scheme of amalgamation provides for an adjustment to the consideration contingent on one or more future events, the amount of the additional payment should be included in the consideration if payment is probable and a reasonable estimate of the amount can be made. In all other cases, the adjustment should be recognised as soon as the amount is determinable [see Accounting Standard (AS) 4, Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date].

A description of the accounting treatment given to the reserves and the reasons for following the treatment different from that prescribed in this Standard.

Ashit C. Mehta Financial Services Ltd. The TPO has included this company as it is engaged into ITES and meets all the qualitative filters applied by the TPO. Before DRP assessee raised an objection that it has a high advertisement and marketing expenses and also functionally different. DRP also held that the company performs broadly the same ITES functions. Before Tribunal, assessee submitted that the employee cost to sales ratio of the company is only 22.40 per cent whereas its employee cost is 47.33 per cent.

This is an altogether new argument and same was not at all either before TPO or DRP. Further it is not submitted how the employee cost to sales ratio as impacted the price or the margin of the assessee vis-à-vis comparables. The assessee relied on the decision of C3i Support Services (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt CIT [2014] 151 ITD 348/46 taxmann.com 453 (Hyd.-Trib) and decision of ITAT of Goldman Sech Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 9 (Bang. - Trib.) wherein both the cases it is submitted that the employee cost to sales if less than 25 per cent, the comparable should be rejected.

There cannot be any dispute with respect to the decisions taken by the co-ordinate benches however; such quantitative filter has not been applied by the assessee while preparing its TP Study Report as well as by TPO. Further, while perusing the decision of the co-ordinate bench in C3i Support Services (P.) Ltd., this comparable has been rejected since it belongs to a different vertical. It is not argued that the company is functionally different and belongs to a different vertical. In view of this the argument of the assessee for the exclusion of this comparable is rejected.

Bodhtree Consulting Limited

This comparable is selected by TPO and held that the company belongs to ITES segment. However, assessee objected submitting that the primary business of company is software development services hence, it cannot be compared with the assessee. Against this the TPO has held that it has considered only the data cleansing services and e-paper activities and has only considered the ITES segment.

Before DRP assessee contended that it is earning extraordinary profit, functionally different and has RPT of 38.54 per cent. The DRP rejected the contention of the assessee holding that TPO has taken into consideration only the ITES segment of the comparable. Before Tribunal, it was submitted that the comparable has the unreliable books of account and therefore same should be rejected. It was also submitted that it is functionally different.

It is undisputed that the comparable company is also engaged in software development services. However the TPO has obtained information under section 133(6) and after that he has excluded the segmental information pertaining to software development services and has only considered the information pertaining to segment of data cleansing solution. The argument of assessee that it has unreliable books and has applied the accounting concept of matching wrongly is a new argument which was neither before TPO and nor before the DRP. However, the assessee has relied on the decision of co-ordinate bench of Ciena India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2015] 59 taxmann 92 (Delhi-Trib) for assessment year 2009-10.

On perusal of said order, it is apparent that co-ordinate benche considered the accounting policy of the comparable with respect to software development services for assessment year 2009-10. However in the present case assessment year involved is 2007-08 and furthermore the segment of the comparable of software development is not at all considered by TPO, he has considered ITES segment of the comparable. Therefore, reliance placed upon the above decision of the co-ordinate bench is misplaced. In view of this the argument of assessee for exclusion of the above comparable is rejected.

Eclerx Services Limited

The assessee submitted that the company is operating in data analytics space and provides operations management, audit and reconciliation service. It was submitted that it falls in the domain of KPO segment. It was further submitted that the company is providing high end services and therefore same should be excluded. For this assessee submitted a corporate presentation of the comparable wherein it is apparent that the company became first KPO in 2008 which is listed on BSE and NSE.

From the above it is apparent that the company is engaged in the KPO business and therefore same is not comparable with the appellant which is carrying on admittedly ITES services. The Delhi High Court in case of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 234 Taxman 573/60 taxmann.com 355 has held that KPO segment cannot be compared with ITES segment. Therefore following the decision of the High Court it is directed to exclude this comparable.

Comparable Manipal Digital Systems Private Limited :

■

The TPO has considered Manipal Digital Systems Private Limited as comparable. The assessee submitted that the revenue of Manipal Digital Systems Private Limited consist of ITES, Sale of e-Books, Distribution of Books and no segmental is available. The annual report of Manipal Digital Systems Private Limited is perused. It is observed that as per the annual report, Manipal Digital Systems Private Limited’s sale consist of ITES, Pre-media work and e-Book/Other Books Distribution. The annual report is studied and no separate figures for ITES, Pre-media work and e-book/other books distribution are available. Therefore, the functions performed by Manipal Digital Systems Private Limited are not comparable to assessee. Comparable CES Limited

■

The assessee submitted that CES Limited is having two segments. The assessee submitted that it is a KPO and hence not comparable. The annual report of the CES Limited is perused. In the annual report, it has mentioned its business as BPO/KPO. There is no segmental available for IT enabled services providing revenue for BPO/KPO separately. It is important to mention here that the TPO in his order, while rejecting Sundaram Business Services Limited has observed that Sundaram Business Services Limited is into ITES and KPO which makes it functionally non-comparable to assessee. Comparable MPS Limited

■

The annual report of the MPS Ltd. is perused. It is observed that the Board of Directors of the company has approved amalgamation of ADI BPO Services Ltd with the MPS Ltd. 10.4-3 Some points to be noted in connection with the deductions:

10.4-3a Section 35DD - Section 44DB refers to deduction under section 35DD which refers to expenses of amalgamation/demerger. However, it applies only to Indian Companies. It is not clear how this section would apply to co-operative banks.

10.4-3b Actual cost of assets in the hands of successor - Explanations 7 and 7A to section 43(1) provide for actual cost to the successor in case of amalgamation/demerger of companies. No such provision is made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3c WDV of the amalgamating/resulting co-operative bank - Explanations 2 and 2B in section 43(6) provides for computation of written down value in the hands of the amalgamated company or resulting company. No such provision has been made for amalgamation/demerger of co-operative banks.

10.4-3d Tax liability under section 41(1) - If an amalgamating company/demerged company has been granted an allowance or deduction and subsequently the amalgamated company/resulting company obtains any amount in respect of such loss or expenditure by way of remission or cessation of such trading liability, the amalgamated company/resulting company is liable to tax under section 41(1) in respect of the said sum. This is because section 41(1) provides inter alia, that, in case of a succession in business (which has been defined to include amalgamation/demerger) the successor is chargeable under section 41(1) even if the deduction was allowed to the person succeeded to. However, no express amendment has been made to cover reorganisation of co-operative banks. It may be noted that Explanation 2(ii) to section 41(1) does provide that where a person is succeeded by any other person, such other person is a successor in business for the purposes of section 41(1). Since amalgamation/demerger result in succession, it may be possible for the revenue to argue that the case of reorganisation of co-operative banks is covered under this general Explanation.

10.4-4 Capital gains to predecessor - Section 47(vica) provides that section 45 is not applicable to transfer of a capital asset in a business reorganization by the predecessor to the successor. Hence, there is no capital gains to the predecessor on transfer of its capital assets to the successor.

If the accumulated loss or unabsorbed depreciation is not directly relatable to the undertaking, the same will be apportioned between the demerged co-operative bank and the resulting co-operative bank in the same proportion in which the value of the assets have been transferred.

CIT [IT Appeal No. 420/Hyd/07] the Tribunal held that there was no dispute to the fact that the employees cost to the total turnover of the selected company worked out to be 1.42% as against the industry's average of 30-40% and the assessee's employees cost to turnover percentage was 43%. This fact implied that the selected company had outsourced major portion of its work to third party vendors. Therefore, the company could not be treated as a comparable.

In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that any company with employee cost less than 25% could not be compared with an ITES company – in this case Vishal IT Limited had been adopted by the TPO. This company outsourced its call centre work and, therefore, the employees cost was less than 25% as was the common practice among other ITES. When company had outsourced its ITES, it could not be said that its business results would be comparable to any other ITES provider rendering the services entirely on its own. In such circumstances the net margins of the two comparables could not be on the same basis.

The TPO added 18 more comparables to the two accepted by him. The TPO worked out the arithmetical mean at 22.28% after making an adjustment to the benchmark for working capital. If nine comparables which according to the assessee were wrongly included were excluded, it would work out to be an arithmetical mean of 7.97% only as against 14.91% disclosed by the assessee, so that there could have been no addition. The DRP affirmed the addition of TPO. The Tribunal found that out of 20 companies chosen by the TPO as comparables only 11 companies were found to be comparables and their arithmetic mean was only 7.97%. During the previous year, there were extraordinary events that took place which warranted exclusion as a comparable;
